﴿O you who believe, fulfil the contracts⦆.

The opening of the surah with the command to fulfil contracts signals that after it there will come rulings and covenants which God had established upon the believers, both in general and in detail; He reminds them of them, because upon them is the duty of fulfilling what they covenanted with God. This is like the opening of royal decrees with the phrase: "This is a noble decree, to be received with obedience and compliance." This is the excellence of an opening (bara'at istihlal).

The definite article in "al-'uqud" (the contracts) is the definite article of genus for comprehensiveness (ta'rif al-jins li'l-istighraq), so it includes the contracts which the Muslims made with their Lord, namely compliance with His law, as in His saying ﴿And remember the favour of God upon you and His covenant with which He bound you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 7], and like what the Messenger used to take the pledge of the believers upon: that they would not associate anything with God, nor steal, nor commit adultery, and he would say to them: "Whoever among you fulfils it, his reward is upon God."

It also includes the contracts which the Muslims made with the polytheists, such as His saying ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months⦆ [al-Tawbah: 2], and His saying ﴿nor [allow] those who make for the Sacred House⦆ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. It also includes the contracts which Muslims make among themselves.

Al-iksa' (fulfilment) is giving a thing in full, i.e., without deficiency. Since the realisation of avoiding deficiency does not occur in common usage except by adding to the required measure, fulfilment came to mean, by custom, justice. This was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards⦆ [al-Nisa': 173] in Surat al-Nisa'.

"Al-'uqud" is the plural of 'aqd with a fatha on the 'ayn, and it is the binding commitment between two parties in some action. Its essential meaning is tying a rope to a pot-handle or the like, and tying the rope itself is also an 'aqd. Then it was used metaphorically for commitment, and its use became predominant until it became a customary reality. Al-Hutay'ah said:

"A people who, when they make a contract with their neighbour, tie the 'inaj and tie above it the karab."

So with the metaphorical 'aqd he mentioned the 'inaj, which is a rope that binds the waterskin, and mentioned the karab, which is another rope for the waterskin; he thus returned the metaphorical 'aqd to its concomitants, imagining with it an 'inaj and a karab, and by all of them he intended the imagery of the metaphor. So 'aqd is originally a verbal noun used to name what is tied, and it was applied metaphorically to a commitment from two sides to a thing and its counterpart. The tied part of a rope is called 'uqdah. The term 'aqd was also applied to the object of the contract, by using the verbal noun for the object; thus covenants are 'uqud, alliances are 'uqud, and sales, hiring and the like are 'uqud, and these are what is meant here. Included in this are the rulings which God has legislated, since they are like contracts, for the one who enters Islam has bound himself to them implicitly, and in them is the covenant of God which He took from people, that they worship Him and not associate anything with Him.

In the terminology of the jurists, 'aqd is applied to the establishing of a transfer or an undertaking from two sides. Sometimes it is the establishing of a transfer, like sale for ready price; sometimes it is the establishing of an undertaking, like hiring for ready wage, and like salam and qirad; and sometimes it is the establishing of an undertaking from both sides, like marriage, since the dower is not regarded as a counter-value, rather the counter-value is each of the spouses undertaking rights toward the other. All contracts require offer and acceptance.

The command to fulfil contracts indicates the obligation of that, so it is established that the contracting party's fulfilment of his contract is a right upon him, and therefore he may be compelled to it, because contracts were legislated to meet the needs of the community; they belong to the category of the complementary necessity (al-hajiyy), so completing them is of the category of need; because what completes each category of the three categories of benefit (al-munasib) takes the same rank as what it completes: if it is essential (darurri), or needed (hajiyy), or embellishing (tahsini). And in the hadith: "Muslims are bound by their conditions, except a condition that makes lawful what is unlawful or makes unlawful what is lawful."

So contracts for which the law requires in their conclusion merely the formula bind one to complete the formula or what stands in its place, such as marriage and sale. What stands in place of the formula includes the sign of a mute person and the mu'atah in sales. Contracts for which the law requires, for their conclusion, commencement of them after the formula bind by commencement, such as al-ju'l and qirad. Distinguishing the particulars of one of the two types from the particulars of the other is an area for ijtihad.

Al-Qarafi said in the Ninth and Two Hundredth Difference (al-Farq al-tasi' wa'l-mi'atayn): the origin of contracts, as such, is binding, and what has been established in the law or by the mujtahids as being based on non-binding by utterance, is so because in some contracts the right undertaken is hidden, so there is fear that deception may enter it, and therefore leniency was extended to the contracting parties in them, so they are not bound except by beginning the action, since beginning is the branch of reflection and deliberation. For this reason the Malikis differed concerning the contracts of mugharasah, muzara'ah and sharikah: whether they are joined to what its benefit requires binding by utterance, or to what its benefit requires binding by commencement. In the Ninety-Sixth and One Hundredth Difference he argued that the origin of contracts is that they be binding by utterance, by His saying ﴿Fulfil the contracts⦆, and he mentioned that the Malikis argued by this verse to nullify the hadith of "the option of the session"; meaning, on the basis that this verse established a principle of the principles of the Shari'ah, namely that the Lawgiver's intent from contracts is their completion; and by this what I have established became preferred according to Malik over the report of single transmitters, so Malik did not take by the hadith of Ibn 'Umar: "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not parted."

Know that a contract may be concluded on the condition of non-binding, as in the option sale (bay' al-khiyar), which the jurists bounded by a period usually needed for choosing the object sold or consulting about its matter.

Among the contracts commanded to be fulfilled are the contracts of reconciliations and truces in wars, the pact to support the oppressed, and every contract made on something not forbidden. The rulings of Islam have made contracting for such things unnecessary, since the Muslims became like one body; so the matter remained tied to fulfilling the contracts concluded in the Jahiliyyah for supporting the oppressed and the like, such as the Pact of the Virtuous (hilf al-fudul). In the hadith: "Fulfil the contracts of the Jahiliyyah, and do not create a contract in Islam." There also remained what the Muslims and polytheists contracted, like the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah between the Prophet ﷺ and Quraysh. It has been related that Furat ibn Hayyan al-'Ijli asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the alliance of the Jahiliyyah, and he said: "Perhaps you ask about the alliance of Lujaym and Taym." He said: "Yes." He said: "Islam only increases it in strength." I say: this is among the greatest things by which Islam was known among them, in fulfilling to one who does not transgress against him. The Khuza'ah were among the Arab tribes who did not wage war against the Muslims in the Jahiliyyah, as mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿Those to whom people said: Indeed the people have gathered against you⦆ [Al 'Imran: 173] in Surat Al 'Imran.

* * *

﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you, not violating the game while you are in the state of ihram. Indeed God decrees what He wills⦆.

The words of some exegetes indicate hesitation about the connection of His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle⦆ with His saying ﴿Fulfil the contracts⦆. In al-Kashshafi's summary, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The meaning of the contracts is what follows His saying ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle⦆," end. It must be that Ibn 'Abbas's meaning is what begins with His saying ﴿except what is recited to you⦆ and the verses following.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement that ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle⦆ is a detailing of the general ﴿Fulfil the contracts⦆, its interpretation is that the whole sentence is a detailing, not specifically the clause ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle⦆; for the permission of cattle is not a contract that must be fulfilled, except in view of what follows it, His saying ﴿except what is recited to you⦆. And in view of the nullification of what the people of the Jahiliyyah forbidden falsely, among what is covered by His saying ﴿God did not ordain any bahirah or sa'ibah⦆ [al-Ma'idah: 103] and the verses that follow.

My view is that the clause ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle⦆ is a preparation for the prohibitions that will come after it, such as His saying ﴿not violating the game⦆ and His saying ﴿and help one another in righteousness and piety⦆ [al-Ma'idah: 2], which are among the contracts of the law of Islam. So beginning with mention of some of what is permitted is a favour and a reassurance for the Muslims, so that they receive the obligations with tranquil souls;
So the meaning: if We forbid you things, We have permitted you more than them; and if We obligate you to things, We have placed you in ease from things more abundant than them, so that they know that God wills from them only their good and their uprightness.

So the clause ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle⦆ is a resumptive sentence, a fresh beginning, since it is an opening of the discourse after its title.

Al-bahimah: the land animal of the four-footed kind, domestic and wild, except predators, so it includes the wild cattle and gazelles. The idafah of bahimah to al-an'am is from the idafah of the general to the specific, and it is explanatory (bayaniyyah), like the expressions "the fly of the bee" and "the city of Baghdad." So the intent is the an'am specifically, because they are the main food of people. As for wild animals, they are included in His saying ﴿not violating the game while you are in the state of ihram⦆. Here it serves to remove the assumption that by an'am is meant specifically camels, due to the common application of the name an'am to them; so bahimah is mentioned to include the four kinds of an'am: camels, cattle, sheep and goats.

The explanatory idafah is in the sense of "min" of explanation, as in His saying ﴿So shun the filth of the idols⦆ [al-Hajj: 30].

The exception in His saying ﴿except what is recited to you⦆ is from the generality of essences and states. "What is recited" is what will be detailed at His saying ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion⦆ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. Likewise His saying ﴿not violating the game while you are in the state of ihram⦆, which occurs as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of address in His saying "Lawful for you," and it is a circumstantial clause specifying the meaning of the exception from the generality of states and places, because hurum is the plural of haram, like radah to rudud. The detailing of this description will come at His saying ﴿God made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a standing for the people⦆ [al-Ma'idah: 97] in this surah.

Haram is a description of one who has entered ihram for hajj or 'umrah, i.e., intended them. It is also a description of one who is residing in the Sacred Precinct (haram). From the application of "muhrim" to one residing in the Haram is the saying of al-Ra'i:

"They killed Ibn 'Affan, the caliph, while in the state of ihram,"

i.e., residing in the sanctuary of Madinah.

The Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) is the area bounded all around Mecca on its sides by known limits. It is the place where game may not be hunted, its trees may not be cut, and its lost property (luqatah) may not be picked up. It is the well-known precinct that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) demarcated, setting up markers (ansab) by which its boundaries are recognized. The Arabs held it in reverence. Qusayy had renewed these markers, and they remained in place until it occurred to the Quraysh to remove them, which happened during the period the Prophet (ﷺ) resided in Mecca. This grieved the Messenger of Allah greatly. Then the Quraysh soon restored them as they had been.

When the year of the Conquest of Mecca came, the Prophet (peace be upon him) sent Tamim ibn Asad al-Khuza'i, who renewed them and then revived them. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab later clarified them in his caliphate in the year seventeen (AH). He dispatched four men from the Quraysh to renew the boundaries of the Sacred Precinct, who used to dwell in the desert of Mecca: Makhramah ibn Nawfal al-Zuhri, Sa'id ibn Yarbu' al-Makhzumi, Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza al-'Amiri, and Azhar ibn 'Awf al-Zuhri. They set up markers which were made into signs on the outline of the Precinct, according to the limits that the Prophet (ﷺ) had defined. It begins at the Ka'bah and extends for the one on foot toward Medina about four miles to al-Tan'im. Al-Tan'im is not part of the Precinct. It extends eight miles along the road going to Iraq, where it ends at a place called al-Maqta'. It goes nine miles along the road to al-Ta'if, where it ends at al-Ji'ranah. From the direction of Yemen it extends seven miles, where it ends at Adat Libn. From the Jeddah road it extends ten miles, where it ends at the far edge of al-Hudaybiyah, and al-Hudaybiyah is within the Precinct. Thus this Precinct is forbidden for hunting, just as hunting is forbidden to one in the state of ihram for Hajj or 'Umrah.

So His saying (﴿And you are in a state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]) may mean those in ihram, and then it is a prohibition of game for the one in ihram, whether inside the Precinct or outside it, and the prohibition of game within the Precinct for one not in ihram is established by the Sunnah. It may also mean those in ihram and those not in ihram within the Precinct, in which case the word is used in two meanings that are united by a common element, which is sanctity (hurmah). This is not the use of a homonym in both its meanings if we hold that such use is invalid; or it is the use of a homonym in both its meanings according to the view of those who validate it, and this is the correct view, as we mentioned in the ninth introduction.

The exception is rhetorically varied in His saying ﴿except what is recited to you﴾ and His saying ﴿not hunting game﴾. The first is introduced with the exception particle, and the second with a circumstantial phrase indicating a state different from the permitted one. The meaning is: except game while you are in ihram, or in the state of ihram.

The ruling on game for the one in ihram is mentioned here because of its relation to being excepted from the cattle of livestock in a specific condition. It is mentioned here because it is an incidental and not an inherent prohibition. Otherwise its proper place would have been together with the prohibited acts connected with the rulings of the sacred state and ihram, at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], and so on. The word "game" (sayd) may here be a verbal noun in its original sense, or it may be used for the passive participle (maf'ul), like "creation" for "what is created." The latter is a common usage, more widespread than its use in its original meaning, and it is the more suitable here so that its occurrences in the Qur'an keep one consistent pattern. The implied sense is: not making lawful for yourselves the hitting of game.

As a verbal noun, sayd is the seizing of an animal that is not tame, by hand or by a restraining means or by a catching instrument, such as nets, snares, spears, arrows, dogs, and falcons. As a passive participle, sayd is the animal that is hunted.

"Ghayr" (not) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in the genitive in His saying "for you" (lakum). The clause "and you are in a state of ihram" (wa antum hurum) is in the place of a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "making lawful" (muhilli). This is a remarkable construction in the arrangement of speech, from which both permission and prohibition are derived: permission applies when one is not in ihram, and prohibition applies to him when he is in ihram.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah ordains what He wills﴾ is a justification for His saying ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾. That is, let not the fact that Allah has legislated for you something burdensome prevent you from fulfilling the contracts, since you have contracted on not disobeying and on hearing and obeying Allah, and Allah ordains what He wills, not what you will. The meaning is that Allah knows better than you what is good for you.

Ibn 'Atiyyah mentions that al-Naqqash related that the companions of al-Kindi said to him: "O philosopher, produce for us something like this Qur'an." He said: "Yes, I will produce for you something like part of it." So he secluded himself from them for days, then came out and said: "By Allah, I am not able to do it, and no one can manage this. I opened the Mushaf and there came out Surah al-Ma'idah. I looked, and behold, He has commanded fulfilment, forbidden breaking of covenants, made lawful in a general way, then made exception after exception, then informed of His power and wisdom in two lines. No one can produce this except in volumes." "Ajlad" is the plural of "jild," meaning large books (asfar).

[p. 82 marker omitted]

﴿O you who believe, do not violate the rites of God, nor the sacred month, nor the offering, nor the garlands, nor those who come to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure.﴾

This is a parenthetical statement between the sentences that precede it and the sentence ﴿But when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾. For this reason the address is repeated with the vocative, "O you who believe" (﴿يا أيها الذين آمنوا﴾). Addressing those who believe, even though it is not supposed that they would make forbidden things lawful, indicates that the intended meaning is a prohibition against transgressing upon the divine rites that the polytheists also observe, just as the Muslims observe them.

The meaning of ﴿do not violate the rites of God﴾ is: do not make lawful among people what is forbidden of them. This is shown by the context of His saying "do not make lawful," so the sense is: do not make lawful what God has made sacred of the rites of God. This is like the saying of the Exalted, concerning making the sacred month lawful through the practice of *nasi'* (intercalation), "so that they make lawful what God has forbidden" (Q. 9:37). Otherwise, among the rites of God are things that are permitted, such as shaving the head, and among them are things that are obligatory. The prohibited things are known.

The "rites" (*sha'a'ir*) is the plural of *sha'ira*. Its explanation has already been given at the words of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the rites of God﴾ (Q. 2:158). All the rites were well known to them, so for this reason the verse departs from enumerating them here. They are places, times, and entities. Al-Safa, al-Marwa, and al-Mash'ar al-Haram are among the places. These have passed in Surat al-Baqara.

The sacred month is among the temporal rites, while the offering and the garlands are among the rites that are entities. Thus the conjunction of the sacred month, the offering, and what follows them as "rites of God" is the conjunction of a part over its whole, for the sake of giving it importance. What is meant by it is the category of the sacred month, because it occurs in a context of negation; that is, the sacred months, the four of them, which are in the Exalted's saying, ﴿Of them four are sacred; that is the upright religion, so do not wrong yourselves therein﴾ (Q. 9:36). So the definite article is the definite article of the genus, which functions like an indefinite noun, applying equally to the singular and the plural.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The more apparent view is that only Rajab was intended, so that the prohibition of making it lawful would be strengthened, since the Arabs did not agree on it. It was singled out for the prohibition of making it lawful because not all the Arabs sanctified it. For this reason it was known as the Rajab of Mudar. Rabi'a, Iyad, and Anmar did not sanctify it." It was also called the month of the Banu Umayya, because the Quraysh sanctified it before all the Arabs, and all of Mudar followed them, according to the saying of 'Awf ibn al-Ahwas:

*"And the month of the Banu Umayya, and the offerings when they are held back, their blood is reddening."*

On this view the definite article is that of anaphora (*'ahd*), and so it does not generalize. The more apparent view is that the definite article is generic, as we have already stated.

The offering (*hady*) is that which is brought as a gift to the rites of the hajj to be slaughtered at the place of sacrifice in Mina, or at al-Marwa, from among the livestock.

The garlands (*qala'id*) is the plural of *qila'da*, which are braids of wool or fur, to which are tied two sandals or a piece of tree bark, that is, its peel, and they are placed on the necks of the offerings, likened to women's necklaces. Their purpose is that the offering be recognized, so that it is not attacked by a raid or the like. Some of the Arabs, when they delayed in Mecca until the sacred months had passed and wished to return to their homeland, would place around their necks a garland of the bark of the trees of the Sanctuary, so that no harm would come to them.

The reason for conjoining the garlands with the offering is the emphasis on honoring it, to the extent that it is forbidden to attack its garland, let alone its substance. This is like the saying of Abu Bakr: "By God, if they withheld from me a cord they used to give to the Messenger of God, I would fight them over it." Moreover, the garlands are of use, since the people of Mecca would make sandals from the garlands for their poor, just as they benefited from the *jilal al-badan*, which are pieces of cloth placed on the saddle of the camel, from which they would make shirts and wrappers for themselves. Therefore the prohibition against making them lawful is like the prohibition against making the offering lawful, because in that there is a neglect of the interests of the inhabitants of the Sanctuary, whose supplication Abraham asked God to answer when he said, ﴿So make hearts from people incline toward them and provide them with fruits﴾ (Q. 14:37). The Exalted said, ﴿God made the Ka'ba, the Sacred House, a standing place for the people, and the sacred month, and the offering, and the garlands﴾ (Q. 5:97).

His saying, ﴿nor those who come to the Sacred House﴾, is a conjunction upon "the rites of God," meaning: nor make lawful those who intend the Sacred House, who are the pilgrims. What is meant is those who intend it for the pilgrimage, because the House is not intended except for the hajj. For this reason He did not say "nor those who come to Mecca," because whoever intends Mecca may intend it for trade or the like. The sanctity of the House includes the sanctity of the one who comes to it. There is no doubt that what is meant is those who come to the House from among the polytheists, because those who come to the House from among the believers are already protected from harm both while intending the House and at other times. There is a report that supports this in the occasions of revelation: that a group of horsemen from Bakr ibn Wa'il came to Medina, and their leader was Shurayh ibn Dubay'a, known as al-Hutam (on the pattern of Zufar), also called Ibn Hind, in reference to his mother Hind bint Hassan ibn 'Amr ibn Murthid. This al-Hutam was from Bakr ibn Wa'il, one of the residents of Yamama. He left his horses outside Medina and entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and [the report says]: "He said, 'To what do you invite?' The Messenger of God said: 'To the testimony that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakat.' Hasan [al-Hutam] said: 'What you invite to is good. I will consider it, and perhaps I will become a Muslim. But I see harshness in your affair, and behind me are people whose matter I will not decide without them.' He left and passed by the pasture of Medina, drove off a large number of camels, and the Muslims pursued him when they were informed, but did not catch him." He composed a rajaz verse about this. It was said that the rajaz belongs to one of his companions, Rushayd ibn Rumayd al-'Anazi, and it is:

*"This is the time for the drive, so drive on, O Zaym!
The night has wrapped it with a driver, al-Hutam.
Not a shepherd of camels, nor of sheep,
Nor a butcher on the back and the side.
They slept, all asleep, but the son of Hind did not sleep,
He is struggling with them, a youth like a stick,
Strong-shanked, quick-footed."*

Then al-Hutam came in the following year, which was the year of the Qada' (the Year of the Settlement). They heard the talbiya of the pilgrims of Yamama, and said: "This is al-Hutam and his companions, and with them is an offering, which he plundered from the camels of the Muslims." They asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to plunder them, and so the verse was revealed prohibiting that. It is therefore a general ruling that was revealed after that event, and the prohibition against touching the offering of al-Hutam was included in what this verse comprises.

The Sacred House is the Ka'ba. Its description with this attribute will come at the words of the Exalted, ﴿God made the Ka'ba, the Sacred House, a standing place for the people﴾ (Q. 5:97) in this surah. The clause ﴿seeking bounty from their Lord﴾ is a qualifier of "those who come" (*amminin*), describing their intention to seek God's bounty and His good pleasure. They are the ones who came for the sake of the hajj, indicating the reason for the sanctity of those who come to the Sacred House.

God has forbidden harming the pilgrims, because the hajj is a seeking of God's bounty and His good pleasure, and the people of the Jahiliyya too intended this by it. Al-Nabigha said:

*"May my Lord greet you, for it is not lawful for us
To engage in the play of women, and religion has resolved."*

*"Girding up on swift camels, lean and tired,
We hope in God, and we hope for righteousness and food."*

They also refrained from foul speech. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*"By the Lord of flocks of pilgrims, restrained
From vain talk and obscene speech."*

They also displayed asceticism and humility. Al-Nabigha said:

*"With companions from Lasaf and Thabra
They visit Ilal, their going is pushed forward.
Upon them are disheveled ones, devoted to their Lord,
So they are like the branches of the Hani, humble."*

The reason for the prohibition against harming the pilgrims, even if they are polytheists, is that the state in which they intend the hajj and enter into ihram is a state of goodness and nearness to faith in God and remembrance of His blessings. Therefore they should be assisted in increasing it, because goodness seeps into the soul gradually, just as evil seeps into it in the same way. For this reason, right after this verse will come His saying, ﴿And help one another in righteousness and piety﴾.

*Fadl* (bounty) is the good of this world, which is the righteousness of action. *Ridwan* (good pleasure) is God's good pleasure with them, which is the reward of the Hereafter. It was said that by *fadl* is meant profit in trade. This is far from being the cause of the prohibition, unless it is meant to enable them to bring their goods to Mecca.

* * *

﴿But when you have come out of ihram, then hunt.﴾

This is an explicit statement of the implication of His saying, ﴿not hunting game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ (Q. 5:1), for the purpose of emphasizing the permission. The imperative in it is for permission, and this is not an imperative that comes after a prohibition, because that issue applies to a prohibition against something that is continuous, and then the command to it is likewise continuous. What is here is a temporary prohibition and a command for the rest of the times. Therefore what is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) about the disagreement over the import of the imperative form that comes after a ban, whether it is permission, recommendation, or obligation, does not apply here. Hunting is permissible by original permission, and it was prohibited during the state of ihram. When that state ends, it returns to its permission.

(*Istadu*) is a verbal form of the *ifti'al* pattern, used in speech with a meaning other than the reflexive sense that is the original meaning of the *ifti'al* pattern. So *ista'ada* in their speech is an intensive of *sa'ada* (to hunt). A parallel is *idtarrahu ila kadha* (he compelled him to such-and-such). Here "hunt" (*isṭadu*) has been treated as an intransitive verb, so no object is mentioned for it.

* * *

﴿And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress.﴾

This is a conjunction upon His saying, ﴿do not violate the rites of God﴾, for the purpose of further affirming its content. That is: do not violate the rites of God even with your enemy, if they do not initiate war against you.

The meaning of (*yajrimannakum*) is "earn for you" or "bring upon you." It is said: *jaramahu yajrimuhu*, like *daraba*. Its original meaning is "earn," from *jaram al-nakhla*, when one cuts its clusters of dates. Since the cutting was for the sake of earning, the use of *jaram* in the sense of *kasaba* (to earn) became common. They say: "Fulan earned for himself such-and-such" (*jarama li-nafsihi kadha*), that is, he earned.

It is transitive to a second object, which is (*an ta'taduu*), and the sense is: "hatred earns you transgression." As for its being transitive with *'ala* in His saying, ﴿let not the hatred of a people lead you to not act justly﴾ (Q. 5:8), this is because it is construed with the meaning of "carry you" (*yahmilannakum*).

*Shana'an* with a fatha on the *shin* and the *nun* in most readings (and the *nun* may also be sukun, either originally or by lightening) means hatred. It was said: intense hatred, and this is the more suitable, due to its conjunction with *al-baghda'* (enmity) in the saying of al-Ahwas:

*"I grow upon enmity and hatred."*

It is one of the verbal nouns indicating agitation and fluctuation, because in *shana'an* there is an agitation of the soul, so it is like boiling and surging.

Al-Jumhur read *shana'anu* with a fatha on the *nun*. Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read it with a sukun on the *nun*. It has been said that the sukun form is an adjective of the pattern of *ghadban* (angry), meaning "enemy," so the sense is: "let not the enemy of a people earn for you." Thus it is an idafa of the adjective to the noun it qualifies. When *shana'an* is a verbal noun, the idafa is of the verbal noun to its object, meaning "your hatred of a people," supported by the context of His saying, "because they barred you," since the one hated is usually the one attacked.

Al-Jumhur read *an sadduukum* with a fatha on the hamza of *an*. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the hamza, as *in* (if) the conditional particle. Then the answer of the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes the condition.

*Al-Masjid al-Haram* is a name made a proper noun by predominance over the area surrounding the Ka'ba, enclosed and having gates. It is an Islamic name; it was not called that in the Jahiliyya, because *masjid* means the place of prostration, and the people of the Jahiliyya did not prostrate at the Ka'ba. This was explained at the words of the Exalted, ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ (Q. 2:144) in Surat al-Baqara, and it will come at the words of the Exalted, ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ (Q. 17:1).

* * *

﴿And help one another in righteousness and piety, and do not help one another in sin and transgression. And fear God; indeed God is severe in punishment.﴾

This is a justification for the prohibition in His words ﴿And let not the hatred of a people prevent you from acting justly﴾ [or: "and let not the enmity of a people lead you to transgress"]. The sentence would ordinarily be detached, but it is conjoined (ʿuṭifat) in order to give preference to the legislative content it carries over the causal (taʿlīl) sense it implies. The meaning is: your obligation is to cooperate among yourselves in righteousness (birr) and God-consciousness (taqwā). Since this is their obligation among themselves, the matter is that they should also assist one another in righteousness and God-consciousness, because cooperating in them instills a love for attaining them, so that attaining them becomes a desire for them. Therefore, it is fitting that they assist in them everyone who strives toward them.

Even if the person is an enemy, and the Hajj is an act of righteousness, then ﴿help one another in righteousness and God-consciousness﴾: they, though they are disbelievers, are to be assisted in what is righteous, because righteousness guides to God-consciousness, so perhaps the repeated performance of it brings them closer to Islam. And since transgression against the enemy only occurs through their cooperating against him, they were alerted that cooperation should not become a means of barring access to the Sacred Mosque, and we have already pointed to this above. Thus the pronoun and the form of mutual action (mufāʿalah) in (taʿāwanū, "cooperate") refer to the Muslims,

[page 88]

that is, let some of you assist one another in righteousness and God-consciousness. The benefit of cooperation is the facilitation of work, the provision of benefits, and the display of unity and mutual support, so that this becomes a character trait (khuluq) of the community. This was before the revelation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only unclean, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this year of theirs﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28].

His words ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ are an emphasis on the content of ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and God-consciousness﴾, because although the command to something includes the prohibition of its opposite, giving attention to the ruling on the opposite requires a specific prohibition against it. The intent is that some of you must restrain one another from wronging a people toward whom you harbor hatred.

His words ﴿And fear God﴾ to the end of the verse are a concluding summation (tadhyīl). His words ﴿Severe in punishment﴾ are an allusive threat (taʿrīḍ bil-tahdīd).

[Page 89]

*Ḥurrimat ʿalaykumu al-maytatu wa al-damu wa laḥmu al-khinzīri wa mā uhilla li-ghayri Allāhi bihi wa al-munkhaniqatu wa al-mawqūdhatu wa al-mutaraddiyatu wa al-naṭīḥatu wa mā akala al-sabʿu illā mā dhakkaytum wa mā dhubiḥa ʿalā al-nuṣubi*

﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that over which any name other than Allah's has been invoked, the strangled animal, the animal beaten to death, the animal that falls to its death, the animal gored to death, and what a beast of prey has eaten, except what you have slaughtered properly; and what is sacrificed on stone altars.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī, a new sentence that clarifies a preceding statement) arising from His words: ﴿Lawful to you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾ [al-Maʾida: 1]. It explains what is not lawful among the cattle. The meaning of the forbiddance of these mentioned items is the forbiddance of eating them, because this is the purpose of this entire list here. They are conditions of cattle that necessitate the prohibition of eating them. Included within them is a type of animal that is not one of the cattle, namely the swine, in order to encompass all forbidden animals. This comprehensiveness is evidence for the permissibility of all else, except what has come in the Sunnah regarding the prohibition of domestic donkeys, though scholars differ on the meaning of its prohibition. The apparent view is that it is a prohibition that considers a particular condition, not the category.

Mālik analogized the horses and mules to them by qiyās (analogical reasoning), and this is an analogy from the lesser (qiyās al-adwan). Also, Allah the Exalted, when mentioning them in the context of favor, said: ﴿And the horses, the mules, and the donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [al-Naḥl: 8]. This is the view of Abū Ḥanīfa, in contrast to his two companions. It is an inference for which no parallel is known in juristic reasoning. Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad said: eating horses is permissible. It is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ (the authentic collection), from Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, who said: «We slaughtered a horse during the time of the Messenger of Allah and we ate it.» It is not mentioned that this was abrogated. And from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh: «The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of donkeys on the day of Khaybar and permitted the flesh of horses.»

As for domestic donkeys, it has been reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ: «The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade eating them during the Battle of Khaybar.» It was said: this was because the donkeys were their means of transport in that expedition. It was also said: he forbade them permanently. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are permissible. Therefore, there is no clear basis in jurisprudence or in the Sunnah for the unrestricted prohibition of these three.

Carrion (al-maytah) is an animal whose life has ceased. Death is a known state that arises from the stopping of the movement of the blood through the malfunction of one of the vital organs, or through its being eaten. The reason for its prohibition is that death arises from causes most of which are harmful due to infection, and distinguishing what is infectious from what is not is difficult. Also, the flesh of a dead animal is generally not known in terms of how long it has been in the state of death; perhaps a period has passed during which the benefits of its flesh and blood have turned into harms. So the ruling was attached to the majority of cases and to what is most reliable.

Blood here is spilled blood, that is, poured out (al-masfūḥ), which is that which can flow, as was stated explicitly in the verse of al-Anʿām, thereby restricting the absolute of this verse to the qualified verse of al-Anʿām. It is the blood that flows from the veins of the animal's body when a vein is cut, along with what is on the skin. It is a viscous red liquid, varying in redness according to age and the different types of veins.

The apparent reason for its prohibition is filth: it acquires a foul odor upon contact with air. For this reason, many jurists held that it is impure in its very substance, though the verse does not address this. Alternatively, it is because it carries harmful elements from the animal's body that cannot be fully known. Or it is because of the habituation to drinking blood, which produces a craving that corrupts human character. The Arabs used to eat blood: during famines they would bleed their camels, mix the blood with wool, and eat it; they called it ʿilhiz (with a kasra on the ʿayn and the hāʾ). They would also fill the stomach with blood, roast it, and eat it. This was mentioned previously in the explanation of His words: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion and blood﴾ [al-Baqara: 173] in Sūrat al-Baqara.

He said ﴿and the flesh of swine﴾ and did not say ﴿and the swine﴾ as He said ﴿that over which any name other than Allah's has been invoked﴾ up to the end of the conjoined items. In all the verses of the Qur'an He mentioned the prohibition of swine only by attaching the word "flesh" (laḥm) to swine, and the exegetes have not offered an explanation for this that satisfies the heart. We clarified this in the parallel phrase in Sūrat al-Baqara. It seems to me that attaching the word "flesh" to swine is to indicate that what is forbidden is eating its flesh, since when flesh is mentioned with a ruling, what is intended is its eating. This indicates that other than eating its flesh, the uses of its parts are like those of any other animal: its hair is pure when removed from it during its life by shearing, its sinew is pure, and its skin is pure when tanned, if we consider tanning as purifying the skin of carrion, by analogy with tanning being like ritual slaughter (dhakāh). The view that the skin of swine is purified by tanning has been reported from Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī and Abū Yūsuf, relying on the generality of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: «Any hide that is tanned has become pure,» narrated by Muslim and al-Tirmidhī from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The reason for the prohibition of swine is that its flesh contains harmful germs that the heat of fire does not kill during cooking. When they reach the blood of the one who eats it, they live in the blood and cause great harms, among them the disease of the worms found in the stomach.

That over which any name other than Allah's has been invoked (mā uhilla li-ghayri Allāh bihi) is that over which a name other than Allah's has been pronounced at the time of slaughter.

Al-ihlāl (invocation) means raising the voice, and from it comes al-ihlāl bi-al-ḥajj, which is the talbiyah (the call "Labbayk") indicating entry into the Ḥajj; and from it comes "istahalla al-ṣabiyy ṣārikhan" (the child cried out loudly). It was said: this is derived from the word hilāl (crescent moon), because when the Arabs saw the crescent of the first night of the month, they raised their voices with it so that people would know the start of the month. It is my view that the word hilāl may have been derived from people's raising their voices upon seeing it. When they slaughtered offerings for the idols, they called out to the idol by its name, saying: "In the name of al-Lāt," "In the name of al-ʿUzzā."

﴿Al-munkhaniqah﴾ is that which something has happened to that strangles it. Al-khanq is blocking the passages of breath by pressure on the throat, or by blocking it. They used to tie the animal near a post, and it might thrash about and be strangled without their noticing, and they did not strangle it intending to kill it. For this reason it was said here "al-munkhaniqah" and not "al-makhnūqah," in contrast to His words ﴿al-mawqūdhah﴾. This is what Ibn ʿAbbās meant by his saying: "The people of the Jāhiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to strangle the sheep and other animals, and when they died, they ate them."

The wisdom behind the prohibition of the strangled animal is that death by suffocation corrupts the blood by trapping the carbonic acids present in it, so that the parts of the flesh containing the blood become harmful to the one who eats it.

﴿Al-mawqūdhah﴾ is that which is struck with a stone or a stick in a manner that kills it without shedding blood. It is the passive participle of waqadha, meaning he struck a violent blow. The feminine form of this adjective is because it is understood as describing an animal. The wisdom behind its prohibition is similar to the wisdom behind the prohibition of the strangled animal.

﴿Al-mutaraddiyah﴾: it is that which fell from a mountain or fell into a well, falling to its death, and the wisdom is the same.

﴿Al-naṭīḥah﴾ is on the pattern of faʿīlah in the sense of maf ūlah (passive). Al-naṭḥ is an animal with two horns striking another animal with its horns. What is meant is the one that another animal gored and it died.

The feminine form of al-naṭīḥah is like the feminine form of al-munkhaniqah, and the feminine marker appeared in these descriptive forms of the pattern faʿīl in the sense of maf ūl because they did not apply to a mentioned noun, so they became like nouns.

﴿Wa mā akala al-sabʿu﴾: whatever animal a beast of prey has eaten. Al-sabʿ is every animal that preys upon other animals, such as the lion, the panther, the hyena, the wolf and the fox. So everything killed by a beast of prey is forbidden to people, because the prey of a beast of prey usually dies without the blood being poured out, but rather by blows to the vital points.

His words ﴿illā mā dhakkaytum﴾ (except what you have slaughtered properly) are an exception from all that was mentioned before it, from His words ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾, because an exception that follows a list of items may be a part of them, and it refers back to all of them according to the majority. It refers only to the last item according to Abū Ḥanīfa and Imam al-Rāzī. Some of the items mentioned before are forbidden in their essence, and some are forbidden because of their attributes. Since the exception is a state and not an essence, because ritual slaughter (dhakāh) is a state, it is necessary that the exception refers to what is other than the flesh of swine, since there is no sense in forbidding its flesh if it is not slaughtered and permitting it if it is slaughtered, because this is the ruling for all animals when eating them is intended. Further, ritual slaughter is a state intended to kill the animal, so it does not apply to a dead animal; thus it is known that the exception does not refer to carrion, because that would be pointless. Likewise, ritual slaughter applies only to what has life in it, so there is no sense in its applying to blood. Similarly, that over which something other than Allah's name has been invoked, because they invoke over it at the time of slaughter, so there is no sense in applying ritual slaughter to its permissibility. Therefore it is determined that what is intended by the exception are: the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and what a beast of prey has eaten. These mentioned items are subject to conditions that lead them to destruction. If they perish in those conditions, eating them is not permitted, because at that point they are carrion. If they are rescued by ritual slaughter before they die, eating them is permitted. The point is that when ritual slaughter is applied to them while they are still alive in that state. This explanation draws attention to the aspect of limitation in His words: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is abomination, or a sin over which something other than Allah's name has been invoked﴾ [al-Anʿām: 145]. Here He mentioned four things on which ritual slaughter has no effect at all, and He did not mention the strangled, the beaten, and what is connected to them here, because they are forbidden only when death occurs due to the cause and not absolutely. So they held firmly to this (ʿaḍḍū ʿalā hadhā bi-al-nawājidh, an idiom meaning to adhere to it tenaciously).

The jurists differed in defining the state in which ritual slaughter takes effect in these five items, with varying expressions. The majority held that it is defined as: that there remains in the animal some breath of life and a sign of life before slaughter or sacrifice, such as the movement of a limb, eye or mouth, a movement that indicates life by custom, and not a movement of the death throes. This is the view of Mālik in the Muwaṭṭaʾ and the narration of the majority of his companions from him. From Mālik also: that these items, if they reach a state where their vital organs are so damaged that their life is not expected if left without slaughter, their slaughter is not valid; but if their vital organs are not destroyed, ritual slaughter takes effect on them. This is the narration of Ibn al-Qāsim from Mālik, and it is one of the two opinions of al-Shāfiʿī. Some jurists said: what is looked at during slaughter is whether the animal is alive or dead, and one does not consider whether such an animal would survive if left without slaughter. This is the view of Ibn Wahb among the companions of Mālik, which Ibn Ḥabīb chose, and one of the two opinions of al-Shāfiʿī. The very exception in the verse indicates that Allah permitted it in a state that is a matter of hesitation regarding the application of ritual slaughter. As for when the vital organs have not been destroyed, it is clear to everyone that eating it is permissible, since at that point it is a crushed or wounded animal, and there is no need to inform of the permissibility of eating it by slaughter, unless one says that the exception here is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), meaning "but," that is: "but eat what you have slaughtered, apart from the mentioned items." This is far-fetched. Some scholars made the exception apply to His words (﴿and what a beast of prey has eaten﴾), according to the view of those who make the exception refer to the last item only, and there is no basis for this except that they were considering the prevalence of this category among the Arabs, for beasts of prey and wolves frequently raided them, and it often happened that they would reach the prey and it would be left with a life still in it, and they would catch it by ritual slaughter.

﴿Wa mā dhubiḥa ʿalā al-nuṣub﴾: this is what they used to slaughter of offerings and sacrifices upon the stone altars (al-anṣāb). Al-nuṣub (with two damma vowels) is a standing stone, so it is a singular noun, and what is meant by it is

[p. 95]

the kind. It is also said that it is a plural whose singular is *nisab*, and it is pronounced *nasb* (with a fatha and then a sukun), as in ﴿as though they were rushing toward a shrine-stone, hastening﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43]. The word may be used as a synonym for *sanam* (idol), and it may be restricted to an idol that has a form, while *nusub* (stone-shrines) refers to a rock that is not shaped into an image, such as Dhu al-Khalasa and Sa'd. The more correct view is that the *nusub* is a stone not regarded as an image of the gods, but placed so that sacrifices and offerings made to the gods and to the jinn would be slaughtered upon it. Idols were counted, had names, and stood in specific places that were visited for worship. The *ansab*, however, were not counted, had no names, and were set up by every tribe, which drew near to them. The leading scholars of Arab reports narrate that the Arabs used to revere the Ka'bah, being the descendants of Isma'il. When some of them dispersed and left Makkah, separation from the Ka'bah weighed heavily on them, and they said: "The Ka'bah is a stone, so we shall set up stones in our settlements that will serve us in the place of the Ka'bah." Thus they set up these *ansab*, and they often circled around them. For this reason they called them *al-Dawwar* (pronounced with a damma on the dal, and with the waw doubled), and they slaughtered upon them the blood-offerings by which they drew near in their religion.

They used to seek out the finest stones for this purpose. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, in Sahih al-Bukhari (the authentic collection of al-Bukhari), said: "We used to worship a stone; whenever we found a better stone than it, we would cast away the first and take the other. If we did not find a stone, that is, in the land of sand, we would heap up a mound of earth, then bring a sheep and milk it over it, so that it would become like a stone, and then we would circle around it."

So the *nusub* are stones prepared for slaughter and for circumambulation, according to the differing beliefs of the tribes, such as the stone of al-Ghabghab that was beside al-'Uzza. They would slaughter upon the *ansab*, cut up the meat, and roast it; they would eat part of it and leave part for the custodians (*sadanah*). Al-A'sha, mentioning the Prophet's ﷺ instructions in his poem composed in praise of him, said:

"And the erected shrine-stone, do not sacrifice upon it."

Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said to the Prophet ﷺ before the mission, when the Messenger offered him a meal to eat with him at 'Ukaz: "I do not eat of what you slaughter upon your *ansab*." In the narration of the Conquest of Makkah: around the House were three hundred and some sixty *nusub*, and whenever they slaughtered upon them, they sprinkled them with blood and sprinkled the Ka'bah with their blood. In earlier law there was also the designation of rocks upon which offerings were to be slaughtered, to distinguish what was slaughtered in devotion from what was slaughtered for eating. From this is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), said to be from the time of Ibrahim, beneath which is a pit called "the well of souls," because blood falls into it, and blood is called *ruh* (spirit). From this too, it is said, is the Black Stone, which was on the ground, then Ibrahim built it into the walls of the Ka'bah. And from it is the Station stone (*Maqam*), according to some. When beliefs became mixed in the Jahiliyyah, they made these altars for slaughtering the offerings drawn near to the gods and the jinn.

In al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas: "*Nusub*: stone-shrines upon which they slaughtered." I say: For this reason Allah the Exalted said ﴿and what is slaughtered upon the *nusub*﴾, using the preposition "upon" (*'ala*), and did not say "for the *nusub*," because the sacrifice is intended for the idols and the jinn and is slaughtered upon the *ansab*, so the *ansab* became among the symbols of polytheism.

As for the reason the phrase ﴿and what is slaughtered upon the *nusub*﴾ is joined to the forbidden things mentioned here, even though this surah was revealed after many years had passed since Islam, and the Muslims had abandoned idol-worship: many Muslims were recent converts to Islam, and although they knew the falsity of idol-worship as the first thing they learned of Islamic belief, during the Jahiliyyah they had not limited slaughtering upon the *nusub* to idol-sacrifices alone. Rather, it also occurred in sacrifices to the jinn and the like, such as those of the *nushrat* (sacrifices to undo spells), sacrifices to avert diseases, and sacrifices to ward off the *tabi'ah* (a jinn that follows a person) from their children. It is said that they sought protection by this from leprosy, elephantiasis, and the touch of the jinn, especially for children. Do you not see what is recorded in the books of the Prophet's biography: that Tufayl ibn 'Amr al-Dawsi, when he embraced Islam before the Hijrah and returned to his people, invited his wife to Islam,

[p. 96]

and she said to him: "Are you afraid for the children from Dhu al-Shara (the idol of Daws)?" He said: "No, I guarantee them," and she embraced Islam, and similar things. Thus, there may have been among them those who persisted in slaughtering some sacrifices upon the *ansab* that were in their tribes, with the intention of seeking cure and blessing. So Allah wished to alert them and to emphasise the prohibition of this and to make it widely known. For this reason it is mentioned at the beginning of this surah and at its end, in His saying ﴿O you who believe, intoxicants, gambling, stone-shrines, and divining arrows are only an abomination of Satan's work﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], and the verses that follow.

* * *

﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows; that is depravity﴾.

The rule regarding conjunction is that the conjoined items must be alike. Therefore this conjoined item is of the same type as the items before it, namely forbidden foods. The meaning here is the prohibition of eating the meat over which they seek decision by arrows, which is the meat of the camel slaughtered in the gambling (*maysir*), because it is obtained through gambling. Thus the *sin* and *ta'* in *tastaqsimu* are extra letters, as they are in their saying *istajaba* and *istraba*. The meaning is: that you divide the meat by the arrows.

Among the seeking of decision by arrows is another type that they practised in the Jahiliyyah, by which they sought to know the outcome of an action they intended to perform: whether it would bring success and benefit or loss and harm. Since the word *istiqsam* includes this as well, it is appropriate that it too be intended by the prohibition, according to the rule of using a homonym in both its meanings. Thus its intention is an incidental inclusion, and the *sin* and *ta'* indicate seeking, that is, seeking a portion (*qism*), meaning a share of good or its opposite, that is, seeking knowledge of it. The Arabs, like other contemporary peoples, were fond of knowing what would happen to them or what was hidden among concealed matters. They imagined that the idols and the jinn knew these unseen things, so the custodians of the idols devised a method to deceive them, and they made arrows (*azlam*). *Azlam* is the plural of *zalam* (with two fathas), also called *qidh* (with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the dal), which is the shaft of an arrow without an iron head.

The method of seeking decision by the gambling arrows was: betting on the portions of a camel that they slaughtered, and they gambled over its parts. These are ten arrows, the discussion of which was given earlier at Allah's saying ﴿They ask you about intoxicants and gambling﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The apparent form would have been to say: "and what you sought decision upon by the arrows," but the style was changed to ﴿and that you seek decision by the arrows﴾, so that it would encompass the prohibition of both methods of seeking decision together, and this is an elegant incidental inclusion.

The most well-known forms of seeking decision are with three arrows. One of them has written on it "My Lord has commanded me" (sometimes they wrote "Do" on it), and they call it the *Amir* (the commander). Another has written on it "My Lord has forbidden me" or "Do not do," and they call it the *Nahi* (the forbidder). The third is *ghufl* (with a damma on the ghayn, a sukun on the fa', and it is the sister of the qaf), meaning blank, without writing. When one of them wished to undertake a journey or an action and did not know whether it would be beneficial or harmful, he went to the custodian of their idol and shuffled the arrows. If the one bearing the writing came out, they did what was inscribed for them; if the blank one came out, they shuffled again. When Imru' al-Qays wished to rise to avenge his father Hujr, he sought decision by the arrows at Dhu al-Khalasa, the idol of Khath'am, and the *Nahi* came out for him. He broke the arrows and said:

"If you had been, O Dhu al-Khalasa, the avenged one, like me, and your sheikh were buried,
you would not have forbidden me from killing the enemy falsely."

It is narrated in the account of the Conquest of Makkah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ found a picture of Ibrahim seeking decision by the arrows, and he said: "They lied, by Allah! He never sought decision by them at all." They had fabricated that picture, or imagined it for that purpose, to exalt the matter of seeking decision by the arrows and to mislead the people who were ignorant.

They also had other arrows with each of their soothsayers and rulers. Among them, at Hubal in the Ka'bah, there were seven, on each of which they had written something of the most important matters that arose for them in their affairs. On one of them they wrote *al-'aql* (blood-money) for when they disagreed about who among them should bear the blood-money. There were arrows for establishing lineage, with one inscribed "from you," another "from other than you," and another "attached" (*mulsaq*). They also had arrows for granting the right to water when they disputed over it. With these, 'Abd al-Muttalib sought decision when he consulted the gods about ransoming his son 'Abd Allah from the vow he had made to slaughter him at the Ka'bah in exchange for ten camels. The arrow fell on 'Abd Allah, and they said to him: "Satisfy the gods." He added ten more, until it reached one hundred camels, and then the arrow fell on the camels, and they slaughtered them. A man might also make arrows for himself, as is recorded in the narration of the Hijrah: "When Suraqa ibn Malik overtook the Prophet ﷺ in order to bring news of him to the people of Makkah, he sought decision by the arrows, and what he disliked came out for him."

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿that is depravity﴾ refers back to the verbal noun, namely ﴿that you seek decision﴾. The demonstrative was used to draw attention to it, so that the judgement falls upon a distinct, specified thing.

*Fisq* (depravity) is departure from religion and from goodness. It has already been discussed at Allah's saying ﴿and He does not lead astray thereby except the depraved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surah al-Baqarah.

Allah made seeking decision by arrows depravity because part of it is gambling, and within it is what belongs to the laws of polytheism, through seeking outcomes without their causes. Seeking decision is not an ordinary, regulated cause, nor a legislated cause, so it becomes purely fabrication. Moreover, what it contains of people's supposition that it reveals Allah's intention toward them is a lie against Allah. This is because Allah established for knowing outcomes rational causes, namely the sciences and knowledge derived from reason or from its proofs, such as experiment; and He made causes whose causal connection is not known except through revelation from Him by the tongue of the messengers, such as making the decline of the sun a cause for prayer. Anything beyond this is falsehood and calumny. For this reason it is depravity, and therefore our jurists said that one who claims knowledge of the unseen is to be discredited.

It is not of this kind to know outcomes from their causes, as one knows that rain falls from clouds, or expects a chick to hatch from an egg at the end of the period of incubation. In a hadith: "When a sea-cloud arises and then becomes ominous, that is a *'ayn ghudayqah*," meaning a cloud from the direction of their sea; and the meaning of *'ayn* is that it is abundant in rain.

As for the arrows of gambling, they are depravity, because they are the consuming of wealth by falsehood.

* * *

﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion, so do not fear them, but fear Me﴾.

This is a parenthetical sentence placed between the earlier verse of forbidden things and the following verse of permission, namely His saying ﴿but whoever is compelled by hunger﴾, because the connection of that verse by the conjunctive *fa'* (of consequence) requires its attachment to what precedes it, and nothing is suitable for attachment to it except His saying ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ and the verse that follows.

The reason for this objection is that when God prohibited matters whose performance was part of the religion of polytheism, namely what was dedicated to other than God, what was sacrificed on the stone altars (*nusub*), and seeking decisions by the arrows (*istiqsam bil-azlam*, divination by arrows), and when many of these prohibitions constrained them by departing from their customs and reducing their sustenance, He followed this hardship with a comforting reminder that all of this completes their religion and brings them out of the states of misguidance of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic age of ignorance). Just as they had been strengthened by a great, tolerant religion in which their welfare lies, they should accept what it contains of hardship, which returns to their reform. Some of its benefit is bodily, and some of its benefit is elevation above the lowliness of disbelief, which is what was dedicated to other than God and what was sacrificed on the stone altars. The seeking of decisions by arrows reminded them of their victory over those who opposed them and of the excellence of their religion and its completion, for completing reform includes applying severity when it is required. They were also reminded of the blessing, following the Qur'an's usual custom of pairing severity with gentleness. For a time, when the polytheists heard the rulings of Islam, they hoped these would weigh heavily on the Muslims so that they would apostatize and return to polytheism, just as the hypocrites said: ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7]. When these rulings were revealed, God sent down this verse as good news for the believers and as a blow to the polytheists. It has been narrated that it was revealed on the day of the conquest of Mecca, as al-Tabari related from Mujahid and al-Qurtubi from al-Dahhak. It was also said that it was revealed on the day of 'Arafa during the Farewell Pilgrimage, together with the verse that follows it, and this is what al-Tabari related from Ibn Zayd and a group, and Ibn 'Atiyya attributed it to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and this is the more correct view.

So "today" (*al-yawm*) may refer to the present day, the day the verse was revealed. If it is meant as the day of the conquest of Mecca, then that day was indeed the most joyful of the days of Islam, and there appeared on it, in the midst of those who remained in polytheism, such strength of the religion that it despaired them of any decline in the affair of Islam. There is no doubt that the hearts of all the Arabs were attached to Mecca and the season of the pilgrimage and its rites, where their social, commercial, religious and literary life lay, the foundation of their affairs, their mutual acquaintance, and the settlement of their disputes. Therefore it was inevitable that the Muslims' taking sole possession of those places would cut off what remained of their hopes, both of the survival of the religion of polytheism and of attempting to weaken the support of Islam. So that day, in reality, was the day of complete despair and the cutting off of hope, whereas before that they had been subject to hope from time to time. Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "Hubal is exalted! Al-'Uzza is ours, and you have no 'Uzza!" And Safwan ibn Umayya, or his brother, said on the day of Hawazin, when the Muslims were thrown into confusion and he thought it a defeat for the Muslims: "Has not sorcery been nullified today?"

The revelation of this verse on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage together with the verse after it is supported by the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in his sermon that day, according to the view of many of the biographers: "O people, Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this land of yours, but he has been content with what is less than that, in the deeds you consider trivial, so beware of him for your own sake."

"Today" may also refer to a specific day, worthy of being remembered for its time, or "today" may be taken in the sense of "now," that is, the time of the present situation, a portion of time in which despair took firm root in the hearts of the people of polytheism after doubt had crept into their souls about this. The Arabs use "today" for the time of the present, "yesterday" for the past, and "tomorrow" for the future. Zuhayr said:

*I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it,*
*but concerning the knowledge of what lies in tomorrow I am blind.*

He means by "today" the present time, by "yesterday" what has passed, and by "tomorrow" what is yet to come. Among this usage is the saying of Ziyad al-A'jam:

*I saw you yesterday as the best of the sons of Ma'add,*
*and you today are better than you were yesterday.*
*And you tomorrow will increase goodness in goodness,*
*just as the lords of 'Abd Shams increase.*

The verb *ya'isa* (to despair) takes *min* (from) before the thing that was previously hoped for, and this is the indication that the entry of *min* (which here marks the verb's complement) before "your religion" is only by way of an implied noun, meaning: they despaired of the affair of your religion, that is, Islam. It is known that the matter they had been hoping to achieve was the weakening of the spread of the religion and the apostasy of its followers from it.

The branching of the prohibition from the fear of the polytheists in His words *so do not fear them* follows on from the report of their despair of harming the religion, because the enemy's despair of attaining what his foe possesses removes his might, extinguishes his zeal, and keeps him from pursuing his foe. In a hadith: "I have been granted victory through terror." So when He informed them of their despair, He reassured the Muslims about the might of their enemy, saying: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾. Or, because the despair had been produced by the effects of the victories of the Muslims, day after day, and that was by God's support for them, God reminded the Muslims of this with His words: ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾, and indeed a group whose might did not avail them anything against God are more deserving of not being feared for their might, and of being feared is rather the one who forsakes them and empowers His friends against them.

His words *﴿so do not fear them, but fear Me﴾* convey the meaning of the form of restriction (*hasr*). Had it been said, "So fear Me alone," it would have followed the more common pattern of restriction, but instead He turned to two clauses, one negative and one affirmative, because the meaning of both clauses is intended, so it is not fitting to omit either of them. This is among the reasons that divert from the form of restriction toward the use of two forms, affirmation and negation, like the saying of al-Samaw'al or 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Harithi:

*Our souls flow along the edges of the swords,*
*and they do not flow except on the edges of the swords.*

Its parallel is His later saying: ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾.

* * *

﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam as a religion for you﴾.

If the verse ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ was revealed on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage after the verse ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾, by about two years, as al-Dahhak said, then it was an independent, new sentence, and its placement in the Qur'an after the one before it was by the instruction of the Prophet (ﷺ), who ordered that it be joined with its counterpart concerning the completion of the matter of the religion, in belief and in legislation. The "today" referred to in this verse is different from the "today" referred to in the one before it, even though both were revealed together on the Day of the Greater Pilgrimage in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, as al-Tabari related from Ibn Zayd and others. In the words of Ibn 'Atiyya it is attributed to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and that is the preferred view upon which the scholars rely. It is the basis for the agreement of the recitation with the order of revelation. The "today" mentioned in this verse and in the one before it was one and the same day. This sentence was an enumeration of another blessing, and its separation from the one before it follows the pattern of sentences used for enumeration of a blessing or for rebuke. For this reason the word "today" was repeated so that it would be attached to the verb "I have perfected," and it did not suffice with the adverbial phrase attached to the verb "despaired," so that it was not said: "And I have perfected for you your religion."

Religion (*din*) is what God has imposed upon the community from the totality of beliefs, deeds, legislation and systems. Its explanation has already been given at His words: ﴿Indeed the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19] in Surat Al 'Imran. So the perfecting of the religion is the perfecting of the clarification of what God intended, which wisdom required to be revealed in stages. It came after the revelation of the rulings of belief, which the Muslims cannot afford to be ignorant of, and after the detailed rulings of the foundations of Islam, the last of which is the pilgrimage, both by word and by deed, and after the explanation of the legislation of transactions and the principles of the Islamic order. After all of that, the clarification that God intended was complete, in His words: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89], and His words: ﴿so that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44]. So the totality of legislation contained in the Qur'an and the Sunna became sufficient for guidance of the community in its worship, its dealings and its governance, in all its ages, according to what its needs call for. The religion was complete at every time for what the Muslims needed. But the conditions of the community of Muslims began simply, then its gathering expanded, so the religion sufficed them for clarifying their needs in their conditions in proportion to their expansion, since the teaching of the religion was by way of gradual progression so that its roots could be firmly established, until the community of Muslims completed all the affairs of the great communities and became a nation in the most complete form a nation can be. Thus there was completed for them, of the clarification of the religion, that by which all their needs are fulfilled. That is the meaning of the perfecting of the religion for them on that day. There is nothing in this that suggests the religion had been deficient, but the conditions of the community in its unlettered state (*al-ummiyya*, the state of having no written scripture or established system) were not yet fully realized, and when they became established the religion was perfected for them. So there is no difficulty with the verse. What was revealed of the Qur'an after this verse perhaps contains no new legislation, but rather a confirmation of what had been established as legislation earlier, through the Qur'an or the Sunna. So what we find in this surah of verses after this one that contain legislation, such as the penalty for hunting by one in the state of ihram (sacred pilgrim state), we are certain were revealed before this verse, and that when this verse was revealed it was commanded to be placed in this position. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "After that day, no permission or prohibition or obligation was revealed to the Prophet." So if the Muslims were to lose every trace of knowledge, God forbid, and nothing remained among them but the Qur'an, they would be able [to derive all they needed from it].

[p. 105]

...the attainment, through it, of what they need in matters of their religion. Al-Shāṭibī (al-Shāṭibī, the Andalusian jurist) said: The Qur'an, despite its brevity, is comprehensive. It could not be comprehensive unless what is gathered within it consists of universal principles, because the Sharī'ah was completed with the completion of its revelation, according to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾. You know that the prayer (ṣalāh), the zakāh, the jihād, and similar matters, were not fully explained in the Qur'an; rather, the Sunnah explained them. Likewise the transactions (al-ʿUqūd) and the penal prescriptions (al-Ḥudūd) and others. When we consider the return of the Sharī'ah to its universal meanings, we find that the Qur'an has comprehensively included them, and they are: the necessities (ḍarūriyyāt), the needs (ḥājiyyāt), the embellishments (taḥsīnāt), and what completes each one of them. Thus, the sources of evidence that lie outside the Book, namely the Sunnah, the consensus (ijmāʿ, the agreement of the scholars), and analogical reasoning (qiyās, deduction by analogy), arose only from the Qur'an. In the Ṣaḥīḥ (of al-Bukhārī and Muslim) it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ūd that he said: "God has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who make hair connections and those who have them made, the women who pluck (their facial hair) for beauty, who alter the creation of God." His statement reached a woman from the Banū Asad called Umm Ya'qūb, who used to read the Qur'an. She came to him and said: "You have cursed such and such," and she mentioned it. ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Mas'ūd) said: "And why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of God?" The woman said: "I have read what is between the two covers of the Muṣḥaf, and I did not find it." He said: "If you had read it, you would have found it. God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Ḥashr 59:7]." End of quotation.

So the statement of Ibn Mas'ūd points to the fact that the Qur'an is the comprehensive collection of the foundations of the rulings, and that it is the proof upon all Muslims, since it has reached all of them, and none of them can excuse ignorance of what is in it. Had the Muslims not possessed any remnant of knowledge other than the Qur'an, it would have sufficed them for the establishment of the religion, because its universal principles and its detailed commands are clear in their indication, and its general (mujmal) statements prompt Muslims to seek to know their explanation by inductive study of the actions of the Messenger and of the earlier generations of the Ummah, who received from him. For this reason, when the Companions differed about the Prophet writing a document for them during his illness, ʿUmar said: "The Book of God is sufficient for us." Had anyone confined himself to the knowledge of the Qur'an, and found ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, ﴿and give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:141], ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:183], and ﴿Complete the ḥajj and the ʿumrah for God﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:196], he would have sought the explanation of these from what had been established by the practice of the earlier generations of the Ummah.

[p. 106?]

Furthermore, the Qur'an teaches the lawful methods of inference, as in His saying: ﴿those among them who derive it would know it﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:83].

There is no doubt that the affair of Islam began weak, then it began to appear like the light of dawn. Throughout all of that it was a religion that explains to its followers what is good, what is forbidden, and what is lawful. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not migrate until many people of Makkah and most of the people of Madīnah had embraced Islam. When the Messenger of God migrated, the religion began to appear in the form of a complete Sharī'ah, containing the explanation of the worship of the Ummah, its etiquette, and the laws of its dealings. Then, when God granted the conquest of Makkah and the delegations came as Muslims, and Islam prevailed over the lands of the Arabs, the religion became firmly established, its strength served it, and its might was feared. He prevented the polytheists from performing the ḥajj after that year. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) performed the ḥajj in the year ten, and there was none with him except Muslims. That was the clearest manifestation of the perfection of the religion, in the sense of the authority of the religion, its establishment, and its preservation. This became evident on the day of the ḥajj on which this verse was revealed.
