The religion was never, at any day, insufficient for its followers, because the religion at every day, from the time of the mission (al-baʿthah), is an expression of the measure that God prescribed for the Muslims day by day. Whoever among the Muslims was taking hold of all that was sent down to them at any time is one who holds fast to Islam. So the completion of the religion on the day of the revelation of the verse is a completion of it with respect to what it is intended for, and before that it was complete with respect to what it required from its present followers.

In this verse there is evidence for the occurrence of the delay of explanation (taʾkhīr al-bayān) until the time of need.

If the verse was revealed on the day of the conquest of Makkah, as is narrated from Mujāhid, then the completion of the religion means the completion of the remaining foundations of Islam of which they had been deprived, since Islam has been explained in the ḥadīth as including the ḥajj. For He enabled them on that day to perform their ḥajj without opposition, and the authority of the religion was also completed by the entry of the Messenger into the land from which they had expelled him, and He enabled him to turn the lands of the Arabs. Thus the intended meaning of "the religion" is the religion of Islam, and its attribution to the pronoun of the Muslims is for their honour.

It is not correct that the intended meaning of "the religion" be the Qur'an, because many verses were revealed after this verse. Sufficient for you as evidence of that is the rest of Sūrat al-Māʾidah and the verse of kalālah at the end of al-Nisāʾ, on the view that it is the last verse revealed. And likewise Sūrat ﴿When the help of God comes﴾ [al-Naṣr 110:1]. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) lived after the revelation of the verse ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ about ninety days, during which revelation continued to come to him.

The meaning of "today" (al-yawm) in His saying ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾ is like its meaning in His saying ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Māʾidah 5:3].

His saying ﴿and I have completed My favour upon you﴾: the completion of a favour is that it becomes pure of what mixes with it, namely hardship and fatigue.

Its apparent sense is that the clause is conjoined (maʿṭūfah) to the clause ﴿I have perfected your religion for you﴾, so that the adverbial phrase, which is "today", is connected to it, and the completion of the favour is accomplished on the day of the revelation of this verse. The completion of this favour is the removal of what they were suffering of fear, so He enabled them to perform the ḥajj in security, as believers, sincere, and He subdued their enemies for them on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage. They had previously been in a favour, and He completed it for them. Therefore He restricted the completion of the favour to that day, because it is the time of the manifestation of this completion. The verse was revealed on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage according to the most correct opinions. If it was revealed on the day of the conquest of Makkah, and that view is weak, then the completion of the favour upon the Muslims in it is that He enabled them over their fiercest enemies and those most eager to exterminate them. But His saying ﴿I have perfected your religion for you﴾ conflicts with this, except through distant interpretations.

The apparent sense of the conjunction requires that the completion of the favour is a separate blessing other than the completion of the religion, namely the favour of victory, brotherhood, and the spoils they obtained, and the completion of the religion is one part of them. So it is a general conjunction after a specific one. Some have permitted that the intended meaning of "favour" is the religion, and its completion is the perfection of the religion, so that the meaning of the two clauses is one; and the conjunction is for mere difference in attributes of the essence, so as to convey that the religion is a favour and that its perfection is a completion of the favour. This conjunction is like that in the verse of a poet which al-Farrāʾ cited in Maʿānī al-Qur'ān:

To the king, the noble, and the son of the great ones,
and the lion of the battalion in the crowded throng.

His saying ﴿and I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾: al-riḍā (approval) with something is leaning towards it and the absence of aversion to it, and its opposite is al-sukhṭ (displeasure). A person may approve of something for himself and say "I am pleased with such-and-such", and he may approve of something for another, and then it means choosing it for him and believing it suitable for him, so it is construed with the preposition lām, to indicate that his approval is for the sake of another, as you say: "I apologised to him" (iʿtadhartu lahu). In the ḥadīth: "God is pleased for you with three things", and similarly here. Therefore He mentioned "for you" (lakum), and "approved" (raḍītu) was construed to "Islam" without the preposition bāʾ. The apparent coherence of the conjoined elements is that the clause "I have approved" is conjoined to the two clauses before it, and that the connection of the adverbial phrase with the first conjoined element extends to the two conjoined elements, so the meaning is: "and I have approved for you Islam as a religion, today." Since the approval of Islam as a religion for the Muslims was established in God's knowledge on that day and before it, the interpretation of attaching that adverbial phrase to "approved" becomes necessary. So the author of al-Kashshāf interpreted it to mean: "I have informed you of that on this day", i.e., I made it known. This interpretation is derived from His saying "today", because what occurred on that day was the announcement of that and the proclamation of it, not the occurrence of God's approval of it as a religion for them on that day, since the approval of it was already present before. This is indicated by many verses preceding this verse. So it is not the case that "approved" is a metaphor for the meaning of "permitted" (adhintu), because that is not sound: the meaning of choosing Islam for them would disappear from it, and that is the intended meaning. Also, it is not suitable to be construed to His saying "Islam". If that is so, then the indication of the statement on the meaning of proclamation is from its indication on a necessary consequence of its meaning by the specific context, so it is of the type of kināyah (allusion) in the construction. If anyone wishes to make this of the use of a statement for a necessary benefit, then just as a statement is frequently used to indicate that the speaker has knowledge of it, it is used here to indicate informing and proclaiming it.

His saying ﴿and I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ may indicate that this religion is an everlasting religion, because the chosen and stored-up thing is not but the most excellent of the religions that have been manifested, and the most excellent is not nullified by anything, since there is no end after it. Thus the verse indicates that the abrogation (naskh) of the rulings has come to an end.

* * *

﴿Whoever is compelled by hunger, without being inclined to sin, then God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

The presence of the particle fa (then/so) at the beginning of this clause, together with the non-suitability of what follows the fa to what preceded it, determines that it is connected to some of the verses that came before. The exegetes made it connected to the verse prohibiting carrion and what is conjoined to it of foods, without addressing in their speech the coherence of the composition of this verse with what precedes it. Only the author of al-Kashshāf singled out the explanation of this, and he made what lies between them a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ).

There is no doubt that he meant by the connection of this clause to what precedes it: the connection of speech that arises from speech before it. So the fa is, in his view, the fa al-faṣīḥah (the expressive fa, which indicates an implied condition), because when the verses included the prohibition of much of what they used to subsist on, and the lands of the Arabs were few in food, exposed to famine when rains were withheld or in the severity of winter's dearth, they did not have among the kinds of food what they could substitute for one another, as their poets' verses have amply shown.

So it is inevitable that the prohibition of much of their customary food would indicate an expectation on their part that this would lead to the hand of destruction reaching them at the time of famine. So it was fitting that it should express this condition which reveals their circumstances, with the implied sense: "If you fear destruction in famine, then whoever is compelled by hunger..." etc. On this view the fa is not suitable for coordination (ʿaṭf), since among the previous clauses of prohibition there is nothing suitable for conjoining "whoever is compelled by hunger" to it.

In my view, the better position is that the placement of "whoever is compelled by hunger" is connected to His saying ﴿and I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾, as the connection of the conjoined to the element it is conjoined to. The fa is for consequence: consequence of a particular favour upon a general favour. God bestowed favour in these three clauses through Islam three times: once by its attribute in His saying "your religion", once by the general term that includes it in His saying "My favour", and once by its name in His saying "Islam". It is established among them that the best of Islam's attributes is tolerance (samāḥah) and gentleness, from many verses before this verse. So when He taught them that they feared hardship in crises after the prohibition of what was forbidden to them of foods, and followed that with favour, then removed immediately what they had apprehended in their souls by His saying "whoever is compelled..." etc., it was fitting that this expansion be conjoined, and made a consequence of His saying ﴿and I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾, and that the general favour be followed by a specific favour.

[End of part 4]

Al-Idtirar: falling into a state of necessity. Its verb is used mostly in the passive form (ughliba 'alayhi al-bina' li-l-majhul), and its meaning was explained earlier, at the words of God, ﴿Then I will drive him to the punishment of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Makhmasa: famine. It is derived from al-khams, which means the shrinking of the belly, because hunger makes the bellies shrink. In a hadith: "They set out in the morning hungry and return in the evening full."

Al-Tajanuf: leaning to one side. Al-Janaf: inclination. God says, ﴿But whoever fears injustice or wrongdoing from a testator﴾ [al-Baqarah: 182], and so on. The meaning is that one is compelled without inclining toward what is forbidden, such as taking people's property or opposing the religion. This condition is stated in order to define the state of necessity, both in acting and in refraining. So one does not rush to eat forbidden things when he has no real need of them, and he does not hold back from eating them when he fears that he will otherwise seize what is in people's hands by usurpation or theft. This is like God's words, ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173], meaning neither desiring nor transgressing against people or against the rulings of the religion.

God's words, ﴿indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 192], stand in place of the answer to the conditional clause, because they serve as its cause and as evidence for it. Dispensing with the answer in this way is common in Arabic speech and in the Qur'an. The full sense is: "Whoever is compelled by famine, without inclining toward sin, then he may eat that; indeed, Allah is Forgiving," just as God said in the similar verse, ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 173].

[Page 111]

Qur'an 5:4: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: The good things have been made lawful for you.﴾

If the people did ask about what had been made lawful for them among foods, whether after they had heard what had been forbidden to them in the preceding verse or before they heard it, and their question is now being answered, then the present tense (al-mudari') is used to indicate the renewal of the question, meaning its recurrence or the expectation of its recurrence. On this basis, the reason the sentence ﴿yas'alūnaka﴾ is disjoined (fasl) is that it is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani) arising from the sentence ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3] and His words ﴿But whoever is compelled by hunger﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3]. Alternatively, it is a resumptive initiatory clause (istinaf ibtida'i), marking the transition from explaining what is forbidden to explaining what is lawful in itself. Even if the question had not actually been asked, and it was intended only as an anticipated question, as if it were said: "If they ask you," then the use of the present tense with the meaning of the future indicates the expectation that people would ask about the regulation of what is lawful, because this is something minds are inclined to master, and to know what might have been forbidden to them beyond what was enumerated for them in the preceding verses. We have explained in earlier passages of this work, at His words ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons﴾ [al-Baqara: 189] in Surat al-Baqara, that the form ﴿yas'alūnaka﴾ in the Qur'an admits both possibilities.

On the first interpretation, the answer has been given by stating what is forbidden first and then what is lawful, or by stating only what is lawful, if the statement of what is forbidden preceded the question. On the second interpretation, the intention is to give particular attention to explaining what is lawful, in a comprehensive manner. So it was introduced in the form of a question, suited to the mention that preceded it.

The word ﴿al-ṭayyibāt﴾ (the good things) is an attributive adjective of an elided noun understood from the context, meaning "the good foods," that is, foods described as good, i.e., those that are wholesome. The original meaning of ṭayyib is purity, wholesomeness, and a good effect on the soul, both immediately and in the future. Thus a thing that is pleasant to taste but noxious is not called ṭayyib, because it leads to pain or harm. Accordingly, the best quality of anything is that it be of the finest kind and the most beneficial. The word ṭayyib has also been applied to what is permitted by the Law, because the Law's permitting something is a sign of its goodness and freedom from harm. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqara: 168]. The meaning of ﴿al-ṭayyibāt﴾ in His words ﴿The good things have been made lawful for you﴾ is its linguistic meaning, so that the verb ﴿uḥilla﴾ (has been made lawful) can properly be attributed to it. Some of the meaning of ṭayyib was discussed earlier at His words ﴿O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good﴾ [al-Baqara: 168] in Surat al-Baqara, and some will come at His words ﴿and the good land﴾ in Surat al-A'raf.

The phrase ﴿al-ṭayyibāt﴾ is a description of foods, joined to the ruling of permissibility (al-taḥlīl). This shows that goodness is the reason ('illa) for permissibility, and it implies that the forbidden is its opposite, namely the foul (al-khabā'ith), as He said in the verse of al-A'raf, describing the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the foul﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed about how to define the description "good things." From Malik: "The good things are the lawful." It must be that his meaning is that lawfulness is what signals the realization of the attribute of goodness in permitted food, because the attribute of goodness may be hidden, so Malik took its sign, which is lawfulness, so that His words "the good things" would not be a reference to something that cannot be fixed among people, such as delight in taste. It follows, then, that His words ﴿The good things have been made lawful for you﴾ are not intended to define what is lawful, but are intended as a favour (imtinan) and an announcement that what God has made lawful for them is good, nullifying what they believed in the time of polytheism: forbidding what has no cause for prohibition, and making lawful what is foul. This is supported by the repetition of the mention of "the good things" together with the mention of the lawful in the Qur'an, such as His words ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 5], and His words in al-A'raf ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the foul﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

From al-Shafi'i: "The good things are the lawful that are pleasant to taste. So everything repugnant, such as the monitor lizard (al-wazagh), is among the foul and is forbidden." Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) said: "The criterion for finding something pleasant and good is people of manliness and good character, for the people of the desert consider it good to eat all animals." This ruling is reinforced by His words ﴿He created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqara: 29]. This requires being empowered to benefit from everything on earth, except that it has been restricted by the prohibition of the foul. Thus this became a great principle in knowing what is lawful and unlawful among foods. Among its applications: the flesh of horses is permitted according to al-Shafi'i, while Abu Hanifa said it is not permitted. The argument of al-Shafi'i is that it is pleasant and good, and knowledge of this is necessary, and if it is so, it must be lawful, according to His words ﴿The good things have been made lawful for you﴾. In Sharh al-Hidaya in Hanafi jurisprudence, by Muhammad al-Kaki, it is stated that what the Arabs find good is lawful, according to His words ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], and what the Arabs find foul is unlawful, according to His words ﴿and makes unlawful for them the foul﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. The people whose judgement of what is good is to be considered are the people of the Hijaz among the urban populations, because the Qur'an was revealed to them and addressed to them. The people of the desert are not considered, because they eat whatever they find out of necessity and hunger. Whatever is found in the cities of the Muslims that people of the Hijaz do not know is referred back to the closest thing resembling it in the Hijaz. End of quotation. This contains an arbitrariness in making the customs of some of the community the standard, to the exclusion of others, which is not appropriate to general legislation. The people of the Hijaz found the flesh of the dhabb lizard repugnant, as shown by the Prophet's ﷺ saying in the hadith of Khalid ibn al-Walid: "It is not from the land of my people, so I find myself repelled by it." Yet he did not make it unlawful for Khalid.

What appears to me is this: God has tied the permissibility of foods to the attribute of goodness. It is therefore certain that this is to be considered in relation to the food itself: that it is not harmful, not repugnant, and not contrary to the religion. The sign that these attributes are combined is that religion does not forbid it, and that it is acceptable to the majority of moderate people among mankind, from everything that humanity considers food and not repugnant, regardless of customs and familiarities, and regardless of deviant natures. We find that different types of people eat some foods from animals and plants, and some of them refrain from eating those. Among the Arabs, some eat the dhabb lizard, the jerboa, and hedgehogs, and some do not eat them. Among nations, some eat frogs, tortoises, and reptiles, and some find that repugnant. The people of the city of Tunis refuse to eat the flesh of female sheep and the flesh of goats. The people of the island of Sharik prefer goat meat. Among the people of the deserts, camel meat and milk are preferred, while among city dwellers some dislike this. Likewise with the creatures of the sea, its turtles, and its snakes. The Law is broader than all of that, so the disposition of one group does not decide the matter for another group. Among the forbidden foods are those that harm the body or mind when consumed, such as poisons, intoxicants, and narcotics like opium and the intoxicating hashish; those that are impure in themselves by the ruling of the Law; and those that are repugnant, such as phlegm, bird droppings, and ostrich dung. Beyond this, you will find no criterion for prohibition other than the forbidden things by their specific identity, and whatever else is in the category of the lawful for anyone who wishes to consume it. The claim that some of them are lawful and others unlawful without a text or analogy (qiyas) is among saying about God what the speaker does not know. What made the gazelle lawful and the hare unlawful? What made the fish lawful and the sea serpent unlawful? What made the camel lawful and the horse unlawful? What made the dhabb and the hedgehog lawful and the tortoise unlawful? What made the locust lawful and the snail unlawful? Unless there is a sound text, or a sound reasoned judgement, anything else is wind. Our purpose in this is to illuminate insight when doubt arises for people of reflection regarding attaching prohibition or permission to what has no text, or to matters of the ambiguous (mutashabihat).

Qur'an 5:4: ﴿And [lawful for you is] what the trained hunting animals, which you train as instructors, catch for you, of what God has taught you. So eat of what they catch for you, and mention the name of God over it, and fear God. Indeed, God is swift in reckoning.﴾

It is permissible for this to be coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿al-ṭayyibāt﴾ as the coordination of a singular noun (ʿaṭf al-mufrad), with an elided genitive understood: the meaning being "and the game of what you have trained from the hunting animals," which is indicated by His words ﴿So eat of what they catch for you﴾. Thus ﴿mā﴾ is a relative pronoun, and the particle fa in ﴿fakulū﴾ indicates a consequence (tafrī').

It is also permissible for it to be a coordination of one sentence with another, and ﴿mā﴾ is then a conditional particle, the response of the condition being ﴿fakulū mimmā amsakna﴾ (so eat of what they catch).

It was singled out for explanation from among the good things because its goodness may be hidden owing to the hidden meaning of the dhakāh (ritual slaughter) in the wounding of game, especially the game caught by hunting animals. This is the point of special attention here, concerning the hunting of trained animals. The hunting by spear or the chase will be mentioned in His words ﴿God will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 94]. The meaning is: "what they caught for you," with the context indicating this, since after His words ﴿So eat of what they catch for you﴾ it is clear that the intended meaning is not the permissibility of eating what trained dogs and birds themselves consume.

The word ﴿al-jawāriḥ﴾ is the plural of jāriḥ or jāriḥa, following the pattern of the plural of the feminine form fā'ila, because animals are treated as having feminine plurals, just as the Arabs called beasts of prey "al-kawāsib" (the seizers). Labid said:

"Grey seizers, whose prey is not given as a favour."

For this reason it is pluralized with the feminine plural, as will come in His words ﴿So eat of what they catch for you﴾.

﴿Mukallibīn﴾ (as trainers of dogs) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿'allamtum﴾ (you have taught), specifying the type of teaching, namely the training of hunting dogs. The word ﴿mukallib﴾, with a kasra on the lam, is the active participle meaning a trainer of dogs. It is said: mukallib, and it is said: kallāb.

Thus ﴿mukallibīn﴾ is a descriptive derived from the solid noun (ism jāmid) "dog" (kalb), derived from the name of the dog in keeping with what is most common in hunting with trained animals. Therefore its being a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿'allamtum﴾ does not restrict the generality implied by His words ﴿what you have taught﴾, so this generality includes animals other than dogs, such as leopards and falcons. Ibn 'Umar disagreed on this. Ibn al-Mundhir reports from him that he restricted the permissibility of eating what the hunting animal has killed to the hunting of dogs, based on His words ﴿mukallibīn﴾. He said: "As for what is hunted with falcons and other birds, whatever you reach its slaughter, slaughter it, and it is lawful for you; otherwise do not eat it." This is also the view of al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

As for dogs, there is no disagreement on the permissibility of the general hunting of trained dogs, except for what was an anomalous opinion of al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Nakha'i, who held it disliked to hunt with a black dog, meaning one that is wholly black, citing the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The black dog is a devil" (reported by Muslim). This is a weak argument, and besides, the Prophet, peace be upon him, called it a dog. Does anyone doubt that the meaning of its being a devil is that it is prone to biting and bad temper? Furthermore, the context of the hadith concerns whether it breaks the prayer when it passes in front of the one praying, and even that is subject to interpretation. From Ahmad ibn Hanbal: "I do not know anyone who grants a concession regarding it," meaning regarding eating its game when it is black, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said the same. And how can one deal with the majority of jurists?

Ibn 'Ashur's words, "Its commentary on the Qur'an" and "Its explanation" (تفسير), ask that every Qur'an reader pay close attention to the "accuracy" (إتقان) of the one who transmits from it...
