And His saying ﴿you teach them from what Allah has taught you﴾ is a second circumstantial clause (ḥāl), intended as a reminder of favour (imtinān), as a lesson (ʿibrah), and of the faculties (mawāhib) that Allah deposited in man, since He made him one who is taught by nature from the day He said, ﴿O Adam, inform them of their names﴾, and the faculties that Allah deposited in some animals, since He made them receptive to learning. Thus, insofar as the meaning of this clause is the same as the meaning of its governing verb, it stands in the position of an emphatic circumstantial clause (al-ḥāl al-muʾakkidah); and insofar as it includes the meaning of favour, it is a establishing clause (muʾassasah). The author of al-Kashshaf said: "In the repetition of the circumstantial clause there is a benefit: that upon everyone who takes knowledge is the obligation not to take it except from the most proficient of its people in knowledge, the most skilled of them in understanding, and the most penetrating of them into its subtleties and realities, even if he has to travel to it on the backs of camels. For how many a one who has taken from a non-proficient person has wasted his days, and bitten his fingertips when meeting the masters."

Ended. And the "fāʾ" in His saying (﴿so eat of what they hold for you﴾) is the fāʾ of al-fasīḥah (the expressive fāʾ), referring back to His saying ﴿and what you have taught of the hunting beasts﴾, if you make "mā" in (wa mā ʿallamtum) a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah). If you make it a conditional (sharṭiyyah), then the fāʾ is the fāʾ linking the apodosis (rābiṭah lil-jawāb).

Page 116

The particle "min" in His saying (﴿of what they hold for you﴾) is partitive (lil-tabʿīḍ), and this is a partitive usage common in the speech of the Arabs when mentioning things that are caught, as in His saying ﴿eat of its fruit﴾ [al-Anʿām: 141]. The intention is not a prohibition against eating everything the hunter catches, nor is it a precaution against eating the feathers, bones, skin, or horns, since none of that would occur to the hearer so that he would guard against it.

The particle "ʿalā" in His saying (﴿of what they hold for you﴾) carries the sense of the causal "lām," as you say: "He was imprisoned for transgression (ʿalā al-iʿtidāʾ)," and "the child was beaten for lying (ʿalā al-kadhib)," and the saying of ʿAlqamah ibn Shaybān:

"We spear the enemies on behalf of our sons, and for our insights, even if we do not see."

That is, we spear on behalf of our realities, i.e., to protect the truth. And from this category is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Keep your wife for yourself﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 37], and His saying ﴿Keep for yourself some of your wealth, for it is better for you﴾.

The meaning of the verse is the permissibility of eating what the hunting beasts catch: from dogs, leopards, and birds of prey such as the falcons and hawks, when they have been trained and they hold the game after the hunter releases them. This is a point on which the scholars of the Ummah agree; they differ only over the verification of these conditions.

As for the condition of training: they agreed that if it is sent and it runs, sprints after the game, comes when called, desists when restrained, and brings the game back to its master, then it is trained. These are degrees of training. For birds of prey, less than that suffices: it is enough that they be commanded and obey. The attributes of training are referred back to the custom of the people of hunting, and once it becomes known to them, that is the recognized standard. On this Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfah, and al-Shāfiʿī said: there is no need to restrict it to two or three times, unlike Aḥmad, Abū Yūsuf, and Muḥammad.

Page 117

As for the condition that it holds the game for its master: this is known by its holding the game after the hunter has sent it, which is the release from his hand if it was tied, or his command to it with a word it is accustomed to understand as a command, such as saying "This is for you," because the release takes the place of the intention of slaughter. Then the beast, as long as it is in pursuit, is considered valid until it returns to its master with the game.

They differed over whether the beast's eating of the game before bringing it to its master invalidates the rule of its holding it for its master. A group of the Companions and the Successors said: if the beast has eaten from the game, the remainder is not to be eaten, because it held only for itself, not for its master. On this meaning is the hadith of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that he "asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the dog, and he said: 'And if it eats, do not eat, for it has only held for itself.'" Al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Abū Thawr, and Isḥāq acted on this. Another group of the Companions said: if the beast eats, its eating does no harm, and what remains is eaten. This is the view of Mālik and his companions, based on the hadith of Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd: "He asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he said: 'Even if it eats from it.'" Some of our companions wished to argue for this from His saying (﴿of what they hold for you﴾), where "min" is used, which denotes partiality, indicating that it is eaten if part of it remains. But this is a weak proof, since we have mentioned just now that "min" enters upon the noun in such a context and the intention is not partiality. And if the dog or beast, when the hunter releases it and it runs and brings the game to its master, has held it for him even though it ate from it, since it may eat out of extreme hunger or forgetfulness. Some scholars inclined in this matter toward verifying whether the beast's eating from the game affects its training; the correct view is that it does not affect its training, provided its actions are in accordance with the actions of trained hunting animals, and that this is merely a lapse or recklessness. A group inclined to permit this only in the case of birds of prey, because they do not grasp of training what the dog grasps. This was reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ḥammād, al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah, and Abū Thawr.

It has arisen from the condition of verifying its holding for its owner the question: if a dog or beast holds a game that its owner did not see, and it left it and returned without it, then the hunter found game in the direction the beast had been searching, or recognized the trace of its dog in it. According to Mālik: it is not eaten; according to some of his companions: it is eaten. As for when the hunter finds his arrow in the vital parts of the game, it is eaten without doubt.

I suppose that His saying (﴿of what they hold for you﴾) is a precaution against someone finding a game that he did not hunt himself, nor saw the beast when it held it, because its death may have been other than the customary way, and so it would not be a valid slaughter; and that it is not forbidden for one who did not hunt to eat game he saw another's dog catch, if the hunter is not nearby, or if he bought it from its hunter, or asked him for it as a gift.

His saying (﴿and mention the name of Allah over it﴾) is a command to mention Allah's name over the game, and its meaning is that one should mention it at the time of release, because it may die from the beast's wound; but if he holds it alive, then slaughtering it becomes required, and then he mentions Allah's name over it. The brevity of the word "ʿalayhi" is remarkably comprehensive, covering both situations. The ruling on forgetting the basmalah and deliberately omitting it is known from the books of fiqh and of disagreement, and "religion is ease."

The jurists differed over whether hunting is a concession (rukhṣah) or an attribute of the legal slaughter (dhakāh). The majority treated it as attached to slaughter, which is the preponderant view, and therefore they permitted eating the game of the People of the Book but not of the Magians. Mālik said: it is a concession for Muslims, so the game of the People of the Book and of the Magians is not eaten, and he recited His saying ﴿O you who believe, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 94]. This is a weak proof, since it is addressed to a context other than the explanation of hunting, rather to the sanctity of the Sacred Precinct. Ashhab and Ibn Wahb, among his companions, disagreed with him. There is no disagreement on not eating the game of a Magian, except a narration from Abū Thawr, since he placed them with the People of the Book; this is a disagreement about the root, not the branch.

His saying (﴿and fear Allah﴾) to the end of the verse is a general conclusion (tadhyīl ʿāmm) with which the verse on hunting is concluded, and it is of general relevance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you, and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them.﴾

The restriction by "today" (al-yawm) here is like what occurs in His saying ﴿Today those who disbelieved have despaired of your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] and His saying ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], apart from the aspect that the act itself actually occurs on that day. So it does not apply here, because the making lawful of the good things is something that preceded, since none of them had been forbidden. Rather, that day was the day of announcing it in a comprehensive manner, so it is like His saying ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], in the connection of the word "today" to it, as has been mentioned before.

The reason for mentioning that after His saying ﴿Today [those who disbelieved] have despaired﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] and ﴿Today I have perfected﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] is that this too is a great favour, because the delivery of the rulings in a comprehensive manner is a blessing in understanding the religion (al-tafaqquh fi al-din).

The discussion of "the good things" has passed just above, so it is repeated in order to build upon it His saying ﴿and the food of those who were given the Book﴾. The conjunction of the clause ﴿and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾ to the clause ﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you﴾ is due to what this concession contains of favour, because of the frequent intermingling of the Muslims with the People of the Book; for if God had forbidden their food to them, that would have been a hardship for them.

"Food" (al-ta'am) in the speech of the Arabs is what a person eats and consumes, and its attribution to the People of the Book is for association, i.e., what the People of the Book prepare by cooking or slaughtering. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Food in which there is no processing, such as wheat, fruit and the like, is not changed by someone's possession of it; and food in which there is a process of preparation, in which religion has no bearing, such as baking dough or pressing oil. If this is avoided from a dhimmi, it is out of disgust." Slaughter (al-tadhkiyah) is what requires religion and intention. Since the analogy would be that their slaughtered animals are not permissible, God granted a concession regarding them to this community and took them out of the analogy. By "analogy" he meant the analogy of their states of slaughter
(page 120)
to their states, which differ from our states. For this reason many scholars said: God here meant by "food" the slaughtered animals, while they agreed that other food is permissible; but these said: other than slaughtered animals is not intended, i.e., because it is not a matter of dispute regarding the permissibility of eating it.

The better view is to interpret the verse in its generality, so that it includes every food that might be thought forbidden to us because their preparation enters into it, and they do not guard against what we guard against, and their slaughter enters into it while they do not stipulate in it what we stipulate. Their hunting (sayd) is included in their food according to the more probable view.

The People of the Book are the followers of the Torah and the Gospel, whether they are among those to whom Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, called to follow the religion, or among those who followed the two religions by choice; for Moses and Jesus called the Children of Israel specifically, and some Arabs have become Jews, such as the people of Yemen, and some Arabs have become Christians, such as Taghlib, Bahra', Kalb, Lakhm, the people of Najran, and some of Rabi'ah and Ghassan. These are among the People of the Book according to the majority, except 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, for he said: "The slaughter of the Christians of Taghlib is not lawful," and he said: "They did not hold to anything of Christianity except drinking wine." Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the view of al-Shafi'i," and al-Rabi' narrated from al-Shafi'i: "There is no good in the slaughter of the Christian Arabs of Taghlib." And from al-Shafi'i: "Whoever was among the People of the Book before the Muhammadan mission is among the People of the Book, and whoever entered the religion of the People of the Book after the revelation of the Qur'an, nothing is accepted from him except Islam, and the poll-tax (jizyah) is not accepted from him," i.e., like the polytheists.

As for the Magians (al-majus), they are not People of the Book by consensus, so their slaughtered animals are not eaten, and whoever considered them People of the Book was an outlier. As for the polytheists and idol-worshippers, they are not People of the Book without disagreement.

The wisdom of the concession regarding the People of the Book is that they are upon a divine religion that forbids the foul things and guards against impurity, and they have in their affairs firmly established and followed rulings
(page 121)
whose violation is not presumed of them, and these are based on divine revelation, unlike the polytheists and idol-worshippers. As for the Magians, they have a book, but it is not divine; among them are the followers of (Zarathustra), who have the book (the Zand-Avesta), and these are the locus of disagreement. As for the Manichaean Magians, they are licentious, so their state does not differ from the state of the polytheists and idol-worshippers, or they are worse than them. Malik said: "Food of the Magians in which there is no slaughter is not forbidden," meaning when they guard against impurity. In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi: Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani "asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the pots of the Magians, and he said to him: 'Scour them with washing and cook in them.'"

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari: Abu Tha'labah "asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the vessels of the People of the Book. He said to him: 'If you find other than them, do not eat in them; and if you do not find, wash them and then eat in them.'" Ibn al-'Arabi said: "So washing the vessels of the Magians is obligatory, and washing the vessels of the People of the Book is recommended." He means: because God permitted us the food of the People of the Book, He knew their state, and doubt only extends to their vessels from their food, and that is permitted; but the food of the Magians was not permitted to us, and this is the source of the distinction between the vessels of the two groups.

Then, food that includes slaughter is only considered food for them if they consider it lawful in their religion, and their rabbis and scholars eat it; and if it were something the Qur'an mentioned that He forbade to them, because they have interpreted their religion with interpretations, and this is the view of Malik. I hold that his evidence is that the verse generalized their food, so its generality is an evidence for the Muslims, and there is no regard for what God related that He forbade it to them and then permitted it to the Muslims; so the generality of their food in our law is permissible, abrogating what was forbidden to them. We do not resort to argument from the law of those before us (bi-shar' man qablana...) except when we have no evidence on its ruling in our law. It was said: what we know to be forbidden to them by the explicit text of the Qur'an is not eaten, and this is the view of some scholars, and it was said to be the view in the school of Malik; the established position from Malik is the disliking of the fat of the cows and sheep of the Jews without prohibition, because God mentioned that He forbade them the fats.
(page 122)
It is known that the slaughter of the People of the Book does not take effect, nor is the permissibility of their food extended, in what God has forbidden to us specifically, such as swine and blood, nor what He has forbidden to us by its description, which is not a slaughter: such as carrion, the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, and what the beast of prey has eaten, when they consider that lawful. As for what their slaughter was in a manner differing from ours by a difference of deficiency, not a difference of addition, that is a matter for consideration, like the animal struck on its head with a blunt object so that it dies, and the one whose neck is twisted so that the veins are torn; the majority of scholars said: it is not eaten. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, from the Malikis, said: it is eaten. He said in al-Ahkam: "If it is said: what they ate not in the manner of slaughter, such as strangling and crushing the head, the answer is: this is carrion, and it is forbidden by the text, and if they eat it we do not eat it, like swine, for it is lawful to them and part of their food, and it is forbidden to us," meaning its permissibility among the Christians. Then he said: "I was asked about a Christian who twists the neck of a chicken and then cooks it: is it eaten with him, or is it taken from him as food? I said: it is eaten, because it is his food and the food of his rabbis and monks, and although this is not slaughter in our view, God the Exalted permitted their food absolutely, and whatever they consider lawful in their religion is lawful for us in our religion." The reconciliation between the two statements of Ibn al-'Arabi was unclear to many observers, but he only intended the distinction between what is among the kinds of cutting the windpipe and the veins, even by strangling, and between such strangling that holds back the breath and crushing the head. And Ibn al-'Arabi's statement is an anomaly.

As for His saying ﴿and your food is lawful for them﴾, the commentators did not turn to explaining the connection of the mention of ﴿and your food is lawful for them﴾. What I see is that God the Exalted, by this, alerted us to ease in our intermingling with them: He permitted us their food, and He permitted us to feed them our food. From these two rulings it is known that the reason for the concession in our eating their food is the need for intermingling with them, and this is also a preparation for His saying afterwards ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾, because that requires close intermingling with them for marrying their women and for affinity with them.

* * *
(page 123)
﴿And the chaste women from among the believers, and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you, when you have given them their wages, being chaste, not fornicating, nor taking secret lovers. And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his work has become void, and he is in the Hereafter among the losers.﴾

"And the chaste women from among the believers" is conjoined to "and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you," as the conjunction of a singular to a singular. The commentators did not turn to explaining the connection of mentioning the lawfulness of chaste women from among the believers in the midst of the permission of the food of the People of the Book and the permission of marrying their women. In my view, it is an allusion that they are more deserving for the believers than chaste women from among the People of the Book, while the intended matter is the ruling on chaste women from among those who were given the Book, for this verse came to permit marriage with Scripturaries. So His saying ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and the food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾. The estimate is: "and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book are lawful for you."

"Chaste women" (al-muhsanat): the women whom chastity has protected, i.e., kept from unchastity or from suspicion, so "ihsan" is applied to those preserved by the protection of husbands, as in His saying in Surat al-Nisa', conjoined to the forbidden ones: ﴿and the chaste women from among women﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], and to the Muslim women, because Islam restrained them from unchastity. The poet said:

"And Islam restrains them from unchastity"

And it is applied to free women, because free women hold themselves aloof from unchastity since the days of pre-Islamic ignorance.

Of these meanings, the first does not fit here, since it is not lawful to marry a woman who has a husband; nor the second, because of His saying ﴿from among the believers﴾, which is apparent in that they are some of the believing women, so the meaning of freedom is determined. Malik interpreted them as free women, and for this reason he forbade a free man to marry a slave woman unless he fears sinning and does not find the means (tawl) to marry free women, and he permitted that for a slave. It seems he made the address here to free persons by context, and by the context of the verse of al-Nisa': ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [the means] to marry chaste believing women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and this is a clear and coherent explanation. The root of this is from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Mujahid. Among the scholars is one who interpreted "chaste women" here as "chaste," and this is reported from al-Sha'bi and others; so they forbade marrying women who are not chaste, because of the weakness of their religion and the badness of their character.

The same applies to the interpretation of His saying ﴿and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾, i.e., free women according to Malik, and for this reason marrying slave women of the People of the Book was forbidden absolutely, for free men and for slaves. Those who interpreted the chaste women as chaste forbade here what they forbade there.

The People of the Book include: the dhimmis, the mu'ahids (those under treaty), and the people of war (ahl al-harb); this is apparent, except that Malik disliked marrying women of the enemy (al-harbiyyat). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse is restricted to other than women of the people of war, so he forbade marrying enemy women. They did not mention his evidence.

"Wages" (al-ujur): the dowries (al-muhur), and they were called here "wages" (ujur) metaphorically, in the sense of compensation for the benefits resulting from the effects of the marriage contract, by way of metaphor or sending metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal). The dowry is an ancient and long-standing mark among humankind to distinguish marriage from mere companionship. If dowries were truly wages, the duration and amount of the benefit would have to be specified, and that is something the marriage contract is free of.

As for the discussion of His saying ﴿being chaste, not fornicating, nor taking secret lovers﴾, it is like the discussion of its counterpart ﴿chaste, not fornicating﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], which has passed in Surat al-Nisa'.

The clause ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deeds have become void﴾ is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) placed between the other clauses. Its purpose is to make clear that permitting marriage to the women of the People of the Book does not imply a endorsement of their state, but is rather a facilitation for the Muslims. It has been mentioned, regarding its occasion of revelation, that

[p. 125]

the women of the People of the Book said: "Had God not been pleased with our religion, He would not have permitted you to marry us."

By "faith" (al-īmān) is meant the well-known faith, namely the faith of the Muslims, by which they were called "the believers." Thus "disbelief" (al-kufr) here means disbelief in the Messengers, that is, denying faith, that is, denying what faith requires of beliefs, since "faith" has become a term (laqab) for the totality of what must be affirmed.

Ḥabṭ, with a sukun on the bā', and ḥubūṭ, means the corruption of something that was previously sound. From it the ḥabaṭ (a disease with two fatḥas) is named, a sickness that afflicts camels from eating green plants at the beginning of spring, causing their intestines to swell, and sometimes they die. The verb ḥabiṭa implies that the one who comes to ḥabṭ was once sound and then turned to corruption. The corruption meant here is loss and invalidation, which is the gravest form of corruption. Thus the verb ḥabiṭa indicates that the deeds were sound, and the qualifier is omitted because the verb indicates it. This is a comparison of the loss of good deeds to the corruption of beneficial substances, the point of resemblance being that their performer gains no benefit from them. What is meant is the loss of their reward and of the recompense the doer expects from them and the attainment of success through them.

The purpose is a warning against apostasy from faith and an encouragement to enter it, so that the People of the Book may know that their acts of devotion and deeds will not benefit them, and the polytheists may know this as well.

[p. 126]

﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. And if you are in a state of major impurity, purify yourselves. But if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it. Allah does not intend to place upon you any difficulty, but He intends to purify you and to complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful.﴾

When we proceed from what has become clear and been sifted out to us, namely that Surat al-Ma'ida is among the last surahs to be revealed, and that it was revealed in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage (hajjat al-wada'), we are certain that this verse was revealed here as a reminder of a great blessing among the blessings of legislation: the grace of prescribing tayammum (dry ablution, the substitute for washing with water) when purification with water is difficult. We are therefore certain that this entire ruling had already been legislated earlier, and that it is mentioned here among the blessings with which Allah showed favor to the Muslims. The reports are authentic that wudu' (ablution) and ghusl (full ritual bath) were legislated together with the obligation of prayer, and that tayammum was legislated in the expedition of al-Muraysi' in the fifth or sixth year (of the Hijra).

Earlier, in our commentary on His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] in Surat al-Nisa', we discussed the disagreement over which verse was the one in which the legislation of tayammum was revealed: is it the verse of Surat al-Nisa' or the verse of Surat al-Ma'ida? We mentioned there that the hadith in the Muwatta', narrated by Malik from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim from his father from 'A'isha, does not specify the verse, but calls it "the verse of tayammum." We also mentioned that al-Qurtubi chose that it is the verse of al-Nisa' because it is known as the verse of tayammum, and al-Wahidi likewise chose this in Asbab al-Nuzul (Occasions of Revelation). We mentioned that the explicit report of 'Amr ibn Huraith from 'A'isha states that the verse revealed in the expedition of al-Muraysi' is His saying ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer﴾ and so on, as al-Bukhari transmitted it from Yahya from Ibn Wahb from 'Amr ibn Huraith from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim. Our chosen view regarding the date of the revelation of Surat al-Ma'ida does not agree with this. If what is in the hadith of al-Bukhari is not an error (sahw) of one of its narrators other than 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim and his father, then it means that he intended to mention the verse ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying, nor while in a state of major impurity, except as travelers, until you have bathed﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], which is the verse of al-Nisa', and so he mentioned the verse ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ and so on. Then its interpretation is determined to be that the verse ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer﴾ had been revealed before the revelation of Surat al-Ma'ida, and then its revelation was repeated in Surat al-Ma'ida, or Allah commanded that it be placed in this position in Surat al-Ma'ida. My preferred view is that what is in the hadith of al-Bukhari is a mistake (wahm) by one of its narrators, because there is a resemblance between the two verses.

[p. 127]

The most evident view is that this verse intends to affirm the legislation of wudu' and the legislation of tayammum as a substitute for wudu', by the explicit text of the Qur'an, because there was no earlier Qur'anic revelation about it, but it had been prescribed through the Sunnah. There is no doubt that wudu' was prescribed before that, for it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) "did not pray any prayer except with wudu'." Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam (Rulings of the Qur'an): There is no disagreement among the scholars that this verse is Medinan, just as there is no disagreement that wudu' was performed before its revelation without being recited. For this reason our scholars said: wudu' was a sunnah (practice) in Mecca, meaning it was by way of the Sunnah. As for its ruling, it was never anything but an obligation (fard). Ibn Ishaq and others have reported that when Allah, glorified is He, made the prayer obligatory upon him on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), Jibril descended at noon on that day to lead them in prayer. He struck his heel, and water gushed forth, and he performed wudu' teaching him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed wudu' with him, and then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed. This is authentic, though the people of the authentic collections did not narrate it, but they left it out because they did not need it. End of quote.

In the Sirah (Biography) of Ibn Ishaq: Then Jibril departed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Khadija and performed wudu' for her in order to show her how purification for prayer is, as Jibril had shown him. End of quote.

As for their saying that wudu' is a sunnah, it was narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. Ibn al-'Arabi interpreted it as meaning that it is established by the Sunnah. Some of our scholars said: For this reason they said, in the hadith of 'A'isha, "then the verse of tayammum was revealed," and they did not say "the verse of wudu'," because they already knew it before the verse.

Thus wudu' is undoubtedly legislated with prayer, since the scholars mention only the legislation of prayer and do not mention the legislation of wudu' after that. So this verse established the ruling of wudu' so that its authority would be by the Qur'an. Likewise ghusl: it was legislated earlier, just as wudu' was legislated, indeed it is even older than wudu', because it is among the remnants of the Hanifiyya (the primordial monotheistic faith of Abraham) which were known even until the days of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). We clarified this in Surat al-Nisa'. For this reason the expression is stated in general terms here and there: here by His saying "fatahharu" (purify yourselves), and there by His saying "faghtasilu" (bathe), so the verse became exclusively devoted to the legislation of tayammum in place of wudu'.

[p. 128]

The meaning of ﴿when you rise to prayer﴾ is: when you resolve upon prayer, because qiyam (rising) is used in the speech of the Arabs to mean beginning an action. The poet said:

"He rose to drive the people away from her with his sword, and said: 'Truly there is no way to Hind.'"

And for resolving upon an action, al-Nabigha said:

"They rose and said: 'Our protected land is not to be approached.'"

That is, they resolved their opinion and said. Qiyam here is likewise, by the indication of its being followed by (ila, "to"), as it implies the meaning of "you intended to" (amadtum ila an tusalli), i.e., you intended to pray.

Malik narrated in the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Aslam that he interpreted qiyam as meaning waking up from sleep, and this is also reported from al-Suddi. These are the aspects of the opinions regarding the meaning of qiyam in this verse, and all of them come back to the view that the requirement of purification is for the sake of performing prayer.

As for what relates to the interpretation of the condition in His saying ﴿when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ and so on: the apparent meaning of the verse is a command to perform wudu' at every prayer, because the command to wash what is commanded to be washed is conditioned by "when you rise," so it requires washing these limbs at every rising to prayer. The command is apparently for obligation. A small number of the early generations (salaf) held to this apparent meaning: it was reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and 'Ikrima that wudu' is obligatory for every prayer, and al-Tabarsi attributed this to Dawud al-Zahiri, but Ibn Hazm did not mention this in al-Muhalla, and I have not seen it attributed to anyone other than al-Tabarsi. Buraydah ibn Abi Burda said: wudu' was obligatory upon the Muslims for every prayer, then this was abrogated (naskh) on the Day of the Conquest (of Mecca) by the act of the Prophet (ﷺ), for he prayed all five prayers on the Day of the Conquest with one wudu', and in the expedition of Khaybar he prayed the 'Asr and the Maghrib with one wudu'. Some said: this ruling is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is a strange view if its holder intends by it to apply the verse to him, since the verse opens with "O you who have believed."

The majority interpreted the verse to mean: when you rise having become in a state of minor impurity (muhdithin). They likely based this on the verse of al-Nisa', which opens with His saying ﴿do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] up to His saying "nor in a state of major impurity," and so on. They understood what the Prophet (ﷺ) used to do of performing wudu' for every prayer as being an obligation specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), not included in this verse, and that its obligation upon him was abrogated on the day of the Conquest of Mecca. Some of them understood it to mean that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to make it a regular practice. They understood what the rightly guided Caliphs and Ibn 'Umar used to do of performing wudu' as being for the merit of renewing wudu' for every prayer, and this is the view that should not be said otherwise. Those who interpreted qiyam as rising from sleep intended to pave the way for the interpretation by making the command dependent upon the existence of the cause requiring wudu'. I am astonished at these routes of interpretation when the verse is self-sufficient without them, because its interpretation is clear in the verse itself: it opens with a condition, namely rising to prayer, so we know that wudu' is a condition of prayer in general. Then it clarified this general statement by His saying ﴿if you are ill﴾ up to His saying ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾ up to His saying ﴿and you find no water, then seek (tayammum)﴾. So He made these matters causes for tayammum when water is not found. From this it is understood by indication (dalalat al-ishara) that the execution of the command continues until one of these mentioned matters occurs: either something that prevents wudu' from the outset, which is illness and travel, or something that removes the ruling of wudu' after it has occurred, which is the breaches (ahdath) some of which are mentioned in His saying ﴿or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself﴾. If water is found, then wudu'; otherwise, tayammum. Thus the implication of the condition, which is His saying ﴿if you are ill﴾, and the implication of the negation, which is ﴿and you find no water﴾, is a clear interpretation in turning this apparent meaning away from its literal sense, rather it is an explanation of this general statement, and a clear clarification for interpreting what the rightly guided Caliphs did as being for the purpose of virtue, not for obligation.

What the Qur'an mentions of the limbs of wudu' is the obligatory part, and what is added to it is a recommended practice that is strongly encouraged (sunnah wajiba). The verse set the limit for the hands by reaching the elbows, because "yad" (hand) is applied to what reaches the wrist, what reaches the elbow, and what reaches the armpit. So the verse removed the ambiguity in wudu' for the purpose of thoroughness in cleanliness, and it was silent regarding tayammum, so we know that the silence is intended, and that since tayammum is based on dispensation (rukhsa), it is satisfied with the form of the action and the apparent limb. For this reason He restricted Himself to saying "wa-aydikum" (and your hands) regarding tayammum in this surah and in Surat al-Nisa'.

This is a case of deriving meaning by contrast (al-istifada bil-muqabala), and it is a wonderful method of conciseness which the scholars of rhetoric (balagha) and the scholars of legal theory (usul) have neglected. So preserve it and attach it to their topics.

[p. 130]

The imams have differed over whether the elbows are washed or left out. The more evident view is that they are washed, because the principle regarding the limit (al-gaya fi al-hadd) is that it falls within what is limited. In al-Madarik it is stated that the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq was asked about the inclusion of the limit within what is limited, and he hesitated over it. Then after some days he said to the questioner: I read the book of Sibawayh and saw that the limit is included within what is limited. In the school of Malik there are two opinions regarding the inclusion of the elbows in the washing, and the preferred of the two is their inclusion. Shaykh Abu Muhammad said: including them in it is more cautious, to remove the burden of precise delimitation. It is reported from Abu Hurayra that he would wash his hands up to his armpits, and this was interpreted as meaning that he intended to lengthen the radiance (ghurra) on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: excess is disliked.

And His saying, ﴿and your feet﴾, was recited with the accusative (*naṣb*) by Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafṣ on the authority of 'Āṣim, Abū Ja'far and Ya'qūb, as a conjunction (*'aṭf*) to ﴿your hands﴾ (*wa-aydiyakum*). In that case the clause ﴿wipe your heads﴾ (*wa-msaḥū bi-ru'ūsikum*) is an interjected clause (*mu'tarriḍa*) placed between the two conjoined elements. The likely purpose of this interjection is to indicate the order of the parts of ablution (*wuḍū'*), because the basic principle of mention-order (*al-tartīb al-dhikrī*) is that it indicates the order of occurrence (*al-tartīb al-wujūdī*). Thus the feet must be washed. The wisdom of ablution, which is cleanliness, purity, hygiene and readiness for intimate communion with Allah, the Exalted, requires that the greatest care be taken in washing what is most exposed to dirt. The feet encounter the dust of the roads, and they excrete waste through the great amount of walking. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) used to order thorough washing of them, and he called out at the top of his voice to the one who had not washed his feet properly: "Woe to the heels from the Fire."

It was recited with the genitive (*khafḍ*) by Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, Ḥamza, Abū Bakr on the authority of 'Āṣim, and Khalaf: ﴿and your feet﴾ (*wa-arjulikum*). Scholars have various interpretations of this recitation. Some took its apparent meaning and made the ruling for the two feet wiping rather than washing. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbās, Anas ibn Mālik, 'Ikrima, al-Sha'bī and Qatāda. It is reported from Anas ibn Mālik that news reached him that al-Ḥajjāj delivered a sermon one day in al-Ahwāz and mentioned ablution, saying: "There is nothing of the son of Adam closer to his filth than his two feet, so wash their soles, their upper surfaces and their heels." Anas ibn Mālik heard this and said: "Allah has spoken the truth and al-Ḥajjāj has lied. Allah said: ﴿And wipe your heads and your feet﴾." Another report from Anas says: "The Qur'an was revealed with wiping, and the Sunnah (practice of the Prophet) with washing." This is the best interpretation of this recitation: the wiping of the two feet is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the Sunnah (*naskh*, abrogation). In the Ṣaḥīḥ it is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw people performing ablution while their heels were gleaming (dry), so he called out at the top of his voice: "Woe to the heels from the Fire," twice.

After the era of the Successors (*tābi'ūn*), the jurists reached a consensus (*ijmā'*) on the obligation of washing the two feet in ablution. None deviated from this except the Imāmiyyah (Imami Shi'ah), who said: "There is nothing for the two feet except wiping." Al-Ṭabarī (Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī) saw an option (*takhyīr*) between washing and wiping, and treated the two recitations as being like two reports in matters of information when it is not possible to prefer one over the other, according to the view of those who hold that there is an option in action when the preferred one is not known. Al-Sha'bī found support for his position in the fact that in tayammum (dry ablution with earth, *tayammum*) what is washed in ablution is wiped, and what is wiped in ablution is dispensed with.

Among those who recited with the genitive are some who interpreted the wiping of the two feet as meaning washing, claiming that the Arabs call a light washing "wiping" (*maskh*). Even if this usage is valid, it cannot be intended here, because the Qur'an distinguished in its expression between washing (*ghasl*) and wiping (*maskh*).

As for the clause ﴿And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves﴾ up to His saying ﴿your hands﴾ from it, the discussion of its parallel has already passed in Sūrat al-Nisā', sufficient to avoid repeating it here.

The clause ﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any hardship﴾ gives the reason for the concession of tayammum. The negation of intention here is a metonymy (*kināya*) for the negation of placing (hardship), because one whose will is not overcome by anything is not prevented from carrying out his will by any obstacle.

The lām in (*li-yaj'ala*, "to place") is followed by an implied *an* (the verbal particle "that"), and it is a lām that frequently occurs after verbs of intention and verbs of the root *amr* (command). It is considered, according to the more preferred view, an extra (*zā'ida*) lām, and it is called *lām an* (the lām of "that"). Its discussion has already been mentioned at His saying, ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisā' 26] in Sūrat al-Nisā', and it is close in position to the lām of denial (*lām al-juḥūd*).

Al-ḥaraj means constriction and severity. A *ḥarajah* is a patch of densely interlaced, cramped trees, and its plural is *ḥaraj*. The hardship negated here is physical hardship, were they obliged to use water with illness or travel, and psychological hardship, were they prevented from performing prayer when unable to use water due to harm, travel or lack of water, for they find rest in prayer and love it.

His saying ﴿but He intends to purify you﴾ is an indication that among the wisdom of commanding washing and ablution is purification. This is physical purification, because it is cleaning, and psychological purification, which Allah placed in it when He made it an act of worship. All acts of worship include several secrets: some of them are grasped by understandings, and we express these by wisdom; and some of them none knows except Allah, such as the fact that the noon prayer has four rak'ahs. When wisdoms of acts of worship are mentioned, the intention is not that wisdoms are restricted to what we know; rather, that is only a part of the whole and a conjecture that does not reach the limit of knowledge. When water is unavailable, it is replaced by tayammum. Had Allah intended hardship, He would have burdened them with seeking water even at a price, or with abandoning prayer until water is found, and then making up all of it. So tayammum contains no physical purification, but it contains the psychological purification found in ablution, since tayammum was made a substitute for ablution, as previously mentioned in Sūrat al-Nisā'.

His saying ﴿and to complete His favor upon you﴾ means: to perfect the blessings that existed before Islam by the blessing of Islam; or He completes the blessing of Islam by increasing its rulings, which return to purification and cleansing, together with ease in many circumstances. Completion is either by increasing kinds of blessings that did not exist, or by multiplying the branches of a type of blessing.

His saying ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾ means: in hope of your thankfulness to Him. He made gratitude the cause (*'illah*) of the completion of the favor by way of metaphor (*majāz*), by borrowing the form of hope (*rajā'*) for a command, in order to urge it and to display it in the form of a command whose realization is near.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 7:

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey." And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾

It is conjoined to the statement ﴿Allah does not intend to make for you any difficulty﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], the verse that serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil) of His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, when you rise to prayer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. The discourse is connected to what the surah opened with, His saying: ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1], because in reminding of the favour there is an implicit urging toward fulfilling (covenants).

He reminded them of favours that had passed, a reminder intended to urge gratitude and fulfilment of covenants. The intended meaning of "favour" is its genus, not a specific favour, and it includes what Islam brought of honour, establishment on earth, the removal of the conditions of the Jahiliyyah, and the betterment of the condition of the Ummah.

Al-mithaq (الميثاق) means covenant ('ahd), and wathaqa means 'ahada (to make a pact). The verb wathaqa is applied to the covenant that the Muslims gave, and to God's promise to them of what He promised in return for their fulfilment of their pledge. Thus in the form "wathaqakum" there is the use of the word in both its literal and figurative sense.

And (إذ) (idh) is a noun of time, made definite here by its attachment to a statement known to the addressees.

The Muslims made several covenants with God during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). The first of them is the covenant of Islam, as has preceded at the beginning of this surah. Among them is the covenant of the Muslims when they met the Messenger (peace be upon him), which was the pledge (bay'ah) that they would not associate anything with Allah, would not steal, would not commit fornication, would not kill their children, would not bring a slander they had invented between their hands and feet, and would not disobey him in what is right. This is the very covenant that the Qur'an mentions in Surah al-Mumtahanah when mentioning the pledge of the believing women, as is related in the Sahih that he used to take the same pledge from the believing men. Among them is the pledge of the Ansar to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the season of Hajj in the thirteenth year of the mission before the Hijrah, and they were seventy-three men who met the Messenger of Allah after the season at al-'Aqabah, with al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib with them. They pledged that they would protect the Messenger of Allah as they protect their women and children, and that they would shelter him if he migrated to them. Before this pledge there were two pledges: one in the eleventh year of the mission, when a group of the Khazraj pledged to him in the season of Hajj; and the second in the twelfth year of the mission, when twelve men of the Khazraj pledged at al-'Aqabah during the Hajj season, to convey Islam to their people. Among the covenants is the pledge of al-Ridwan at al-Hudaybiyah under the tree in the sixth year after the Hijrah. In all of these they made a covenant to hear and obey, in ease and in hardship.

The meaning of "We hear and we obey" is the acknowledgement of having received the message, and the acknowledgement that they heard what was demanded of them in the covenant. So "hearing" is meant as knowledge of what they pledged to, and it is permissible that "sami'na" be a figurative usage for compliance, with "wa-ata'na" as its emphasis. This is from the usage of sami'a, and from it is their saying: "They pledged upon hearing and obedience." An-Nabighah said, describing the state of one who was stung by a snake while people began to recite charms over him:

تَناذَرَها الرّاقُونَ مِن سُوءِ سَمْعِها

That is, the charm-reciters warned one another of its bad hearing, meaning its bad obedience to the charm, i.e., the failure of the charm against its poison. He followed this with the command to taqwa, because a favour deserves that its giver be thanked, and thanking Allah is to fear Him.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyil) serving as a warning against concealing disobediences and against the illusion that Allah knows only what appears from them.

The particle (إنّ) indicates that the clause is the cause (ʿillah) of what precedes it, in the manner established in rhetoric, as in the verse of Bashshar:

إنَّ ذاكَ النَّجاحَ في التَّبْكِيرِ

[Page 135]

When He had reminded them of the blessing, He followed it with a demand for gratitude to the Benefactor and obedience to Him. So He addressed them by the attribute of faith, which is the source of the blessings they had received.

This sentence is therefore a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) that arises from the listeners' anticipation after the enumeration of blessings.

The parallel of this verse has already appeared in Surat al-Nisa', but the verse in Surat al-Nisa' says ﴿Be steadfast in upholding justice, witnesses for Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 135], whereas what is here is the reverse.

The reason is that the verse in Surat al-Nisa' came after verses about judgment concerning rights, beginning with His words ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you﴾ [al-Nisa': 105], and then it dealt with the affair of the Banu Ubayriq in His words ﴿and do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [al-Nisa': 105]. Then it was followed by rulings on dealings between men and women. Thus what was most important in it was the matter of justice and then testimony. For this reason it placed first ﴿be steadfast in upholding justice, witnesses for Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. So *al-qist* (justice) there means justice in judgment, and for this reason it was made to govern the object by the preposition *bi* (with), when He said ﴿be steadfast in upholding justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 135].

As for the verse we are explaining, it comes after the reminder of Allah's covenant. So the primary position was exhortation to standing up for Allah, that is, fulfilling to Him the covenants they had made with Him. For this reason His words "*qawwamīn*" (steadfast) were governed by the preposition *li* (for). Since the covenant is a form of testimony, He followed His words ﴿steadfast for Allah﴾ with His words ﴿witnesses in justice﴾, that is, witnesses to justice, testimony free of any partiality, and the most fitting testimony of this kind is their testimony to Allah, exalted is He.

From the two verses together arises the obligation to stand for justice and bear witness to it, and the obligation to stand for Allah and bear witness to Him.

The meaning of ﴿and let not the hatred of a people lead you to deviate﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2] has already been discussed shortly before, but here it explicitly uses the particle *'alā* (against), which we clarified there. The discussion of justice has already occurred in His words ﴿and when you judge between people, judge with justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 58].

The pronoun in His words ﴿it is nearer﴾ refers to justice, which is understood from *ta'dilū* (you act justly). This is because a pronoun may be satisfied with whatever is understood, even to the extent that it may refer to something not mentioned, as in His words ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]. Moreover, the Arabs make a verb stand in place of a verbal noun in several levels:

The first level: the verb is preceded by *an* (the verbal particle that turns it into a verbal noun).

The second level: the *an* is omitted and the verb remains in the accusative by means of it, as in the verse of Tarafa:

*Unquestioningly, O you who rebuke me, "Attend the battle, and witness the pleasures; will you make me immortal?"*

Here *ahḍura* is in the accusative in one narration, and this is indicated by the coordination *"wa an ashhada"* (and to witness).

[Page 136]

The third level: the *an* is omitted and the verb is put in the nominative, by way of an inference from context, as is narrated in the verse of Tarafa with *ahḍuru* in the nominative. From this is the proverb "Hearing of al-Mu'ayyidi is better than seeing him," and in a hadith: "Helping your brother with his mount is charity."

The fourth level: the pronoun returns to the verb with the meaning of the verbal noun, as in this verse. Grammarians have limited themselves to this verse as an example, so that the observer imagines it to be a unique model in its category. That is not so; rather, from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and to warn those who said, "Allah has taken a son"﴾ [al-Kahf: 4]. Its examples are numerous. Among them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they have no knowledge of it﴾, where the pronoun *bihi* (of it) refers to the saying derived from "they said." Also among them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That, and whoever honours the sacred rites of Allah, it is better for him with his Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], where the pronoun in "*fa-huwa*" (it) refers to the honouring derived from the verb "yu'azzim." And the verse of Bashshar:

*By Allah, Lord of Muhammad, I never betrayed, nor did I intend it.*

That is, the betrayal.

As for the meaning of ﴿nearer to piety﴾, it means nearer to complete piety, with which nothing of goodness goes astray. This is because justice is the foundation for restraining the self from desire, and that foundation is the basis of piety.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 9–10:

﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim)﴾.

Their matter is followed by the command to be mindful of God (taqwa) with the mention of what God has promised to the God-conscious (muttaqun), as encouragement to comply, and the state of the opposites of the God-conscious is conjoined to it as a warning. Thus the sentence is resumed as an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani).

The second object of "wa'ada" (promised) is omitted, the verb being treated as if it were transitive to one object.

The clause "﴿lahum maghfirah﴾" (for them is forgiveness) explains the clause "﴿Allah has promised those who believe﴾", so the explanation dispenses with the object. The sense thus becomes: Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward, for them. He departed from this arrangement because establishing forgiveness for them through a nominal sentence carries the meaning of permanence and certainty.

The restriction in His saying "﴿those are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾" is a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i), because when they were the most deserving of the Blazing Fire and were abiding in it, they were made as though they were exclusively its own. Or it is a real restriction (qasr haqiqi) when the idafa of "ashab" (companions) indicates an added degree of exclusive attachment to a thing, as they said regarding its synonym, "dhu" (possessor of), as they pointed out in His saying "﴿And Allah is Mighty, Possessor of retribution﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4]". The aspect of this exclusivity is then that they are the ones who remain in the Blazing Fire forever.

﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them is forgiveness and a great reward﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — those are the companions of the Blazing Fire (al-Jahim)﴾.
