Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 11:

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands toward you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear Allah; and upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾

After His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 7], He repeated their reminder of another great favor upon all of them, since in it was their safety. That is the favor of casting terror into the hearts of their enemies, because it is a favor through which victory is achieved without bearing the hardships of war and its losses. The opening of the new statement with the call (al-nida') is so that the listeners' attention to hearing it is obtained. The phrase "O you who have believed" and the plural pronouns that accompany it indicate that the incident concerns the whole community of believers. He stated the favor in general terms and then specified it with His saying: "﴿when a people determined to extend their hands toward you﴾".

The exegetes have mentioned several possibilities for identifying the people referred to in this verse. What appears to me is that the intended people are a group known to the Muslims at that time; it is therefore necessary that it refer to a well-known event or one close in time to the revelation of this surah. I have not found in what they mentioned anything that satisfies the soul. What I think is that it is a reminder of the Day of the Confederates (Yawm al-Ahzab), because it resembles His saying: "﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when hosts came against you, so We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9]" and the rest of the verse.

It is also possible that the reference is to the intention of the people of Makkah to treach the Muslims when the Muslims alighted at al-Hudaybiyah in the year of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah, and then they turned away from that. The verse has indicated this: "﴿And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah﴾ [al-Fath: 24]" and the rest of the verse. It is also possible that the reference is to the determination of the people of Khaybar and their helpers from Ghatafan and Banu Asad to fight the Muslims during the siege of Khaybar, then they turned back from their determination and laid down their arms; this is what the verse indicated: "﴿Allah promised you many spoils that you will take, and He hastened this for you, and He withheld the hands of the people from you﴾ [al-Fath: 20]."

From Qatadah: the cause of the verse is what Banu Muharib and Banu Tha'labah intended on the day of Dhat al-Riqa' of attacking the Muslims during the afternoon prayer; so Allah informed His Messenger of that, the prayer of fear was revealed, and Allah withheld their hands from the believers.

As for what is mentioned other than this, that Banu al-Nadir intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) when he came to them seeking help regarding the blood money of the two men of Banu Amir, and they conspired to kill him, so Allah revealed that to him and he left, with his companions, that is not appropriate to the address "those who have believed"; and it does not fit the story of the Bedouin who drew the sword of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was napping upon his return from one of his expeditions, because the one who intended to kill was one person, not a people.

The spreading of the hand is a metaphor for striking (al-batsh), as He said, exalted is He: (﴿And they would extend toward you their hands and their tongues with evil﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2]). It is also used figuratively for authority, as in their saying: enjoining good and forbidding evil is obligatory upon everyone whose hand is extended in the land; and for generosity, as in His saying, exalted is He: (﴿Rather, His hands are extended﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]). It is literal in the sense of attempting to grasp something, as in His saying, exalted is He, relating the words of the son of Adam: (﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I will not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 28]).

As for withholding the hand, it is a metaphor for turning away from evil specifically: ﴿and He withheld the hands of the people from you﴾ [al-Fath: 20].

The command to be mindful of Allah (taqwa) following this is because it is the most evident form of gratitude (shukr). So He conjoined the command to taqwa with the conjunction "wa" (and) to indicate that taqwa is intended for its own sake, and that it is gratitude to Allah, by the indication that the command comes right after the reminder of a great favor.

His saying: ﴿and upon Allah let the believers rely﴾ is a command to them to depend upon Allah alone, not others. That reliance (tawakkul) requires carrying out the commands and avoiding the prohibitions, so it is fitting with taqwa. And among its manifestations was that favor they were reminded of.

[p. 140]

The mention of the covenant of the Children of Israel follows the mention of the covenant of the Muslims in His words, ﴿and His covenant by which He bound you﴾ [al-Ma'idah 7], as a warning that our covenant should not become like theirs. The point of the admonition is His words, ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves after that has indeed strayed from the right way﴾. This is the Qur'an's manner: variety, delivering guidance in the form of narratives, and moving from one style to another.

The emphasis of the verbal statement with *qad* (indeed) and the *lam* of emphasis expresses concern for it, just as emphasis with *inna* comes to express concern, when there is no doubter and no one treated as a doubter.

The mention of the covenants of the Children of Israel has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-ba'th* (sending forth, raising up) originally means directing and dispatching. It is used figuratively for establishing and rousing, as in His words, ﴿Who has raised us from our resting place?﴾ [Ya-Sin 52], and His words, ﴿This is the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Rum 56]. Then this figurative usage became so common that another figurative usage was built upon it, by applying it to figurative establishing, as in ﴿When He raised among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran 164]. Then it was applied to stirring up things and generating thoughts in the soul. Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah said:

*"I said to them: sorrow only stirs up sorrow."*

That is, grief stirs up another grief. Here it may carry the first meaning and the third meaning.

The shift from the third person in His words, ﴿Allah had taken﴾, to the first person in His words, *"wa ba'athna"* (and We raised up), is an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person).

*Naqib* (leader, chief) is a form of *fa'il* in meaning. It is either from *naqaba*, meaning to dig, used figuratively, or from *naqqaba*, meaning to send out, as in ﴿So they traversed the lands﴾ [Qaf 36]. In the latter case, forming *fa'il* from it is contrary to analogy, but it occurs, just as *sami'* (hearing) was formed from *asma'* (to make hear), as in the words of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

*"From Raihanah, the caller who hears?"*

That is, the one who makes hear.

Describing Him as *al-Hakim* (the Wise) means the One who firmly establishes affairs. The *naqib* is the one entrusted with managing the people, because this makes him seek out their conditions. So the term is applied to the head, to the commander of an army, and to the scout. From this is what is in the hadith of the Pledge of al-'Aqabah, that the *nuqaba'* (leaders) of the Ansar on that day were twelve men.

The meaning of "the *nuqaba'* of the Children of Israel" here may be heads of armies, and it may be scouts and spies, and both occurred in the events of the Children of Israel.

As for the first, it suits that the *ba'th* (raising up) in it means establishing. Musa (peace be upon him) appointed from the Children of Israel twelve chiefs over the army of the Children of Israel, according to the number of the tribes that were enlisted, so he made one *naqib* for each tribe, and he made two *nuqaba'* for the tribe of Yusuf,

and he did not make a *naqib* for the tribe of Levi, because the Levites were not counted in the army, since they were the guardians of the Law. It has come in the beginning of the Book of Numbers: "The Lord spoke to Moses: Count all the congregation of the children of Israel by their families, by the number of names, from twenty years old and upward, every one that is able to go forth to war in Israel; you and Aaron shall number them by their armies. And with you there shall be a man of every tribe, every one head of the house of their fathers." And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: "Only the tribe of Levi you shall not number, nor take the sum of them among the children of Israel; but appoint the Levites over the tabernacle of testimony and over all its furniture." This was in the second month of the second year after they came out of the land of Egypt, in the wilderness of Sinai.

As for the second, it suits that the *ba'th* in it has its original meaning. Musa sent twelve men from the tribes of Israel to investigate the conditions of the peoples around them in the land of Canaan. These are other than the twelve *nuqaba'* whom he appointed as chiefs over their tribes. Among these was Yusha' ibn Nun from the tribe of Ephraim, and Kalib ibn Yafinah from the tribe of Judah. These are the two mentioned in His words, Most High: ﴿Two men of those who feared, on whom Allah had bestowed favour, said: "Enter upon them through the gate"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 23], as will come in this Surah. Their names have been mentioned in the thirteenth chapter of the Book of Numbers. The apparent meaning here is the *nuqaba'* who were appointed over the army of Israel.

The *ma'iyyah* (being with) in His words, ﴿I am with you﴾, is figurative, an image of care, protection and support. He, Most High, said: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you"﴾ [al-Anfal 12]. He said: ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha 46]. He said: ﴿He is with you wherever you are, and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ [al-Hadid 4]. The apparent meaning is that this statement was a promise of reward for fulfilling the covenant.

The clause ﴿If you establish prayer﴾ and the verse that follows is a pure *isti'naf* (resumptive new sentence). Nothing in it is connected to any of the words of the sentence before it; rather, the governing verb, which is the verb of saying, has joined them, so both are things said. For this reason it is good to stop at His words, "I am with you," and then begin again with His words, ﴿If you establish prayer﴾ to the end. The *lam* in ﴿la-in aqamtum﴾ is a preparatory *lam* for an oath, and the *lam* in *la-ukaffiran* is the *lam* of the answer to the oath.

[p. 142]

Perhaps this is part of what the covenant included, just as His words, ﴿I will surely remove from you your misdeeds﴾, are part of what His words "I am with you" encompassed.

The *zakah* here means what was obligatory upon the Children of Israel: giving a tenth of the produce of their fruits and crops, as is mentioned in the eighteenth chapter of the Book of Numbers, and the fourteenth and nineteenth chapters of the Book of Deuteronomy. The discussion of it has already passed at His words, Most High, ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah 43] in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Al-ta'zir* means support. It is said: *'azarahu* (without doubling) and *'azzarahu* (with doubling). It is an intensification of *'azarahu*, meaning he supported him. Its root meaning is restraint, because the supporter restrains the aggressor against the one he supports.

The meaning of ﴿and lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ is voluntary charities, other than what is obligatory.

The expiation of misdeeds is forgiveness of what they had committed of disobedience to the Messenger. He made obedience and repentance expiators for sins.

His words, ﴿then he has certainly strayed from the right way﴾, mean he has swerved from the straight path. There is no excuse for the traveller in this when he is led astray, because the straight road does not require the traveller on it to resort to twisting aside onto paths that may become confused for him and lead him to wandering in error.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 13:

﴿So for their breaking of their covenant We cursed them, and We made their hearts hard. They distort words from their places, and they have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of. And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except for a few of them. So pardon them and overlook. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.﴾

His saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant We cursed them﴾. The discussion of its like has already preceded in His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant and their disbelief﴾ [an-Nisa: 155], and His saying: ﴿For wrongdoing from those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things﴾ [an-Nisa: 160], in Surat an-Nisa.

And la'n (cursing) is distancing, and what is meant here is distancing from the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, and from His guidance, since they deserved the wrath of Allah on account of breaking the covenant.

﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾. The hardness of the heart is a metaphor, since its origin is solidity and severity, so it was borrowed for the hearts not being affected by admonitions and warnings. It has already preceded in His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. The majority (al-Jumhur) read qasiyah (قاسِيَةً) in the form of the active participle. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read qasiyyah (قَسِيَّةً), which then is on the pattern fa'iilah from qasa yaqsu.

The clause ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ is either a resumptive clause (isti'naf) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "la'annahum".

And tahrif (distortion) is inclining a thing toward a harf, and the harf is the side. The Arabs have often used the metaphors of walking and what relates to it for the meanings of action and guidance and their opposite. Among this are their saying: al-suluk (the way of conduct), al-sirah (conduct), and al-sa'y (striving). Among this are their saying: al-sirat al-mustaqim (the straight path), and (siratan sawiyyan) [Maryam: 43], and sawa' al-sabil (the even way), jaddat al-tariq (the main road), al-tariqah al-wadihah (the clear method), and sawa' al-tariq. And in the opposite of that they said: al-murawaghah (evasion), and al-inhiraf (deviation). They said: bunayyat al-tariq (side paths), ya'budu Allah 'ala harf (he worships Allah on an edge), and yusha'ibu al-umur (he splits matters). Likewise is what is here, that is, they turn the prophetic words away from their places, so they walk with them on other than their paths, and this is the alteration of the meanings of their heavenly books. This distortion is generally by bad interpretation following desire, and it may be by concealing many rulings to accommodate the desires of the common people. It was said: it may also be by changing the wordings of their books. And from Ibn 'Abbas: what indicates that tahrif is the corruption of interpretation. The discussion of this has already preceded at His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿From those who were Jews, they distort words from their places﴾ [an-Nisa: 46], in Surat an-Nisa.

The present tense was used to indicate their continuity.

The clause ﴿and they have forgotten a portion﴾ is conjoined to the clause "yuharrifuna". And forgetting is meant as neglect that generally leads to forgetting. It was expressed with the past verb because forgetting does not renew itself; when it occurs, it has passed, until a reminder reminds of it. And although neglect is what is meant by it, its formulation in the past form is a further development (tarshih) of the metaphor or the kinaya, due to their carelessness regarding the reminder.

And hazz (portion) is share, and its indefiniteness here is for magnification or multiplication, by the indicator of blame. And what they were reminded of is the Torah.

The verse has gathered, from the indications of their little concern with religion and the weakness of their adherence to it, three principles: they deliberately breaking what they had pledged to comply with, delusion through bad interpretation, and forgetting arising from little attention to the religion and little concern for it.

The purpose of this is that we take warning from their condition and admonish ourselves against falling into the like of it. The scholars of Islam, may Allah be pleased with them, have guarded this religion from every channel of distortion; they distinguished the explicit (mansusah) and the analogically derived (maqisah) rulings and set titles to distinguish between them. For this reason they said regarding a ruling established by analogy: it is permissible to say: this is the religion of Allah, but it is not permissible to say: Allah said it.

His saying: ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾ is a transition from mention of their breaking of the covenant of Allah to their betrayal of their covenant with the Prophet ﷺ. The verb "la tazal" indicates continuity, because the present tense indicates the continuance of the action, as it is equivalent to saying: "your discovery continues." So al-ittila' (discovery) is a well-known metaphor for knowledge of a matter, and al-ittila' here is a kinaya for the thing discovered, meaning: they continue to betray, so you discover their treachery.

Al-ittila' is an ifti'al form from tala'a, and al-tulu' is ascending. The ifti'al form in it is for mere intensification, since its verb is not transitive so as to have a corresponding derived form (mutawi'); so "ittala'a" is equivalent to "tatalla'a," meaning he undertook ascending for the purpose of looking over.

The meaning: you will not cease to uncover and witness a treachery from them.

And khai'nah (treachery) is khiyanah; it is a verbal noun on the pattern of al-fa'ilah, like al-'aqibah and al-taghiyah. From it: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ [Ghafir: 19]. The origin of khiyanah is not fulfilling a covenant, and perhaps its origin is displaying the opposite of what is inward. It was said: "khai'nah" is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning a treacherous group.

He excepted "a few of them," who were created upon fidelity. The Jews of Madinah broke their covenant with the Messenger of Allah and the Muslims, and supported the polytheists at the Battle of the Confederates. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Scripture who supported them from their fortresses﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26]. His command to pardon them and overlook is understood as referring to noble character, and that concerns their ill treatment of the Prophet ﷺ. The context is not the context of mentioning national or religious hostility, so this is not contradicted by His saying in Bara'ah: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day and who do not consider unlawful what Allah and His Messenger have made unlawful and who do not adopt the religion of truth from those who were given the Scripture until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled﴾ [at-Tawbah: 29], because those are rulings on general dealings, so there is no need to say that this verse was abrogated by the verse of Bara'ah.

[Page 146]

After the mention of the covenant of the Jews, the covenant of the Christians is mentioned. The sentence takes the form of the construction called *ishtighal* (the verb is preoccupied with a pronoun referring back to its object), since the complement "أخذنا ميثاقهم" (*akhadhna mithaqahum*, "We took their covenant") is placed first, and there is an explicit noun in it. The pronoun is attached to the verb for the sake of a rhetorical purpose that calls for *ishtighal*: fixing the complement and establishing it in the mind, since the ruling is connected both to the explicit noun and to its pronoun. The meaning is therefore: "And We took from those who say, 'We are Christians,' their covenant." Placing the prepositional phrase first does not serve to restrict the meaning. It has also been said that the pronoun in "mithaqihim" refers to the Jews, and that the *idafa* (construct phrase) has the sense of comparison, meaning: "From the Christians We took a covenant like the covenant of the Jews," that is, its equivalent. This would be an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*) in which the particle has been omitted, so the compared element is put in the accusative. But this is remote, because the covenant of the Jews was not detailed in the preceding verse, so that the covenant of the Christians could be compared to it.

The Christians are referred to as "﴿الذين قالوا إنا نصارى﴾" (*alladhina qalu inna nasara*, "those who say, 'We are Christians'") here and in His words, which come later: "﴿ولتجدن أقربهم مودة للذين آمنوا الذين قالوا إنا نصارى﴾" ("And you will find the nearest of them in affection to the believers those who say, 'We are Christians'") [al-Ma'ida: 82]. This is to record against them that the name of their religion points to one of its foundations, which is that its followers should be helpers (*ansar*) of what Allah commands: "﴿كما قال عيسى ابن مريم للحواريين من أنصاري إلى الله قال الحواريون نحن أنصار الله﴾" ("As Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, 'Who are my helpers for Allah?' The disciples said, 'We are helpers of Allah'") [al-Saff: 14]. Among this is that they should support the one who upholds the religion after Jesus from among his followers, such as Paul, Peter and others from the callers to guidance. Greater than all of that is that they should support the prophet foretold in the Torah and the Gospel, who comes after Jesus before the end of the world and frees people from misguidance: "﴿وإذ أخذ الله ميثاق النبيين لما آتيتكم من كتاب وحكمة ثم جاءكم رسول مصدق لما معكم لتؤمنن به ولتنصرنه﴾" ("And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: 'Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him'") [Al 'Imran: 81], and so on. Thus all the followers of the messengers are bound by what their prophets committed to, and the Christians in particular. Therefore this title, which is "Christians," is a proof against them, established upon them and inseparable from all of their community.

The word "qalu" ("they said") also implies, by way of allusive implication (*kinaya ta'ridiyya*), that this statement has been fulfilled and that it must be fulfilled. This is the case if "al-nasara" is the plural of *nasari* or *nasrani*, in the sense of attribution to victory (*nasr*) for emphasis, as in their saying *sha'rani* and *lihyani* (meaning: one who is very strong in his hair or his beard), that is, the one who is very strong in victory. But if "al-nasara" is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) of *nasari*, in the sense of "one attributed to al-Nasiri," and al-Nasiri is Jesus, because he appeared from the city of Nazareth, then al-Nasiri is an epithet by which the Messiah, peace be upon him, was known in the books of the Jews, because he appeared with the call to his message from the town of Nazareth in Palestine. Therefore, attribution to him means attribution to his way and his law. Whoever deviates from his law is not truly entitled to be attributed to him except by a false claim. For this reason He said, "﴿قالوا إنا نصارى﴾." It has also been said that "al-nasara" is the plural of *nasrani*, attributed to *nasr* (victory), as they said *sha'rani* and *lihyani*, because they said, "We are the helpers of Allah." Accordingly, the meaning of "﴿قالوا إنا نصارى﴾" is that they claimed this with their words, without supporting it with their deeds.

Allah took a covenant from the Christians through the tongue of the Messiah, peace be upon him. Some of it is mentioned in passages of the Gospels.

His words "﴿فأغرينا بينهم العداوة﴾" ("so We caused among them animosity"): the literal meaning of *al-igra'* (inciting) is to urge someone to an action and to make it attractive to him so that he does not slacken in achieving it. The word is used figuratively for establishing the constant presence of enmity and hatred in their souls, meaning their continuing among themselves. The establishment of enmity and hatred, with their persistence among them, is likened to one person inciting another to an action he performs, a likeness of an intelligible thing to a perceptible one. Since the adverbial phrase "بينهم" (*baynahum*, "among them") indicates that these two were incited among them, mention of the object of "أغرينا" is dispensed with. The sentence in full would be: "So We incited enmity and hatred upon them, existing between them." It seems that the shift from transitivizing "أغرينا" with a preposition to linking it with the adverbial phrase is either an indication or a stripping away, to show that what is meant by "أغرينا" is "ألقينا" (*alqayna*, "We cast").

What occurs in al-Kashshaf of interpreting "أغرينا" as meaning "ألصقنا" (*alsaqna*, "We stuck") is a deviation from the intended meaning toward a smell of derivation from *al-ghira'*, which is the grease with which wood is glued. This meaning has been forgotten in usage. The enmity, and the pronoun in the genitive attached to "بين" (*bayn*), refer back to the Christians so that the pronouns are consistent.

"Al-'adawa" (enmity) and "al-baghda'" (hatred) are two nouns for two meanings from the category of intense dislike. Thus they are opposites of love.

The apparent conjunction of one of the two nouns to the other in several places of the Qur'an, in this verse and in the two verses after it in this surah, and in a verse of Surat al-Mumtahana, shows that they are not synonyms, because the adherence to conjunction in this order is unlikely to be merely for emphasis. So the conjunction of one of them to the other is not like the conjunction of synonyms merely for emphasis, as in the words of 'Adi:

*"And he found her words to be lies and falsehood."*

The scholars of language left the explanation of the distinction between *al-'adawa* and *al-baghda'* unexplained, and the commentators followed them in this. You will not find anyone who undertook to distinguish between them except Shaykh Ibn 'Arafa al-Tunisi, who said in his tafsir: "Enmity is more general than hatred, because enmity is a cause of hatred. A brother may be hostile to his brother without persisting in it until hatred arises from it, and he may persist in it." End of quote.

It occurred to Abu al-Baqa' al-Kafawi, in his book *al-Kulliyyat*, that he said: "Enmity is more specific than hatred, because every enemy is a hater, while one may hate someone who is not an enemy." This contradicts the words of Ibn 'Arafa. In both of their explanations there is clear begging of the question (*musadara*). If enmity is more general than hatred, the benefit of the conjunction increases, because it becomes like a safeguard against misunderstanding (*ihtiras*). If enmity is more specific than hatred, the conjunction is only for emphasis, because emphasis is achieved by mentioning a word that indicates a general part of the meaning of the emphasized term, so the meaning is confirmed, even if in a more general or more specific aspect, and the sense of emphasis is achieved thereby.

In my view, neither of the two positions is evident. What I see is that between the meanings of *al-'adawa* and *al-baghda'* there is opposition and disparity. *Al-'adawa* is a dislike that proceeds from its bearer: treating someone harshly, severing ties, or causing harm, because *al-'adawa* is derived from *al-'adw*, which means transgression and distance. All derivatives of the root (ʿ-d-w) revolve around separation and the absence of harmony. As for *al-baghda'*, it is the intensity of hatred, and in the root (b-gh-d) there is nothing but the general meaning of dislike, so there is no way to know the derivation of its word from its root. Yes, it is possible to refer to it by the method of metathesis (*qalb*), which is one of the signs of derivation, since the inverted form of *baghida* becomes *ghadiba* (to be angry) and nothing else. So *al-baghda'* is intense dislike not accompanied by hostile action; it is hidden within the soul. When this is the case, it is not valid for the meanings of enmity and hatred to be combined in one subject at one time. Therefore it is necessary that their casting among them be in the sense of distribution, meaning: We incited enmity among some of them and hatred among others.

Thus in this arrangement there is a wonderful concision (*ijaz*), because it rests on the listeners' knowledge that the two meanings cannot coherently combine in one subject.

[Page 149]

Among the subtleties is what Ibn Hisham mentioned, in his commentary on the poem of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, at Ka'b's words:

*"But it is a friendship whose blood has been shed by bereavement, passion, breaking, and change."*

That al-Zamakhshari said: he saw himself in a dream saying, "Enmity is derived from *'udwat al-wadi*," meaning its side, because the two who are hostile to each other are separated from each other, so that each of them is in enmity (*'adawa*). End of quote. Thus it would be derived from a non-derivative noun (*ism jamid*), and this is remote.

The casting of enmity and hatred among them was a punishment in this world, as shown by His words: "﴿إلى يوم القيامة وسوف ينبئهم الله بما كانوا يصنعون﴾" ("until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah is going to inform them of what they used to do"), as a recompense for their breaking the covenant.

The causes of enmity and hatred are severe disagreement. Thus it arises from their disagreement over religious sects, among the Ya'qubiyya (Jacobites), the Malkaniyya (Melkites), the Nasturiyya (Nestorians), and the Haratiqa (Protestants), and it arises from envy over authority and worldly goods, as occurred among the kings of Christianity, and between them and the heads of their religion.

If it is said: How could enmity be cast among them when they have never ceased to be a united front (*alb*) against the Muslims? The answer is that enmity is established among them in religion through their division into sects, as we mentioned in Surat al-Nisa' in the words of the Most High: "﴿وكلمته ألقاها إلى مريم وروح منه﴾" ("And [He is] His word which He directed to Mary and a soul [created at a command] from Him") [al-Nisa': 171]. That division draws enmity upon them, and they abandoned one another. Moreover, their states were divided and at war with each other, and they continued in that condition. They only united against the Muslims in the Crusades, and then they soon abandoned one another and fought each other, and the matter remains so among them until now. How many efforts of those striving to gather them under one word and to forge a unity among them have been wasted! Their disagreement was a kindness to the Muslims throughout the different eras of Islamic history. Moreover, their agreement upon another nation does not negate the entrenchment of enmity among them, and that is sufficient as a punishment for them for forgetting what they were reminded of.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to both groups, that is, between the Jews and the Christians, and there is no difficulty in the enmity between the two religions being real.

His words "﴿وسوف ينبئهم الله﴾" ("And Allah is going to inform them") are a threat, because the intended meaning of "informing" is informing them of the retribution for their conduct, as in His words: "﴿فسوف تعلمون﴾" ("then you are going to know") [al-An'am: 135]. This may occur in the Hereafter, in which case "informing" has its literal meaning. It may also occur in this world, in which case "informing" is a figurative expression for God's decree upon them of events through which they will come to know the evil of their deeds.

﴿O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture, and pardoning much. There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book.﴾ ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His pleasure to the paths of peace, and brings them out of darknesses into the light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path.﴾

After mentioning the circumstances and reports of the two groups of the People of the Book, which none knows except their scholars and which they cannot deny, He turned to them with direct address and admonition. This is because the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ had become evident, which makes it easier to establish the proof against them. For this reason, the description of the Messenger began with his making clear to them much of what they used to conceal of the Scripture, and then it was followed by his pardoning much.

The meaning of ﴿yaʿfu﴾ (يَعْفُو) is: he turns away and does not make manifest. This is the root sense of the root ʿ-f-w. It is said: ʿafā al-rasm (عفا الرسم), meaning it was not visible, and ʿaffāhu, meaning he removed its visibility. Then they said: ʿafā ʿan al-dhanb (عفا عن الذنب), meaning he turned away from the sin, and then they said: ʿafā ʿan al-mudhnib (عفا عن المذنب), meaning he concealed his sin from him. It is also permissible that the meaning here be forgiveness and pardon, i.e., "and he overlooks many of your sins," that is, "he makes your religion clear to you and pardons your ignorance."

[Page 151]

The clause ﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light﴾ is a badal (apposition) of the clause ﴿There has certainly come to you Our Messenger﴾, a badal al-ishtimal (apposition of inclusion), because the coming of the Messenger included the coming of the guidance and the Qur'an. Its pattern is like the pattern of (ʿilmuhu) in their saying: "Zayd benefited me, his knowledge" (nafaʿanī Zaydun ʿilmuhu). For this reason it is separated from it, and the particle (qad) that enters upon the clause being substituted is repeated, in addition to confirming the content of the apposing clause, because the connection of the badal al-ishtimal to the word it substitutes is weaker than the connection of the badal that corresponds fully.

The pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ (به) refers either to the Messenger or to the Clear Book.

Subul al-salam (سُبُلُ السَّلامِ) are the paths of safety, in which there is no fear for the traveler. The Arabs had known roads famous for safety and roads famous for fear, such as Wadi al-Sibaʿ (the valley of wild beasts), about which Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi said:

*And I passed by Wadi al-Sibaʿ, and I see no valley like Wadi al-Sibaʿ when it grows dark,*
*A valley in which a caravan that came to it has been few, in its fearfulness, and more fearful, except for one traveler whom Allah protected.*

Thus ﴿subul al-salam﴾ is a metaphor (isti'arah) for the paths of truth. The darknesses and the light are a metaphor for misguidance and guidance. And ﴿al-sirat al-mustaqim﴾ (the straight path) is used metaphorically for faith.

[Page 152]

This is one of the forms of failing to keep the covenant of God, exalted is He.

The greatest of the Christians' errors was their claim that ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) is divine. Refuting this belief is therefore the most important aspect of bringing them out "from darkness into light" and guiding them to "the straight path." So the phrase ﴿Certainly, those have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Maryam"﴾ begins a new sentence of clarification (istiʾnāf al-bayān). The relative pronoun is required here because the aim is to explain the disbelief contained in this statement, not to explain the misguidance the Christians are in, since their misguidance necessarily follows once this statement is disbelief.

Their statement is rendered in Arabic through the sentence ﴿inna Allāha huwa al-Masīḥu ibnu Maryam﴾, which is a precisely meaningful construction. The commentators have not given it its due in explaining the meaning derived from its structure: that the two names refer to one and the same referent, by making both the subject and the predicate definite through proper-name definiteness (ʿalamiyya). The context indicates that the speech is not intended to inform about events happening to distinct beings. In terminology, this is called ḥaml ishtiqāq (predication by derivation) only in the wrong sense; rather it is ḥaml muwāṭaʾa (predication of identity), which logicians call ḥaml (huwa huwa), "is-is" predication. This occurs when both the subject and the predicate are known to the addressee and the purpose is to state that they are one thing. An example is when you say, "Ziyād said," and your listener asks, "Who is Ziyād?" and you reply, "Ziyād is al-Nābigha." Similar examples are: "Maymūn is al-Aʿshā," "Ibn Abī al-Simṭ is Marwān ibn Abī Ḥafṣa," "al-Muraʿʿath is Bashshār," and the like. Thus the mere definiteness of both parts of the predication is sufficient to convey identity. The insertion of the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl, "huwa") between the subject and predicate in such examples is a well-known usage that almost never fails to be used deliberately to emphasise identity. Hence such a construction does not indicate that one part is restricted to the other (qaṣr), and the separating pronoun in it conveys nothing except emphasis. Likewise the presence of the particle ﴿inna﴾ is for added emphasis. A parallel is the verse of Ruwaysh ibn Kathīr al-Ṭāʾī, one of the poets of the Ḥamāsa:

"Say to them: hasten to make excuses, and seek a word that will clear you; indeed I am Death."

Here there is none of the scholarly disagreement of the rhetoricians (ʿulamāʾ al-maʿānī) over whether the separating pronoun restricts the subject, which is the more correct view, or the reverse, which is rare. This is because the situation of the identity of the two names levels the two possibilities and turns away from intending restriction. The author of al-Kashshāf alluded to this meaning subtly when, after quoting ﴿those who said, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Maryam"﴾, he said: "its meaning is a decisive statement that the reality of Allah is the Messiah and nothing else." The point of evidence in al-Kashshāf's words is everything except his phrase "and nothing else," because the apparent meaning of "and nothing else" points to deriving the sense of restriction from such a construction, which is far-fetched. It may be said, however, that he meant that the sense of exclusivity is necessarily implied by the sense of identity and does not arise from a restrictive formula.

Their statement conveys that they made the reality of the true, known God unified with the reality of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), in the manner of two names for one named object. Their intention was the fusion of the divine reality into the person of ʿĪsā. Since the divine reality is designated among all religious people by the name of majesty (ism al-jalāla, "Allah"), the speakers made the name "Allah" the subject and the name "ʿĪsā" the predicate, to indicate that God has united with the person of the Messiah.

The report of the statement from them shows clearly that they said it openly out of conviction, since the belief in the union of the divine nature (lāhūt) with the human nature (nāsūt) of ʿĪsā spread among them to the point that they believed that God, glorified is He, had united with ʿĪsā and the existence of God had merged with the existence of ʿĪsā. This is an exaggeration in the belief of incarnation (ḥulūl). The Christians have a basis for depicting this incarnation or union: that God, exalted is He, is one substance, which is the totality of three hypostases (aqānīm, singular uqnūm, with a initial hamza and a sukūn on the qāf, a Greek word meaning "origin," as in the Qāmūs). These three are the hypostasis of essence, the hypostasis of knowledge, and the hypostasis of life. They divided over how these hypostases are united with the essence of ʿĪsā into three doctrines: the doctrine of the Malkites, who are the Chalcedonians (the Catholics); the doctrine of the Nestorians; and the doctrine of the Jacobites. Its details are in the book al-Maqāṣid. It was discussed in detail earlier, when commenting on His words, exalted is He: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say, "Three"﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 171], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. This is the view of the Yaʿqūbiyya among the Christians, who are followers of Yaʿqūb al-Barḏaʿānī, who was a monk in Constantinople. His doctrine appeared after the doctrine of the Malkites. The Jacobites are also called "the people of the single nature," and all the Christians of Abyssinia followed this way. There is no doubt that the Christians of Najrān were on this path.

Because the Abyssinians, its adherents, were close to the lands of the Arabs, the Qur'an addressed the refutation of this belief here and in the next verse of this sūra. We have already explained the true nature of the Christian belief in the union of the divine and human natures, and in the gathering of the hypostases, at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And His word which He directed to Maryam and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 171], in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

Allah showed His messenger the proof against them through His words: ﴿Say, "Then who could prevent Allah at all?"﴾, and so on.

[Page 154]

The fāʾ here is conjunctive for the rhetorical interrogation (istifhām inkārī) following their statement "indeed Allah is the Messiah," to show that the denial is consequent upon this monstrous statement. It is thus fāʾ of mention-based sequence (taʿqīb dhikrī). This usage is common in their speech, so there is no need for what has been said: that the fāʾ conjoins with an omitted element indicated by the context, meaning "the matter is not as you claim," nor that it is the answer to an implied condition, meaning "if what you say is true, then who can prevent Allah at all..." and so forth.

The meaning of "possesses anything" (yamlik shayʾan) here is "is able to do anything." The phrase is therefore used for its necessary implication by way of kināya (metonymy). This implication is multiple: possession, and so the capacity to transform or alter. This is a common usage, and an instance of it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Who could prevent Allah from you in anything if He intended harm for you?"﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 11], and so on, in Sūrat al-Fatḥ. In a ḥadīth, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn: "Can I prevent Allah from removing mercy from your heart?" because the one who possesses disposes of what he owns however he wishes.

The indefiniteness in His words "shayʾan" (anything) expresses minimisation and belittlement. Since the interrogation here has the sense of negation, the negation of a small thing necessarily entails the negation of a great thing, a fortiori. So the meaning is: "who is able to do anything against Allah, that is, against His act and disposal, to turn it away from Him?" A parallel is ﴿and I cannot avail you anything against Allah﴾ [Yūsuf: 67]. Another usage of "yamlik" will come in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses for you neither harm nor benefit?"﴾ [al-Māʾida: 76] in this sūra, and a close usage will come in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever Allah intends for trial, you will not possess for him anything against Allah﴾ [al-Māʾida: 41] in this sūra.

The conditional particle in His words "in arāda" (if He intends) is used merely for stating a condition, without indicating futurity. This is because the destruction of the Messiah's mother has indeed occurred, without dispute. And because the destruction of the Messiah, that is his death, is accepted by those who argue with this statement, it is appropriate to give them free rein in this matter in order to establish the proof. It is also accepted in one opinion of a group of Muslim scholars who said that God caused him to die and raised him up, without letting the Jews reach him, as was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 157], and His words: ﴿Indeed, I will take you in death and raise you to Myself﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 55]. Accordingly, in the stating of this condition there is no indication of futurity.

[Page 155]

The present-tense verb preceded by "an" (anna yuhlika, "that He destroy") is used merely for the verbal-nominal sense (maṣdariyya). By "those who are on earth" here is meant all who were on earth in the time of the Messiah and his mother; they all perished, by necessity. The sense is: "who could prevent Allah, if He intended to destroy the Messiah, his mother, and those on earth at that time?"

It is also possible to maintain that the conditional refers to the future, by taking "wa man fī al-arḍi jamīʿan" (and all who are on the earth) to mean the human species as a whole. Then the conditioning applies to the totality of the objects of "yuhlik" (destroys) by way of taghlīb (predominance of one part over the rest). Some of these objects have already perished, namely the mother of the Messiah, while others have not yet perished and will perish, namely the destruction of all who are on earth, that is, the destruction of the entire species. This has not occurred, but it is possible.

The summary is that the use of this conditional is among the strange uses of conditionals in Arabic. It returns to the use of a conditional form in a literal sense and in a figurative sense, with the literal sense given predominance, since "man fī al-arḍ" (whoever is on earth) includes all, and this is the majority. The commentators have not given it its due explanation. Maryam, the mother of the Messiah (peace be upon them both), died at a time not precisely known, after the raising of the Messiah.

The concluding statement, His words: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. He creates what He wills﴾ contains the magnification of the status of Allah, exalted is He. It is also another refutation against them: that Allah is He who created the heavens and the earth and possessed what is in them before the Messiah appeared. So Allah is the true God, and He creates what He wills; He is the one who created the Messiah in an unusual manner, and this was the cause of the misguidance of those who attributed divinity to him. Likewise is His words: ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (*al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr*) on Surah 5, verse 18:**

﴿The Jews and the Christians said, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones." Say, "Why then does He punish you for your sins? Rather, you are mortals of those whom He has created. He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and to Him is the final return."﴾

Another statement, shared between them and the Jews, indicates their foolishness in disbelief, since they say what does not befit the majesty of Allah, the Exalted. Moreover, it contradicts their other statements. It is conjoined to the statement specific to the Christians, which is the phrase ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary."﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 17]. The expression "sons of Allah" occurs in the Torah and the Gospel. In the first chapter of the fourteenth section of the Book of Deuteronomy, there is the saying of Moses: "You are children of the Lord your Father." As for the Gospels, they are full of describing Allah, the Exalted, as the Father of the Messiah and the Father of those who believe in him, and of calling the believers "sons of Allah." In Matthew, in the third chapter: "And a voice from heaven saying, 'This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'" In the fifth chapter: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God." In the sixth chapter: "And your heavenly Father feeds them." In the tenth chapter: "For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." All of these are expressed in a manner of figurative comparison (*tashbīh*), but their common folk took them literally and held their apparent meaning.

The conjunction of "and His beloved ones" with "sons of Allah" indicates that they intended that they are beloved sons, since a son may be one with whom anger is directed.

Allah taught His Messenger to refute their claim with two premises. The first is from the Law, and it is His saying: ﴿Say, "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾, meaning that they affirm that a portion of punishment reaches them for their sins. Had they been the sons and beloved ones of Allah, He would not have punished them for their sins. It is the nature of a lover not to punish his beloved, and it is the nature of a father not to punish his sons. It is narrated that al-Shiblī asked Abū Bakr ibn Mujāhid: "Where do you find in the Qur'an that a lover does not punish his beloved?" Ibn Mujāhid could not find it, so al-Shiblī said to him, regarding the verse: ﴿Say, "Why then does He punish you for your sins?"﴾.

The intent of this is not to answer them by the occurrence of punishment upon them in actual fact, from the decree of punishment for them in the Hereafter because of their disbelief, since they do not acknowledge that, and it is not suitable for refutation by it, for the refutation would become a *muṣādara* (begging the question). Rather, the intent is to refute them by the occurrence of a punishment that they believe to occur according to the doctrines of their religion, whether it is the punishment of the Hereafter or the punishment of this world. As for the Jews, their books are overflowing with mention of punishment in this world and the Hereafter, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80]. As for the Christians, I have not found in the Gospels any mention of the punishment of the Hereafter, except that in their doctrines they hold that all the children of Adam deserved the punishment of the Hereafter because of the sin of their father Adam. Then Jesus, son of Mary, came as a redeemer and intercessor, and he exposed himself to crucifixion in order to expiate for mankind their inherited sin. This obliges them to acknowledge that punishment would have been written upon all had it not been for the atonement of Jesus. Thus the refutation was achieved against them by their own belief, let alone our belief.

Then the conclusion was drawn from the proof by His saying: ﴿Rather, you are mortals of those whom He has created﴾, meaning: what befalls all of mankind befalls you.

In this there is also an allusion (*taʿrīḍ*) that the Messiah is a mortal, because what befalls mankind of accidents and fear befell him, and they claimed that crucifixion and killing befell him.

The clause ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ is like a precautionary insertion (*iḥtirās*). Since He had based the punishment befalling them on their being mortals, He removed the Christians' assumption that mortality necessitates deserving punishment through inheriting the consequence of Adam's sin. So He said: ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾, meaning from among mankind, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾.

[Page 158]

God repeated His admonition and His call to them after He had made clear to them the corruption of their beliefs and the delusion of their souls, with a clarity that leaves no one who is fair-minded holding on to those misguidances. He had admonished and called them in the same way just before, following the mention of their breaking of the covenants. So the placement of this verse repeats the placement of His words: ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15] and what follows, except that here He mentions the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by describing his coming "after an interval of messengers." This is to remind them that their own books explicitly foretell the coming of a messenger after their messengers, and to show them that his coming was no novelty among the messengers, since messengers had been coming after intervals among them. There, the Messenger was mentioned by describing his making clear what they concealed of the Scripture. Here, what precedes the admonition has already indicated the equality of the messengers in being human and the equality of the nations in their need for a message. What preceded the admonition there was only an announcement of the secrets of their books and of what they hide from people because of its disgrace to them and the bad reputation it brings them. The object of "yubayyinu" (he makes clear) is omitted because it is evident that what is meant is the making clear of the Law. Thus the speech is an address to the People of the Scripture, which serves as an emphasis of the sentence ﴿O People of the Scripture, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 15]; for this reason it is separated (from what precedes).

His words ﴿after an interval of messengers﴾ are a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿makes clear to you﴾, so it is a fixed adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr). It may also be a free adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) connected to "jaakum" (has come to you). It may also be connected to the verb "yubayyinu" (makes clear), because the making clear had ceased during the period of the interval.

"'Ala" (upon) here denotes figurative elevation in the sense of "after" (ba'da), because the one who is elevated settles after the thing above which he is elevated has settled; so his settling after it is likened to his being elevated over it, and the particle that indicates elevation is borrowed for it.

Al-fatrah (the interval) is the cessation of a certain activity.

The particle "min" in His words ﴿of the messengers﴾ indicates the starting point, meaning an interval of time whose beginning is the period of the existence of the messengers, that is, the days of the sending of the messengers.

The word "al-majy'" (coming) is used figuratively for the Messenger's being commanded to convey the religion. Just as the Messenger was called a messenger (rasul), his conveying was called a coming, by analogy with the coming of one who is sent from one person to another.

By "the messengers" is meant the messengers of the People of the Scripture who succeeded one another from the time of Moses to the Messiah, or the Messiah alone is intended. The interval between the mission (of Moses) and the raising up of the Messiah was about five hundred and eighty years. As for people other than the People of the Scripture, messengers came to them as well, such as Khalid ibn Sinan and Handhalah ibn Safwan.

His words ﴿lest you say﴾ are a causal clause (ta'lil) for His words ﴿there has come to you﴾, to explain some of the wisdoms behind the sending of the Messenger. These wisdoms are cutting off the excuses of the People of the Scripture when they are called to account in the Hereafter, or rebuking them in this world for what they changed of their laws, so that one of their excuses would not be that they had become accustomed to the succession of messengers to guide them and renew the religion. So they might plead that after a period had passed without the sending of a messenger, no blame could be directed at them for neglecting their law, and that had a messenger come to them, they would have been guided. The meaning, then, is: "lest you say, 'No messenger came to us during the interval after Moses or after Jesus.'" It is not intended that they should say, "No messenger came to us at all," for they do not claim that, and how could they, since Moses and Jesus came to them? Thus His words ﴿lest you say, "There came not to us any bringer of good tidings or warner"﴾ are a causal clause for the coming of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to them, and it is connected to the verb in ﴿there came not to us﴾. It was necessary to supply the lam of causation before (an), and this supplying is what the meaning requires. Such supplying of a dropped preposition before (an) is common, as an obligatory omission, and the context determines the omitted particle; so the omitted particle here is the lam.

The meaning of the verse may be problematic, since the reason for sending the Messenger to them is the negation of their saying ﴿There came not to us any bringer of good tidings or warner﴾, not the affirmation of it, as is clear. So why did He not say, "lest you not say, 'There came not to us any bringer of good tidings or warner'"? There are parallels to this verse in the Qur'an, and in the poetry of the Arabs, such as the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We hastened the hospitality, lest you insult us"

He meant: "lest you insult us." The grammarians differed about what must be supplied for the meaning to be complete in these verses and others. The Basrians held that a noun suitable to be an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) should be supplied for the verb "jaakum," and they supplied: "out of dislike that you say." The author of al-Kashshaf and most of the commentators who followed him from among the majority of exegetes adopted this view. The Kufans held that a negating particle is omitted after (an), and the supplied form is: "lest you not say." Some commentators such as al-Baghawi adopted this, and it would then be an instance of concise omission relying on the evidence of the context and situation. Ibn Hisham, in Mughni al-Labib, claimed that this is a forced interpretation, and he mentioned that some grammarians held that one of the meanings of (an) is to be in the sense of (li-alla, lest).

[Page 160]

In my view, what drove the grammarians and the commentators to this interpretation is their assumption that (an) makes the present tense verb specific to the future, so that the saying of the People of the Scripture, "There came not to us any bringer of good tidings or warner," is not realized at the time of the revelation of the verse, and its occurrence is presumed to be in the future. It appears that the function of (an) in making the present tense refer to the future is a mostly common usage and not an invariable rule. Abu Hayyan adopted this view and mentioned that Abu Bakr al-Baqillani also held it. Indeed, (an) may simply indicate the verbal-noun function, as in the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], and the words of Imru' al-Qays:

"If you see me unable to close my eyes for an hour of the night, except that I bow down and doze off"

He does not mean that he will doze off in the future. The turning of (an) away from indicating the future depends on contextual indicators, so the meaning here is that the People of the Scripture had given this excuse to those who blamed them, such as the followers of the hanifiyyah, like Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt and Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, or that the Jews said it to the Christians of the Arabs.

His words ﴿so there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾: the fa' here is the explanatory fa (fa al-fasihah). Its excellence in placement has become clear through what it establishes about the meaning of causation, that is: "If you say that, then your saying has been refuted, since there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner." A parallel to this is the words of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

"They said: Khurasan is the farthest that is aimed at for us, then the return. So we have come to Khurasan."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah al-Māʾidah, verses 20–22**

[Quranic text]

﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else in the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will turn back as losers."﴾ ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants, and we will never enter it until they leave it. And if they leave it, then we will enter."﴾

[p. 161]

This is the story following on from the narratives and admonitions. The discussion of similar instances of "And when [he] said" has already been given in several places, among them the saying of Allah, ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾ (al-Baqarah: 30), in al-Baqarah.

The connection of the position of these verses here is that the story contains a reminder of Allah's blessings upon them and an exhortation to fulfil what they had pledged to Allah of obedience, as a preparation for seeking their compliance.

Mūsā (peace be upon him) placed his command to the Children of Israel to fight the Canaanites after reminding them of Allah's blessing upon them, so as to prepare their souls to accept this great matter that was imposed on them, and to give them confidence in victory if they fought their enemies. He mentioned Allah's blessing upon them and enumerated three great blessings. The first: that among them were prophets. The meaning of Allah placing prophets among them may be that in the lineage of their forefathers in the past there were such figures as Yūsuf, the Patriarchs (al-Asbāṭ), Mūsā and Hārūn. It may also mean that He placed prophets among those addressed. In that case, he may have meant himself, after the death of his brother Hārūn, because this story took place after Hārūn's death. Thus his saying "prophets" (anbiyāʾ) would be a plural used to denote the category (jins), so that the singular and the plural are equal. For when the category is intended by the plural, the sense of plurality is cancelled out, and this category was restricted to a single individual at that time. This is like the saying of Allah, ﴿by which the prophets who submitted judge for those who were Jews﴾ (al-Māʾidah: 44), which means Muḥammad (ﷺ). Or he may have meant the prophets who appeared in the time of Mūsā. Maryam, the sister of Mūsā, was a prophetess, as is clearly stated in the Torah (Exodus, ch. 15). Likewise, Eldad and Medad were two prophets in the time of Mūsā, as in the Torah (Numbers, ch. 11). The place of the blessing in the establishment of prophets among them is that this ensures for them guidance and conformity to the will of Allah concerning them, and it also brings them good renown among the nations and in the record of the generations.

The second: that He made them kings. This is an eloquent metaphor (tashbīh balīgh), meaning as kings in their control over themselves and their freedom from the servitude that they had suffered at the hands of the Copts. He also made them masters over the peoples through whom they passed: the Amorites, the Anakites, the Heshbonites, the Rephaim, the Amalekites and the Canaanites. Or the verb "He made you" (jaʿalakum) may be used in the sense of the future, like the saying of Allah, ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ (al-Naḥl: 1), intended to affirm the report, so that the report is a good tiding to them of what will be theirs.

[p. 162]

The third blessing: that He gave them what He had not given anyone else in the worlds. The referent of "what" (mā) may be one particular thing that Allah singled out for the Children of Israel, or it may be a collection of things. He gave them the sound Sharīʿah, wide in guidance and protected, supported them with victory on their path, provided their sustenance of manna and quails for forty years, and took charge of the training of their souls through His messengers.

His saying, ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land﴾, is the purpose of the address. It is like the aim after the introduction. For this reason, he repeated the wording with which he began his speech, which is the call "O my people", to increase the attentiveness of their minds.

The command to enter is a command to strive for its causes, that is, prepare yourselves to enter. "The Holy Land" means the purified, blessed land, that is, the land in which Allah placed blessing, or because it was sanctified by the burial of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) in the first village of its villages, which is Ḥabrūn (Hebron). Here it refers to the land of Canaan from the desert of Sin up to the entrance of Ḥamāh and up to Ḥabrūn. This land is the land of Palestine, lying between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River and the Dead Sea, extending to Ḥamāh in the north and to Gaza and Ḥabrūn in the south. Describing it as ﴿which Allah has prescribed﴾ is an incitement to advance to enter it.

The meaning of "Allah prescribed" (kataba Allāh) is that He decreed and ordained. There is no writing here, but it is a common figurative expression in the language, because when the one bound by a matter affirms it, he "writes" it. As al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah said:

*"Can desires undo what is written in the scrolls?"*

So "writing" was used for what cannot be annulled. This is because Allah promised Ibrāhīm that He would give it to his offspring, and Allah's promise is not broken.

His saying, ﴿and do not turn back on your heels﴾, is a warning against what causes defeat, because the army turning back on its heels is among the greatest causes of abandonment and failure. The verb "irtidād" is a reflexive form derived from "radd" (to return), as one says: "He turned him back, so he turned back." "Radd" means causing a traveller to cease advancing on his journey and returning him to the place from which he set out. "Adbār" is the plural of "dubur", which means the back. "Irtidād" means returning, and returning "on the backs" means towards the backs, that is, backward, because they would be going to the place that a walker walks on, which is behind him. They say: "He retreated on his heels," "they rode on their backs," and "they turned back on their backs and on their heels." So it is governed by "ʿalā" (on), which indicates elevation, that is, the elevation of the road of travel. The backs, in whose direction travel takes place, were treated as the road along which one journeys.

"Inqilāb" means returning. Its original sense is returning to one's dwelling, as Allah says, ﴿So they returned with a blessing from Allah and grace﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 174). Here it means simply the outcome or destination.

The pronouns in "fīhā" and "minhā" refer to the Holy Land.

By "the people" (al-qawm) who were tyrants in the land, they meant its inhabitants: the Canaanites, the Amalekites, the Hittites, the Jebusites and the Amorites.

"Jabbār" means strong. It is derived from "jabr" (compulsion), because the strong one compels people to do what he wants.

The spies of Mūsā, the twelve whom he sent to explore the land, had informed the people of the richness of the land and the strength of its inhabitants. This is a metonymy (kināyah) for their fear of the nations who dwelt in the Holy Land. So they refrained from storming the town out of fear of its people, and they strongly affirmed their refusal to enter the enemy's land, using the force of "inna" (indeed) and "lan" (never) in ﴿Indeed we will never enter it﴾ (al-Māʾidah: 24), confirming their fear.

His saying, ﴿but if they leave it, then we will enter﴾, is an explicit statement of the implied meaning (mafhūm al-ghāyah) of his saying, ﴿and we will never enter it until they leave it﴾, aiming to affirm the promise of entering it once it is cleared of the tyrants who are in it.

This verse alludes to what is in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters of the Book of Numbers: that Allah commanded Mūsā to send twelve men as spies to search the land of Canaan, which Allah had promised to the Children of Israel, one man from each tribe. Mūsā appointed twelve men, among them Joshua son of Nun from the tribe of Ephraim, and among them Caleb son of Jephunneh from the tribe of Judah, and the rest of the spies were not named. They explored through the land from the desert of Sin to Ḥamāh and found the land full of fruits, vines, milk and honey, and they found its inhabitants powerful, of great stature, and their cities fortified. When the Children of Israel heard this, they were dismayed, wept, and complained against Mūsā, saying, "If only we had died in the land of Egypt, it would have been better for us than that our women and children be taken as spoil." Joshua and Caleb said to the people, "If Allah is pleased with us, He will bring us into this land. But do not disobey the Lord, and do not fear its people, for Allah is with us." But the people refused to enter the land, and Allah became angry with them. He said to Mūsā, "No one from twenty years old and upward shall enter this land, except Joshua and Caleb. All of you will be buried in this wilderness, and your children will be shepherds in it for forty years."

[End of passage]

But the people refused to enter the land, and Allah became angry with them. He said to Mūsā, "No one from twenty years old and upward shall enter this land, except Joshua and Caleb. [End of passage]

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah al-Māʾidah, verses 20–22**

[Quranic text]

﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else in the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will turn back as losers."﴾ ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed there are in it a people of tyrants, and we will never enter it until they leave it. And if they leave it, then we will enter."﴾

[p. 161]

This is the story following on from the narratives and admonitions. The discussion of similar instances of "And when [he] said" has already been given in several places, among them the saying of Allah, ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels﴾ (al-Baqarah: 30), in al-Baqarah.

The connection of the position of these verses here is that the story contains a reminder of Allah's blessings upon them and an exhortation to fulfil what they had pledged to Allah of obedience, as a preparation for seeking their compliance.

Mūsā (peace be upon him) placed his command to the Children of Israel to fight the Canaanites after reminding them of Allah's blessing upon them, so as to prepare their souls to accept this great matter that was imposed on them, and to give them confidence in victory if they fought their enemies. He mentioned Allah's blessing upon them and enumerated three great blessings. The first: that among them were prophets. The meaning of Allah placing prophets among them may be that in the lineage of their forefathers in the past there were such figures as Yūsuf, the Patriarchs (al-Asbāṭ), Mūsā and Hārūn. It may also mean that He placed prophets among those addressed. In that case, he may have meant himself, after the death of his brother Hārūn, because this story took place after Hārūn's death. Thus his saying "prophets" (anbiyāʾ) would be a plural used to denote the category (jins), so that the singular and the plural are equal. For when the category is intended by the plural, the sense of plurality is cancelled out, and this category was restricted to a single individual at that time. This is like the saying of Allah, ﴿by which the prophets who submitted judge for those who were Jews﴾ (al-Māʾidah: 44), which means Muḥammad (ﷺ). Or he may have meant the prophets who appeared in the time of Mūsā. Maryam, the sister of Mūsā, was a prophetess, as is clearly stated in the Torah (Exodus, ch. 15). Likewise, Eldad and Medad were two prophets in the time of Mūsā, as in the Torah (Numbers, ch. 11). The place of the blessing in the establishment of prophets among them is that this ensures for them guidance and conformity to the will of Allah concerning them, and it also brings them good renown among the nations and in the record of the generations.
