[End of passage]

[p. 165]

These four clauses are arranged in the manner of dialogue (*muhawara*), as we explained earlier in Surat al-Baqara. The two men were Yusha' and Kalib. The two men are described as "of those who fear" (*min alladhina yakhafun*). The word "fear" in His saying "yakhafun" may mean fear of the enemy. In that case the relative pronoun refers to the Children of Israel. Their identification by means of the relative clause serves as a rebuke to them for the blameworthy trait of fear and lack of courage. The "min" in ﴿of those who fear﴾ is then *ittisaliyya* (indicating affiliation), of the kind found in the expression "you are not from me and I am not from you," meaning that they belong to those who fear. The meaning is not that the two men themselves were characterized by fear, as shown by the fact that they urged their people to fight the enemy. On this reading, His saying ﴿God bestowed His favour upon them both﴾ means that God bestowed upon them courage, and the object of the verb "bestowed" (*an'ama*) is omitted, the context being sufficient to indicate it.

It is also possible that "fear" refers to fear of God, Exalted is He. That is, their saying to their people ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾ arose from their fear of God, Exalted is He. This would be an implicit rebuke that those who disobeyed them do not fear God, Exalted is He. His saying ﴿God bestowed His favour upon them both﴾ would then be an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*) clarifying the source of their fear of God, Exalted is He: that is, fear of God is a favour from Him upon them both. This implies that courage in defending the religion is a favour from God upon its bearer.

The meaning of ﴿God bestowed His favour upon them both﴾ is that He bestowed upon them the removal of fear from their souls and knowledge of the truth.

"Al-bab" (the gate) may refer to the entrance to the Holy Land, that is, the passages through which one travels to the land of Kan'an. It is the frontier and the narrow pass through which one proceeds to the dwelling of the tribe, lying between two rugged mountains, since in the land they were commanded to enter there is no city but rather a territory, as His saying indicates: ﴿Enter the Holy Land﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 21]. So the two men meant: when you cross the frontier and tread the land of the enemies, you will overcome them in battle in their own abodes. The sea frontier is also sometimes called a gate, as in Bab al-Mandab, and people have named a place in the direction of Bukhara "al-Bab." The commentators understood "al-bab" in its well-known common sense, the gate of the city within its wall, and they said: they meant the gate of their city, because conquering the city of the land is considered possession of all that land. It is apparent that this city was Ariha (Jericho) or Qadish, the principal city of the Amalaqa (Amalekites) at that time, and it is the one mentioned in Surat al-Baqara. In this sense, the gate is a great door made of planks, attached to the two sides of a wall or rampart in a manner that allows the plank to block that opening when it is desired to close it, and to be opened when it is desired to open it. Thus closing is called *ghalq* and removing the closure is called *fath* (opening).

After they commanded the people to take the causes and means, they commanded them to rely upon God and to depend on His promise, His help, and the report of His Messenger. For this reason they concluded with the words ﴿if you are believers﴾, because doubt concerning the truthfulness of the Messenger nullifies faith.

[p. 166]

They addressed Musa (Moses) only after the exhortation of the two men to them, returning to their earlier refusal with which they had confronted Musa when they said ﴿Indeed, therein are a people of tyrants﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 22]. Or it may be that, because they paid little attention to the words of the two men, they emphasized the second refusal to enter after the dialogue with the utmost emphasis. Three intensifiers in Arabic indicate its strength: *inna* (indeed), *lan* (never), and the word *abadan* (ever).

As for their saying ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here﴾: if it is addressed to Musa, its meaning is that they asked him for a miracle, as they were accustomed to victory, so they asked that God destroy the tyrants by the supplication of Musa.

It was also said that they intended by these words to belittle Musa. This is far-fetched, because they did not doubt his mission. Had they intended belittling, they would have disbelieved, and in the words of Musa that follow, there is no response to their statement except his description of them as ﴿the defiantly disobedient﴾ (*al-fasiqin*). Fisq (defiant disobedience) is applied to a major sin, since disobeying God's command to fight is a major sin. For this reason He, Exalted is He, said ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾. And on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad came to the Prophet while he was supplicating against the polytheists on the day of Badr, and said: "O Messenger of God, we will not say as the Children of Israel said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting here﴾." The hadith continues.

Do not, however, suppose from this that this verse was being recited among them on the day of Badr, because Surat al-Ma'ida is among the last to be revealed. Rather, al-Miqdad spoke of a report they used to hear from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, when he related to them about the Children of Israel. Then this verse was revealed with that wording.

He said, that is Musa, conversing with his Lord or in the hearing of the people in order to make them aware of their non-compliance with the command of their Lord: ﴿My Lord, I control none except myself and my brother﴾. It may mean: I have power only over myself and my brother. He did not count the two men who had said ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾, because he feared that their people would lead them astray. What is in the books of the Jews is that Harun (Aaron) had died before this event. It is possible that by "his brother" he meant Yusha' ibn Nun, because he was constantly with him in his affairs, and God named him his servant (*fata*) in His saying: ﴿And when Musa said to his servant...﴾ [al-Kahf: 60], and so on. He coupled him here with himself because he was urging the people to enter the town.

[p. 167]

The meaning of ﴿So part between us and the defiantly disobedient people﴾ is: do not hold us accountable for their sin. He feared that a punishment in this world would befall them and destroy everyone, so he sought salvation. It cannot be that he meant a separation between them in the Hereafter, because it is known that God does not hold the innocent accountable for the sin of the guilty, and because the innocence of Musa and his brother from approval of what their people did is a matter known to God. It is possible that by "separating between them" is meant judging between them and making the misguided aware of their error.

God's saying to him ﴿Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years﴾, and so on, is an answer to Musa's words ﴿So part between us and the defiantly disobedient people﴾, and it is an answer that comprehends everything contained in Musa's statement. God informed Musa of the punishment with which He would afflict those who disobeyed His command, thereby calming the apprehension of his fear that a punishment would befall them all, and the punishment of those who disobeyed was realized as a vindication of Musa. If you say: this punishment also affected Musa, since he remained with them in the wilderness until he died, I reply: that was light for Musa, because his staying with them was for guiding them and reforming them, which is the distinguishing feature of his mission, so the hardship in that increased his rank, whereas they were in hardship.

The desert was called *tayha'* and was called *tih*. The Children of Israel remained living in narrow areas, walking slowly on a path without order, until they reached the mountain of Nibu (Nebo) near the river Jordan (al-Urdunn). There Musa, peace be upon him, died, and there he was buried. The location of his grave is unknown, as stated in the text of the Jewish book. They did not enter the Holy Land until they crossed the Jordan under the leadership of Yusha' ibn Nun, the successor of Musa. God, Exalted is He, excepted him and Kalib ibn Yafanna, because they had not said: "We will never enter it." As for the rest of the scouts whom Musa had sent to examine the land, they agreed with their people in refusing to enter it.

This implies that courage in defending the religion is a favour from God upon its bearer.

The meaning of ﴿God bestowed His favour upon them both﴾ is that He bestowed upon them the removal of fear from their souls and knowledge of the truth.

"Al-bab" (the gate) may refer to the entrance to the Holy Land, that is, the passages through which one travels to the land of Kan'an. It is the frontier and the narrow pass through which one proceeds to the dwelling of the tribe, lying between two rugged mountains, since in the land they were commanded to enter there is no city but rather a territory, as His saying indicates: ﴿Enter the Holy Land﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 21]. So the two men meant: when you cross the frontier and tread the land of the enemies, you will overcome them in battle in their own abodes. The sea frontier is also sometimes called a gate, as in Bab al-Mandab, and people have named a place in the direction of Bukhara "al-Bab." The commentators understood "al-bab" in its well-known common sense, the gate of the city within its wall, and they said: they meant the gate of their city, because conquering the city of the land is considered possession of all that land. Then this verse was revealed with that wording.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 27–30:

﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when each offered an offering, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Allah only accepts from the righteous."﴾ ﴿"If you extend your hand against me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So his soul permitted him the murder of his brother, and he killed him, and he became among the losers.﴾

He linked one report to another, so that this would serve as an introduction to the warning against killing a soul, banditry and theft. It is followed by the prohibition of wine, the rules of bequest, and other matters. This also makes the transition smooth from the reports and narratives that were digressed into, which are all occasions of lessons and are all arranged under the consequences of delusion. The relation between this and the story before it is a relation of similarity and a relation of contrast.

As for similarity, both contain disregard for what Allah the Exalted has decreed. The Children of Israel disobeyed the command of their messenger, who told them to enter the Holy Land, and one of the two sons of Adam disobeyed the ruling of Allah the Exalted, that his offering was not accepted, because he was not among the righteous. In both there is audacity toward Allah after disobedience. The Children of Israel said, "Go, you and your Lord," and the son of Adam said, "I will surely kill the one whom Allah accepted from."

As for contrast, in one of them there is a blameworthy boldness on the part of the son of Adam, and in the other a blameworthy reluctance on the part of the Children of Israel. In one there is the agreement of two brothers, Musa and his brother, on obeying the command of Allah the Exalted, while in the other there is the disagreement of two brothers over righteousness and corruption.

The meaning of "the two sons of Adam" here is his two children. As for "son of Adam" in the singular, it may refer to one of mankind, such as: "O son of Adam, indeed, as long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I will forgive you," or in the plural, such as ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment﴾ (Qur'an 7:31).

[Page 169]

The preposition "bi" in His saying "bil-haqq" (in truth) is for accompaniment, related to "utlu" (recite). The meaning of "al-haqq" here is truthfulness, from "haqqa al-shay'" when a thing is established. Truth is what is established, and falsehood has no establishment in reality, as He said: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾ (Qur'an 18:13). It is also possible that "al-haqq" is the opposite of falsehood, meaning seriousness rather than jest. That is, recite this report while accompanied by truth, meaning with a correct purpose, not merely for amusement and idle entertainment. It is also possible that His saying "bil-haqq" refers to what has been surrounded the story of additions that the storytellers among the Children of Israel added concerning the causes of the killing of one brother by the other.

"Idh" is an adverb of time referring to "naba'" (report), meaning their report that occurred at the time they offered an offering. So "idh" is in the accusative as an adverbial of time.

The verb "qarraba" here is derived from "qurban" (offering), which has become like a fixed noun. Its origin is a verbal noun, like "shukran," "ghufran," and "kufran." It is used to name what a person offers to his Lord to draw near to Him, whether charity, a sacrifice, or prayer. So "qarraba" is derived from "qurban," just as "nasaka" is derived from "nusk," "dahha" from "udhiyya," and "ʿaqqa" from "ʿaqiqa." "Qarraba" here does not mean "brought near," since that meaning makes no sense here.

In the Torah they are (Cain) and the Arabs call him Qabil, and his brother (Abel) and the Arabs call him Habil. Qabil was a farmer on the land, and Habil was a shepherd of sheep. Qabil offered an offering from the fruits of his cultivation, and Habil offered an offering from the firstlings of his flock. We do not know whether the offering among them was given to the poor and the like, or whether it was left for people in general. Allah accepted the offering of Habil and did not accept the offering of Qabil. The apparent view is that the acceptance of one offering and not the other occurred through revelation from Allah to Adam. The reason Allah did not accept the offering of Qabil is that he was not a righteous man, but had sins. It was said that he was a disbeliever, but this contradicts his offering an offering.

The word "qurban" is used in the singular in the verse to indicate the genus. Each of them offered an offering, and it was not a shared offering. Allah the Exalted did not name the one from whom it was accepted or the one from whom it was not accepted, since naming them would serve no purpose in the context of the lesson.

What moved him to kill his brother was envy of the other's distinction of acceptance. Envy is the first crime that appeared on earth.

His saying in reply, ﴿Allah only accepts from the righteous﴾, is an admonition, an allusion, and a disavowal of what would require his killing. It means: acceptance is the act of Allah and not the act of anyone else, and He accepts only from the one who is righteous, not from anyone else. He implicitly suggests that the other is not righteous, and that is why Allah did not accept from him. A sign of this is that he intends to kill a soul. Therefore, the one whose offering Allah accepted has committed no offense that would require killing. The statement of the son of Adam implies a restriction of acceptance to the deeds of the righteous. If "al-muttaqin" (the righteous) means its well-known sense in the Shari'a, as expressed by the wording that signifies the meaning the son of Adam intended, then the restriction indicates that the deed of one who is not righteous is not accepted. It is possible that this was their law, and then it was abrogated (naskh, meaning the replacement of a ruling by a later one) in Islam by the acceptance of good deeds from a believer, even if he is not righteous at all times. It is also possible that "al-muttaqin" means those who are sincere in their deeds, so that non-acceptance is a sign of non-sincerity. This involves taking the word "taqwa" out of its common usage. It is also possible that by "acceptance" is meant a particular kind of acceptance, namely complete acceptance, indicated by the burning of the offering, so that it is like His saying, ﴿a guidance for the righteous﴾, meaning complete guidance for them, and His saying, ﴿and the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous﴾ (Qur'an 43:35), meaning the complete Hereafter. It is also possible that He means the acceptance of offerings specifically. It is possible too that "al-muttaqin" refers to the offering itself, meaning those who intend by it the fear of Allah, while his brother intended by his offering mere show.

The meaning of this restriction is that Allah does not accept from those who are not righteous, and that was the law of their time.

His saying, ﴿If you extend your hand against me to kill me﴾ and so on, is an admonition to his brother, to remind him of the gravity of this crime he was about to commit. It implies that he was able to defend himself, but the fear of Allah the Exalted prevented him from doing so. The apparent view is that this was Habil's own judgment regarding the enormity of the crime of killing a soul, even if the killing were in self-defense. The two brothers knew what killing is, from what they knew of slaughtering animals and hunting, so killing was known to them. For this reason Qabil resolved upon it, while Habil saw a sanctity in souls even if they were wrongdoers, and he regarded submitting to the one seeking his killing as a way of preserving souls, so that Allah's purpose of populating the earth might be fulfilled. It is possible that they received from their father the injunction to preserve souls, whether small or great, even at the time of self-defense. For this reason he said, ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾ So his saying, ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah﴾ indicates that defense that leads to killing was prohibited, and that this is an abrogated law, because the laws permit the one who is attacked to defend himself, even by killing the aggressor, but he must not exceed the limit by which defense is achieved. As for the hadith, "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire," that refers to fighting over rule and intending mutual domination, in which the aggressor refrains upon the other's surrender to him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the better of the two parties to surrender to the other and to bear the responsibility, to avoid strife. This is the stance that 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) took, hoping for reconciliation.

The meaning of "uridu" (I want) is: I want, by my restraint from defending myself.

The word "iradah" (wanting) is used for resolve, as in His saying, ﴿He said, "Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ (Qur'an 28:27), and His saying, ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾ (Qur'an 2:185). So the clause is an explanation of the one before it, and for this reason it is separated and introduced with "inna," which indicates explanation, in the sense of the connective "fa."

"Tabu'a" means to return, and this is a figurative return, meaning you acquire that from your act. It is as if he went out seeking for himself, and so he returned with two sins.

﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when each offered an offering, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Allah only accepts from the righteous."﴾ ﴿"If you extend your hand against me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand against you to kill you. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So his soul permitted him the murder of his brother, and he killed him, and he became among the losers.﴾

He linked one report to another, so that this would serve as an introduction to the warning against killing a soul, banditry and theft. It is followed by the prohibition of wine, the rules of bequest, and other matters. This also makes the transition smooth from the reports and narratives that were digressed into, which are all occasions of lessons and are all arranged under the consequences of delusion. The relation between this and the story before it is a relation of similarity and a relation of contrast.

As for similarity, both contain disregard for what Allah the Exalted has decreed. The Children of Israel disobeyed the command of their messenger, who told them to enter the Holy Land, and one of the two sons of Adam disobeyed the ruling of Allah the Exalted, that his offering was not accepted, because he was not among the righteous. In both there is audacity toward Allah after disobedience. The Children of Israel said, "Go, you and your Lord," and the son of Adam said, "I will surely kill the one whom Allah accepted from."

As for contrast, in one of them there is a blameworthy boldness on the part of the son of Adam, and in the other a blameworthy reluctance on the part of the Children of Israel. In one there is the agreement of two brothers, Musa and his brother, on obeying the command of Allah the Exalted, while in the other there is the disagreement of two brothers over righteousness and corruption.

The meaning of "the two sons of Adam" here is his two children. As for "son of Adam" in the singular, it may refer to one of mankind, such as: "O son of Adam, indeed, as long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I will forgive you," or in the plural, such as ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment﴾ (Qur'an 7:31).

Truth is what is established, and falsehood has no establishment in reality, as He said: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾ (Qur'an 18:13). It is also possible that "al-haqq" is the opposite of falsehood, meaning seriousness rather than jest. That is, recite this report while accompanied by truth, meaning with a correct purpose, not merely for amusement and idle entertainment. It is also possible that His saying "bil-haqq" refers to what has been surrounded the story of additions that the storytellers among the Children of Israel added concerning the causes of the killing of one brother by the other.

"Idh" is an adverb of time referring to "naba'" (report), meaning their report that occurred at the time they offered an offering. So "idh" is in the accusative as an adverbial of time.

It is used to name what a person offers to his Lord to draw near to Him, whether charity, a sacrifice, or prayer. The loss here refers to the agitation, bad condition, and disappointment of hope that appear on the perpetrator, so this indicates that the killing took place in the morning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 27–30:

﴿And recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when each offered an offering, and it was accepted from one of them but not accepted from the other. He said, "I will surely kill you." He said, "Allah only accepts from the righteous."﴾ ﴿"If you extend your hand against me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand against you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, and thus be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So his soul permitted him the murder of his brother, and he killed him, and he became among the losers.﴾

He linked one report to another, so that this would serve as an introduction to the warning against killing a soul, banditry and theft. It is followed by the prohibition of wine, the rules of bequest, and other matters. This also makes the transition smooth from the reports and narratives that were digressed into, which are all occasions of lessons and are all arranged under the consequences of delusion. The relation between this and the story before it is a relation of similarity and a relation of contrast.

As for similarity, both contain disregard for what Allah the Exalted has decreed. The Children of Israel disobeyed the command of their messenger, who told them to enter the Holy Land, and one of the two sons of Adam disobeyed the ruling of Allah the Exalted, that his offering was not accepted, because he was not among the righteous. In both there is audacity toward Allah after disobedience. The Children of Israel said, "Go, you and your Lord," and the son of Adam said, "I will surely kill the one whom Allah accepted from."

As for contrast, in one of them there is a blameworthy boldness on the part of the son of Adam, and in the other a blameworthy reluctance on the part of the Children of Israel. In one there is the agreement of two brothers, Musa and his brother, on obeying the command of Allah the Exalted, while in the other there is the disagreement of two brothers over righteousness and corruption.

The meaning of "the two sons of Adam" here is his two children. As for "son of Adam" in the singular, it may refer to one of mankind, such as: "O son of Adam, indeed, as long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I will forgive you," or in the plural, such as ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment﴾ (Qur'an 7:31).

[Page 169]

The preposition "bi" in His saying "bil-haqq" (in truth) is for accompaniment, related to "utlu" (recite). The meaning of "al-haqq" here is truthfulness, from "haqqa al-shay'" when a thing is established. Truth is what is established, and falsehood has no establishment in reality, as He said: ﴿We relate to you their story in truth﴾ (Qur'an 18:13). It is also possible that "al-haqq" is the opposite of falsehood, meaning seriousness rather than jest. That is, recite this report while accompanied by truth, meaning with a correct purpose, not merely for amusement and idle entertainment. It is also possible that His saying "bil-haqq" refers to what has been surrounded the story of additions that the storytellers among the Children of Israel added concerning the causes of the killing of one brother by the other.

"Idh" is an adverb of time referring to "naba'" (report), meaning their report that occurred at the time they offered an offering. So "idh" is in the accusative as an adverbial of time.

The verb "qarraba" here is derived from "qurban" (offering), which has become like a fixed noun. Its origin is a verbal noun, like "shukran," "ghufran," and "kufran." It is used to name what a person offers to his Lord to draw near to Him, whether charity, a sacrifice, or prayer. So "qarraba" is derived from "qurban," just as "nasaka" is derived from "nusk," "dahha" from "udhiyya," and "ʿaqqa" from "ʿaqiqa." "Qarraba" here does not mean "brought near," since that meaning makes no sense here.

In the Torah they are (Cain) and the Arabs call him Qabil, and his brother (Abel) and the Arabs call him Habil. Qabil was a farmer on the land, and Habil was a shepherd of sheep. Qabil offered an offering from the fruits of his cultivation, and Habil offered an offering from the firstlings of his flock. We do not know whether the offering among them was given to the poor and the like, or whether it was left for people in general. Allah accepted the offering of Habil and did not accept the offering of Qabil. The apparent view is that the acceptance of one offering and not the other occurred through revelation from Allah to Adam. The reason Allah did not accept the offering of Qabil is that he was not a righteous man, but had sins. It was said that he was a disbeliever, but this contradicts his offering an offering.

The word "qurban" is used in the singular in the verse to indicate the genus. Each of them offered an offering, and it was not a shared offering. Allah the Exalted did not name the one from whom it was accepted or the one from whom it was not accepted, since naming them would serve no purpose in the context of the lesson.

What moved him to kill his brother was envy of the other's distinction of acceptance. Envy is the first crime that appeared on earth.

His saying in reply, ﴿Allah only accepts from the righteous﴾, is an admonition, an allusion, and a disavowal of what would require his killing. It means: acceptance is the act of Allah and not the act of anyone else, and He accepts only from the one who is righteous, not from anyone else. He implicitly suggests that the other is not righteous, and that is why Allah did not accept from him. A sign of this is that he intends to kill a soul. Therefore, the one whose offering Allah accepted has committed no offense that would require killing. The statement of the son of Adam implies a restriction of acceptance to the deeds of the righteous. If "al-muttaqin" (the righteous) means its well-known sense in the Shari'a, as expressed by the wording that signifies the meaning the son of Adam intended, then the restriction indicates that the deed of one who is not righteous is not accepted. It is possible that this was their law, and then it was abrogated (naskh, meaning the replacement of a ruling by a later one) in Islam by the acceptance of good deeds from a believer, even if he is not righteous at all times. It is also possible that "al-muttaqin" means those who are sincere in their deeds, so that non-acceptance is a sign of non-sincerity. This involves taking the word "taqwa" out of its common usage. It is also possible that by "acceptance" is meant a particular kind of acceptance, namely complete acceptance, indicated by the burning of the offering, so that it is like His saying, ﴿a guidance for the righteous﴾, meaning complete guidance for them, and His saying, ﴿and the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous﴾ (Qur'an 43:35), meaning the complete Hereafter. It is also possible that He means the acceptance of offerings specifically. It is possible too that "al-muttaqin" refers to the offering itself, meaning those who intend by it the fear of Allah, while his brother intended by his offering mere show.

The meaning of this restriction is that Allah does not accept from those who are not righteous, and that was the law of their time.

His saying, ﴿If you extend your hand against me to kill me﴾ and so on, is an admonition to his brother, to remind him of the gravity of this crime he was about to commit. It implies that he was able to defend himself, but the fear of Allah the Exalted prevented him from doing so. The apparent view is that this was Habil's own judgment regarding the enormity of the crime of killing a soul, even if the killing were in self-defense. The two brothers knew what killing is, from what they knew of slaughtering animals and hunting, so killing was known to them. For this reason Qabil resolved upon it, while Habil saw a sanctity in souls even if they were wrongdoers, and he regarded submitting to the one seeking his killing as a way of preserving souls, so that Allah's purpose of populating the earth might be fulfilled. It is possible that they received from their father the injunction to preserve souls, whether small or great, even at the time of self-defense. For this reason he said, ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾ So his saying, ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah﴾ indicates that defense that leads to killing was prohibited, and that this is an abrogated law, because the laws permit the one who is attacked to defend himself, even by killing the aggressor, but he must not exceed the limit by which defense is achieved. As for the hadith, "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire," that refers to fighting over rule and intending mutual domination, in which the aggressor refrains upon the other's surrender to him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the better of the two parties to surrender to the other and to bear the responsibility, to avoid strife. This is the stance that 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) took, hoping for reconciliation.

The meaning of "uridu" (I want) is: I want, by my restraint from defending myself.

The word "iradah" (wanting) is used for resolve, as in His saying, ﴿He said, "Indeed, I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ (Qur'an 28:27), and His saying, ﴿Allah intends for you ease﴾ (Qur'an 2:185). So the clause is an explanation of the one before it, and for this reason it is separated and introduced with "inna," which indicates explanation, in the sense of the connective "fa."

"Tabu'a" means to return, and this is a figurative return, meaning you acquire that from your act. It is as if he went out seeking for himself, and so he returned with two sins.

The more apparent meaning of His saying "bi-ithmi" (with my sin) is the sins that preceded in his life. That is, I hope that my sins are forgiven and that they are placed upon you. In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection, the wrongdoer and the wronged are brought, and good deeds are taken from the wrongdoer and added to the good deeds of the wronged until he is compensated. If he has no good deeds, then some of the wronged person's evil deeds are taken and cast upon him." Related by Muslim. If he said this on knowledge from revelation, then it was like what was legislated in Islam. If he said it by his own reasoning, then he was correct in his judgment and inspiration, and he spoke like one who has the character of prophecy.

The object of "an tabu'a" is the object of "uridu." That is, I want, by refraining from killing you, if you proceed to kill me, that my sin should fall upon you. So "ithm" (sin) is used in a generic sense, meaning whatever sin he might have. By this he intended to admonish his brother, and therefore he joined to it His saying, ﴿and your sin﴾, to remind him of the grievous outcome of his deed, like His saying, ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾ (Qur'an 16:25). So the conjunction of "wa-ithmika" is an idmaj (a grammatical insertion, meaning an incorporation) that mentions what actually results, though it is not what he wants. Likewise His saying, ﴿and you would be among the companions of the Fire﴾ is a reminder to his brother of what may restrain him from transgression.

The meaning of "among the companions of the Fire" is: among those whose punishment in the Fire is prolonged, since the companions of the Fire are those who abide in it.

His saying, ﴿So his soul permitted him the murder of his brother﴾: the "fa" indicates sequence and consequence, and "tawwa'a" indicates that there was a wavering in Qabil's soul and a struggle between the impulse of envy and the impulse of fear. So we understand that the thing that follows from it is omitted. Its estimated meaning is: he hesitated for a long time, or he watched for opportunities, and then his soul made it easy for him. It has been said that he remained for a time waiting for his brother. "Tawwa'a" means he made it obedient, that is, he enabled it to be made obedient. "Taw" and "tawa'iyya" are the opposite of compulsion, and "tatwi'" is the attempt at obedience. He likened the murder of his brother to something refractory to Qabil that does not obey him, because of the opposition of reason and fear. The impulse to kill in Qabil's soul was likened to a person who helps him and makes the refractory killing easy for him. So "tawwa'at" is a metaphorical allegorical image (istiʿara tamthiliyya, an allegorical metaphor), and the meaning produced by this image is that Qabil's soul made the killing of his brother seem fine to him after resistance.

In His saying, ﴿So his soul permitted him the murder of his brother, and he killed him﴾, the style of elaboration (iṭnab, expansion) is used. The style of concision would require omitting ﴿So his soul permitted him the murder of his brother﴾ and limiting it to His saying, "and he killed him." But this was avoided in order to express the horror of the killer's state, by depicting his evil thoughts and the hardness of his heart, since he was contemplating killing one whose nature was compassion and gentleness toward him. Therefore this is not mere elaboration.

[Page 173]

The meaning of ﴿and he became among the losers﴾ is: he became. The loss here may mean the loss of the Hereafter, that is, by that killing he became among those who lost the Hereafter. It is also permissible to keep "asbaha" in its literal sense, that is, he became a loser in this world. The loss here refers to the agitation, bad condition, and disappointment of hope that appear on the perpetrator, so this indicates that the killing took place in the morning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 31:

﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal his brother's corpse. He said, "Woe to me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal my brother's corpse?"﴾

The verb "ba'th" (sending) is used here in the sense of inspiration (ilham) to fly to that place; that is, Allah inspired a crow to alight where Qabil could see it. The choice of the crow for this task was either because burying was a known practice among crows beforehand, or because Allah chose it for this purpose in keeping with what the onlooker feels at the sight of its black colour, namely the sense of unease that the regretful loser feels, a constriction of the soul. Perhaps this is the origin of the Arabs' pessimism about the crow, which is why they said: "ghurab al-bayn" (the crow of separation).

As for the hidden pronoun in "yuriyahu" (to show him): if it refers back to the Name of Majesty (Allah), then the causation indicated by the lam and the attribution of the will are both literal. If it refers back to the crow, then the lam is used in the sense of the fa' of consequence (fa' al-tafri'), and the attribution of the will to the crow is metaphorical, because it is the cause of the sight, so it is as though it were the one who shows. As for "kayfa" (how), it may be unrestricted from interrogation with the meaning of manner, or it may be interrogative; the meaning is: that he might show him the answer to "how he conceals".

"Sau'ah" means that whose sight is hateful, and here it refers to the change in the smell of the slain man and the dismemberment of his body.

The phrase "ya waylata" is one of the formulas of invocation used to express astonishment. Its original form is "ya lawaylati", and the alif was substituted for the lam of invocation, as in the common expression "ya 'ajaba" (how strange!). It is also permissible to treat the alif as a substitute for the ya' of the speaker, which is a dialect, and for the address to be metaphorical, the woe being treated as though it were something addressed, as in His saying: ﴿Alas, my regret over what I neglected concerning Allah﴾ [al-Zumar: 56].

The interrogative in "a'jiztu" (Am I unable) is one of denial.

This great scene is the scene of the first civilisation among mankind, and it belongs to the category of seeking to conceal disagreeable sights. It is also the scene of the first knowledge that mankind acquired through imitation and experience, and the scene of the first manifestation of mankind receiving its knowledge from realms weaker than itself, just as people imitated animals in adornment, so they wore fine coloured hides and crowned themselves with coloured feathers, flowers and precious stones. How much of lesson for history, religion and morality is in this verse!

* * *

﴿So he became among the regretful.﴾

The discussion of it is like the discussion of ﴿So he became among the losers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 30]. The meaning of "min al-nadimin" (among the regretful) is that he became regretful in the strongest regret, because "min al-nadimin" is more indicative of regret taking firm hold of his self than saying "nadiman" (regretful). This was already explained at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and he was among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34] and His saying ﴿so you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35] in Surah al-Baqarah.

Regret (nadam) is the grief of the doer over an action that proceeded from him, which he did not perceive the harm in for himself. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance and then become, over what you have done, regretful﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6]. That is, he regretted what he had committed of killing his brother when he saw the crow busying itself with honouring its dead brother and saw himself daring to kill his brother; his hastening to imitate the crow in burying his brother was nothing but the beginning of regret and love of honour for his brother.

It is possible that this regret did not arise from fear of the punishment of Allah nor from intent to repent, and therefore it did not benefit him. There came in the Sahih: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing." It is possible that this is evidence for those who said that the killer's repentance is not accepted, which is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. This was already discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell, abiding therein﴾ [al-Nisa': 93] in Surah al-Nisa'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 32:

[175] ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain all mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all mankind.﴾ It is necessarily the case that "min ajl dhalik" (because of that) is a causal clause tied to "kataba-na" (We prescribed), and it is the beginning of the sentence, while the end of the preceding sentence is His saying: ﴿among the regretful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31]. The phrase "min ajl dhalik" is not connected to "al-nadimin" (the regretful) as its cause, because the meaning of the fa' in His saying ﴿so he became﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31] makes it unnecessary.

"Min" here denotes the starting point (ibtida'). "Al-ajl" (the cause, the reason for an offence) is originally the verbal noun of ajala, ya'julu and ya'jilu (like nasara and daraba), meaning janā (to commit an offence) and iktasaba (to earn). It was said that it is specific to acquiring a crime, so it is synonymous with jana and jarama, and from it come al-jinayah (crime) and al-jarimah (offence). However, the Arabs extended usage, applying "al-ajl" absolutely to what is acquired, by the relation of generality.

The sense of origin for which "min" is used here is figurative: it likens the cause of a thing to the beginning of its emergence. This is the source of the statement that among the meanings of "min" is causation (ta'lil), since its frequent occurrence before the word "ajl" has given it the meaning of causation, and the frequent omission of the word "ajl" after it has given it the meaning of causation as well, as in the saying of al-A'sha:

"So I swore I would not show pity to her for any weariness, nor for any exhaustion, until I meet Muhammad."

Causation is derived from the content of the sentence. Causation expressed by "min ajl" is stronger than causation by the lam alone, and therefore it is chosen here to indicate that this event was the cause of the aggravation of the matter of killing and the manifestation of its evils.

In the use of the demonstrative "dhalik" (that), which is specific, there is the intention of encompassing everything mentioned.

[176] Al-Jumhur read "min ajl dhalik" with a sukun on the nun of "min" and with the hamza of "ajl" pronounced. The reading of Warsh from Nafi' is with a fatha on the nun and deletion of the hamza of "ajl" according to his method. Abu Ja'far read "min ajli dhalik" with a kasra on the nun of "min" and deletion of the hamza of "ajl" after transferring its vowel to the nun, so that it is not pronounced.

The meaning of "kataba-na" is "we legislated," as in His saying: ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183].

The object of "kataba-na" is the content of the clause ﴿that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain all mankind﴾. The "anna" in His saying "annahu" is with a fatha on the hamza, a sister of "inna" with a kasra on the hamza, and it indicates the verbal (masdariyyah) function. The pronoun in "annahu" is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), meaning: "We prescribed upon them a matter of great importance, namely the equivalence of killing one soul without right with the killing of all people by the killer." The way this meaning is obtained from this structure becomes clear by explaining the position of the particle "anna" with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the nun: this particle occurs in speech only as a governed element after a governing word preceding it that requires it. Hence it is determined that the clause after "anna" is in the position of a single governed noun, and so the clause after "anna" must be interpreted as a verbal noun that is formed (yusbak), i.e., it is taken from the predicate of "anna."

The scholars of Arabic have agreed that "anna" with a fatha on the hamza and a shadda on the nun is a sister of "inna" with a kasra on the hamza, and that it expresses emphasis just as its sister does.

They have also agreed that "anna" with a fatha on the hamza is one of the five literal relative particles after which what follows is formed into a verbal noun. By this, "anna" with a fatha exceeds "inna" with a kasra.

The predicate of "anna" in this verse is the clause ﴿whoever kills a soul without a soul﴾ and so on. And it, together with that, explains the pronoun of the matter.

The object of "kataba-na" is taken from the conditional clause and its response, and its estimated form is: "We prescribed the resemblance of killing a soul without a soul, etc., to the killing of all mankind in the enormity of the crime."

[177] This is the way in which the commentators and grammarians have proceeded. It has occurred in the speech of the Arabs, according to al-Farra', that the essence of it is: when "anna" comes after "qala" (to say) and its derivatives, and it is an explanation of the saying and not a quotation of it, you put it in the accusative (i.e., you open its hamza), as in your saying: "I have said to you a good word, that your father is noble." You open "anna" because it explains "kalaman," which is accusative, i.e., the object of the verb "qultu," so its explainer is likewise accusative as an object, because the explanation takes the case of what is explained. Thus al-Farra' attributes to the particle "anna" the meaning of explanation (tafsir) in addition to the meaning of verbal-noun formation that all grammarians attribute to it. By combining the two opinions, the particle "anna" regularly indicates the meaning of emphasis, and with it indicates the meaning of verbal noun at times and the meaning of explanation at other times, according to the context. Perhaps al-Farra' tends to the view that the particle "anna" with a fatha on the hamza is composed of two particles: the particle "inna" with a kasra on the hamza and a shadda on the nun, and the particle "an" with a fatha on the hamza and a sukun on the nun, which is sometimes verbal and sometimes explanatory. The fatha of its hamza is due to considering its composition from "an" with a fatha on the hamza and sukun on the nun, as verbal or explanatory, and the shadda on its nun is due to considering its composition from "inna" with a kasra on the hamza and shadda on the nun. Its original form is "an inna," and when the two were composed, their letters merged, as some grammarians said: the original of "lan" (never) is "la an" (not that).

This is an explanation that the killing of a soul without right is a monstrous crime, like the monstrousness of killing all people. The purpose is to prepare for the legitimacy of retaliation (qisas) expressed in the following verse: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], and so on.

The purpose of reporting what was prescribed for the Children of Israel is to show the Muslims that the rule of retaliation is an ancient law and a divine intent from of old, for knowing the history of the laws offers insight to those who seek understanding, reassurance to the hearts of the addressees, and removal of doubts that might arise concerning rulings whose wisdoms are hidden, such as the legitimacy of retaliation. It may appear to shallow views to be a cure with the same kind of disease that is being treated, so much so that this suspicion led some nations to abolish the rule of retaliation on the ground that they do not punish a guilty person with another crime. This is a heedlessness whose path is subtle, failing to see that the deterrence from killing is not confined to the certainty of being repaid with death.

[178] For souls are created to love survival and to love satisfying the irascible faculty. When someone, in anger, knows that if he kills his punishment is death, he is restrained; and if he hopes that the punishment will be less than death, he proceeds to satisfy his irascible faculty, then he persuades himself that what is less than retaliation can be endured and avoided. This was common among the Arabs and widespread in their sayings and deeds. Their poet, Qays ibn Zuhayr al-'Absi, said:

"I have healed my soul from Hamal ibn Badr, and my sword has healed me from Hudhayfah."

Therefore God Most High said: ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life, O people of understanding﴾ [al-Baqarah: 179].

The meaning of the comparison in His saying ﴿it is as if he had slain all mankind﴾ is an exhortation to the whole community to pursue the killer of a soul, to seize him wherever he is found, and to refrain from sheltering him or concealing him, each addressee according to his capacity and the extent of his reach in the land, from the rulers down to the common people. The purpose of that comparison is to magnify the crime of killing; it does not mean that he has literally killed all people. Do you not see that he may be pardoned by the particular heirs of the blood, without the rest of the people? Moreover, it contains a noble psychological meaning: the motive that drives the killer to kill is the preference for satisfying the emotional impulse arising from anger and the love of revenge over the considerations of respecting the right, restraining the self, and reflecting on the consequences of the act within the order of the world. Whoever's habit is to prefer that trivial impulse over all these noble meanings is one whose soul is about to constantly lead him to infringe upon rights; whenever the opportunity presents itself, he kills, and if it impelled him to kill all people, he would do so.

You may also take the purpose of the comparison to be the direction of the rule of retaliation and its rightness, and that it is considered for the right of the one killed, such that if he were able, he would accept nothing but the repayment of his killer with a crime like his. Thus no one should marvel at the rule of retaliation, saying: "How do we reform the world with the same thing by which it was corrupted, and how do we cure a disease with another disease?" So He made clear to them that the killer of a soul, in the sight of the victim's guardian, is as if he had slain all people.

Some explanations of the meaning of the comparison have been mentioned which the reasoning does not accept.

The meaning of ﴿and whoever saves it﴾ is whoever rescues it from death, since it is evident that giving life after death is not within human power. That is: whoever takes care to rescue it and to defend it, it is as if he has given life to all people by that direction we have just explained; or whoever overcomes the restraint of law and wisdom over the impulse of anger and desire and refrains from killing in anger.

[179] * * *

﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs; then indeed many of them after that are transgressors in the land.﴾

This is a conclusion (tadhyil) to the ruling of the law of retaliation for the Children of Israel. It is a statement used figuratively (kinayah) for their turning away from the law, and that, despite the severity imposed upon them concerning killing, they continued to kill, as His saying "ba'da dhalik" (after that) indicates, that is, after Our messengers came to them with clear proofs. The complement of "musrifun" (transgressors) is omitted for the purpose of generality. What is meant is that they are transgressors in corruptions, among which is the killing of souls, by the indication of His saying "in the land," since the Qur'an frequently mentions "in the land" together with mention of corruption.

The clause ﴿then indeed many of them﴾ is coordinated (atf) with the clause ﴿And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾. The "thumma" (then) is for delay in rank, because the coming of the messengers with clear proofs is a wondrous matter, and transgression in the land after those clear proofs is more wondrous still. "In the land" is mentioned to portray this transgression to the hearer and to make it appear more abhorrent, as in His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption in the land after its reform﴾ [al-A'raf: 56]. Fronting "fi al-ard" (in the land) is for emphasis, and it indicates an increase in the abhorrence of transgression within it, along with the importance of its matter.

Al-Jumhur read "rusulu-na" with a damma on the sin. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the sin.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 33–34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is that they be killed or crucified or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be exiled from the land. That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ .
Page 180
This is a transition to the legislation of the punishment of those who wage war (muharibun), who are a category of criminals guilty of the crime of killing. This verse and the one after it have no connection to the reports about the Children of Israel. This verse was revealed concerning the ruling of the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the 'Uraniyyin, and this is indicated by the practice of al-Bukhari, for he gave this verse as the chapter heading in the Book of Tafsir, and he cited immediately after it the hadith of Anas ibn Malik concerning the 'Uraniyyin. The text of the hadith from several places in his Sahih is: "A group from 'Ukl and 'Urayna came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embraced Islam, then they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said, 'This land has made us ill.' He said to them, 'These are our camels; go out among them and drink their milk and urine.' So they went out among them and drank from their urine and milk and recovered. Then they turned upon the herdsman, killed him, drove off the camels, and apostatized. So the Messenger of Allah sent after them. He sent Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah with horsemen, and they caught up with them when they had reached their territory. The day had not yet ended when they were brought back. He ordered them punished: their hands and feet were cut off, their eyes were branded with heated nails, and then he imprisoned them until they died." And it was said: "He ordered them to be thrown into al-Harra, where they asked for water and were not given water until they died." A group said: This happened in the sixth year after the Hijra, before the revelation of the verse of al-Ma'ida. Mawla Ibn al-Talla' transmitted that in the book Al-Aqdiya al-Ma'thura with his chain of narration to Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Sirin. Accordingly, its revelation abrogates the penalty which the Prophet (ﷺ) imposed, whether it was by revelation or by his own ijtihad, because when he exercised ijtihad and Allah did not change it for him before the action was carried out
Page 181
it was established as law. Allah permitted him this severe punishment because they intended to be an example for the polytheists in deception by displaying Islam in order to reach a plot against the Muslims, and because they combined in their act many crimes. Abu Qilaba said: "Then who should be spared of these? They killed a soul, waged war against Allah and His Messenger, and terrified the Messenger of Allah." In a narration of al-Tabari: it was revealed concerning a people from the People of the Book who had a covenant with the Muslims, then broke it, cut off the road, and spread corruption in the land. He transmitted this from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak. The correct view is the first. In any case, that ruling was abrogated by this verse.
So the restriction with (innama) in His saying "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war..." etc., according to the more sound of the two reports on the occasion of revelation, is a relative restriction (hasr idafi), a qasr that has been reversed to nullify, i.e., to abrogate the punishment which the Messenger (ﷺ) had ordered for the 'Uraniyyin. And according to what al-Tabari transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, the restriction means that there is no penalty for them except that, so the purpose of the restriction then is that it should not be reduced below that penalty, which is one of the four matters. It may also be that the restriction is to refute a supposed belief, namely the belief of one who considers this penalty too severe and inclines toward lightening it. Likewise, it is so if the verse was not revealed concerning any occasion at all.
Whatever the occasion of revelation, the verse requires the obligation of punishing those who wage war by what Allah mentioned in it, because restriction conveys the emphasis of the attribution. And emphasis may be counted among the indications of the obligation of an act, some of which are enumerated in the principles of jurisprudence, because it makes the ruling definite.
The meaning of "yuharibun" is that they become fighters with weapons, in aggression, for the purpose of plunder, like the case of the one who initiates war, because the reality of war is fighting. The meaning of waging war against Allah is waging war against His law and intending aggression against His rulings. It is known that no one wages war against Allah, so mentioning Him in the context of war serves to make the matter appear heinous, as a war against one for whom Allah is angry when he is fought, namely the Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning of waging war against the Messenger is aggression against his ruling and authority, for the 'Uraniyyin attacked the camels of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which were held for equipping the armies of the Muslims, and he had granted them the benefit of them, yet they did not observe this because of their disbelief. So the punishment the Messenger inflicted on the 'Uraniyyin
Page 182
was a punishment for a specific kind of war, which is pure hatred of Islam. Then Allah legislated a ruling for the war that occurs in the time of the Messenger of Allah and after him, and made its punishment equal, so it became necessary that the interpretation of "they wage war against Allah and His Messenger" be war against the community of Muslims. A penalty was assigned to it identical to the penalty for apostasy, because apostasy has a different penalty; thus we know that the penalty is for the sake of waging war. For this reason the scholars regarded it as the penalty for one of the Muslims who commits this crime, and for this reason Allah did not make it the penalty for the disbelievers who fought the Messenger out of obstinacy toward the religion. On this basis "yuharibun" is followed by "Allah and His Messenger" so that it becomes clear that they did not intend war against any specific people nor war against a group.
And "they strive upon the earth in corruption" is conjoined to explain the purpose of their war against Allah and His Messenger, so the penalty is based on both matters together. The combination of the two matters is a compound cause for the punishment, and each of the two matters is a partial cause which does not by itself require this particular punishment.
The scholars differed over the reality of hirabah. Malik said: it is carrying weapons against people to take their property, without enmity, grudge, or prior dispute between the one who wages war (the muharib) and the one against whom war is waged (the muharab), whether in the desert or in the city. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Thawr also held this. Others said: the muharib in a city is not a muharib; this is the view of Abu Hanifa, Sufyan al-Thawri and Ishaq. What Malik considered was the general meaning of the word hirabah, while what his opponents considered was the predominant usage, because hirabah is rare in cities. A case occurred in Tunis concerning a thief named Wannas, who terrorized the people of Tunis with his tricks in theft and who carried weapons; he was sentenced under the ruling for the muharib during the reign of Amir Muhammad al-Sadiq Bey, and he was hanged at the gate of Suwayqa.
The meaning of "they strive upon the earth in corruption" is that they acquire corruption, reap it and commit it, because sa'y (striving) has been used in the sense of earning and gathering, as He, exalted is He, said: "And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its striving" [al-Isra: 19]. They say: "So-and-so strove for his family," meaning he earned for them. And He, exalted is He, said: "So that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives" [Ta-Ha: 15].
Page 183
The author of al-Kashshaf took it here to mean walking, so he made "fasadan" a circumstantial accusative (hal) or an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). He considered that most of the muharib's activity is striving and moving about, and the verb is thus treated as intransitive, the object of purpose indicating it. He also allowed that sa'a could mean "corrupted," making "fasadan" an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). But the use of sa'a in the sense of "corrupted" is not known.
Corruption (fasad) is the destruction of lives and property, so the muharib kills a man to take the clothing on him and the like.
"Yuqattalu" is an intensive form of "yuqtalu," as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
"In the fragments of a heart that has been slain (muqattal)"
The intensification here is intended to convey inflicting the punishment without leniency or gentleness, as a severity against them; the same applies to His saying "yusallabu."
Crucifixion (salb) is placing the offender who is to be killed tied to a piece of wood, then killing him upon it by stabbing him with a spear at the place of killing. It was also said that crucifixion is after killing. The first is the view of Malik, and the second is the position of Ashhab and al-Shafi'i.
The "min" in His saying "min khilaf" is initial (ibtida'iyya) and in the position of a circumstantial clause relating to "aydihim wa arjulahum," so it is a restriction on the cutting: the cutting begins in a state of alternation. It is known that the limb cut off is the opposing limb, so it is determined that it opposes another cut limb; otherwise opposition could not be conceived. If no limb has previously been cut, then alternation is impossible, so the first limb is cut immediately, and the alternation proceeds afterward. And it is known from His saying "min khilaf" that from the muharib only one hand or one foot is cut off, and not both hands or both feet, because if it were so, the meaning of cutting "from opposite sides" would not be conceivable. This construction is an example of marvelous concision. It is apparent that cutting from opposite sides is facilitation and mercy, because that makes it easier for the rest of the body to move after healing, by supporting oneself with the remaining hand on a staff on the side of the cut foot.
Page 184
Our scholars said: his hand is cut for the sake of taking property, and his foot for the sake of terror, because the hand is the limb by which taking occurs, and the foot is the limb by which terror occurs, that is, walking behind people and waylaying them.
Exile from the land (nafy min al-ard) is banishment from the place which is one's homeland, because nafy means non-existence. The intended meaning is banishment, because it is removal from the people whom he fought. One says: "They exiled so-and-so," meaning they expelled him from among them, and he was rejected. Al-Nabigha said:
"Let it be pleasing to you that you have expelled us from our homes"
meaning you have removed us from your dwellings. No meaning of nafy other than this is known in the speech of the Arabs. Abu Hanifa and some scholars said: nafy is imprisonment. What led them to this distant interpretation was the wish to avoid repelling the harm of the muharib from one people by directing his harm onto another people. This is a consideration that requires interpretation, but the scholars have made clear that exile achieves the removal of harm, because when someone was removed from his homeland among the Arabs, he was humbled and his strength was broken. Imru' al-Qays said:
"The wolf howls over him like a disgraced, impoverished outcast"
This condition is not specific to the Arabs, for a person in his own land and among his own people has a boldness that he does not have outside his land.
Moreover, some scholars said: they are exiled to a distant land isolated in a direction, such that in it they are as though confined. Abu al-Zinad said: exile used to be to Dahlak and to Ba'id, which are two islands in the Yemeni sea.
Page 185
The verse indicates two matters. The first is that the punishment of the muharibun is optional (takhyir), because the basic function of "aw" is to indicate one of two things or several things in occurrence, and in the case of commands and the like this requires optionality, as in His saying: "So a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice" [al-Baqara: 196]. Many scholars have adhered to this apparent meaning, including Malik ibn Anas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, 'Ata', Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, and Abu Hanifa; and what is transmitted from Malik is that this optionality applies to the hirabah itself. If during the period of his waging war he committed a proven crime that requires the most severe penalty, such as killing, he is killed without option, and this is a clear basis. Then it is incumbent upon the imam after that to impose a penalty approximating the gravity of the muharib's offense and the extent of his persistence in corruption. Others said that "aw" in the verse is for division (taqsim) and not for option, and that the things mentioned are grades of penalties according to what the muharib has committed: whoever kills and takes property is killed and crucified; whoever neither kills nor takes property is disciplined (ta'zir); whoever only terrorizes the road is exiled; and whoever only takes property has his hand cut off. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Suddi and al-Shafi'i. Their disagreement is close to agreement.
The second matter is that these penalties are for the sake of hirabah and are not for the sake of the rights of individuals among the people, as is indicated by His saying afterward: "Except for those who repent before you gain power over them" etc. This is clear. Therefore, if the aggrieved parties waive their rights, the penalty of hirabah does not thereby lapse from the muharib.

That is their disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter they will have a great punishment. (Note: this is the translation of the preceding clause; the passage itself begins below.)

Translation of the passage:

And His saying: ﴿That is for them a disgrace in this world﴾, meaning: the punishment is a disgrace for them in this world. Al-khizy (disgrace) is humiliation and degradation. ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Imran: 194]. The verse indicates that these warring criminals have two punishments: a punishment in this world and a punishment in the Hereafter. If what is meant by "those who wage war" in the verse is specifically the warriors from among the people of disbelief, such as the 'Uraniyyun, as has been said, then their deserving of both punishments is clear. But if what is intended includes the warrior from among the people of Islam, the verse would conflict with what is reported in the authentic hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, from the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he took the pledge from the believers, concerning what is contained in the verse ﴿When believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 12], etc., when he said: "Whoever among you fulfils it, his reward is with Allah, and whoever incurs any of that and is punished for it, that is an expiation for him, and whoever incurs any of it and Allah conceals it, it is up to Allah: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him." So his saying, "that is an expiation for him," is evidence that the prescribed penalty (hadd) removes the punishment of the Hereafter. Therefore it is permissible that what is in the verse is an intensification against the warriors beyond the rest of the sins, and it is permissible that the interpretation of what is in this verse is by way of detail, meaning: they have disgrace in this world if they are seized by it, and they have a great punishment in the Hereafter if they are not seized by it in this world.

The exception with His saying ﴿except those who repent﴾ refers to both rulings, the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, by the indication of His saying ﴿before you gain power over them﴾, because the effect of repentance in salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter is not restricted to what comes before gaining power over them. The exception particle has indicated the removal of the penalty from the warrior in this state; thus the speech is complete with it, because the exception is an independent utterance that does not need additional explicit statement that the ruling stated for the excepted subject is negated for the excepted one, in the usage of the Arabs and according to the majority of scholars. So the excepted is not silent about, as the Hanafis say. And had it not been for the exception, the verse would not indicate the removal of the penalty of the warrior mentioned. So if it were said, "If they repent," it would only indicate the acceptance of their repentance in removing the punishment of the Hereafter.

The meaning of ﴿before you gain power over them﴾ is what comes before the warrior is certain of being seized, or the siege is tightened upon him, or he is pursued throughout the lands and pressed. If he comes before all of that, sincerely and regretful, the penalty that Allah prescribed for him falls away from him, because this indicates the transformation of his state from corruption to righteousness, so there remains no wisdom in punishing him. And since the verse does not address compensation for what he destroyed by his warfare, it is known that repentance does not affect the removal of what he had been involved in of the rights of people, of property or blood, because that is known from other evidences.

His saying ﴿Know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reminder after the completion of the speech and a rebuttal to the wonder of one who is amazed at the falling away of the punishment from them. The fa' is ṣafīḥa (indicating an implied condition) for what the exception indicates of the removal of the penalty despite the magnitude of the crime, and the meaning is: if the removal of the penalty from one who repents before being overpowered seems great to you, then know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

His saying "fa-'lamū" (know) indicates treating the addressees as those who do not know that, in view of their magnification of this pardon. You have seen that the nature of the verb (i'lam) is to indicate the importance of the news, as will come in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart﴾ [Al-Anfal: 24] in Surat al-Anfal, and His saying in it ﴿And know that whatever you gain as spoils﴾ [Al-Anfal: 41].
