The second matter is that these penalties are for the sake of hirabah and are not for the sake of the rights of individuals among the people, as is indicated by His saying afterward: "Except for those who repent before you gain power over them" etc. This is clear. Therefore, if the aggrieved parties waive their rights, the penalty of hirabah does not thereby lapse from the muharib.

That is their disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter they will have a great punishment. (Note: this is the translation of the preceding clause; the passage itself begins below.)

Translation of the passage:

And His saying: ﴿That is for them a disgrace in this world﴾, meaning: the punishment is a disgrace for them in this world. Al-khizy (disgrace) is humiliation and degradation. ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Al-Imran: 194]. The verse indicates that these warring criminals have two punishments: a punishment in this world and a punishment in the Hereafter. If what is meant by "those who wage war" in the verse is specifically the warriors from among the people of disbelief, such as the 'Uraniyyun, as has been said, then their deserving of both punishments is clear. But if what is intended includes the warrior from among the people of Islam, the verse would conflict with what is reported in the authentic hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, from the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he took the pledge from the believers, concerning what is contained in the verse ﴿When believing women come to you pledging allegiance to you﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 12], etc., when he said: "Whoever among you fulfils it, his reward is with Allah, and whoever incurs any of that and is punished for it, that is an expiation for him, and whoever incurs any of it and Allah conceals it, it is up to Allah: if He wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him." So his saying, "that is an expiation for him," is evidence that the prescribed penalty (hadd) removes the punishment of the Hereafter. Therefore it is permissible that what is in the verse is an intensification against the warriors beyond the rest of the sins, and it is permissible that the interpretation of what is in this verse is by way of detail, meaning: they have disgrace in this world if they are seized by it, and they have a great punishment in the Hereafter if they are not seized by it in this world.

The exception with His saying ﴿except those who repent﴾ refers to both rulings, the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, by the indication of His saying ﴿before you gain power over them﴾, because the effect of repentance in salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter is not restricted to what comes before gaining power over them. The exception particle has indicated the removal of the penalty from the warrior in this state; thus the speech is complete with it, because the exception is an independent utterance that does not need additional explicit statement that the ruling stated for the excepted subject is negated for the excepted one, in the usage of the Arabs and according to the majority of scholars. So the excepted is not silent about, as the Hanafis say. And had it not been for the exception, the verse would not indicate the removal of the penalty of the warrior mentioned. So if it were said, "If they repent," it would only indicate the acceptance of their repentance in removing the punishment of the Hereafter.

The meaning of ﴿before you gain power over them﴾ is what comes before the warrior is certain of being seized, or the siege is tightened upon him, or he is pursued throughout the lands and pressed. If he comes before all of that, sincerely and regretful, the penalty that Allah prescribed for him falls away from him, because this indicates the transformation of his state from corruption to righteousness, so there remains no wisdom in punishing him. And since the verse does not address compensation for what he destroyed by his warfare, it is known that repentance does not affect the removal of what he had been involved in of the rights of people, of property or blood, because that is known from other evidences.

His saying ﴿Know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a reminder after the completion of the speech and a rebuttal to the wonder of one who is amazed at the falling away of the punishment from them. The fa' is ṣafīḥa (indicating an implied condition) for what the exception indicates of the removal of the penalty despite the magnitude of the crime, and the meaning is: if the removal of the penalty from one who repents before being overpowered seems great to you, then know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

His saying "fa-'lamū" (know) indicates treating the addressees as those who do not know that, in view of their magnification of this pardon. You have seen that the nature of the verb (i'lam) is to indicate the importance of the news, as will come in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart﴾ [Al-Anfal: 24] in Surat al-Anfal, and His saying in it ﴿And know that whatever you gain as spoils﴾ [Al-Anfal: 41].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 35:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him and strive in His cause; perhaps you will succeed.﴾

This is an interjection between the verses on the threat against those who wage war and the rulings on their recompense, and what follows it, His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—if they had all that is on earth entirely...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 36], the verse. He addressed the believers with encouragement after warning them against corruption, following the Qur'an's custom of interweaving its purposes with exhortation, encouragement and warning. This is a method of oratory (khitabah) for capturing souls, as al-Hariri said: "So when they buried the dead and the words 'would that' had passed, a shaykh came from Rabawa, tucking his cudgel under his arm, and said: 'For the like of this let the workers work.'" etc. Thus the ruling on the warriors from among the people of disbelief was followed by commanding the believers to piety and to seeking what brings them to the pleasure of Allah. And it set against blameworthy fighting a fighting whose doer is praised in this world and the next.

Al-wasilah (the means, a term meaning what brings one close) is like al-wasilah (waṣīlah). The verb wasala is close in meaning to the verb waṣala (to connect, to reach). So al-wasilah is nearness (al-qurbah), and it is of the form fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ulah, meaning "that by which one seeks connection," i.e., follow the means of drawing near to Him, that is, by obedience.

"Ilayhi" (to Him) is connected to al-wasilah, meaning "the means to Allah, exalted is He." So al-wasilah is intended to mean that by which one reaches Allah. The Muslims know that reaching Allah is not reaching by distance, but reaching by nearness (zulfa) and good pleasure (ridan). Thus the definite article in "al-wasilah" is the definite article of the genus, meaning: everything you know brings you near to Allah, that is, causes you to attain His good pleasure and the acceptance of your deeds in His presence. So al-wasilah is that which brings the servant near to Allah by acting upon His commands and prohibitions. In the hadith qudsi: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him," etc.

The prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿and seek the means to Him﴾ is connected to "seek" (ibtaghu). It may also be connected to al-wasilah, and it was placed before its complement for restriction (al-hasr), meaning: do not seek means except to Him, not to other than Him. This would be an allusion against the polytheists, because the Muslims are not suspected of anything that would require this restriction.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 36–37:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—if they had whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them. And for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿They will wish to exit from the Fire, but they will not be able to exit from it, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾

The more apparent view is that this sentence is connected to the sentence ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33] by way of explanation (ittisal al-bayan). It explains the preceding sentence, magnifying the punishment with which Allah threatened them in His saying: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33]. For those combatants concerning whose recompense that verse was revealed had disbelieved after their Islam and waged war against Allah and His Messenger. So when their recompense was mentioned, it was followed by mention of a recompense that encompasses them and encompasses their likes among those who disbelieve. This does not conflict with the fact that the preceding verse is intended to include the Muslim combatants.

The condition in His saying ﴿if they had whatever is on the earth﴾ is implied by a verb indicated by (anna), since the implied meaning is: "if whatever is on the earth were established as their possession." For (law), by virtue of its specialization with the verb, it is correct to dispense with mentioning the verb after it when (anna) follows it. His saying ﴿and the like of it with it﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "whatever is on the earth," and there is no need to make it a direct object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), since it is dispensed with by His saying "ma'ahu" (with it). The lam in ﴿to ransom themselves thereby﴾ indicates the purpose of the implied verb, i.e., "if whatever is on the earth were established for them for the sake of ransoming themselves with it, not for the sake of hoarding it or giving it away."

The pronoun in His saying "bihi" (thereby) is singular, although the things mentioned are two: "whatever is on the earth" and "the like of it." This is either on the basis that the pronoun refers only to "whatever is on the earth," and His saying ﴿and the like of it with it﴾ is a coordinated phrase placed earlier by inversion. The original wording would be: "if they had whatever is on the earth to ransom themselves thereby, and its like with it." What indicates that it is to be considered as placed earlier by inversion is the singular form of the pronoun governed by the preposition (bi). The purpose of the inversion is to hasten their despair of ransom, even if what is on the earth were multiplied.

Or—and this is the more apparent view in my opinion—the pronoun refers to ﴿and the like of it with it﴾, because that like encompassed what is on the earth and more, so there remained no benefit in supposing ransom with what is on the earth, since it is included within the like that is with it.

It is permissible for the pronoun to be treated like the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara) in the correctness of using it in the singular while referring to a plural, by interpreting it as referring to what has been mentioned. This is common with the demonstrative, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68], meaning between the cow in its prime and the virgin. And His saying: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], where "that" refers to what was mentioned in His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], because the demonstrative is suitable for one thing or for many things. This is rare with the pronoun, because the forms of pronouns are many and suited to what they refer to, so departing from that is a deviation from the original convention. It is rare but eloquent. From it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah should take your hearing and your sight and seal over your hearts, what deity other than Allah could bring them back to you?﴾ [al-An'am: 46], meaning "with the mentioned." In al-Kashshaf, he treated it as carried upon the demonstrative noun, and Ru'bah likewise interpreted it when he recited his verse:

In it are lines of black and white, as if on the skin is the blotch of leprosy.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: I said to Ru'bah, "If you mean the lines, say 'ka'annaha'; if you mean the blackness, say 'ka'annahuma'." He said: "I mean ka'anna dhalika, woe to you." And from it, in the pronoun, is His saying the Exalted: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift; but if they give you part of it willingly﴾ [al-Nisa': 4]. This was mentioned earlier at His saying the Exalted: ﴿neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68] in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾ means perpetual, as an emphasis on His saying: ﴿and they will not be able to exit from it﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 38–39:

﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, and as an exemplary punishment from Allah. Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿The recompense of those who wage war…﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33]. ﴿Wa-al-sariq﴾ ("and the thief") is the subject (mubtada').

[Page 190]

Its predicate (khabar) is omitted according to Sibawayh. The implied sense is: "Among what is recited to you is the ruling on the thief, male and female: cut off their hands." Al-Mubarrad said: the predicate is the clause ﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾ ("cut off their hands"), and the fa' (fa, "then") entered the predicate because the subject implies the meaning of a conditional (shart), since its implied form is: "the one who steals and the one who steals (female)." When a relative construction (mawsul) is intended to be general, it is treated as a conditional, i.e., the "al" in it is taken as a relative pronoun, so it becomes like the verse ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring four witnesses against them from among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it, harm them﴾ [al-Nisa': 16]. Sibawayh said: This applies when the context shows that the subject is mentioned in the course of narrative, ruling, or obligations, such as ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness…﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], ﴿And the two of you who commit it…﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], and ﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾, since the implied sense in all of these is: "And the ruling on those who commit…" or "And the recompense for the thief, male and female."

Ibn al-Hajib mentioned this in al-Kafiyah and summarized it with his saying: "The fa' is for the conditional according to al-Mubarrad, and it is two clauses according to Sibawayh." He means: according to al-Mubarrad it is a conditional clause with its response, so it is as if it were one clause; otherwise the preferred reading is the accusative (nasb). He pointed to the reading of 'Isa ibn 'Umar, "wa-al-sariqa wa-al-sariqata" with the accusative, which is an irregular reading (qira'ah shadhdhah) that is not relied upon, so the Qur'an is not to be interpreted by it. Ibn al-Hajib erred in his saying "the preferred reading is the accusative."

His saying ﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾: the plural pronoun of address is directed at those in authority (wulat al-umur), by the indication of the context, as in His saying: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer, flog each one of them with a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. The pronoun does not refer back to "those who believe" in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 35].

The hands (al-aydi) are in plural in view of the individuals of the category of thief. The pronoun is in dual in view of the two genders, male and female; so the plural here is intended to mean the dual, as in His saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

The reason for mentioning the female thief alongside the male is to remove the suspicion that the masculine form in "thief" restricts the hadd (prescribed punishment) for theft to men only. The Arabs did not give women any weight, so they did not apply the prescribed punishments to them. This is also what calls for mentioning the female in His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. The woman of Makhzum stole in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he ordered her hand to be cut off. This was grave for Quraysh, and they said: "Who will intercede for her with the Messenger of Allah except Zayd ibn Harithah?" When he interceded for her, he (ﷺ) rejected it and said: "Will you intercede in one of the limits of Allah?" Then he gave a sermon and said: "What destroyed those before you was that when a noble person stole among them they left him, and when a weak person stole they cut off his hand. By Allah, if Fatimah had stolen, I would have cut off her hand."

[Page 191]

Establishing the meaning of theft, the threshold amount of stolen property that makes the hadd obligatory, and the manner of amputation, is a field for the jurists (ahl al-ijtihad) among the scholars of the early generations and the leaders of the legal schools (a'immat al-madhahib), and it is not the aim of the exegete.

It is not the custom of the Qur'an to define the legal meanings (al-ma'ani al-shar'iyyah) and their details. Rather, it establishes their foundations, and it refers what lies beyond that to what is customary among the people of the language, in knowing their realities and distinguishing them from what resembles them.

So al-sariq is the one characterized by theft. Theft (al-sariqah) is well known among the Arabs and is distinguished from raiding (al-ghaarah), usurpation (al-ghasb), seizure by force (al-ightisab), and snatching (al-khilsah). Holding someone accountable for it returns to considering the stolen item as something that most people are stingy about.

So theft is: a person taking something he does not own, secretly from its owner, removing it from a place that is the protected place (hirz) of its like, without the taker having been permitted to enter it.

The stolen item is what has a benefit that people do not tolerate losing. The scholars defined its minimum by reference to the value of the least thing for which the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled that the hand of the one who stole it be cut off. It is established in the Sahih that he ruled to cut off the hand of the thief of a hajafah, with a ha' without dots and a jim, both vowelled with fatha (a shield made of leather), which is worth a quarter of a dinar according to the majority, a dinar according to Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, and Ibn 'Abbas, and half a dinar according to some jurists.

[Page 192]

The Qur'an does not mention any punishment for the thief other than the cutting off of the hand.

Cutting off the hand of the thief was a ruling from the time of Jahiliyyah, decided by al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and Islam approved it, as is in the verse. No sound report in the Sunnah has come except regarding the cutting off of the hand.

The first man whose hand was cut off in Islam was al-Khiyar ibn 'Adi ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf, and the first woman whose hand was cut off was al-Makhzumiyyah, Murrah bint Sufyan.

The jurists agreed that the first thing with which the punishment for theft begins is that the hand be cut off. The majority said: the right hand. A group said: the left hand. If he steals a second time, the majority of the imams said: his leg on the side opposite to the cut-off hand is cut off. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: he is not cut, but he is imprisoned and beaten. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab ruled accordingly, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. 'Ali said: "I am indeed ashamed to cut off his other hand, for then with what will he eat and cleanse himself? Or his leg, for then on what will he rely?" If he steals a third and fourth time, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: his other hand and his other leg are cut off. Al-Zuhri said: "There has reached us in the Sunnah only the cutting off of a hand and a leg, and nothing is added to that." This was also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Thawri, and Hammad ibn Salamah. It is obligatory to judge according to the view of Abu Hanifah, for the hadd punishments are averted by doubts (shubuhat), and what doubt is greater than the disagreement of the recognized imams of jurisprudence?

Recompense (al-jaza'): the requital for an action with what suits that action, of good or evil. Allah said: ﴿Indeed for the God-fearing there is a place of success﴾ [al-Naba': 31], up to His saying: ﴿a recompense from your Lord, a gift reckoned﴾ [al-Naba': 36], in Surat al-Naba'; and He said: ﴿The recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], in Surat al-Shura.

Exemplary punishment (al-nakal): a severe punishment whose nature is to restrain the one punished from returning to a deed like the one for which he was punished. It is derived from recoiling from a thing (al-nukul 'an al-shay'), meaning shrinking back from it and fearing it.

[Page 193]

So al-nakal is a kind of evil recompense, and it is its most severe form. It was discussed at His saying ﴿So We made it an exemplary punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 66] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word jaza' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) or as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and nakalan is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for jaza', a badal ishtimal (partial substitution).

The wisdom behind prescribing amputation is that it is a recompense for theft, intended as a deterrent and to prevent recurrence; that is, a recompense that is not revenge but reform (istislah). Whoever supposed that amputation is a compensation for the stolen property has gone astray, and he said, in two verses attributed to al-Ma'arri, which are not in al-Saqt or al-Luzumiyyat:

A hand whose blood-money was set at five hundred gold pieces, why was it cut off for a quarter of a dinar?

Its answer is attributed to the scholar 'Alam al-Din al-Sakhawi:

The honour of trustworthiness has raised its value and lowered it, the humiliation of betrayal, so understand the wisdom of the Creator.

His saying ﴿fa-man taba min ba'di zulmihi wa-aslaha fa-inna Allaha yatubu 'alayhi﴾ means: whoever among the thieves repents after the theft, Allah will turn to him, that is, his repentance will be accepted. Its meaning was discussed at His saying ﴿Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He turned to him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] in Surat al-Baqarah. There is nothing in the verse indicating that the punishment for theft is dropped from the thief if he repents before his punishment, because the apparent meaning of "repented" and "Allah turned to him" is that it concerns what is between the servant and his Lord in the recompense of the Hereafter. So His saying ﴿whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾ is an encouragement to these sinners to repent and good news for them. There is no evidence in the verse for nullifying the ruling of punishment in some cases, as in the verse about those who wage war (muharibun). Therefore, the majority of scholars said: the repentance of a thief does not drop the amputation, even if he comes repentant before being able to be apprehended. What supports the validity of their view is that the Prophet (ﷺ) cut off the hand of the woman of Makhzum, and there is no doubt that she was repentant.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Because the one who wages war acts independently with his own strength, and the imam cannot reach him except by pressing forward with horses and mounts. So his punishment is dropped by repentance, as a means of bringing him down from that state, just as Allah forgives all that preceded for the disbelievers, to win them over to Islam. As for the thief and the adulterer, they are in the grip of the Muslims." End of quotation.

[Page 194]

'Ata' said: if a thief comes repentant before he can be apprehended, the amputation is dropped from him. This is reported from al-Shafi'i, and it is a case of applying the absolute (mutlaq) to the restricted (muqayyad), by analogy with the ruling on the one who wages war. This seems to be a case of a unified cause with differing rulings. The verified view is that the verse on waging war is not among the restricted texts; rather it is a ruling derived independently, and that waging war and theft are not one cause. So the matter is not one of a unified cause, nor of an absolute text whose restricted counterpart applies.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 38–39:

﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they have earned, and as an exemplary punishment from Allah. Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾ ﴿But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿The recompense of those who wage war…﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 33]. ﴿Wa-al-sariq﴾ ("and the thief") is the subject (mubtada').

[Page 190]

Its predicate (khabar) is omitted according to Sibawayh. The implied sense is: "Among what is recited to you is the ruling on the thief, male and female: cut off their hands." Al-Mubarrad said: the predicate is the clause ﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾ ("cut off their hands"), and the fa' (fa, "then") entered the predicate because the subject implies the meaning of a conditional (shart), since its implied form is: "the one who steals and the one who steals (female)." When a relative construction (mawsul) is intended to be general, it is treated as a conditional, i.e., the "al" in it is taken as a relative pronoun, so it becomes like the verse ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring four witnesses against them from among you﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], and His saying: ﴿And the two of you who commit it, harm them﴾ [al-Nisa': 16]. Sibawayh said: This applies when the context shows that the subject is mentioned in the course of narrative, ruling, or obligations, such as ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness…﴾ [al-Nisa': 15], ﴿And the two of you who commit it…﴾ [al-Nisa': 16], and ﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾, since the implied sense in all of these is: "And the ruling on those who commit…" or "And the recompense for the thief, male and female."

Ibn al-Hajib mentioned this in al-Kafiyah and summarized it with his saying: "The fa' is for the conditional according to al-Mubarrad, and it is two clauses according to Sibawayh." He means: according to al-Mubarrad it is a conditional clause with its response, so it is as if it were one clause; otherwise the preferred reading is the accusative (nasb). He pointed to the reading of 'Isa ibn 'Umar, "wa-al-sariqa wa-al-sariqata" with the accusative, which is an irregular reading (qira'ah shadhdhah) that is not relied upon, so the Qur'an is not to be interpreted by it. Ibn al-Hajib erred in his saying "the preferred reading is the accusative."

His saying ﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾: the plural pronoun of address is directed at those in authority (wulat al-umur), by the indication of the context, as in His saying: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer, flog each one of them with a hundred lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. The pronoun does not refer back to "those who believe" in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 35].

The hands (al-aydi) are in plural in view of the individuals of the category of thief. The pronoun is in dual in view of the two genders, male and female; so the plural here is intended to mean the dual, as in His saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

The reason for mentioning the female thief alongside the male is to remove the suspicion that the masculine form in "thief" restricts the hadd (prescribed punishment) for theft to men only. The Arabs did not give women any weight, so they did not apply the prescribed punishments to them. This is also what calls for mentioning the female in His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178]. The woman of Makhzum stole in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he ordered her hand to be cut off. This was grave for Quraysh, and they said: "Who will intercede for her with the Messenger of Allah except Zayd ibn Harithah?" When he interceded for her, he (ﷺ) rejected it and said: "Will you intercede in one of the limits of Allah?" Then he gave a sermon and said: "What destroyed those before you was that when a noble person stole among them they left him, and when a weak person stole they cut off his hand. By Allah, if Fatimah had stolen, I would have cut off her hand."

[Page 191]

Establishing the meaning of theft, the threshold amount of stolen property that makes the hadd obligatory, and the manner of amputation, is a field for the jurists (ahl al-ijtihad) among the scholars of the early generations and the leaders of the legal schools (a'immat al-madhahib), and it is not the aim of the exegete.

It is not the custom of the Qur'an to define the legal meanings (al-ma'ani al-shar'iyyah) and their details. Rather, it establishes their foundations, and it refers what lies beyond that to what is customary among the people of the language, in knowing their realities and distinguishing them from what resembles them.

So al-sariq is the one characterized by theft. Theft (al-sariqah) is well known among the Arabs and is distinguished from raiding (al-ghaarah), usurpation (al-ghasb), seizure by force (al-ightisab), and snatching (al-khilsah). Holding someone accountable for it returns to considering the stolen item as something that most people are stingy about.

So theft is: a person taking something he does not own, secretly from its owner, removing it from a place that is the protected place (hirz) of its like, without the taker having been permitted to enter it.

The stolen item is what has a benefit that people do not tolerate losing. The scholars defined its minimum by reference to the value of the least thing for which the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled that the hand of the one who stole it be cut off. It is established in the Sahih that he ruled to cut off the hand of the thief of a hajafah, with a ha' without dots and a jim, both vowelled with fatha (a shield made of leather), which is worth a quarter of a dinar according to the majority, a dinar according to Abu Hanifah, al-Thawri, and Ibn 'Abbas, and half a dinar according to some jurists.

[Page 192]

The Qur'an does not mention any punishment for the thief other than the cutting off of the hand.

Cutting off the hand of the thief was a ruling from the time of Jahiliyyah, decided by al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and Islam approved it, as is in the verse. No sound report in the Sunnah has come except regarding the cutting off of the hand.

The first man whose hand was cut off in Islam was al-Khiyar ibn 'Adi ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf, and the first woman whose hand was cut off was al-Makhzumiyyah, Murrah bint Sufyan.

The jurists agreed that the first thing with which the punishment for theft begins is that the hand be cut off. The majority said: the right hand. A group said: the left hand. If he steals a second time, the majority of the imams said: his leg on the side opposite to the cut-off hand is cut off. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: he is not cut, but he is imprisoned and beaten. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab ruled accordingly, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. 'Ali said: "I am indeed ashamed to cut off his other hand, for then with what will he eat and cleanse himself? Or his leg, for then on what will he rely?" If he steals a third and fourth time, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: his other hand and his other leg are cut off. Al-Zuhri said: "There has reached us in the Sunnah only the cutting off of a hand and a leg, and nothing is added to that." This was also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Thawri, and Hammad ibn Salamah. It is obligatory to judge according to the view of Abu Hanifah, for the hadd punishments are averted by doubts (shubuhat), and what doubt is greater than the disagreement of the recognized imams of jurisprudence?

Recompense (al-jaza'): the requital for an action with what suits that action, of good or evil. Allah said: ﴿Indeed for the God-fearing there is a place of success﴾ [al-Naba': 31], up to His saying: ﴿a recompense from your Lord, a gift reckoned﴾ [al-Naba': 36], in Surat al-Naba'; and He said: ﴿The recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], in Surat al-Shura.

Exemplary punishment (al-nakal): a severe punishment whose nature is to restrain the one punished from returning to a deed like the one for which he was punished. It is derived from recoiling from a thing (al-nukul 'an al-shay'), meaning shrinking back from it and fearing it.

[Page 193]

So al-nakal is a kind of evil recompense, and it is its most severe form. It was discussed at His saying ﴿So We made it an exemplary punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 66] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word jaza' is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) or as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi), and nakalan is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for jaza', a badal ishtimal (partial substitution).

The wisdom behind prescribing amputation is that it is a recompense for theft, intended as a deterrent and to prevent recurrence; that is, a recompense that is not revenge but reform (istislah). Whoever supposed that amputation is a compensation for the stolen property has gone astray, and he said, in two verses attributed to al-Ma'arri, which are not in al-Saqt or al-Luzumiyyat:

A hand whose blood-money was set at five hundred gold pieces, why was it cut off for a quarter of a dinar?

Its answer is attributed to the scholar 'Alam al-Din al-Sakhawi:

The honour of trustworthiness has raised its value and lowered it, the humiliation of betrayal, so understand the wisdom of the Creator.

His saying ﴿fa-man taba min ba'di zulmihi wa-aslaha fa-inna Allaha yatubu 'alayhi﴾ means: whoever among the thieves repents after the theft, Allah will turn to him, that is, his repentance will be accepted. Its meaning was discussed at His saying ﴿Then Adam received words from his Lord, and He turned to him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] in Surat al-Baqarah. There is nothing in the verse indicating that the punishment for theft is dropped from the thief if he repents before his punishment, because the apparent meaning of "repented" and "Allah turned to him" is that it concerns what is between the servant and his Lord in the recompense of the Hereafter. So His saying ﴿whoever repents after his wrongdoing﴾ is an encouragement to these sinners to repent and good news for them. There is no evidence in the verse for nullifying the ruling of punishment in some cases, as in the verse about those who wage war (muharibun). Therefore, the majority of scholars said: the repentance of a thief does not drop the amputation, even if he comes repentant before being able to be apprehended. What supports the validity of their view is that the Prophet (ﷺ) cut off the hand of the woman of Makhzum, and there is no doubt that she was repentant.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: "Because the one who wages war acts independently with his own strength, and the imam cannot reach him except by pressing forward with horses and mounts. So his punishment is dropped by repentance, as a means of bringing him down from that state, just as Allah forgives all that preceded for the disbelievers, to win them over to Islam. As for the thief and the adulterer, they are in the grip of the Muslims." End of quotation.

[Page 194]

'Ata' said: if a thief comes repentant before he can be apprehended, the amputation is dropped from him. This is reported from al-Shafi'i, and it is a case of applying the absolute (mutlaq) to the restricted (muqayyad), by analogy with the ruling on the one who wages war. This seems to be a case of a unified cause with differing rulings. The verified view is that the verse on waging war is not among the restricted texts; rather it is a ruling derived independently, and that waging war and theft are not one cause. So the matter is not one of a unified cause, nor of an absolute text whose restricted counterpart applies.

This is a explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), an answer to one who asks about the change in the thief's state from punishment to forgiveness after repentance, despite the greatness of his offence, [the answer being] that God is the Disposer of what is in the heavens and the earth and what is between them, so He knows the places of punishment and the places of pardon.

[Page 195]

This is a resumptive, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) that serves to ease the distress of the Prophet ﷺ over the gathering of the hypocrites and the Jews around falsehood, their wavering in dealing with the Messenger ﷺ, and their evil intentions toward him. It expands his breast (bi-sharh sadr) regarding what might grieve him from the recklessness and contempt of the Jews and the hypocrisy of the hypocrites.

The address opens with the noblest of attributes, which is the attribute of messengerhood from God.

The occasion of revelation of these verses took place during the period in which this surah was revealed, so the verses revealed before them were followed by them. The occasion of revelation of this verse, and what it refers to, is what Abu Dawud, al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, and al-Tabari in his Tafsir narrated, in summary: "The Jews disagreed about the penalty for the adulterer when a man among them committed adultery with a woman from the people of Khaybar or the people of Fadak, between stoning and flogging with tahmim (blackening the face). The disagreement drove them to send to the Jews of Medina" to ask that they have the Messenger of God judge the matter. They said: "If he rules with tahmim, we will accept his ruling, and if he rules with stoning, do not accept it." The Messenger of God said to their rabbis in Medina: "What do you find in the Torah concerning one who commits adultery when he is muhsan (married)?" They said: "He is blackened, flogged, and paraded about." The Prophet ﷺ denied them and informed them that the ruling of the Torah is stoning for the one who is muhsan. They denied this, so he ordered the Torah to be unfolded (tunshar), meaning its folds opened, for they used to roll it around a stick in a cylindrical shape. One of them began to read it while placing his hand on the verse of stoning, that is, reading it for those who understood it. The Messenger of God said to him: "Raise your hand," and he raised his hand, and beneath it was the verse of stoning. The Messenger of God said: "I shall surely be the first to revive the ruling of the Torah." So he ruled that the man and the woman be stoned. In the narrations of Abu Dawud, the words of God Most High, "O Messenger, let not those grieve you who race to disbelief," were revealed concerning that matter. Al-Wahidi and al-Tabari also narrated likewise.

They did not mention anything that indicates the reason for the reference to the hypocrites at the beginning of this verse with the words: "from those who say, 'We believe,' with their mouths, while their hearts have not believed." Perhaps the hypocrites who concealed Judaism were participants with the Jews in this matter, or they were waiting for there to be no ruling on stoning the adulterer in the Torah, so they might take that as an excuse to display what they concealed of disbelief, under the pretext of denying the Messenger ﷺ.

I reckon that the Jews' resort to having the Messenger ﷺ judge in that matter was not because they believed in his messengerhood, nor because they regarded his ruling as a preference in their disagreement, but because they regarded him as a ruler (wali al-amr) in that domain and what follows from it. In the rules of their dealings and the estimations of their rabbis, they were to obey the authorities who ruled over them from outside their religious community. So when they disagreed about the ruling of their religion, they made the judgment belong to someone who was not among the disputants, because the ruling of the ruler is obeyed among them. Thus the Messenger of God issued a ruling that combined holding them to the consequence of their own choice of arbitration with showing their error in turning away from the ruling of their own Book. For this reason God Most High called it justice (qist) in His words: "And if you judge, judge between them with justice" [al-Ma'idah: 42].

It is also possible that it arose from the opinion of those among them who affirm the messengerhood of Muhammad ﷺ and say that he is a messenger to the Gentiles (ummiyyin) only. These are the Jews of the Eisawiyyah sect (al-yahud al-'isawiyyah), so his ruling would be supportive of them, since it is regarded as an informing about the Torah. What supports this is what Abu Dawud narrated from Abu Hurayrah: that a Jewish man committed adultery with a Jewish woman, and some of them said to others: "Come, let us go to Muhammad, for he was sent with leniency. If he issues a fatwa of flogging without stoning, we will accept it and argue with it before God, and say: 'The fatwa of a prophet from among your prophets.'" It is also possible that this was a kind of reinforcement by agreement with the law of Islam, so the preference for one of the two interpretations would be by its agreement with another law. What supports this is what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated: that they said, "Our sovereignty has gone, so we disliked killing." It is also possible that they had turned away from the ruling of their law, hesitating at the conflict, so they inclined toward arbitration. Perhaps that was permissible in their law. What supports this is that it occurs in the hadith of al-Bukhari and others that when they asked the Prophet ﷺ for a fatwa, he set out with his companions until he came to al-Midras, which is the house where the Jews are taught, and he debated with them concerning the ruling of stoning. Two rabbis among them, called the sons of Suriya (ibn Suriya), answered him by acknowledging that the ruling of stoning is established in the Torah. It is also possible that they had arbitrated the Prophet ﷺ deliberately to test him regarding what he claimed of knowledge through revelation, and the ruling of stoning was concealed among them, known only to the select of their rabbis, and forgotten and not mentioned among their scholars. So when he ruled against them with it, they were confounded. What supports this is what appeared of their intention in their denial of the existence of the ruling of stoning. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, they denied that the ruling of stoning was in the Torah, and the Prophet ﷺ came to al-Midras and ordered the Torah to be unfolded, and their reader began to read while placing his hand on the verse of stoning. The Prophet ﷺ was informed by God of this, so he ordered him to raise his hand, and the verse of stoning was read, and the two sons of Suriya acknowledged it. Whatever the case, this incident indicates the breakdown of the order of the law among the Jews at that time and the weakness of their confidence in their knowledge.

The meaning of "let not those grieve you who race" is a prohibition against his being made to grieve by those who race in disbelief. The grieving is the act of those who race in disbelief, and the prohibition against an act of another is only a prohibition against its causes. That is: do not let them grieve you, meaning do not concern yourself with what they do that is of a nature to bring grief upon you. This is a common usage, and it is one of the cases of using a compound expression in its metonymic (kinayah) meaning. A parallel to it is the saying: "I shall not find you doing such and such," meaning: do not do it until I find out. And the saying: "I shall not find you here," and "I shall not see you here."

Ascribing the grieving to "those who race in disbelief" is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), for which there is no literal (haqiqah) sense, because those who race are a cause of the grief, while the actual stirrer of grief in the soul of the one grieved is not known in common usage. Therefore it is one of the metaphors for which there is no literal sense. As for God being the originator of all things, that is not something upon which a literal and a metaphorical sense are based, for if it were so, most ascriptions would be rational metaphors, and that is not the case. This is something in which many students err in determining a literal rational sense for some instances of rational metaphor. Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir excelled when he said in Dala'il al-I'jaz: "Know that it is not necessary in this that the verb should have an agent in estimation; if you transfer the verb to something, it becomes literal. For you do not find in your saying, 'Its land brought me near to you, a right of mine upon so-and-so,' an agent other than the right. Likewise his saying:

'Your desire has made me, and in me the ailment has become proverbial'

and:

'His face increases you in beauty.'

You should not claim that it has an agent from which the verb was transferred and given to desire and to the face." End of quote.

Al-Imam al-Razi erred in explaining the words of 'Abd al-Qahir, and he began bringing evidences showing that verbs have been ascribed to a metaphorical agent although their real agent is God Most High. The Shaykh was not unaware of this, but he was seeking the agent to which the verb is literally ascribed in the common usage of people, both believers and disbelievers. His saying "if you transfer the verb to it," that is, ascribe it to it, indicates this.

The meaning of racing in disbelief is the manifestation of its effects at the slightest occasion and in every opportunity. He likened its repeated manifestation to the hastening of one walking toward something, as one says: "Grey hair hastened toward him," and the saying: "When the fool is admonished, he runs toward it."

It was followed by "in" (fi), which denotes location, to indicate that the hastening is a metaphor in the sense of penetrating deeply, so "in" serves as the indicator of the metaphor, as in the sayings: "Corruption hastened into the thing," and "Grey hair hastened into the head of so-and-so." He made disbelief like a container, and made their floundering in it and the intensity of their immersion in it like the movement of a thing within a container, moving with vigor and speed. A parallel is His saying: "They race in sin" [al-Ma'idah: 62], and His saying: "We hasten for them in good things" [al-Mu'minun: 56], and "They race to good things" [al-Mu'minun: 61]. These are repeated metaphors in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech. What is stronger than them will come, which is His saying: "You see them racing toward them" [al-Ma'idah: 52].

His saying: "from those who say, 'We believe,' with their mouths," etc., is an explanation of "those who race in disbelief." Those who say "We believe" with their mouths while their hearts have not believed are the hypocrites.

His saying: "and from those who are Jews" is coordinated with His saying: "from those who say 'We believe.'" The pause is at His saying: "and from those who are Jews."

His saying: "listeners to falsehood" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "they are listeners to falsehood." The apparent meaning is that the omitted pronoun refers to both groups, the hypocrites and the Jews, by the indication of the discourse concerning both groups.

Omitting the subject (musnad ilayhi) in this kind of context is an omission in which usage is followed; that occurs after they mention a subject being spoken of, or after something strange has proceeded from something, and they come with reports about it in a sentence whose subject is omitted, like their saying to one who hits by accident, "An arrow from one who is not an archer," and the saying of Abu al-Ruqayish:

"Quick to the cousin, his face is slapped,
but he is not quick to the caller of generosity."

And the saying of one of the poets of the Hamasah:

"A youth whose wealth is not hidden from his friend,
nor does he show complaint when the sandal slips."

following his saying:

"I shall thank 'Amr if my death is delayed,
for favors that were not bestowed upon me, even if they were great."

Al-sammā' (listener, one who listens much) means one who listens much, that is, to what is said to him. Hearing (al-sam') is used in its literal sense, meaning that they lend their ears to false speech while knowing it to be false, that is, they take an interest in it and seek it out, so their hearing of it multiplies. In this there is a kinayah for the spread of falsehood among their community, between the listener and the fabricator, because the abundance of hearing entails the abundance of speech. By falsehood is meant the lies of their rabbis who claimed that the ruling for fornication in the Torah is tahmim.

The clause "listeners to a people others who have not come to you" is a second predicate of the omitted subject. The meaning is that they accept what another people commands them, who conceal their purpose from the Prophet ﷺ, so that if he rules in accordance with what they desire they follow him, and if he rules against their desire they disobey him. That is, they are followers of a people who are concealed, and they are the other people, namely the people of Khaybar and the people of Fadak, who sent the question and none of them came to the Prophet ﷺ.

The lam in "li-qawm" (for a people) is for reinforcement, because the active participle is weak in governing the object.

The clause "they distort the words" is a second attribute of "a people others" or a circumstantial clause (hal). You may also make it a circumstantial clause of "those who race in disbelief."

The discussion of distorting words was previously presented at His saying: "From those who are Jews, they distort words from their places" [al-Nisa': 46] in Surat al-Nisa', and that distortion is inclining toward a letter, that is, a side, meaning moving it from its place to another side.

وقال هنا ﴿مِن بَعْدِ مَواضِعِهِ﴾، وفي سورة النساء ﴿عَنْ مَواضِعِهِ﴾ [المائدة: 13]، لأن آية سورة النساء في وصف اليهود كلهم وتحريفهم في التوراة، فهو تغيير كلام التوراة بكلام آخر عن جهل أو قصد أو خطأ في تأويل معاني التوراة أو في ألفاظها. فكان إبعادًا للكلام عن مواضعه، أي إزالةً للكلام الأصلي، سواء عُوِّض بغيره أو لم يُعوَّض. وأما هذه الآية ففي ذكر طائفة معينة أبطلوا العمل بكلام ثابت في التوراة، إذ ألغَوْا حكم الرجم الثابت فيها دون تعويضه بغيره من الكلام، فهذا أشد جرأة من التحريف الآخر، فكان قوله: ﴿مِن بَعْدِ مَواضِعِهِ﴾ أبلغ في تحريف الكلام، لأن لفظ (بَعْدَ) يقتضي أن مواضع الكلم مستقرة، وأنه أُبطل العمل بها مع بقائها قائمةً في كتاب التوراة.

والإشارة التي في قوله: ﴿إنْ أُوتِيتُمْ هَذا﴾ إلى الكَلِم المُحرَّف. والإيتاء هنا: الإفادة، كقوله: ﴿وآتاهُ اللَّهُ المُلْكَ والحِكْمَةَ﴾ [البقرة: 251].

والأخذ: القبول، أي إن أُجبتم بمثل ما تهوون فاقبلوه، وإن لم تُجابوه فاحذروا قبوله. وإنما قالوا: ﴿فاحْذَرُوا﴾، لأنه يفتح عليهم الطعنَ في أحكامهم التي مضَوْا عليها، وفي حكامهم الحاكمين بها.

وإرادة الله فتنةَ المفتون قضاؤها له في الأزل، وعلامةُ ذلك التقدير عدمُ إجداء الموعظة والإرشاد فيه. فذلك معنى قوله: ﴿فَلَنْ تَمْلِكَ لَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيْئًا﴾، أي لا تبلغ إلى هَدْيه بما أمرك الله به من الدعوة للناس كافةً.

وهذا التركيب يدل في كلام العرب على انتفاء الحيلة في تحصيل أمرٍ ما. ومدلول مفرداته أنك لا تملك، أي لا تقدر على أقلّ شيء من الله، أي لا تستطيع نيل شيء من تيسير الله لإزالة ضلالة هذا المفتون، لأن مادة المِلك تدل على تمام القدرة، قال قيس بن الخطيم:

مَلَكْتُ بها كفِّي فأنهرَ فتْقَها

أي شددتُ بالطعنة كفّي، أي ملكتها بكفي. وقال النبي (ﷺ) لعُيينة بن حصن: «أوَأملك لك أن نزع الله من قلبك الرحمة». وفي حديث دعوة الرسول (ﷺ) عشيرتَه: «فإني لا أغني عنكم من الله شيئًا». و(شيئًا) منصوب على المفعولية.

وتنكير (شيئًا) للتقليل والتحقير، لأن الاستفهام لما كان بمعنى النفي كان انتفاءُ ملك شيء قليل مقتضيًا انتفاءَ ملك الشيء الكثير بطريق الأَوْلى.

والقول في قوله: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ أنْ يُطَهِّرَ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ كالقول في قوله: ﴿ومَن يُرِدِ اللَّهُ فِتْنَتَهُ﴾.

والمراد بالتطهير التهيئةُ لقبول الإيمان والهدى، أو أراد بالتطهير نفسَ قبول الإيمان.

والخِزْي تقدم عند قوله تعالى: ﴿إلّا خِزْيٌ﴾ [البقرة: 85] في سورة البقرة، وقوله: ﴿رَبَّنا إنَّكَ مَن تُدْخِلِ النّارَ فَقَدْ أخْزَيْتَهُ﴾ [آل عمران: 192] في سورة آل عمران.

وأعاد ﴿سَمّاعُونَ لِلْكَذِبِ﴾ [المائدة: 42] للتأكيد، وليُرتِّب عليه قوله: ﴿أكّالُونَ لِلسُّحْتِ﴾ [المائدة: 42].

ومعنى ﴿أكّالُونَ لِلسُّحْتِ﴾ [المائدة: 42] أخّاذون له، لأن الأكل استعارةٌ لتمام الانتفاع.

[صفحة 202]

والسُّحْت بضم السين وسكون الحاء: الشيءُ المَسحوت، أي المُستأصَل. يقال: سَحَته إذا استأصله وأتلفه. سُمي به الحرامُ لأنه لا يُبارَك فيه لصاحبه، فهو مسحوتٌ وممحوقٌ، أي مقدَّرٌ له ذلك، كقوله: ﴿يَمْحَقُ اللَّهُ الرِّبا﴾ [البقرة: 276]. قال الفرزدق:

وعَضُّ زمانٍ يا ابنَ مروانَ لم يَدَعْ ∗∗∗ مِنَ المالِ إلّا مُسْحَتٌ أو مُجَنَّفُ

والسُّحْت يشمل جميعَ المال الحرام، كالربا والرشوةِ وأكلِ مال اليتيم والمغصوب. وقرأ نافعٌ، وابنُ عامرٍ، وعاصمٌ، وحمزةُ، وأبو جعفرٍ، وخلفٌ ﴿سُحْتٌ﴾ بسكون الحاء، وقرأه الباقون بضم الحاء إتباعًا لضم السين.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 42:

﴿If they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them. And if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all. And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.﴾

This is a consequence of what His statement ﴿They are listeners for another people who have not come to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41] implies, and His statement ﴿They say: If you are given this, then take it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. This indicates that there was a dialogue among them concerning the sending of a group of them to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to seek judgment on a matter of their affairs, in which their inclinations tended toward changing the ruling of the Torah on it through interpretation or concealment. Some of those who objected to them, or demanded that they produce evidence for their interpretation, so they hoped to find in the Prophet's ﷺ judgment something to support them. The apparent sense of the conditional implies that Allah informed His Messenger of their disagreement concerning the ruling on the prescribed punishment for fornication, and of their resolve to bring it to his judgment before the ones they consulted reached him. Some exegetes have said this, so this verse is among the signs of prophethood. It is also possible that what is meant is: if they come to you a second time, then judge between them or turn away from them.

Allah Most High gave His Messenger ﷺ the choice between judging between them and turning away from them. The reason for the choice is the conflict of two causes: the cause of establishing justice requires judgment between them, and the cause of treating them with the opposite of their intent, namely testing or attempting to have the judgment coincide with their desires, requires turning away from them, lest the Prophetic judgment be exposed to contempt.

صفحة ٢٠٣

The beginning of the choice in the wording of the verse is with the part that implies he judges between them, as an indication that judging between them is preferable. This is supported by His later statement ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾, meaning with truth, which is the Islamic ruling of the prescribed punishment. As for His statement ﴿And if you turn away from them, they cannot harm you at all﴾, this is reassurance to the Prophet ﷺ, lest he say to himself: how can I turn away from them, so that they make that an argument against us, saying: "We relied on you and were content with your judgment, and you turned away from us, so we will not heed your call hereafter." This is something the Prophet ﷺ was concerned with, because it would lead to their leaders repelling their common people from the call to Islam. So Allah Most High reassured him that if he does that, no harm will arise from it. Perhaps in this reassurance there is an indication that they have no hope of their faith in any circumstance. The harm meant is not the harm of enmity or injury, because the Prophet ﷺ is not concerned with that nor fears it from them, contrary to what the exegetes have said here.

The indefinite "شَيْئًا" (shay'an, "anything") is for belittling, as it is in similar expressions, such as ﴿then you would not avail him anything from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. It is in the accusative as an absolute object, because it is in the intent of being attached to a verbal noun, meaning "anything of harm," so it stands in for the verbal noun.

The discussion of the position of the word "شَيْءٍ" (shay', "thing") has already been made at His statement ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 155] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The verse implies the choice of the rulers of the Muslims in judging between the People of the Book when they bring their disputes to them, since the permission of this choice for other than the Messenger among the rulers is equal to its permission for the Messenger. The scholars differed on this question and on the question of the ruling of Muslim judges concerning the disputes of non-Muslims. Inductive study has shown that the basic principle regarding judging between non-Muslims when some of them dispute with others is that their own community's judges judge between them. If they bring their case to Muslim judges, then if what occurred is of the kind of injustice, such as killing, usurpation, and everything from which corruption spreads, there is no disagreement that it is obligatory to judge between them. On this basis, the choice in the verse is restricted by consensus. If it is not of that kind, such as disputes over divorce and transactions:

Some scholars said: the ruling of this choice is definitive and not abrogated, and they said: the verse was revealed concerning the story of stoning which Malik related in the Muwatta', and al-Bukhari after him, namely that a Jewish man committed fornication with a Jewish woman, and they all said: "Let us ask Muhammad about this." So they brought their case to him, and Allah Most High gave him the choice. The proponents of this view differed. A group of them said: the Jews in Medina at that time were people of truce (muwada'ah) and were not people of protection (dhimmah), so the choice remains with the likes of them, those who are not included under the protection of Islam. Unlike those who entered under the protection of Islam, for these, if they bring their case to the Muslims, it is obligatory to judge between them. This is the view of Ibn al-Qasim in the narration of 'Isa ibn Dinar, because the two Jews were from the people of Khaybar or Fadak, and they were at that time in the House of War under a truce. The majority said: this choice is general, including the people of protection as well. This is the view of Malik and a narration from al-Shafi'i. Malik said: turning away is preferable.

It was also said: they are not to be judged in matters of the prescribed punishments (hudud), and this is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i.

It was also said: the choice is abrogated by His later statement ﴿And that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49], and this is the view of Abu Hanifah. It was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, al-Nakha'i, and 'Ata' al-Khurasani. This is far-fetched, because the context of the verses indicates that they were revealed in a single sequence, so it is unlikely that the last of them abrogates the first.

His statement ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾ means with equity. Justice is the judgment that conforms to the Islamic law. It is possible that Allah forbade His Messenger from judging between them by what is in the Torah, because it is a law abrogated by Islam. This is what Malik related. On this basis, the incident in which they brought their case to the Messenger of Allah, he did not judge against the two fornicators; rather his judgment was limited to explaining to the Jews the reality of their law in the Torah, so the invalidity of what they were judging by became clear, since it did not conform to their law nor to the law of Islam. So it is a ruling against the Jews that they had concealed. And what occurred in the hadith of the Muwatta' and al-Bukhari, that the man and the woman were stoned, was only by the judgment of their rabbis. It is also possible that Allah commanded him to judge between them by what is in the Torah, because it agrees with the ruling of Islam; he had judged with stoning before this incident or after it. It is also possible that Allah permitted him to judge between them by their law when they brought the case to him. Some scholars said this, as related by al-Qurtubi. The proponent of this view says: this was abrogated by His statement ﴿And that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49], and this is the view of a group of the Successors. There is no need to claim abrogation, and perhaps they meant by it what includes clarification, as we will mention at His statement ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48].

What is derived from jurisprudence concerning judging between non-Muslims without their seeking judgment is this: the Community has agreed that the people of protection (dhimmis) are under the authority of Islam, and that the covenants of protection require leaving them to what their religions prescribe in the affairs occurring among themselves, according to what their laws have defined for them. Therefore the matters they engage in fall into four categories.

The first category: what is specific to the dhimmi's own person, such as his worship, his prayer, his slaughter, and other matters within what is lawful and unlawful. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the leaders of the Muslims do not intervene to prevent them from it, unless it involves general corruption, such as killing a soul.

The second category: what occurs among them of transactions that relate to what is lawful and unlawful in Islam, such as types of marriage, divorce, drinking wine, and actions which they consider permissible but which Islam prohibits. These too they are left to. Malik said: the hadd punishment for fornication is not established against the dhimmis; if a Muslim commits fornication with a female People of the Book, the Muslim is punished and the female People of the Book is not punished. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: the imam does not send a messenger to them, nor summon the opponent to his session.

The third category: what extends beyond them to others of corruption, such as theft and aggression against lives and honour. The scholars of the Community have unanimously agreed that this category falls under the rulings of Islam, because we have not made a covenant with them concerning corruption, and Allah Most High said ﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205]. For this reason we prevent them from selling wine to Muslims and from openly displaying prohibited things.

The fourth category: what occurs among them of transactions in which some of them aggress against others, such as crimes against persons, debts, and disputes between spouses. As for this category, if they consent among themselves, we do not intervene with them. But if one of them seeks the support of the Muslim ruler against the other, Malik said: the Muslim judge judges between them in it obligatorily, because in aggression there is a form of injustice and corruption. Al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, and Zufar said likewise. Abu Hanifah said: he does not judge between them until both litigants consent together.

How could they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah, and then turn away after that? And those are not believers.

This sentence is coordinated with the sentence "But if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them" [al-Ma'idah: 42]. The interrogative is for expressing wonder (ta'ajjub), and the object of wonder is the content of His saying, "then they turn away after that": that is, it is strange that they abandon their own Book and yet ask you to judge, while they do not believe in you, and then turn away after your judgment if it does not satisfy them. The reference in "after that" (min ba'di dhalika) is to the judgment implied by "they make you judge," meaning they combine both the lack of contentment with their own law and with your judgment. This is the extreme of obstinacy that deserves wonder in both states, just as Allah described the condition of the hypocrites in His saying: "And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away" [al-Nur: 48], "But if the right is theirs, they come to him willingly" [al-Nur: 49].

It is also possible that the interrogative is denunciatory (inkari), meaning: they do not truly make you judge. The point of denial is the basic meaning the verb indicates, namely that its doer is serious; that is, their judging is not sincere but a mere show (tahkim suwari), by which they seek what agrees with their desires. For they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of what they have made you judge concerning, which is the judgment of Allah, and they have discarded it because it does not agree with their desires. Therefore they have also considered rejecting your judgment if it does not agree with their desires. So they are not truly judging. Thus the verb "they make you judge" is used in the sense of making a show of something without it actually occurring, like His saying, Exalted is He: "The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down about them informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: Mock on" [al-Tawbah: 64], and so on. It is also permissible on this view that the reference in "after that" be to the whole of what has been mentioned, namely the judging and the presence of the Torah with them,

Page 207
that is, they turn away from your judgment when the clear proof has appeared, which is the agreement of your ruling with the judgment of the Torah.

The clause "and those are not believers" is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to the pronoun of subject in "they make you judge." The negation of faith from them, with the omission of its complement, indicates that they did not believe in the Torah nor in Islam, so how could their judging be sincere?

The pronoun in "fiha" refers to the Torah. Its feminine form is in agreement with the name Torah, although its referent is a book; but the pattern fa'lah is well known among feminine nouns, like mawma'ah. The reason for naming their book Torah has been discussed earlier, at His saying, "And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel" [Al 'Imran: 3], in Surah Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 44 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light. By it the prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged for those who were Jews, and the rabbis and the scholars [also judged], by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah, and they were witnesses over it. So do not fear the people, but fear Me. And do not exchange My verses for a small price. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - those are the disbelievers.﴾

When he described the Torah as containing the judgment of Allah, he began a new praise of it and of those who judge by it. He described it as having been "sent down" to indicate that it is a revelation from Allah. So "descent" was used metaphorically for the arrival of revelation, because it is the arrival of something from a great source, and the great is imagined as high, as was mentioned more than once before.

"Light" is a metaphor (isti'arah) for clarity and truth, and for this reason it is conjoined with "guidance." Its rulings are guiding and clear. The expression of location (al-zarfiyyah) is literal, and guidance and light are their indicators. You may also take "light" here as a metaphor for faith and wisdom, as in His saying: ﴿He brings them out of darkness into light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257].
[p. 208]
In that case, there is a general and specific relationship between it and guidance, in which light is more general, and the conjunction is for the sake of that difference in generality.

As for what is meant by "the prophets": it is possible that they are the prophets of the Children of Israel, Moses and the prophets who came after him. Then what is meant by "those who submitted" is those whose particular law was like the law of Islam in sameness, because they were specifically given rulings different from the rulings of the general community of their people, but rather these rulings resemble Islam, and they are the true upright religion (al-hanifiyyah al-haqq). This is because there is no doubt that the prophets were in the most perfect condition of worship and dealing. Do you not see that wine was not forbidden in any law before Islam, and yet the prophets never drank it at all? Rather, the Torah forbade it to the priests of the Children of Israel, so what do you think about the Prophet? Perhaps this is what is meant by Abraham's charge to his sons with His saying: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132], as was mentioned there before. Yusuf, peace be upon him, also said in his supplication: ﴿Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous﴾ [Yusuf: 101]. The purpose of the description by His saying "those who submitted," in this way, is to point to the nobility and excellence of Islam, since it was the religion of the prophets.

It is also possible that by "the prophets" is meant Muhammad ﷺ, and he was referred to with the plural form to honor him.

The lam in His saying "for those who were Jews" is for the purpose (li-l-ajal), and it is not for transitivity of the verb "judges," since judgment in reality belongs to them and is upon them. "Those who were Jews" are the Jews, and this is a term that is synonymous with the meaning of "Israelites," except that its original sense is specific to the sons of Judah among them, and then it came to dominate over them later, as we mentioned earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians and the Sabians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], the verse, in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-rabbaniyyun is the plural of rabbani, who is the scholar attributed to the Lord (al-Rabb), that is, to Allah, may He be exalted. Based on this, the rabbani is a nisba (relative adjective) to the Lord not according to the regular analogy, as they said: sha'rani for one with much hair, and lihyani for one with a large beard. It was also said: the rabbani is the scholar who trains (al-murabbi), who begins
[p. 209]
people with the small parts of knowledge before its large parts. This explanation occurs in Sahih al-Bukhari. It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿But be rabbani [people] who teach the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79], in Surat Al 'Imran.

Al-ahbar is the plural of habr, which is the scholar in the Israelite religion (al-milla al-isra'iliyyah). It is pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the ha', but later scholars restricted it to the fatha in order to distinguish it from the name of the ink with which one writes. The rabbaniyyun and the ahbar are conjoined to "the prophets" because they are the inheritors of their knowledge, and it was from them that they received the religion.

Al-istihfaz (entrusting to preserve) means to be entrusted, and entrusting of the Book means the trust of understanding it in its true sense, by what its verses indicate. The term istihfaz, which is the seeking of preservation, is metaphorically used for the meaning of the command to understand well and to convey it to the community as it is.

So the ba' in His saying "by what they were entrusted" is for accompaniment (al-mulaabasah), meaning a judgment accompanying the truth, connected to it, not altered, not changed, and not interpreted in a way that serves desire. Among the subtle points of the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad is what 'Iyad related in al-Madarik, from Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Muntab, who said: "I was with Isma'il one day when he was asked: Why was alteration permitted for the people of the Torah but not for the people of the Qur'an? He said: Because Allah, may He be exalted, said regarding the people of the Torah: ﴿by what they were entrusted of the Book of Allah﴾, so He entrusted its preservation to them. And He said regarding the Qur'an: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ [al-Hijr: 9]. So Allah undertook its preservation, and alteration was not permitted for the people of the Qur'an." He said: "I mentioned that to al-Muhamili, and he said: There is no better statement than this."

The min in "of the Book" is explanatory (mubayyinah) for the vagueness of ma in His saying "by what they were entrusted." The Book of Allah is the Torah, so it is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun, in order to allow the definition through the genitive construction, which gives the honor of the Torah and its exaltation by attributing it to the name of Allah, may He be exalted.

The pronoun in "and they were" refers to the prophets, the rabbis and the scholars, meaning the ones mentioned were witnesses over the Book of Allah, that is, witnesses over its preservation from alteration. So the particle 'ala (over) here indicates the sense of firm establishment (al-tamakkun), and it is not the 'ala that verbs of witnessing take to introduce the one who is in the right, as that verb takes the lam to introduce the one witnessed for, namely the one who is righteous.
[p. 210]
Rather, it is here like the 'ala that verbs of guarding and watching take, meaning: they were guardians over the Book of Allah and protectors of it from misunderstanding and wrong interpretation, and they would lead its followers to the correct understanding of it and the correct practice of it.

For this reason, He followed it with the sentence ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾, which is connected by the fa' to His saying "and they were witnesses over it," since the one who is a guardian over a thing, faithful to the utmost degree of trust, does not fear anyone in carrying out the requirements of his trust, but he fears the one who entrusted him. So the address in His saying ﴿So do not fear the people﴾ may be to the Jews of the time of the revelation of the verse, and the fa' is for the consequence of what is related about the conduct of the earlier prophets and believers, so that they would be an example for their successors of both groups. The sentence on this view is parenthetical (mu'taridah). It may also be that the address is to the prophets, the rabbis and the scholars, and then it is according to an implied saying (ta'diru al-qawl), meaning: We said to them: ﴿So do not fear the people﴾. The consequence arises from the content of His saying ﴿by what they were entrusted of the Book of Allah﴾, because the complete fulfillment of entrustment appears in not caring about the people, whether they are pleased or angry, and in limiting regard to the pleasure of Allah, may He be exalted.

The discussion of the meaning of ﴿and do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾ has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - those are the disbelievers﴾ may be part of what is related by His saying ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾, because the meaning of fearing the people here is to oppose the rulings of the law of the Torah, or of other books of Allah, in order to please the desires of the people. It may also be a new statement to which these great admonitions were appended. On both views, the intended referents are the Jews and the warning to the Muslims against acting as they did.

The relative pronoun "whoever" (man) may refer to the specific group addressed by His saying ﴿and do not exchange My verses for a small price﴾, who are those who concealed some rulings of the Torah, such as the ruling on stoning. So Allah described them as disbelievers because of what they denied of their known law. The meaning is that they had already been characterized by disbelief before. So when they do not judge by what Allah has revealed, that is one of the effects of their earlier disbelief.
[p. 211]
It is also possible that by it is meant the category in general, and the relative clause is then an indication of the reason why they are disbelievers, which requires that everyone who does not judge by what Allah has revealed is a disbeliever. This has entailed two propositions: the first is that the one who abandons judgment by what the Torah contains, of what Allah revealed to Moses, is a disbeliever, or the one who abandons judgment by everything Allah revealed to the messengers is a disbeliever. The second is restricting the description of disbelief to the one who abandons judgment by what Allah has revealed.

As for the first proposition: those who declare the perpetrator of a major sin a disbeliever take the apparent meaning of this, because injustice in judgment is a major sin, and a major sin is disbelief according to them, and they call it "disbelief of ingratitude" (kufr ni'mah), in which all the major sins share. This is a false doctrine, as we have established more than once. As for the majority of Muslims, who are the People of the Sunnah from the Companions and those after them, it is for them an unspecified (mujmalah) proposition, because abandoning judgment by what Allah has revealed occurs in many conditions. So clarifying its generality is through the many texts that indicate the non-declaration of disbelief for sins, and the context of the verse clarifies its generality. For this reason, the majority of scholars said: what is meant by "whoever does not judge" here is specifically the Jews. This was said by al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and he related it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Muslim recorded it in his Sahih. On this view, "whoever" (man) is a relative pronoun, and it has the meaning of the lam of prior reference (lam al-'ahd). The meaning according to it is: whoever abandons judgment by what Allah has revealed with an abandonment like this abandonment, which is abandoning judgment accompanied by disparagement of its validity. The Jews were known for frequently opposing their judges to the rulings of their Book, based on their alteration of it, believing that its rulings did not fit their circumstances, as they did regarding the punishment for fornication. So the restriction is claimed (ad'a'i) and this is the one appropriate to the occasion of revelation of the verses of which this was an appendix. So the relative pronoun serves to define the people of this relative clause, and it is not the cause for the predicate. The fa' was added to its predicate because it resembles a conditional in the necessity of its predicate following it, meaning: those who are known by this description are the ones who, if you ask about the disbelievers, they are precisely them, because they disbelieved and did evil.
