And a group said: what is meant by ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ is whoever abandons judgment by it out of denial of it, or contempt for it, or disparagement of its truth, after it has been established as the judgment of Allah by mass transmission (tawatur) or by hearing it from the Messenger of Allah, heard by the responsible person himself. This is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn
[p. 212]
'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan. On this view "whoever" (man) is conditional, and abandoning judgment is general, and its explanation is in other evidences. Beneath this is another situation, which is the commitment not to judge by what Allah has revealed within oneself, like the act of a Muslim in whose land the legal rulings are established but who enters under non-Islamic courts by his own choice. That commitment is more severe than opposition in particular matters, especially if his act is not for the sake of obtaining a worldly benefit. Greater than that is compelling people to judge by other than what Allah has revealed, by the rulers, and these are graded levels, some of which may entail the implication of apostasy if they indicate contempt for or disparagement of the judgment of Allah.

Some scholars went to a figurative interpretation of the meaning of disbelief. It was said that disbelief is used to mean disobedience, as the wife of Thabit ibn Qays said: "I hate disbelief in Islam," meaning adultery. That is, he committed an act resembling the acts of disbelievers and not fitting for believers, and this was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Tawus said: it is a disbelief lesser than [full] disbelief, and it is not a disbelief that removes one from faith, because the one who does not judge by what Allah has revealed may do so out of desire, and that is not disbelief but disobedience. He may also do it because he did not regard the text as definitive in its indication of the ruling, just as many scholars abandoned taking the apparent meanings of the Qur'an and judged by the implications of their interpretation. This is common.

This verse and the one after it concern the judges. As for the consent of the litigants to the judgment of Allah, it has been discussed in His saying: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge concerning that over which they dispute among themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], the verse, and we explained its aspects. It will come in His saying: ﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away﴾ [al-Nur: 48], to His saying: ﴿Rather, those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Nur: 50], in Surat al-Nur.

The second matter: the restriction (qasr) here is intended to emphasise the gravity of this great sin, which is expressed figuratively by the word "disbelief" (kufr), or to affirm that they have reached the highest degrees of disbelief, namely the disbelief that is joined by oppression and the alteration of rulings. Know that what is meant here by the relative clause (silah), or by the conditional verb (fi'l al-shart) since both are negated, is the attribute of the opposite of each of them. That is: "And whoever judges by other than what God has sent down." This is a third interpretation of the verse, because whoever neither judges by what God has sent down nor judges by anything else, by abandoning judgment among people or by calling for reconciliation, the community does not differ that he is neither a disbeliever nor a sinner. Otherwise it would follow that every ruler would be a disbeliever whenever he is not actually engaged in judging, and that everyone who is not a ruler would be a disbeliever. The meaning, then, is: "And whoever judges, but does not judge by what God has sent down."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 45:

﴿And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life, and an eye for an eye, and a nose for a nose, and an ear for an ear, and a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds is retaliation. But whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾

The clause "And We prescribed" (kataba-na) is conjoined (ʿutifat) to the clause "We sent down the Torah" (anzalna al-Tawrat). The occasion for conjoining this ruling to what preceded it is that they (the Jews) altered the rulings of retaliation (qisas) just as they altered the rulings of the prescribed punishment for fornication (hadd al-zina), distinguishing between the slain and the wounded, as will come. For this reason He appended it with His words: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾, just as He appended the verse indicating the alteration of the ruling of the prescribed punishment for fornication with His words: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is they who are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44].

The word "kataba" (prescribed/written) here is a metaphor for legislating and obligating, indicated by its construction with the particle (ʿala) "upon", i.e., We obligated upon them therein, meaning in the Torah, the content of ﴿that the life is for the life﴾. This ruling is likewise recorded in the Torah. As the construction of the verb (kataba-na) with the particle (fi) "in" requires, it is the use of the expression in both its literal and figurative senses.

In this there is an indication that this ruling cannot be denied, because it is written, and writing adds firmness to speech, as was mentioned previously at His words, exalted is He, ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, then write it down﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282] in Surat al-Baqarah. And al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Do the desires nullify what is in the scrolls?"

Page 215
The thing prescribed upon them is the verbal noun (masdar) derived from (anna). In such a case, the verbal noun is taken from the meaning of the letter of ba' (bi), which is compensation (taʿwid), i.e., We prescribed the compensation of life for life, that is, the slain life for the killing life, i.e., We prescribed upon them the equivalence of retaliation.

The reciters agreed on opening the hamzah of (anna) here, because what was prescribed in the Torah is not the very wording of these sentences, but the meaning derived from them, which is compensatory equivalence and parity within them.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿and the eye for the eye﴾ and what is conjoined to it in the accusative, as a conjunction (ʿataf) upon the subject of (anna). Al-Kisa'i read it in the nominative. This is permissible when (anna) has completed its predicate, so the conjunction is considered to be upon the whole clause.

Al-nafs (the self/soul) means the essence (dhat), and it was discussed previously at His words, exalted is He, ﴿and you forget yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44] in Surat al-Baqarah. "Al-udhun" (ear) is with a damma on the hamzah and sukun on the dhal, and also with a damma on the dhal. The intended meaning of the first "nafs" is the self of the one who was wronged, and likewise in "and the eye" etc.

The ba' in His words "bi-al-nafs" and its four counterparts is the ba' of compensation, and all the words governed by ba' are predicates of (anna). The complement of the prepositional phrase in each of them is omitted, being a specific state (kawn khass) indicated by the context of the speech; so it is estimated: the slain life is compensated by the life of the killer, and the destroyed eye is compensated by the eye of the destroyer, i.e., by its destruction; and likewise the life is destroyed by the life; the eye is gouged out by the eye; the nose is cut off by the nose; the ear is cut off by the ear.

The definite article in the five places attaches to the organ of the one wronged, and the five objects of the ba' are the organs of the aggressor.

Limiting the mention to these organs, rather than other parts of the body such as the hand, the foot, or the finger, is because cutting usually occurs during striking with the intent of severing the neck; the sword may swerve from cutting the head and strike some of the organs connected to it, such as an eye, a nose, an ear, or a tooth. Likewise in close combat, because the face confronts the attacker. Al-Huraysh ibn Hilal said:

"We expose to the swords, when we meet, faces that are not exposed to the slaps."

Page 215
His words, "And for wounds is retaliation," inform concerning retaliation for wounds by an omitted genitive construction, i.e., wounds that are subject to retaliation.

"Qisas" is the verbal noun of qasasahu, which indicates reciprocity, because the one wronged retaliates against the aggressor and the aggressor retaliates against the one wronged, i.e., each of them cuts off the claim of the other by this. It is also permissible for "qisas" to be a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, like "khalq" meaning "makhluq" and "nasb" meaning "mansub", i.e., some of them are retaliated against by others. Qisas means equivalence, i.e., the punishment of the aggressor for wounds by inflicting upon him a wound like the wound he inflicted deliberately. The meaning is: when that is possible, i.e., when one is secure from exceeding equivalence in the punishment, as when he wounds him with a head-wound (ma'mumah) on the head, for he does not know, when striking the aggressor's head, what the extent of the blow will be, so it may cause his death, and he would then pass to the full blood-money or part of it.

All of this concerns deliberate offenses. As for unintentional killing, the verse does not address it, because the intended point is that they did not establish the ruling of the Torah concerning the offense.

Nafi', Hamzah, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read "wa al-jurooha" in the accusative as a conjunction upon the subject of (anna). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it in the nominative as a resumptive (isti'naf), because it is a general statement of the ruling on wounds after having detailed the ruling on cutting off organs.

The benefit of informing about what Allah legislated for the Children of Israel regarding retaliation here is to further record their opposition to the rulings of their own Book. That is because the Jews in Madinah had entered into the wars of Bu'ath, where Qurayzah and al-Nadir were at war; then they disengaged, and Qurayzah was defeated. Al-Nadir stipulated upon Qurayzah that the blood-money of a Nadiri is double the blood-money of a Qurazi, and that a Qurazi is killed for a Nadiri, but a Nadiri is not killed for a Qurazi. So Allah exposed their distortion of their Book. This is like His words, exalted is He, ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 84] up to His words: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85]. It is also permissible that by this is intended also the confirmation of the Islamic law, since it came with the equivalence of retaliation and nullified the tribal inequality in bloodshed that existed in the Jahiliyyah and among the Jews.

Page 216
There is no doubt that confirming the law by another law makes it more acceptable to souls. It also indicates that this ruling is an old intention of Allah, exalted is He, and that its benefit is constant and does not vary with the differences of peoples and times, because the Arabs have always had within their souls reluctance at equalizing a noble with a weak person in retaliation, as Kabshah, sister of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib, said, seeking vengeance for her brother 'Abd Allah ibn Ma'di Karib:

"He would kill by compulsion a man who had no equal to him in blood-price, but there is no equivalence in blood."

She means: we are content that a man named Jabr be killed for a great man who is not his equal; but Islam nullified the inequality in blood. "Takayul" among them is an expression for estimating a soul as equal to a number of souls. The elders of Banu Asad valued the blood of Hujr, father of Imru' al-Qays, at the blood-money of ten leaders of Banu Asad, but Imru' al-Qays refused to accept this valuation and said to them: "You know that Hujr was not one for whom anything could be a counterpart." Muhalhil, when he killed Bujayr, said: "Let him pay with the thong of the sandal of Kulayb." Al-Ba' means equal counterpart.

The verse has enumerated in retaliation items whose striking is frequent in disputes, because the head contains them, and the killer intends the head initially.

His words, "But whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him," are part of what He informs concerning the Children of Israel. So the meaning of "whoever forgoes" is whoever among them forgoes, and the pronoun in "it" refers to what the ba' of compensation indicates in His words "bi-al-nafs" etc., i.e., whoever forgoes the right that he has, that is, relinquishes the compensation.

The pronoun in "for him" refers to "whoever forgoes." The intended meaning of "forgoing" is pardon, because since pardon concerns a established right in the hand of the one entitled to retaliation, its waiver is treated as a gift, to indicate its great reward.

Page 217
By this it becomes clear that the meaning of "it is an expiation for him" is that it expiates for him great sins, because of what this pardon contains of winning hearts, removing grudges, and preserving the lives and organs of the community.

He returned to warn against opposing the ruling of Allah, saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾, to point out that encouragement to pardon does not imply belittling the ruling or nullifying its practice, because the ruling of retaliation was legislated for great wisdoms: among them deterrence, among them the consoling of the heart of the one wronged, and among them the averting of the wronged parties' watching for vengeance against the aggressors or their peoples. So nullifying the ruling of retaliation eliminates these benefits, and it is injustice, because it is a disregard of the right of the one wronged or his guardian. As for pardoning the offender, it realizes all these benefits and adds the benefit of mutual affection, because it is out of goodwill. The dullness of the judges of the Children of Israel had covered their understanding, so they made nullifying the ruling equivalent to pardon. This is the reason for the repetition of the warning after the recommendation of pardon. The commentators have not drawn attention to this. And by this it is determined that the return of this warning is to the Children of Israel, like its predecessor.

His words, "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - it is they who are the wrongdoers," the discussion of it is like the discussion of its counterpart mentioned earlier. The intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" is the disbelievers, because wrongdoing is applied to disbelief, so this is a confirmation of what is in the previous verse. It is also possible that what is intended by it is oppression, so that the attribution of the quality of wrongdoing is for added condemnation of them in their disbelief, because they are disbelievers who are wrongdoers.

[Page 218]

This is a conjunctive continuation of the statement ﴿Indeed, We revealed the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 44], shifting to the condition of the Christians, given His words: ﴿Let the people of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾. It also explains another type of the Jews' turning away from the rulings that Allah had prescribed for them. Having mentioned two types related to their distortion of the rulings of the Torah, the first being what they distorted and then wavered about, so that in the end they doubted and resorted to having the Messenger judge between them, and the second being what they distorted and turned away from, refusing to be troubled by it, namely the nullification of the rulings of retaliation (qisas),

this is a third type: their turning away from Allah's judgment entirely, by their denial of what Jesus, peace be upon him, brought.

Al-taqfiya (the act of following) is the verbal noun of qaffa, meaning he made him follow (yaqfu), i.e., come after him. Its unaugmented verb is qafa, with a light fa', and qafahu means he went toward his back (qafa), that is, he went behind him. Thus taqfiya means following, derived from qafa (the back), just as tawajjaha (he faced) is derived from wajh (face), and ta'aqqaba (he followed on the heel) from 'aqib (heel).

The doubled form qaffa is the intensive of the single form qafa. The basic function of doubling is to make the verb transitive to an object it did not previously take. When the doubling in qaffayna here is taken as making the verb transitive, it requires two objects: the first is the one that was the object before doubling, and the second is the one the verb has now been made to reach. This follows the pattern of the bab kasa (the verb form of kasa, to clothe, taking two objects). In that case the proper construction would be: "wa-qaffaynahum 'Isa ibn Maryam" (And We made them follow Jesus, son of Mary). The preposition ba' in bi-'Isa would then serve for emphasis, as in ﴿wa-msahu bi-ru'usikum﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 6], "and wipe your heads." If, however, the doubling is not for transitivity but merely to indicate repetition of the action, as in jawwaltu (I roamed about) and tawwaftu (I circled about), then the proper construction would be: "wa-qaffaynahum bi-'Isa ibn Maryam." The Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) follows the first view, making the ba' in bi-'Isa a transitive particle. On both views, the object of qaffayna is elided, indicated by His words ﴿upon their traces﴾, because it contains the pronoun of the elided object. This is the verification of his statement, and the commentators who glossed his work accepted it.

His words "upon their traces" are an emphasis on the meaning of the verb qaffayna and convey the speed of the following.

The pronoun in "their traces" refers to the prophets, the rabbis and the scholars. Jesus was sent in the line of Zakariyya, the guardian of his mother Maryam and the father of Yahya. It is also possible that "upon their traces" means "upon their way and guidance."

Al-musaddiq (the confirmer) is one who informs of the confirmation of an informant. Here it is intended to mean the supporter and affirmer of the Torah.

He placed it "between his hands" because it preceded him, and what precedes is said to be "between the hands" of whoever came earlier. "Min al-Tawrat" (of the Torah) is an explanation of "ma" (what).

The discussion of the meaning of Torah and Gospel has already passed in the beginning of Surat Al 'Imran.

The clause ﴿in it is guidance and light﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). The meaning of guidance and light has already been mentioned.

"Musaddiqan" (confirming) is also a circumstantial clause, relating to the Gospel. There is therefore no repetition between it and His words ﴿with Jesus son of Mary, confirming﴾, since the subject of the circumstance differs and the manner of confirmation differs. Jesus' confirmation of the Torah is his command to revive its rulings, which is a real confirmation. The Gospel's confirmation of the Torah is its containing what agrees with its rulings, which is a metaphorical confirmation. This confirmation does not contradict the fact that he abrogated some rulings of the Torah, as Allah related of him: ﴿and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50], because an affirmative verb has no general implication.

Al-maw'iza (admonition) is speech that softens the heart and restrains one from committing what is forbidden.

The clause "wa-liyahkum" (and let them judge) is conjoined to "ataynahu" (We gave him). The majority of readers recite "wa-liyahkum" with a sukun on the lam and a jussive verb, taking the lam as the imperative lam (lam al-amr). There is no doubt that this command predates the coming of Islam, so it is among what Allah commanded those to whom Jesus was sent, namely the Jews and Christians. It is therefore known that the clause contains an implied saying, which is the thing conjoined to ﴿and We gave him the Gospel﴾, meaning: "We gave him the Gospel, described with those great attributes, and We said: let the people of the Gospel judge." This completes the preparation for His words that follow: ﴿and whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾. Thus the indicators for the implied saying are numerous and mutually supporting.

Hamza recited "li-yahkuma" with a kasra on the lam and a fatha on the mim, taking the lam as the lam of purpose (lam kay li-l-ta'lil). In this reading, the clause "li-yahkuma" is conjoined to His words "in it is guidance," which is a circumstantial clause. The purpose is conjoined to the circumstance by a verbal conjunction that does not share the ruling, because the explicit lam of purpose is an indicator that it is not correct to share the ruling through conjunction, so its conjunction is like the conjunction of clauses with differing meanings. The author of the Kashshaf assumed in this reading an elided verb after the waw, meaning "and We gave him the Gospel," which is indicated by his earlier words ﴿and We gave him the Gospel﴾. This is an estimate of the meaning, not an estimate of the structure of the sentence.

The "fasiqun" (defiantly disobedient) means the unbelievers, since fisq is used for disbelief, and so it is of the same kind as in the first verse. It is also possible that it means departing from the rulings of their law, whether they disbelieved in it or believed in it but opposed it. In that case it is a rebuke of the Christians for their laxity regarding the rulings of their scripture, which is less severe than the rebuke of the Jews.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 48:

﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming that which preceded it of the Book and as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed and do not follow their desires, away from what has come to you of the truth. For each of you We have made a law and a method. And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one nation, but [He did it] to test you in what He has given you. So race to [all that is] good. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.﴾

The preceding verses made a circuit through the mention of the revelation of the Torah and the Gospel, and then returned from them to the intended subject, which is the sending down of the Qur'an. This was like the return of the last part of a verse to its first part (radd al-ʿajuz ʿala al-ṣadr), with respect to His saying: ﴿O Messenger, do not let grieve you those who race to disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], to make clear that the Qur'an came abrogating what preceded it, and that the Jews' being held to account for abandoning the practice of the Torah and the Gospel is a holding to account for them on account of their actions before the coming of Islam. It also informs them that they should not hope that Muhammad ﷺ would judge between them by other than what Allah has legislated in Islam. Thus His saying ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ came as an arrangement of the sending down of the heavenly books and as a preparation for His saying ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾.

And His saying ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ occurred in the position of the intended transition (takhallus), so all the verses came orderly, coherent and harmonized in the most wonderful manner.

The first "Book" is the Qur'an, so its definiteness is for a known referent (al-ʿahd). The second "book" is a genus that includes the earlier books, so its definiteness is for the genus (al-jins). "Confirming" (muṣaddiq) has already been explained.

As for "muhaymin" (guardian), the more apparent view is that its hamza-root letter (hāʾ) is original and its verb is of the pattern fayʿala, like sayṭara (to dominate). However, no bare verb from it has been heard, so *hamana* has not been heard. The lexicographers said: there is no parallel to this verb except *haynama* (when one calls out or recites), and *bayqara* (when one leaves the Hijaz for Syria), and *sayṭara* (when one overpowers). There is no parallel to it in the pattern mufayʿil except the active participles of these verbs, and they added *mubayṭir*, the name for a veterinarian, though *bayṭara* has not been heard, but *baṭara* has; and *mujaymir*, the name of a mountain, which Imru' al-Qays mentioned in his saying:

"As if the peaks of the head of Mujaymir at dawn,
from the flood and the debris, were a spindle's whorl."

Muhaymin has been explained as "the elevated" and "the watchful guardian," and among the names of Allah, the Exalted, is al-Muhaymin.

It has also been said: muhaymin is derived from *amina*, and its origin is an active participle from *aminahu ʿalayhi* in the sense of "he entrusted him with it to guard it," so it is a metaphor in its necessary meaning, which is supervision (al-raqabah). Its original form is *muʾʾamin*, and it seems they wanted to distinguish it from the active participle of *āmana* in the sense of "believed" and in the sense of *āmanahu*, because this figurative meaning became an independent literal meaning. So they changed the second hamza into a yāʾ and the first hamza into a hāʾ, as they said for *arāqa* becoming *harāqa*, and they said: *haymana*.

The verse has indicated the two states of the Qur'an in relation to the books before it. It is confirming (muṣaddiq) of some of what is in the laws, establishing it, and affirming in every ruling whose benefit is universal, whose benefit does not differ according to differing nations and times. It is in this description "confirming," that is, verifying and affirming. It is also nullifying (mubṭil) of some of what is in the earlier laws, and abrogating many rulings of everything whose benefits were particular and temporary, in which the circumstances of specific peoples were taken into account.

His saying ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ means: by what Allah has revealed to you in the Qur'an, or by what He has inspired to you, or "judge between them by what Allah revealed in the Torah and the Gospel, as long as Allah has not abrogated it with a new ruling," because the law of those before us is law for us when Allah has established its law for those before us. Thus the Prophet's ruling against the two Jews by stoning was a ruling by what is in the Torah. It is possible that it was supported by the Qur'an, if at that time His saying had already come: "The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit adultery, stone them both." It is also possible that it was not supported, but Allah revealed to His Messenger that the ruling of the Torah concerning such a case is stoning, so he judged by it, and informed the Jews of their concealment of this ruling. The meaning of His saying ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ is connected with the meaning of His saying ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]. There is nothing in this verse that requires the abrogation of the ruling conveyed by His saying ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]. Rather, it is an explanation which some of the early scholars called by the name of abrogation (naskh), before the boundaries of technical terms were fixed.

The prohibition of following their desires, that is, the desires of the Jews when they made him the judge, hoping that he would rule against them according to what had become established among their customs, is intended as a prohibition against judging by other than the ruling of Allah when they resort to him for judgment, since it is not permissible to judge by anything other than it, even if it were an earlier law, because the sending down of the Qur'an as a guardian nullified what contradicts it, and its sending down as confirming affirmed what agrees with it and approved what it does not contradict.

It is not permissible for the Messenger to judge by other than the law of Allah. Therefore the purpose of this prohibition is either: an announcement of that, so that people will know it and those who are hoping will despair that he would judge for them according to what they desire; so the address to the Prophet ﷺ with His saying ﴿and do not follow their desires﴾ is meant to establish that in the knowledge of people, like His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿If you associate others with Allah, your deeds will surely be lost﴾ [al-Zumar: 65]. Or it is Allah's clarification to His Messenger of the way of preferring one of two proofs when evidences conflict, namely that the desires of the adversaries should not be the means of preference. This is because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, out of his intense eagerness for the guidance of people, might hesitate in deciding this arbitration, since they had promised that if he judged against them by what had become established among their customs, they would believe in him. It may be said: when they agreed to his judgment, why should they not be held to it, given the evident benefit of that, which is their entry into Islam? So Allah made clear to him that matters of the Shari'ah are not to be treated lightly, and that the benefit of respecting the Shari'ah among its adherents outweighs the benefit of

صفحة ٢٢٣
a group entering Islam, because Islam is not fitting for it to be weak for its seekers. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has conferred a favor upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you should be truthful﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17].

His saying ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ serves as a justification for the prohibition, meaning: if their desires are in following their own law or their customs, then leave them to what they are accustomed to, and hold fast to your law.

Ash-shir'ah and ash-shari'ah: abundant water of a river or valley. It is said: "the shari'ah of the Euphrates." The religion was called a shari'ah by way of analogy, because in it is the healing and purification of souls. The Arabs often liken things to water and its conditions, as we have already mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿would have known it from those among them who derive it﴾ [al-Nisa': 83] in Surat al-Nisa'.

Al-minhaj: the broad road. Here it is an imaginative image (takhyil), by which is meant the path of a people to the water, as in the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"And I sent my bucket into the water with its rope."

Mentioning the rope is a mere imaginative image. It is also possible to make for it a companion in the likened item, by likening the customs derived from the Shari'ah, or the indicators of derivation from the Shari'ah, or the methods of understanding it, to the road that leads to the water. So the method of the Muslims does not contradict their connection to Islam; it is like the method of those guided to the water. The method of others deviates from their religion, just as the Jews had made customs contrary to their Shari'ah; that is like a road leading to other than the watering place. In this statement there is an ambiguity intended to alert both groups to the difference between their two states, and by reflection it becomes clear to them.

His saying ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one nation﴾. "Making" (al-jaʿl) here means determining. Otherwise, Allah commanded people to be one nation upon the religion of Islam; but He arranged laws and natural dispositions, and caused the guidance of one group and the misguidance of another, and He knew that according to what He created in them of readiness, expressed by success or abandonment, inclination or turning away, resolve or obstinacy. There is no excuse for anyone in that, because the knowledge of Allah is not known to us; it becomes manifest to us only by what appears in events.

The "ummah" is a great community whose religion and belief are one; this is according to the technical usage of the Shari'ah. The original sense of ummah in the speech of the Arabs is a large number of people who trace back to one lineage and speak one language. That is, if He had willed, He would have created you upon one measure, as He created the kinds of animals, which are not receptive to increase or to self-development.

The meaning of ﴿to test you in what He has given you﴾ is what we have indicated concerning the creation of readiness and the like. "Balaʾ" means experience (al-khibrah). Here the intended meaning is that the effect of that may appear to people, and the intended meaning is a necessary implication by way of metonymy (kinayah), like the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i:

"I came while the spear swayed between us,
to know who among us is the coward and who is the brave."

He did not intend only "to know," but intended "so that it would become manifest to me and to people." Its meaning is that Allah entrusted the choice between the paths of good and their opposites to people's intellects and their acquisition, as a wisdom from Him, the Exalted, so that people would compete in putting their intellectual gifts into action; thus the effects of knowledge appear, those of knowledge increase in knowledge, and sound proofs are established for correct belief. All of this manifests what Allah placed in human nature of capacity for good and guidance according to readiness, and that is of the nature of testing. That is why He said ﴿to test you in what He has given you﴾, that is, in everything He has given you of intellect and reflection. Thus the superiority among individuals of the human species becomes manifest, until some of them reach high ranks; and among the laws which He has given you, so that the extent of your acting by them becomes manifest, and reward is given according to the measure of action.

He made ﴿so race to the good﴾ a consequence of "﴿to test you﴾", because by that racing the effect of success becomes clearer and more evident.

Al-istibaq: competition. Here it is a metaphor for rivalry, because the one who does good does not prevent another from doing the like or more, so it resembles racing. And because the verb "istabiqu" is construed by implication with the meaning of "take" or "hasten to," the verb is governed directly by "the good things" (al-khayrat), though its proper construction would be with "ila," as in His saying: ﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [al-Hadid: 21].

His saying ﴿then He will inform you about that over which you used to differ﴾, that is, concerning the disagreement over accepting the religion.

It is possible that his saying, "And [that] judge between them by what Allah has revealed," is coordinated as a conjunction of clause upon clause, by being made coordinate with the clause ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed and do not follow their desires﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 48). In that case it is a return to that command for its emphasis, and his saying ﴿and beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾ is built upon it, just as his saying ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 48) was built upon its counterpart. The "an" would then be explanatory (tafsiriyyah, "an" introducing an explanation). The explanatory "an" serves to strengthen the connection of the explanation to what is explained, because it can be dispensed with, as when you say, "I sent to him, do such-and-such," or "I sent to him that he should do such-and-such." When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He had sent down the Book to His Messenger, He made the command to judge by what was revealed in it follow from it by means of the particle fa', saying ﴿So judge between them﴾. This shows that judging by what is in it is one of the effects of its revelation. He then coordinated with it something indicating that the Book commands judgment by what is in it, by means of what the explanatory "an" indicates in His saying ﴿and [that] judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. The purpose is thereby reinforced by mentioning it twice, with variety and freshness of style. The sense becomes: "We sent down to you the Book with the truth, [namely] that you judge between them by what Allah has revealed; so judge between them by it." What made the coordination of explanation good here is the length of the intervening speech between the explaining verb and its explanation.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) took it as coordination of single words (ʿaṭf al-mufradat). He said: "[The clause] an uhkum ("that judge") is coordinated upon 'the Book' in His saying ﴿and We sent down to you the Book﴾, as if it were said: 'And We sent down to you that judge.'" He therefore made "an" a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle entering upon the imperative verb. The meaning would then be: "And We sent down to you the command to judge by what Allah has revealed," as He said in ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, that warn your people﴾ (Nuh: 1), meaning: We sent him with the command to warn. In the commentary on Surah Yunus, at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and that you set your face toward the religion as a ḥanīf﴾ (Yunus: 105), he explained that this is the view of Sibawayh, who permitted the verbal "an" (maṣdariyyah) to be joined to the imperative and prohibitive verbs, because the purpose of joining it is to join it to what carries the sense of a verbal noun, and the imperative and prohibitive indicate the sense of a verbal noun. Here he gave as the reason: "Because the command is a verb like other verbs." Yet taking it as explanatory is preferable and more eloquent, and "an" would be inserted between the two clauses, explaining the verb "sent down" in His saying ﴿So judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 48); for "sent down" (anzala) includes the sense of "saying" (qawl), so the explanatory particle has a place here.

His saying ﴿and do not follow their desires﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 48) is like His saying before it, ﴿and do not follow their desires, away from the truth that has come to you﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 48).

His saying ﴿and beware of them, lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾ is intended to expose their scheming and to make them despair of what they hoped for. This is because the Prophet's (ﷺ) caution against that does not require a command, since he is protected (ʿiṣmah) from opposing the judgment of Allah.

It is also possible that it is intended to refute what appears to be a benefit in judging between those who come to him for judgment from among the Jews according to their customs, if it is correct what is related: that some of their rabbis promised the Prophet (ﷺ) that if he ruled in their favour in that matter, they would believe in him and the Jews would follow them in imitation. Allah therefore showed him that the benefit of preserving the sanctity of the rulings of the religion, even among those who are not its adherents, takes precedence over the benefit of the faith of a group of Jews. This is because it is the nature of faith that it should not bargain with people over following it, as we have stated just above. The aim, in addition, is to warn the Muslims against imagining such a thing.

For this reason He placed His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ as a consequence of it, meaning: if you judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, and they turn away, then know (fa-ʿlam), that is, that this is a sign that Allah intends for them wretchedness and punishment for some of their sins, and there is no blame upon you for their turning away. By "some of their sins" He meant some unspecified part; that is, some of their sins suffice for their being afflicted, and their turning away from your judgment is a sign of Allah's abandonment (khidhlān) of them.

He concluded it with His saying ﴿and indeed many of the people are defiant transgressors﴾, so that their persistence in their error would be made light for him, since this is the habit (shanshanah) of most people, meaning: these are among them. The statement is thus a metonymy (kinayah) for their being defiantly transgressive.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 50:

﴿Do they then seek the judgment of ignorance? And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾

The fa' (fa, "then") is a consequence of the import of His words, ﴿But if they turn away, then know﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49] etc., as a question about what they intend by that turning away. The interrogation is one of denunciation (istifham inkari), because they sought the judgment of ignorance (hukm al-jahiliyyah). The judgment of ignorance is what was established among the Jews of the practice of blood-money equalization (takayul al-dima'), which passed down to them from the rulings of the people of Yathrib, who were a people of jahiliyyah. For the Banu al-Nadir did not accept equality with Qurayzah, as has preceded; and [it is also] what they had instituted of rulings among the people of jahiliyyah, namely the deviation from stoning, which is the judgment of the Torah.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read yabghun with the ya' of the third person, the pronoun referring back to (man) in His words, ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 47]. Ibn 'Amir read it with the ta' of address, on the basis that it is an address to the Jews according to the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

The waw in His words, ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment﴾, is the waw of the circumstantial clause (waw al-hal), and it is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh). The interrogation is one of denunciation, carrying the sense of negation, i.e., there is none better than Him in judgment. It is addressed to the Muslims, since there is no benefit in addressing the Jews with this.

As for His words, ﴿for a people who are certain﴾, the lam in it is not connected to "judgment" (hukman), since the intended referent of what it governs is not the one judged for; nor is it the lam of emphasis (lam al-taqwiyah), because "for a people who are certain" is not, in meaning, an object of "judgment". This lam is called the lam of clarification (lam al-bayan) and lam al-tabyin, and it is the one that enters upon the intended meaning of the speech, whether it is a report or a directive. It occurs in expressions such as their saying: saqyan laka (may you be given water), wa-j'dan lahu (may he be cut off), and in the hadith: "Tabban wa-suhqan liman baddala ba'di" (ruin and destruction upon whoever changes after me), and His exalted words: ﴿Far, far is what you are promised﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 36], and haasha lillah (far be it from Allah). This is because the intended purpose is to draw attention to the meaning of the speech. From it is His exalted words about Zulaykha: ﴿And she said, "Come, I am ready for you"﴾ [Yusuf: 23], because her readiness for him was strange and would not occur to Yusuf's mind, so he did not know what she intended, and she said to him ﴿Come, I am ready for you﴾ [Yusuf: 23], if (haytu) is a verb-like particle with the sense of "I have prepared myself." Similar to His exalted words here: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain﴾. The intended meaning may be known yet its concealment is feared, so the lam is brought for the increase of clarification, as in haasha lillah; and in that case it is worthy of the name lam al-tabyin, like the one entering upon the addressee in direct address, as in their saying: saqyan laka wa-ra'yan, and similar, and in His words: (Hayta) is a verb-like particle of command with the sense of "come." It was not made a lam of emphasis in some of these instances, because the lam of emphasis can be dispensed with while its governed element is mentioned, whereas in these instances the governed element of the lam is not mentioned except together with it.

[Page 229]

Those who believed were prepared to accept the prohibition against allying with the People of the Book, after they had heard of the turmoil of the Jews regarding their religion, their attempts to mislead the Muslims, and their manipulation of affairs against the Messenger (ﷺ). So He addressed them directly with His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾, and so on, because allegiance (wilayah) is founded on agreement, harmony and connection. Those people are not fit to be allies of the Muslims, because of the great distance between their religious ethics and the Muslims' ethics, and because they conceal scheming against the Muslims. The prohibition here is stripped of any explanation or guidance, being sufficient with what preceded it.

The sentence is an independent new sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a fresh beginning). The cause of the prohibition was what the Jews had done. But when the prohibition was intended in general, it was not restricted to them, lest the Muslims suppose they were permitted to ally with the Christians. To prevent this, the Christians are conjoined with the Jews here, because the factor calling for non-alliance is one in both groups, namely the difference of religion and the aversion arising from their denial of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). Although the Christians did not at that time cause harm like the Jews, it was likely that harm would come from them when its cause appeared.

In this there is an indication of the reason for combining here the prohibition against allying with the Christians with His saying later: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believed are those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82]. There is no doubt that this verse was revealed after the Battle of Tabuk or close to it, when the Muslims had come to border the territories of the Arab Christians. It is reported from al-Suddi that after the Day of Uhud some Muslims resolved to ally with a Jew, and another resolved to ally with a Christian, as will come, so the mention of the Christians is then not an incidental insertion (idmaj).

He follows this with His saying: ﴿some of them are allies of others﴾, meaning that they are more deserving of allying with one another, that is, each group's allegiance to some of its own people, because the individuals of each group are close to one another in morals and deeds, so agreement among them is easy. The meaning is not that the Jews are allies of the Christians. The tanwin on "ba'd" (some) is the tanwin of compensation (tanwin 'iwad), meaning "allies of some of them." This is a metaphor (kinayah) for the denial of their allegiance to the believers and for the prohibition on the believers allying with either group.

Allegiance here is allegiance of affection and support, and it has no connection with inheritance. For this reason Malik did not hold that a Jew inherits from a Christian or the reverse, adopting the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The people of two religions do not inherit from one another." Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa held that some people of religions inherit from others, and they regarded disbelief as one religion, adopting the apparent meaning of this verse. This is also the view of Dawud.

As for His saying: ﴿And whoever of you allies with them, then indeed he is of them﴾, "whoever" (man) is a conditional particle, which requires that everyone who allies with them becomes one of them. He made their allegiance the cause of the one allying becoming one of them. Apparently this requires that allegiance to them is entry into their religion, because the sense of "being of them" here cannot stand except by being in their religion. Since the believer who holds the creed of faith and follows the Messenger, without hypocrisy, is necessarily a Muslim, the verse requires interpretation (ta'wil). The commentators have interpreted it in one of two ways.

The first is to take allegiance in His saying "whoever allies with them" as the complete allegiance, which is approval of their religion and denigration of the religion of Islam. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Whoever allies with them by their creed and religion, he is of them in disbelief and in eternal abiding in the Fire."

The second is to interpret His saying "then indeed he is of them" as a eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh), meaning that he is like one of them in deserving punishment. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Whoever allies with them by their actions, such as assisting them, without holding their creed and without damaging his faith, he is of them in the hatred and blame that falls upon them." End of quotation. This generality in His saying "then indeed he is of them" is an exaggeration in warning against allying with them at the time the verse was revealed. God was not pleased with the Muslims at that time allying with the Jews and the Christians, because that would mix them up with the hypocrites. The affairs of the Muslims at that time were in confusion, since around them were the hypocrites, the weak among the Muslims, the Jews and the polytheists. Therefore it was necessary, to preserve the community's unity, to be free of anything that might cast suspicion upon them.

The scholars of the Sunnah have agreed that what falls short of approving disbelief and colluding with its people in it, from allegiance, does not expel one from the Islamic bond, but it is a great misguidance. And it has degrees of strength according to the strength of the allegiance and the differing conditions of the Muslims.

The greatest of these degrees is the matter that occurred among some Muslims of the people of Granada, about which the jurists of Granada were asked: Muhammad al-Mawwaq, Muhammad ibn al-Azraq, 'Ali ibn Dawud, Muhammad al-Ja'dalah, Muhammad al-Fakhkhar, 'Ali al-Qalsadi, Abu Hamid ibn al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Sarhunah, Muhammad al-Mushadhdhali, 'Abd Allah al-Zalījī, Muhammad al-Haddam, Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Jalil, Muhammad ibn Fath, Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Barr, and Ahmad al-Baqqani, concerning a band of the commanders and knights of al-Andalus who fled to the lord of Castile (the land of the Christians) after the incident of "al-Lisanah" (so they say), and sought his aid against the Muslims, and clung to the rope of his protection, and settled in the land of the Christians. They asked: Is it permissible for anyone among the Muslims to assist them, or for the people of a city or fortress to give them shelter? They answered that their leaning toward the disbelievers and seeking their help had brought them under the threat of His saying, ﴿And whoever of you allies with them, then indeed he is of them﴾. Whoever assists them is therefore assisting in disobedience to God and His Messenger. This applies as long as they persist in their actions. If they repent and return from what they are upon of dissension and opposition, then it is obligatory upon the Muslims to accept them.

Their use of this verse in their answer indicates that they interpreted it to mean that he is "of them" in deserving hatred and blame. What they did, and what the jurists answered about it, is the greatest type of allegiance after allegiance to disbelief. The lowest degree of allegiance is close association and involvement, such as in trade and the like. Below that is what is not allegiance at all, which is dealing (mu'amalah). The Prophet (ﷺ) dealt with the Jews of Khaybar through musaqah (an agreement to care for palm trees for a share of the produce), on the palms of Khaybar. We have explained some detail of this at His saying, ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28] in Surah Al 'Imran.

The sentence ﴿Indeed God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a concluding sentence (tadhyil) for the prohibition. The generality of "the wrongdoing people" includes the Jews and the Christians, and the position of the concluding sentence requires that the Jews and the Christians are among the wrongdoing people by way of metaphor (kinayah). What is meant by "the wrongdoers" is the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them﴾ is a branching (tafri') from a condition of their allegiance, the description of which is intended for the Prophet (ﷺ) because it occurred in his presence.

"Disease" here is applied to hypocrisy, as already mentioned in His saying ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾ in Surah al-Baqarah. It was called a disease because it is a disbelief that corrupts faith.

"Hastening" was explained earlier in His saying ﴿Let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. In the genitive phrase there is an omitted genitive construction (mudaf mahdhuf), indicated by the context, because hastening does not occur toward essences. So the meaning is: they hasten concerning their affair of allegiance to them or concerning supporting them.

The statement in "they say, 'We fear that a calamity will befall us'" is a spoken statement, because 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said that, as is narrated from 'Ata' al-Hufi, al-Zuhri and 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn Qatadah, that the verse was revealed after the Battle of Badr or after the Battle of Uhud, and that it was revealed when the Messenger of God resolved to fight the Banu Qaynuqa'. The Banu Qaynuqa' were allies of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit. "When 'Ubadah saw the Messenger of God's resolve, he came and said: 'O Messenger of God, I disassociate myself before God from the alliance and allegiance of the Jews, and I ally with none but God and His Messenger.' 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy was present and said: 'As for me, I will not disassociate myself from their alliance, for I cannot do without them. I am a man who fears the turns of fortune.'"

It is possible that their saying, "We fear that a calamity will befall us," is an inner statement, meaning they say to themselves. The calamity feared is the fear that the Muslims would turn against the hypocrites. In that case this saying is part of the disease in their hearts. It is reported from al-Suddi that when the defeat at the Day of Uhud occurred, the Muslims became frightened, and some of them said: "Let us take an alliance with the Jews so that they will support us if some calamity from Quraysh strikes us." A man said: "I am going to the Jew so-and-so, and I will take refuge with him and become a Jew with him." Another said: "I am going to so-and-so the Christian in Syria, and I will take refuge with him and become a Christian with him." So the verse was revealed. In this case the disease here is weakness of faith and little trust in God's support. On this view, this verse was revealed before the revelation of this surah, so either it was revealed again, or it was ordered to be placed in this position.

The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿So God may bring victory or a decision from Him, and they will become regretful for what they concealed within themselves﴾ supports the first report, and it supports our interpretation of it that the statement is an inner statement.

The word "dā'irah" (calamity) is the active participle from "dāra," meaning that he reversed his course, so "dā'irah" is a change of condition. Its use became predominant for a change of condition from good to bad. The "cycles of time" (dawa'ir al-dahr) are its vicissitudes and turns of fortune. God said: ﴿and wait for you to undergo the cycles﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98], meaning the changing of your condition from victory to defeat. Concerning His saying ﴿upon them is the cycle of evil﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98], they said that the annexation of "dā'irah" to "al-sū'" (evil) is an explanatory annexation (idafat bayan). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "If the calamity were not annexed to 'evil,' its meaning would be known from it." Its feminine form originally was for the single occurrence, then it became predominant for change, remaining in the feminine form.

As for His saying: "those who believed say," the majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaqulu" without a waw at its beginning, as a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani, a sentence answering an implied question) answering the question of one who asks: what will those who believed say at that time?

That is, when the victory or a matter from the strength of the Muslims and the weakness of the Jews comes, those who believed will say. 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "wa-yaqulu" with a waw and with the nominative "yaqulu," coordinated with "fa-'asa Allah" (so God may). Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub also read it with a waw, but with the accusative "yaqula," coordinated with "an ya'tiya" (that He may bring). The interrogative in "a-Ha'ulā'" (are these?) is used in the sense of wonder at their hypocrisy.

"Ha'ulā'" (these) is a pointing to a group whose occurrence is assumed at the time of the victory, namely the group of those in whose hearts is a disease. The apparent meaning is that "alladhīna" (those who) is the predicate about "ha'ulā'," because the interrogative is for wonder, and the object of wonder is their oath that they are with the believers. This wonder indicates that on the day the victory comes, the believers will see in the condition of the hypocrites what exposes their affair, so they will wonder at their swearing of sincerity to the believers.

The first is to take allegiance in His saying "whoever allies with them" as the complete allegiance, which is approval of their religion and denigration of the religion of Islam. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Whoever allies with them by their creed and religion, he is of them in disbelief and in eternal abiding in the Fire."

The second is to interpret His saying "then indeed he is of them" as a eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh), meaning that he is like one of them in deserving punishment. The affairs of the Muslims at that time were in confusion, since around them were the hypocrites, the weak among the Muslims, the Jews and the polytheists. Therefore it was necessary, to preserve the community's unity, to be free of anything that might cast suspicion upon them.

They answered that their leaning toward the disbelievers and seeking their help had brought them under the threat of His saying, ﴿And whoever of you allies with them, then indeed he is of them﴾. What is meant by "the wrongdoers" is the disbelievers.

"Disease" here is applied to hypocrisy, as already mentioned in His saying ﴿in their hearts is a disease﴾ in Surah al-Baqarah. It was called a disease because it is a disbelief that corrupts faith.

Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub also read it with a waw, but with the accusative "yaqula," coordinated with "an ya'tiya" (that He may bring). The interrogative in "a-Ha'ulā'" (are these?) is used in the sense of wonder at their hypocrisy.

This usage became common in their speech, and then it was employed in the verse with the meaning of the most emphatic and severe oaths, i.e., they swore the strongest oath, and this is by emphasis, repetition, and similar things by which an oath is made severe according to custom. I have not seen the application of jahd in this sense before the Qur'an.

"Jahd" is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), because, by its being annexed to "al-aymān" (the oaths), it became a kind of oath, so it is an absolute object specifying the type.

In al-Kashshāf, in the commentary on Surat al-Nūr, he made it a verbal noun (maṣdar) replacing its verb, and made the implied construction: "They swore by Allah, exerting their oaths with an exerting (jahdan)." So when the verb was deleted and the absolute object was made a substitute for it, the absolute object was placed before the direct object and annexed to it.

The clause "ḥabiṭat aʿmāluhum" (their deeds have become void) is a resumptive (istiʾnāf) clause, whether it is part of the speech of those who believed, in which case it is among the reported speech introduced by "al-qawl," or whether it is part of the speech of Allah the Exalted, in which case it is not part of that reported speech. "Ḥabiṭat" means it was lost and corrupted. It has already been mentioned in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So those—their deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 54:

﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills. And Allah is all-Encompassing, Knowing.﴾.

The warning against their enemies in matters of religion and their avoidance of the causes of weakness in it has concluded. He turns to alert them that this is out of concern for their welfare in adhering to the religion and defending it. Allah is not benefited by it. If a group or a band of them were to apostatize, it would not harm Allah in the least. This religion will have followers and helpers even if whoever turns away from it turns away. This is like His saying, ﴿If you disbelieve, then Allah is free of need of you, and He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾ [az-Zumar: 7], and His saying, ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have accepted Islam. Say, "Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, Allah has done a favor to you that He guided you to faith, if you are truthful"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17].

The sentence ﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion﴾ and so on is an interjection (i'tiradah) between what precedes it and the sentence ﴿Your guardian is only Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 55]. Its interjection was prompted by the connection to the warning in His saying, ﴿And whoever among you takes them as allies, then indeed he is one of them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51]. Its placement after this interjection indicates that taking the Jews and Christians as allies is a means (dhari'ah) to apostasy (ridda, reversion from Islam), because the continuation of a group in alliance with the Jews and Christians, from among the hypocrites and those weak in faith, makes it feared that a group may slip away from faith. It also informs the hesitant, weak in faith, that Islam is independent of them if they resolve to revert to disbelief.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read ﴿man yartadid﴾ with two dal's, by unassimilating (fakk al-idgham, separating the two identical consonants instead of merging them). This is one of two permissible forms in such cases, and it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. It is also written this way in the Medinan and Syrian codices. The rest read it with a single, doubled dal, with idgham (assimilation), which is the dialect of Tamim. They also vowel the dal with a fatha as a fath takhallus (a vowel inserted to escape the meeting of two sukun consonants), because the fatha is light. This is also how it is written in the Meccan, Kufan and Basran codices.

Al-ridda (apostasy) is the reflexive form (mutawi') of radd, and radd is returning something to a place or a state. He, Exalted, says, ﴿Return them to me﴾ [an-Naml: 33]. Radd may also be used in the sense of making something become: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject old age﴾ [an-Nahl: 70]. In applying the term ridda to disbelief after Islam, consideration is given to what they were upon before Islam, such as polytheism and other things. Then the term ridda came to dominate for leaving Islam, even if the apostate had not previously adopted another religion before it.

The clause ﴿So Allah will bring forth a people﴾ and so on is the answer to the conditional (jawab al-shart). From it has been omitted the pronoun referring back to the nominal conditional, and it is a promise that this religion will never lack righteous and sincere followers. The meaning of this promise is to show independence from those in whose hearts is a disease, and from the hypocrites, and to show little concern for them, as in His saying, ﴿Had they gone forth among you, they would not have increased you except in corruption﴾ [at-Tawbah: 47]. It also reassures the Messenger and the sincere believers that Allah will replace the apostates with better people than them. This is the intended meaning of the answer to the conditional, so it has been dispensed with by mentioning what it implies, to the point that the conditional has two answers.

The revelation of this verse at the end of the life of the Messenger (ﷺ) contains an allusion to what would happen of the apostasy of many Arabs from Islam, such as the followers of al-Aswad al-Ansi in Yemen, the followers of Talhah ibn Khuwaylid among Banu Asad, and the followers of Musaylimah ibn Habib al-Hanafi in al-Yamamah. Then it alludes to what happened after the death of the Messenger (ﷺ) of the apostasy of many tribes, such as Fazarah, Ghatafan, Banu Tamim, Kindah and others.

It is said: "Only the people of three mosques remained: the Mosque of Medina, the Mosque of Mecca and the Mosque of Juwatha in Bahrain" (meaning, of the Islamic cities at that time). Allah indeed fulfilled His promise and granted victory to Islam, so He replaced it with generations rooted in it, standing in its support.

His saying ﴿Allah will bring forth a people﴾: the word "bringing forth" (ityan) here means creating (ijad), that is, He brings into existence peoples to follow this religion with hearts that love it, that bring good to it and to the believers, and that drive their enemies away from them. These people may be from among those who apostatized, when they return to Islam with hearts purified of the aversion that had been mixed into them, like most of the Arab tribes and their chiefs who returned to Islam after the apostasy in the time of Abu Bakr. Their collective is not the same as the collective of those who apostatized, so it is valid that they are among those included in the word "a people," and the attribute, which is Allah's love for them and their love for their Lord and His religion, is realized in them. The two loves follow changes in the states of hearts, not changes in persons. 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib, who was among the greatest rebels of the apostasy, became among the greatest supporters of Islam on the day of al-Qadisiyyah, and so on.

Included in the word "a people" are the peoples who entered Islam after that, such as the Arabs of Syria from the Ghassanids, the Arabs of Iraq and their Nabatean, the people of Persia, the Copts, the Berbers, the Franks of Spain, Sicily, Sardinia and the borders of France, as well as the Turks, the Mongols, the Tatars, the Indians, the Chinese, the Greeks and the Romans, among the nations that had a great role in serving Islam, expanding its domain through conquests, supporting it with sciences, and spreading its civilization among great nations. So every nation, group or people in whom the description ﴿whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah, and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾ is realized, they are among the people who have been named. As for the believers who existed before and remained steadfast, they are greater in rank and stronger in faith, and the supporters came to them "in groups and individually."

The love of Allah for His servant is His good pleasure with him and facilitating goodness for him. The love of the servant for his Lord is the soul's inclination toward magnifying Him, delighting in remembering Him, complying with His command, and defending His religion. It is a quality that arises in the servant from frequently contemplating the greatness of Allah, the Exalted, and His blessings, until it settles in his heart. Its source is hearing and contemplation. It is not like the love of the self's approval of something. Do you not see that we love the Prophet (ﷺ) because of how much we hear of his virtues and his concern for our good in this world and the Hereafter? This love grows in proportion to the frequency of practicing his sayings, mentioning his qualities, conduct and guidance. Likewise, we love the four Caliphs because of how much we hear of their love for the Messenger and their exerting utmost sincerity for the good of the Muslims. Likewise, we love Hatim (al-Ta'i) because of what we hear of his generosity. Hind bint 'Utbah, the wife of Abu Sufyan, said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "No household was more beloved to me than that they be humbled among the people of your household, and now I have become such that no household is more beloved to me than that they be honored among the people of your household."

Al-adhillah (humble) and al-a'izzah (mighty) are two opposites, by which the people are described according to the difference in what each relates to. Al-adhillah is the plural of dhalil, which is one characterized by dhull (humiliation). Dhull, with a dammah or kasrah on the dhal, means abasement and submission, and it is the opposite of 'izz (might): ﴿Allah had already helped you at Badr when you were humble﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 123]. In some tafsirs it is said: dhull with a dammah on the dhal is the opposite of 'izz, and with a kasrah on the dhal is the opposite of difficulty (su'ubah). No linguistic evidence is known for this distinction. The plural of dhalil is adhillah, and the abstract noun is dhull: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility from mercy﴾ [al-Isra': 24]. Dhull is also used for gentleness of disposition and humility, which is figurative, and this verse is of that type.

So the meaning here is dhull in the sense of gentleness of disposition and lowering oneself, which is intense mercy and striving for benefit. For this reason, His saying "toward the believers" is attached to it. Because "humble" (adhillah) is construed to imply "compassionate and yearning," it is followed by 'ala (toward) rather than li (for), or for harmony with the second 'ala in His saying "mighty over the disbelievers."

Al-a'izzah is the plural of 'aziz, who is characterized by 'izz, which is strength and self-sufficiency. Because of the strength in the nature of the Arabs, 'izz in their speech came to indicate the sense of aggression. In the proverb: "Whoever is mighty plunders" (man 'azz bazz). The two descriptions have become opposites, so al-Samaw'al or al-Harithi said:

"Our being few does not harm us, and our neighbor is mighty, and the neighbor of the many is humiliated."

The affirmation of two opposite attributes for the people is an Arabic rhetorical art (sina'ah badi'iyyah), called tibaq (antithesis), by which the eloquent among the Arabs produce beauty, and it is rare in their speech. Much of it occurs in the Qur'an. In this there is an allusion that their attributes are guided by sound judgment, so they are not impelled to any act except with insight, and they are not among those whose character springs from a single disposition, being gentle in every situation. This is the meaning of the "most upright character" (al-khuluq al-aqwam), which is that which fits each situation as appropriate. The poet said:

"Forbearing, when forbearance adorns its people, and with forbearance, in the eye of the enemy, he is awe-inspiring."

And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

His saying ﴿striving in the cause of Allah﴾ is a third attribute, and it is among the greatest signs indicating the truthfulness of faith. Jihad is the exerting of effort (juhd), that is, the capacity, in repelling the enemy. The extreme of exertion is exposing oneself to being killed, and for this reason it is given in the form of the verbal noun of fa'ala, because one shows his exertion to one who shows him the same. His saying ﴿and not fearing the blame of any blamer﴾ is a fourth attribute, which is not fearing blame, that is, in matters of religion, as the context indicates.

Al-lawmah (a single instance of blame) is one instance of lawm. Here it is used for the bare verbal noun, like al-lawm, because when it occurs in a negative context, it becomes general, and the sense of unity is removed from it, just as the sense of plurality is removed from a generalized plural by the entry of the generic al- (al-jinsiyyah), because la (no) in the generality of negation is like al- in the generality of affirmation. That is, they do not fear any kind of blame from any blamer, since blame can be severe, like rebuke, or light. Blamers include the frightening blamer and the loving one. So He negated fear of every kind of blame. Thus in the sentence there are three generalities: the generality of the verb in a negative context, the generality of the object, and the generality of the genitive. This attribute is a sign of the truthfulness of their faith, to the point that it has permeated their hearts such that nothing turns them from it, neither enticement nor blame, because submitting to blame is a sign of weakness of certainty and resolve.

Turning away from the blame of blamers has always been a sign of self-confidence and originality of judgment. Our jurists have counted among the qualifications of a judge that he be one who disregards blame, according to one of two interpretations in the expressions of the earlier scholars. The possibility of two interpretations is evidence that both are considered valid in the Law.

His saying ﴿That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil). The demonstrative ("that") refers to the totality of the mentioned attributes of perfection.

"Wasi'" (all-Encompassing) is an attribute of vastness, that is, the absence of limit in the connection to His attributes that have connection (to objects). Its explanation has already preceded in His saying, ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is all-Encompassing, Knowing﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 73], in the surah of Ali 'Imran.

The sentence "Indeed, your protector is Allah and His Messenger and those who believe..." through to its end is connected to the sentence "O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as protectors; they are protectors of one another" [al-Ma'idah: 51], and to what follows from it, His saying: "So you see those in whose hearts is a disease" [al-Ma'idah: 52], up to His saying: "and so they became among the losers" [al-Ma'idah: 53]. The sentence "O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion" [al-Ma'idah: 54] came between these verses as a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), and then the discourse rejoined the sentence "Indeed, your protector is Allah and His Messenger." The position of this sentence is that of a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition, because their guardianship by Allah and His Messenger is established among them. Whoever has Allah as his protector cannot have the enemies of Allah as his protectors. This sentence also gives emphasis to the prohibition against taking the Jews and the Christians as protectors. It also contains an honouring of the believers, by stating that they are the protectors of Allah and His Messenger, by way of emphasising the negation or prohibition through commanding its opposite, because His saying "Indeed, your protector is Allah and His Messenger" implies a command to affirm this guardianship and maintain it. So it is a statement used in the sense of a command. The restriction (qasr) conveyed by "innama" (indeed/only) is a restriction of an attribute to a subject, and it is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi).

The meaning of "those who believe" being protectors of "those who believe" is that the believers are protectors of one another, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "The believing men and believing women are protectors of one another" [al-Tawbah: 71]. The two attributes "who establish the prayer and give the zakat" are applied to "those who believe" in order to praise them. Likewise the clause "while they are bowing (rakti'un)."

Page 240

His saying "while they are bowing" is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the relative clause (sila). The apparent meaning of this clause is that it is the same meaning as "who establish the prayer," since the intended meaning of "bowing" (raki'un) is "those who pray," not "those who perform the part of the prayer called ruku' (bowing)." This coordination has been explained in two ways. Either the intended meaning of "bowing" is the bowing of the supererogatory prayers (nawafil), that is, those who establish the five obligatory prayers and draw near to Allah through the supererogatory prayers; or the intended meaning is what the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) indicates of continuity and steadfastness, that is, those who persist in establishing the prayer. He followed this by saying that they give the zakat, hastening to honour the zakat, as is the custom of the Qur'an. This is what Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) derived when he said: "I will certainly fight whoever distinguishes between the prayer and the zakat." Then Allah praised them, saying that they do not fall short in performing the prayer. So the "wa" (and) is coordinating one attribute upon another attribute, and it is permissible to make the clause a circumstantial phrase (hal). The bowing here means humble submission (khushu').

Among the exegetes is one who made "while they are bowing" a circumstantial phrase referring to the pronoun in "they give the zakat" [Fussilat: 7]. There is no meaning in this, since zakat is not given while in the state of bowing. They constructed this meaning upon a report whose narrations are many, and all of them are weak. Ibn Kathir said: "None of them is authentic at all, because of the weakness of their chains and the obscurity of their narrators." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "In this statement, that is, this narration, there is scrutiny." He said: al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: "Ibn Salam, that is, Abdullah, and a group of his people, those who believed, that is, from the Jews, came and complained to the Messenger (ﷺ) about the distance of their homes and the hostility of the Jews towards them, so the verse was revealed: 'Indeed, your protector is Allah and His Messenger.' Then the Messenger went out to the mosque and saw a beggar, and he said to him: 'Has anyone given you anything?' He said: 'Yes, a silver ring, which that one standing and praying gave me,' and he pointed to Ali. The Prophet (ﷺ) said 'Allahu akbar,' and this verse was revealed," and the Messenger of Allah recited it. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. And it was said: it was revealed concerning the Muhajirun and the Ansar.

His saying "then indeed the party of Allah, they are the victorious" [al-Ma'idah: 56] is an indication of the answer (jawab) of the conditional clause, by mentioning the reason for the answer, as if it were said: "They are the victorious, because they are the party of Allah."
