**[Resumptive clause]** (istiʾnaf: a new sentence that resumes and emphasizes part of the meaning of the preceding discourse). His saying, ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 51) is a warning against allying with the People of the Book, so that the Muslims may be distinguished. This verse is a warning against allying with the Jews and the polytheists who were in Medina. The Christians have no place in it, since there were no Christians in Medina who would mock the religion.

He turned away from the word "Jews" to the relative pronoun (mawsul) and its relative clause (silah), which is ﴿those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game﴾, and so on, because the relative clause contains an indication of the reason that makes the prohibition necessary.

Religion (dīn) is what a person holds of beliefs and of actions that arise from belief. It is the mark of the religious person's mind, the guide of his hopes, and the motive of his deeds. So whoever takes a man's religion as a mockery has taken that religious man as a mockery and looked at him with contempt, since he regarded the greatest thing in him as a subject of ridicule. Then what is lesser than that is all the more so. One who looks upon others in this way is not worthy of being taken as an ally, because the condition of alliance is sameness in thinking, and because mockery and belittling are contempt, whereas affection requires honouring the one who is loved.

By "the disbelievers" (al-kuffār) in his saying, "and the disbelievers," is meant the polytheists. This is the Qur'anic usage of the term "disbelievers." What is meant by this are the polytheists of the people of Medina who showed Islam while hiding hypocrisy, such as Rifāʿah ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Ḥārith. Some Muslims used to befriend them, deceived by their outward condition. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that some Jews and polytheists laughed at the Muslims during their prostration. Al-Kalbī said: when the caller of the Messenger of Allah called out, they said, "A shout like the shout of a donkey," and they laughed. So Allah revealed this verse.

Page 242

The majority of readers read "wal-kuffāra" (and the disbelievers) in the accusative, as a conjunction with ﴿those who have taken your religion﴾, which is explained by his saying, ﴿from those who were given the Book before you﴾. Abū ʿAmr, al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read "wal-kuffāri" in the genitive, as a conjunction with ﴿those who were given the Book before you﴾. The outcome of the two readings is one.

His saying, ﴿and fear Allah, if you are believers﴾, means: beware of Him by obeying what He has forbidden you. Mentioning this condition is a stirring up of resolve to stop, and an incitement of the souls of the believers so that they may show that they are believers, because the nature of the believer is obedience. This condition has no implicit contrary meaning (mafhūm) here, because the statement is a directive (inshāʾ), and because the predicate of "kāna" (is/are) is an epithet (laqab), which has no implicit meaning since it was not intended to describe the one who is affirmed. That is because the negation of piety does not negate faith according to those scholars of Islam who are regarded and who understood the aim of Islam in its comprehensiveness in the fullest understanding.

If by the forbidden alliance is meant complete alliance, in the sense of agreement in religion, then the command to piety, meaning caution against falling into what they were forbidden, is conditioned on their being believers in an evident way. The conclusion is that the verse is explained or interpreted according to what was previously stated in its preceding context: ﴿Whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 51).

The call to prayer (al-niddāʾ ilā al-ṣalāh) is the adhān, and the Qur'an expresses it only by the term "niddāʾ." The verse indicates that the adhān is a known thing. So it confirms the legitimacy of the adhān and does not itself establish it, because it was legislated by the Sunnah.

His saying, ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, is a belittling of them, since there is nothing in the call to prayer that requires mockery. Making it a cause of mockery is a sign of the foolishness of their minds.

By "the disbelievers" (al-kuffār) in his saying, "and the disbelievers," is meant the polytheists. This is the Qur'anic usage of the term "disbelievers." What is meant by this are the polytheists of the people of Medina who showed Islam while hiding hypocrisy, such as Rifāʿah ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Ḥārith. Some Muslims used to befriend them, deceived by their outward condition. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that some Jews and polytheists laughed at the Muslims during their prostration. Al-Kalbī said: when the caller of the Messenger of Allah called out, they said, "A shout like the shout of a donkey," and they laughed. So Allah revealed this verse.

Page 242

The majority of readers read "wal-kuffāra" (and the disbelievers) in the accusative, as a conjunction with ﴿those who have taken your religion﴾, which is explained by his saying, ﴿from those who were given the Book before you﴾. Abū ʿAmr, al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read "wal-kuffāri" in the genitive, as a conjunction with ﴿those who were given the Book before you﴾. The outcome of the two readings is one.

His saying, ﴿and fear Allah, if you are believers﴾, means: beware of Him by obeying what He has forbidden you. Mentioning this condition is a stirring up of resolve to stop, and an incitement of the souls of the believers so that they may show that they are believers, because the nature of the believer is obedience. This condition has no implicit contrary meaning (mafhūm) here, because the statement is a directive (inshāʾ), and because the predicate of "kāna" (is/are) is an epithet (laqab), which has no implicit meaning since it was not intended to describe the one who is affirmed. That is because the negation of piety does not negate faith according to those scholars of Islam who are regarded and who understood the aim of Islam in its comprehensiveness in the fullest understanding.

If by the forbidden alliance is meant complete alliance, in the sense of agreement in religion, then the command to piety, meaning caution against falling into what they were forbidden, is conditioned on their being believers in an evident way. The conclusion is that the verse is explained or interpreted according to what was previously stated in its preceding context: ﴿Whoever among you takes them as allies, then he is one of them﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 51).

The call to prayer (al-niddāʾ ilā al-ṣalāh) is the adhān, and the Qur'an expresses it only by the term "niddāʾ." The verse indicates that the adhān is a known thing. So it confirms the legitimacy of the adhān and does not itself establish it, because it was legislated by the Sunnah.

His saying, ﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, is a belittling of them, since there is nothing in the call to prayer that requires mockery. Making it a cause of mockery is a sign of the foolishness of their minds.

Page 243

These sentences are parenthetical, placed between what precedes them and His words, "And when they come to you." The meaning of the verse does not become fully clear, nor does the reason for Allah's command to His Messenger (ﷺ) to confront them with harsh speech become evident, [a command given] even though He is the One who said, ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech except by one who has been wronged﴾ [an-Nisa': 148], and He is the One who said, ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best, except for those who have wronged among them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 46], except after knowing the occasion of revelation of this verse, whereby it becomes known that they had wronged by their attacks on Islam and the Muslims. Al-Wahidi and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "A group of Jews came to the Prophet, among them Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, Rafi' ibn Abi Rafi', 'Azar, Zayd, Khalid, Azar ibn Abi Azar, and Ash'a, and they asked him about which of the Messengers he believes in. When he mentioned 'Isa ibn Maryam, they said: 'We do not believe in one who believed in 'Isa, and we know no religion worse than your religion, and we know no people less fortunate in this world and the Hereafter than you.' So Allah revealed, ﴿Say, 'O People of the Scripture, do you resent us only because we believed in Allah'﴾ up to His words: ﴿and further astray from the sound way.'"

He singled out the People of the Scripture for this debate because the disbelievers' argument does not establish anything against them, and by the People of the Scripture is meant specifically the Jews, as indicated by the relative pronoun and its clause in His words, ﴿whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry﴾ and what follows. This debate with them was that what they resent in the believers in their religion, when they reflect, they find nothing but belief in Allah, and in what is with the People of the Scripture, plus additional belief in what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ).

The interrogative is both denunciatory and expressive of wonder. The denunciation is indicated by the exception, and the wonder is indicated by the fact that all the objects of "you resent" (tanqimun) are praiseworthy things which do not merit resentment; that is, you do not find anything you resent other than what has been mentioned, and all of that is not worthy of being resented. As for belief in Allah and in what was revealed before, it is evident that they were pleased with it for themselves, so they do not resent it in one who shares it with them.

Page 244

As for belief in what was revealed to Muhammad, it is likewise, because that is something the Muslims were pleased with for themselves, and it does not concern the People of the Scripture. The Messenger invited the People of the Scripture to it, so whoever among them wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve; so what is the basis for resenting it? The verb "tanqimun" is transitive to its complement by the preposition (min), which is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), and it may also be transitive by (ʿalā).

As for the conjunction of His words, ﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, all the readers recited it with the opening of the hamza of (anna), as being conjoined to ﴿that we believed in Allah﴾.

The exegetes have been perplexed in interpreting it, because its apparent meaning requires the defiant disobedience of most of the addressees, while that is not acknowledged by its own people; and even if they acknowledged it, that is not among the things resented against the believers, since the believers have no action in it; and even if it were among the things resented against the believers, its resentment against them is not a place for the denunciation and wonder that is the context of the speech.

The exegetes went in various directions in interpreting the position of this conjoined phrase. It is said: it is conjoined to the complement of "we believed" (āmannā), that is, "we believed in Allah and in the defiant disobedience of most of you," meaning you resent us for the combination of these two matters. This loses the sense of denunciatory wonder, because the believers' belief that most of the addressees are defiantly disobedient makes the addressees excusable in resenting it, so it is not marvelled at and they are not rebuked for resenting it; and that contradicts the context, which emphasizes a matter by something resembling its opposite, so the conjunction between the two conjoined elements is then like combining the lizard and the nun; this is a distant view.

It is said: it is conjoined to the exception, that is, "you resent us only for our belief and the defiant disobedience of most of you," meaning you resent the difference between our two states, so it is resentment of envy, and for this reason the placement of the denunciatory wonder is apt. This view was mentioned and preferred by al-Kashshaf, and it is good were it not for the word "minna," because the difference of the two states is not something resented from believers, since it is not of their doing but from the coincidence of time.

It is said: a genitive complement has been omitted, indicated by what is mentioned, and the estimate is: "Do you resent us only for belief because you are unjust and most of you are defiantly disobedient?" This is an explanation along an unfamiliar style, since omission of the conjoined-to element is not known in such a case. Two other views have been mentioned, which are not accepted.

Page 245

What appears to me is that His words, ﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾, be conjoined to ﴿that we believed in Allah﴾, as is the most immediate reading, and the speech is then sarcasm: you resent from us that we believed as you believe, and affirmed your messengers and your books, and that is a strange resentment; and that we believed in what was revealed to us, and that does not concern you. And you resent from us that most of you are defiantly disobedient, that is, while we are righteous; that is resentment of envy, meaning we do not hold it in our power to make you righteous. Thus the indication of sarcasm became manifest, and the interrogative contains denunciation, then wonder, then sarcasm, each of them arising from the other, and all of them arising from the use of the interrogative in its figurative meanings or in allusive senses; and with this the view put forward by the author of al-Kashshaf is completed.

Then he continued in sarcasm toward them and wonder at the poverty of their opinion, while reminding them of their faults, so he said, ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of [something] worse than that as to reward from Allah"﴾ etc. "Sharr" is an elative noun, its origin being "asharr," and it denotes increase in the quality; its hamza was dropped for lightness due to frequency of use, and increase requires sharing in the basic quality, so it requires that the Muslims have a share of evil. It came in this manner as sarcasm toward the Jews, because they said to the Muslims: "There is no religion worse than your religion," and this is among what was expressed by the verb "tanqimun." This is a matching of harshness with harshness, as it is said: "You said, so you incurred [the consequence]."

The reference in His words "from that" is to the belief in His words, ﴿Do you resent us only that we believed in Allah﴾ etc., in terms of its being resented on the basis of supposition and estimation.

Since the nature of what is resented is that it be evil, the sarcasm was built upon it in His words, ﴿Shall I inform you of [something] worse than that﴾, that is, of what is far worse in evil.

"Mathubah" is derived from thaba yathubu, meaning he returned; it is on the pattern of mafu'alah, and the name was given to the thing by which a person returns to his home when he obtains it as a recompense for a deed he did or an effort he exerted. Its original form is "mathub bihā," and they considered the feminine form in it in view of its interpretation as a gift or a reward; then the complement was omitted for frequency of use.

Its original form indicates that it is used only of an existent thing which the agent gives and which he carries with him, so it is not applied to beating or cursing, because that is not something by which a person returns to his home; and because the Arabs build their speech on their dispositions, and they are a people of generosity toward their guests, so they do not intend by "mathubah" anything but a beneficial gift. Its application is valid to a precious thing and to a base thing of every kind by which the giver returns. So making it in this verse a specification for the comparative of evil is sarcasm, because cursing, wrath, and transformation are not rewards; and this is like the words of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"We hosted you, and hastened your hospitality before dawn, a mirdaah that was pounded."

And the words of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"And cavalry against which I advanced with cavalry; their greeting among them is painful striking."

His words, ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾, are a subject (mubtada'), intended to explain who is worse in reward; and there is an omitted genitive, indicated by the context, and its estimate is: "the reward of one whom Allah has cursed." The turning away from saying "you" or "the Jews" to bringing the relative pronoun is for knowledge of the intended meaning from the relative clause, because the Jews know that some of their forebears were struck by the curse and the wrath from the time of their prophets, and its proofs are established in the Torah and the books of their prophets; so the relative pronoun is a metonymy for them.

As for their being made apes and swine, the discussion of its reality was already presented in Surat al-Baqarah. As for their worshipping Taghut, it is that they worshipped idols after they had been people of monotheism; among that is their worship of the calf.

Taghut means idols, and it was mentioned earlier at His words, ﴿they believe in Jibt and Taghut﴾ [an-Nisa': 51], in Surat an-Nisa'.

The majority read ﴿and worshipped Taghut﴾ with the verbal form of the past tense in "'abada" and with the opening of the ta' in "Taghut" as the object of "'abada," and it is conjoined to the relative clause in His words, ﴿whom Allah has cursed﴾, that is, and those who worshipped Taghut. Hamzah alone read it with an opening of the 'ayn, a damma on the bā', an opening of the dal, and a kasra on the final ta' of the word "Taghut," as "'abud," being the plural of "'abd," a rare analogical plural; in this reading it is conjoined to ﴿apes and swine﴾.

The purpose of mentioning this here is to rebuke the Jewish debaters against the Muslims with the faults of their forebears, in order to silence them from insolence. Moreover, if that was their character in the times when the Messengers and Prophets were among them, then after that they were in a worse state and more deserving of being the worst; so the speech is a condemnation of the whole group. Moreover, many of the causes of the curse, wrath, and transformation were committed by their descendants; and further, they insulted the Muslims with what they claimed was their religion, so it is right that they be insulted with what we believe about them.

﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe," but they entered with disbelief and they left with it. "When they come to you" is conjoined to His saying: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as mockery﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 58], and these attributes are specific to the hypocrites among the Jews from among those who took the religion as mockery and play. Thus the warning is completed against those whose attributes these are, both the openly declared ones among them and the hypocrites. It is not correct to conjoin it to the attributes of the People of the Book in His saying: ﴿And He made some of them apes﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], because the meaning would not be sound; with this, one is spared the strain of finding a justification for this conjunction.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿they entered with disbelief and they left with it﴾ is that faith did not mix with their hearts even for the blink of an eye; that is, they entered as disbelievers and left in the same state, due to the severe hardness of their hearts. The intended sense is the encompassing of both times and what lies between them, because that is what is customary, for when a state changes, its change continues. In this there is a recording of the lie in their saying "We believe." The Arabs say: "He went out in other than the manner in which he entered."

The seeing in His saying "You see" (wa-tara) is visual, that is, their condition in this matter is such that it is hidden from no one. The address is to everyone who hears.

The meaning of "hastening" (yusari'un) has been given earlier at His saying: ﴿Let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41].

Al-ithm (sin): the corruptions of speech and action; here it is intended to mean lying, as His saying indicates: ﴿from their saying of sin﴾. Al-'udwan (transgression): injustice, and what is meant by it is aggression against the Muslims, if they are able to do it.

As-suht (unlawful gain) has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿listeners to falsehood, consumers of unlawful gain﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42].

"Lawla" is a reproach-laden exhortation (tahdid), intended to rebuke.

Al-rabbaniyyun (rabbis) and al-ahbar (scholars): their meanings were explained earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44] and so on.

In rebuking the rabbis, mention is limited to their failure to forbid them from saying sin and consuming unlawful gain, and transgression is not mentioned, as an indication that the transgression is restrained by the Muslims, who do not depend on others in restraining them, because reliance for support on someone other than the one wronged is weakness.

The clause ﴿Evil is what they have been producing﴾ is a new sentence, a condemnation of the conduct of the rabbis and scholars in keeping silent about changing the evil. "Yasna'un" (producing) is in the sense of "ya'lamun" (knowing). What is used here differs from what preceded it in the previous verse only for variety of expression; it was also said that "yasna'un" is more indicative of firm establishment in the action than "ya'malun" (doing).

The lam here is the lam of oath.

The intended sense is the encompassing of both times and what lies between them, because that is what is customary, for when a state changes, its change continues. In this there is a recording of the lie in their saying "We believe." The Arabs say: "He went out in other than the manner in which he entered."

The seeing in His saying "You see" (wa-tara) is visual, that is, their condition in this matter is such that it is hidden from no one. The address is to everyone who hears.

The meaning of "hastening" (yusari'un) has been given earlier at His saying: ﴿Let not those who hasten into disbelief grieve you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41].

Al-ithm (sin): the corruptions of speech and action; here it is intended to mean lying, as His saying indicates: ﴿from their saying of sin﴾. Al-'udwan (transgression): injustice, and what is meant by it is aggression against the Muslims, if they are able to do it.

As-suht (unlawful gain) has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿listeners to falsehood, consumers of unlawful gain﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42].

"Lawla" is a reproach-laden exhortation (tahdid), intended to rebuke.

Al-rabbaniyyun (rabbis) and al-ahbar (scholars): their meanings were explained earlier at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿by which the prophets judged﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44] and so on.

In rebuking the rabbis, mention is limited to their failure to forbid them from saying sin and consuming unlawful gain, and transgression is not mentioned, as an indication that the transgression is restrained by the Muslims, who do not depend on others in restraining them, because reliance for support on someone other than the one wronged is weakness.

The clause ﴿Evil is what they have been producing﴾ is a new sentence, a condemnation of the conduct of the rabbis and scholars in keeping silent about changing the evil. "Yasna'un" (producing) is in the sense of "ya'lamun" (knowing). What is used here differs from what preceded it in the previous verse only for variety of expression; it was also said that "yasna'un" is more indicative of firm establishment in the action than "ya'malun" (doing).

The lam here is the lam of oath.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 61–63:

﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe," but they entered with disbelief and they left with it. And Allah is most knowing of what they were concealing.﴾ ﴿You see many of them hastening toward sin and transgression and consuming the unlawful gain. Evil is what they have been doing.﴾ ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their saying of sin and their consuming of the unlawful gain? Evil is what they have been producing.﴾

"When they come to you" is conjoined to His saying: ﴿And when you call to prayer, they take it as mockery﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 58], and these attributes are specific to the hypocrites among the Jews from among those who took the religion as mockery and play. Thus the warning is completed against those whose attributes these are, both the openly declared ones among them and the hypocrites. It is not correct to conjoin it to the attributes of the People of the Book in His saying: ﴿And He made some of them apes﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], because the meaning would not be sound; with this, one is spared the strain of finding a justification for this conjunction.

"Yasna'un" (producing) is in the sense of "ya'lamun" (knowing). What is used here differs from what preceded it in the previous verse only for variety of expression; it was also said that "yasna'un" is more indicative of firm establishment in the action than "ya'malun" (doing).

The lam here is the lam of oath.

[p. 249]

It is coordinated with the clause ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:61]. Since those people were from among the Jews and the hypocrites, he moved on to their corrupt belief and the wickedness of their inner dispositions, to show the extreme contradiction between their belief and the belief of the people of Islam. This is the statement of the open Jews, not the hypocrites, and therefore it is attributed to the name "the Jews."

[p. 249 continued]

The meaning of ﴿The hand of God is chained﴾ is a description of stinginess in giving, because the Arabs express giving by the hand. They use the extending of the hand as a metaphor (isti'arah) for generosity and munificence, and they use the opposite of extending as a metaphor for stinginess. So they say: "He held back his hand" (amsaka yadahu) and "He closed his hand" (qabada yadahu). We have not heard from them "He chained his hand" (ghalla yadahu) except in the Qur'an, as here, and in the statement ﴿Do not let your hand be chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra' 17:29] in the surah of al-Isra'. This is a strong metaphor, because a person whose hand is chained cannot extend it even for the briefest time. Therefore it is necessarily a metaphor for the utmost stinginess and miserliness.

The Jews are people of faith and religion, so it is not permissible in their religion to describe God the Exalted with attributes of blame. Their statement here is either one that took the form of mockery of the Muslims, as an argument ad absurdum against this corrupt claim of theirs, as it is narrated that they said this when the Muslims were in hardship in the early period of the Hijrah, and the Messenger imposed the charities (sadaqat) upon them, and he may have sought the help of the Jews regarding blood-money (diyat). And as it is narrated that they said it when there was revealed the statement of God the Exalted, ﴿Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:245], so they said: "Verily the Lord of Muhammad is poor and miserly." A similar statement from them has been related in His saying the Exalted, ﴿God has indeed heard the saying of those who said: "Verily God is poor and we are rich"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:181]. And this is supported by His saying after it: ﴿And surely many of them will increase in what has been revealed to you from your Lord in rebellion and disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:68]. Or they said it in a state of anger and despair. It has been narrated concerning the occasion of its revelation that the Jews were struck by severe hardship, and famine and distress befell them, so Fin-has ibn 'Azura said this statement. Then either the common people took it from him, following the custom of the ignorant masses, or the statement of their rabbi was attributed to all of them, because they follow him and imitate him.

God the Exalted has blamed them under both interpretations, since the first is a belittling of Islam and of their own religion as well, since it is obligatory to declare God the Exalted free of such statements, even if they were intended as an argument ad absurdum against an opponent. The second is evident in its arrogance and its displeasure at the actions of God. So God answered their statement with a curse upon them. This is blame in the manner of the Arabs.

The clause ﴿Their hands were chained﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) between the clause ﴿And the Jews said﴾ and the clause ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾. It is a performative speech (insha') of condemnation against them.

[p. 250]

From the figurative chaining (al-ghull al-majazi) is derived its literal counterpart (al-ghull al-haqiqi) in supplication, according to the manner of the Arabs in drawing the supplication from the word of its cause or the like. As the Prophet ﷺ said: "The 'Usayyah disobeyed God and His Messenger, and Aslam, may God grant them safety; and Ghifar, may God forgive them." [Hadith]

The clause ﴿And they were cursed for what they said﴾ may be a performative speech of supplication against them, and it may be a report that God cursed them on account of this statement of theirs, like what is in His saying the Exalted, ﴿They call upon none but a rebellious devil﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:117], ﴿God cursed him﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:118], in the surah of al-Nisa'. His saying ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ is a refutation of their words and an affirmation of the breadth of His bounty, the Exalted. The extending of the two hands is a figurative representation (tamthil) of giving, and it implies the comparison of bestowal to things that are given by two hands.

The mention of "hand" here in the dual form is for the sake of intensifying the emphasis on generosity. Otherwise, the hand, when used metaphorically for generosity or stinginess, is not intended as singular or as a number. So the dual is used to express repetition in general, as in His saying the Exalted, ﴿Then return your gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk 67:4], and the expression of the Arabs "Labbayka wa sa'dayka" (at Your service, again and again). And a poet, whom he (al-Zamakhshari) cited in al-Kashshaf without attributing him, nor did his commentators, said:

"The sanctuary was generous, with both hands outstretched, with a downpour whose gifts were praised by its plains and its valleys."

The clause ﴿He spends as He wills﴾ is an explanation of the metaphor ﴿His two hands are outstretched﴾. "How" (kayf) is a noun indicating a state, and it is built (mabni) in a position of accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

In His saying "as He wills" there is an added indication that His restriction of provision upon some of His servants is for a benefit, such as punishment for ingratitude toward blessing. God the Exalted said, ﴿Had God extended provision to His servants, they would have rebelled in the earth﴾ [al-Shura 42:27].

* * *

﴿And surely many of them will increase in what has been revealed to you from your Lord in rebellion and disbelief﴾.

It is coordinated with the clause ﴿And the Jews said, "The hand of God is chained"﴾. It came as a parenthetical clause between the response to them with the clause ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ and the clause ﴿And We have cast among them enmity and hatred﴾.

[p. 251]

This is an explanation of the cause that moved them to that abominable statement. That is, envy blinded them, so it increased them in rebellion and disbelief. In this there is a preparation for the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, to take precaution against them, and a consolation to him that the extreme of their rage is what made them utter that monstrous statement.

* * *

﴿And We have cast among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection﴾.

It is coordinated with the clause ﴿And they were cursed for what they said﴾ as the coordination of a report upon a performative speech according to one of the two possibilities in it. In this report there is an allusion that God punished them in this world for their hatred of the Muslims by casting hatred among them, one toward another. So it is a recompense of the same kind as the deed. It is also a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ that the matter of their enmity toward him should not trouble him, for hatred is their innate disposition, even among their own peoples. And this attribute remains permanent for them, like the attributes whose possessors have become blind to treating them through good character. The discussion of its parallel has preceded just above.

* * *

﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it, and they strive in the land for corruption; and God does not love the corruptors﴾.

The construction ﴿they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾ is a figurative representation (tamthil). By it is likened the state of preparing for war, readying for it, and being eager in its matter, to the state of one who kindles a fire for a need, and then it goes out. For the metaphors of the meanings of inflaming, heating, and fire and the like for war had spread, and from it come the sayings "the oven (hamiya al-wati) has heated," "so-and-so is a kindler of war (mis'ar harb)," and "a burner of war (mihashsh harb)." So His saying ﴿they kindled a fire for war﴾ is of this kind, and there is no fire in reality, since it is not reported from the Arabs that they had a fire specific to war counted among the fires of the Arabs that they kindled for purposes. Whoever thought it was literal has erred, and the verifying scholars have warned against his error.

And he likened the state of the dissolving of their resolve or their defeat, and the swiftness of their turning back from it, and their holding back from confronting their enemies, to the state of one whose fire that he kindled has been extinguished.

[p. 252]

Among the wonders of this figurative representation is that it is suitable to be considered in both its unity and its division: it may be made one representation for a collective state, or two representations for two states. And the acceptance of the representation for division is more complete in eloquence. The meaning is that the matter of war does not come together for them, and they are not able to inflict harm on an enemy, and if they fight or are fought, they are defeated. So the meaning of the verse according to this is like His saying: ﴿Humiliation is decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:112].

As for what is narrated, that all of Ma'add, when they fought Madhhij on the day of Khazaza, and their leadership was for Taghlib with their commander Kulayb, Kulayb ordered them to kindle a fire on the mountain of Khazaza so that the army could be guided by it because of its size. They set a sign between them: if the armies of Madhhij attacked them, they would kindle two fires on Khazaza. When Madhhij attacked them, they kindled the fire, and all of Ma'add gathered to the field of battle, and Madhhij was defeated. This is what 'Amr ibn Kulthum pointed to with his saying:

"And we, on the morning when the fire was kindled at Khazaza, gave more than the gifts of the givers."

That is a special sign they agreed upon on that day, and it is not counted as a custom in all wars. And where a fire for war is not known, the reading of the figurative representation becomes necessary, and therefore the commentators agreed upon it in this verse. So the speech is neither literal nor a kinaya (allusion).

And His saying ﴿and they strive in the land for corruption﴾: the discussion of it is like the discussion of its parallel that preceded just above, at His saying the Exalted, ﴿The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger and strive in the land for corruption is only that﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:33].

[Page 253]

It follows its prohibition and condemnation of them with a call to good, in the manner of allusion (ta'rid), since it used the particle of counterfactual conditional (harf al-imtina', the particle indicating that the consequent is negated by the negation of the antecedent), saying: ﴿If the People of the Scripture had believed and been mindful of God, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss﴾. The intended people are the Jews. By His saying "believed" is meant belief in Muhammad (ﷺ). In a hadith: "Two will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Scripture who believed in his prophet and then believed in me (i.e., when the Muhammadan call reached him), so he has two rewards; and a man who had a slave-girl whom he disciplined well, taught, then freed and married, so he has two rewards."

The lam in His saying "We would have removed from them" and His saying "and admitted them" is the lam of emphasis (lam al-ta'kid), which frequently occurs in the answer to "law" (if) when the verb is a affirmative past verb, to emphasize the certainty of the necessary connection between the condition of "law" and its answer. The answer to "law" often occurs without the lam, as will come later at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿If We willed, We would have made it salty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70] in Surat al-Waqi'ah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 66:

﴿Had they truly upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet.﴾

*Iqamah* (establishing) a thing means making it standing (qā'im), as was explained at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. The term *iqamah* is used metaphorically for not neglecting something, because a neglected thing lies discarded, which is why it is called *shay' laqan* (a thing cast aside). It is also because a person standing is more capable with regard to things, which is why they say *qamati al-suq* (the market stood up, i.e., became active). Thus the meaning of *iqamat al-Tawrah wa al-Injil* may be establishing their legislation before Islam, i.e., had they obeyed God's commands and acted upon them, they would have been spared His wrath, and He would have lavished His blessings upon them. The Jews believed in the Torah but did not uphold its rulings, as was mentioned just before, and they disbelieved in the Gospel and rejected it. That is more severe in failing to uphold it, and also in regard to the Qur'an. The verse hints that the cause of the constriction of the Jews' livelihood was the wrath of God upon them for their neglect of the Torah and their disbelief in the Gospel and the Qur'an. That is, the retribution became inevitable for them after the revelation of the Qur'an.

It is also possible that the intended meaning is: had they upheld these Books after the coming of Islam, i.e., by acknowledging what is in the Torah and the Gospel of the good news of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), so that they would believe in him and in what he brought. In that case the verse refers to the constriction of their livelihood after the Messenger's migration to Medina. This is supported by what is narrated about the occasion of revelation of His saying: ﴿And the Jews said, "The hand of God is chained."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], as was mentioned before.

Page 254

The meaning of ﴿they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ is the generalization of the directions of provision, i.e., they would have been provided for from every way. *Akalu* (they would have eaten) here means *ruziqu* (they would have been provided for), like His saying: ﴿And you devour the heritage with greedy devouring.﴾ [al-Fajr: 19]. It has also been said that what is eaten "from above" is the fruit of trees, and "from beneath" are grains and vegetables. In that case, eating is in its literal sense, i.e., abundance would have persisted among them.

In the meaning of this verse is His saying: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from heaven and earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they had earned.﴾ [al-A'raf: 96], in Surah al-A'raf.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿la-akalu min fawqihim﴾ and so on is like the *lam* in the verse before it.

* * *

﴿Among them is a moderate community, but many of them—evil is what they do.﴾

This is a fair assessment of a group among them, after those blameworthy traits had applied to most of them.

*Al-muqtasid* (the moderate) is applied to the obedient, i.e., one who does not extravagantly commit sins, and who stops at the limits of their Book, because he moderates the excess of his own soul. The evidence for this is its contrast with His words in the other part: ﴿evil is what they do.﴾ It is known from the Qur'anic usage that *israf* (extravagance) is used to express persistence in sins. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God."﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. Therefore it is contrasted with *iqtisad* (moderation), i.e., caution against sins. *Al-muqtasid* was chosen because the obedient among them before Islam were not reaching the utmost degree of obedience, as in His saying: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds by God's permission.﴾ [Fatir: 32].

So the meaning here is a division of the People of the Book before Islam, because after Islam they were two kinds: one of evil deeds, namely those who did not embrace Islam; and one foremost in good deeds, namely those who did embrace Islam, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq. It has also been said that *al-muqtasid* refers to those who were not extreme in hating the Muslims, namely those who neither believed with them nor harmed them. Their opposite are those who harmed the Muslims through their deeds, such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf.

Page 255

The former's hatred is inward, while the latter's hatred is both inward and expressed in evil deeds. *Al-muqtasid* is also applied to one who is balanced in matters, since it is derived from *al-qasd*, which means balance and the absence of excess. The meaning is "moderate in opposition and in hostility toward the Muslims," derived from His saying: ﴿But surely many of them will increase in rebellion and disbelief by what is revealed to you from your Lord.﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68].

The more apparent view is that His saying *sa'a* (ساء) is a verb meaning "was evil," and *ma ya'malun* (ما يعملون) is its subject, as Ibn 'Atiyyah assigned. In al-Kashshaf, it is taken to mean *bi'sa* (بئس, "how evil"), so he supposed an implied statement in order for the reporting about it to be valid concerning His saying "and many of them," based on the commitment that it is invalid to conjoin a performative (insha'i) sentence with a declarative (khabari) one, which is a matter of dispute. In that case *ma ya'malun* would be specifically for blame. What prompted him to this is that he saw interpreting it as the performative expression of blame to be more emphatic in censuring them, i.e., every speaker would say that about them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 67 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people. Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

The placement of this verse in this surah is problematic. Surat al-Ma'idah is among the last surahs to be revealed, if not the very last. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had conveyed the Sharia and everything that had been revealed to him by the day this surah was revealed. Had this verse been revealed at the beginning of the period of prophethood, we would say it is a reassurance for the Messenger and a lightening of the burdens of revelation upon him, just as the saying of the Exalted was revealed: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-Hijr: 94], ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾ [al-Hijr: 95], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will confer upon you a heavy word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5], up to His saying: ﴿and be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10], and so on. But since this surah is among the last surahs revealed, and the Messenger of Allah had already delivered the message and perfected the religion, there is nothing in the present circumstance that requires him to be commanded to convey. So we are, then, between two possibilities:

[p. 256]

The first is that this verse was revealed due to a specific cause that required reaffirming the Messenger's steadfastness in conveying something that was burdensome for him to convey.

The second is that this verse was revealed before the revelation of this surah, and this is what the reports concerning its occasion of revelation (asbab al-nuzul, the circumstances in which a verse was revealed) agree upon.

As for this second possibility, it should not be taken into account, because it would require that this verse remained for years without being attached to a surah, and it is not permissible for it to have been recited on its own. By this, all the reports concerning the occasions of revelation that mention events which all took place in times before the revelation of this surah are refuted. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) has mentioned ten opinions on this, and al-Tabari has mentioned two other reports, so they become twelve opinions.

Al-Fakhr said, after mentioning the ten opinions: "Although these narrations are numerous, the better view is to interpret the verse as meaning that Allah protected him from the plotting of the Jews and the Christians, because what precedes it and what follows it is speech addressed to the Jews and the Christians, so it is improbable to place this single verse in between, making it unrelated to what precedes it and what follows it." End of quotation. As for what is reported in the Sahih that the Messenger of Allah used to be guarded until there was revealed ﴿and Allah will protect you from the people﴾, it does not indicate that the whole of this verse was revealed on that day. Rather, the narrator confined himself to a part of it, namely His saying: ﴿and Allah will protect you from the people﴾. So perhaps what 'A'ishah related was that Allah informed His Messenger that He would protect him from the people, and when the narrator related it, he related it in the wording found in this verse.

It is therefore necessary to rely on the first possibility: either the cause of its revelation was an event mentioned in this surah, so it is in the manner of the Exalted's saying: ﴿O Messenger, do not let those grieve you who race to disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41] and His saying: ﴿And do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 49]. Just as that verse described the condition of the hypocrites, so this verse is recited to describe the condition of the People of the Book. The two groups were united against the Messenger (ﷺ): one group openly, and another group secretly. So the address returned to the Messenger a second time,

[p. 257]

to reaffirm his heart and expand his breast, by persisting in conveying the Sharia, striving in that, and not caring about the detractors among the People of the Book and the disbelievers. This is because this surah was revealed at the end of the Prophet's (ﷺ) period, and because Allah is ever steadfast in protecting him from his enemies. These are the ones whose matter He made light of in His saying: ﴿O Messenger, do not let those grieve you who race to disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41]. They are the ones meant by "the people" in this verse. Thus, what is commanded to be conveyed is a specific part of the Qur'an.

It is known from the character of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he loved gentleness in matters and said: "Indeed Allah is gentle and loves gentleness in all matters," as came in the hadith of 'A'ishah when the Jews greeted him and said: "As-samm 'alaykum" (death be upon you), and 'A'ishah said to them: "As-samm 'alaykum wa al-la'nah" (death and the curse be upon you). When Allah commanded him to say to the People of the Book ﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59], and ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from Allah? Those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He has become angry﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60], up to the end of the verse, that statement was an open denunciation of them with evil, which Allah informed him was not gentleness. So it does not fall under the manner in which he dealt with them, which was disputing in the best manner. Therefore this verse specifies what is in the hadith of 'A'ishah, and it falls under the exception in the Exalted's saying: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil in speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾ [al-Nisa': 148].

For this reason, the address to him was reopened with the description "the Messenger", which indicates the utmost of his honor, since he was an intermediary between Allah and His creation, and the one who reminds him to turn away from anyone other than the One who sent him. This description in this second address carries an additional significance beyond its significance in the first address: it contains an allusion to the reason for the structure of the speech that follows it, which is His saying ﴿and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾, just as the Exalted said: ﴿The Messenger has no duty except to convey﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 99].

Just as his heart was strengthened by the first address not to be concerned with the schemes of his enemies, so he was warned by the second address against softening toward them in conveying to them the striking verses of the Qur'an, or against fear of their turning away from him when something from the Qur'an concerning them is revealed, since perhaps it would increase them in obstinacy and disbelief. This is indicated by His saying at the end of this verse: ﴿And what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68].

[p. 258]

Then this was followed by a further strengthening of his heart, that he should not be concerned with their plotting, by His saying ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾, and that their plotting is turned away from him by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. Thus there was achieved at the end of this address a return of the final part to the beginning (radd al-ajuz 'ala al-sadr) relative to the first address, which contained His saying ﴿Do not let those grieve you who race to disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], for they are the disbelieving people and those who race to disbelief.

So the conveying commanded in this manner is the conveying of what has been revealed of the Qur'an in rebuke of the People of the Book. The referent of ﴿what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68] is something known from the verses of the Qur'an, namely the verses preceding this verse.

The referent of ﴿what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68] is everything of the Qur'an that was revealed before that day.

Conveying (al-tabligh) means causing something to reach its destination. Arrival (al-buluugh) is reaching the place intended to be reached, and here it is a metaphor for relaying the message to the one to whom it is sent, from the expressions "the news reached" and "the need reached."

The command to convey is used to request continuity, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 136]. Since the revelation of the Sharia is intended for the community to act upon it, whether the revealed matter concerns an action or not, such as what is revealed describing the conditions of the hypocrites, or the virtues of the believers, or stories and the like, because all of that was revealed for benefits whose knowledge is necessary for the achievement of the purposes for which it was revealed. Moreover, the Qur'an has another distinctive feature, which is its inimitability, and that it is an act of worship to recite it. So the need for all that is revealed of it is established regardless of what it contains of rulings, admonitions, and lessons. Since the meaning of the message is the conveying of what was revealed to those who need to know it, namely the whole community, for this reason the object of "convey" (balligh) was omitted to intend generality, meaning: convey what has been revealed to you to all who need to know it, and that is the whole community, since one does not know when some part of the community will need some of the rulings. Furthermore, many of the rulings are needed by the whole community.

[p. 259]

Conveying is achieved by that which ensures that the one who needs to know a ruling is enabled to know it at the time of need or before it. For this reason, the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, would recite the Qur'an to the people when a verse was revealed, and command them to memorize it by heart and to write it down, and he commanded the people to recite it and to listen to it. He also sent Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr to Madinah before his migration to teach the Ansar the Qur'an. He would also command the one who heard his speech to convey it to whoever had not heard it, which ensures that the whole Sharia reaches the generations of the community. For this reason, the caliphs after him used to give people stipends according to the amount of Qur'an they had. For this reason, Abu Bakr ordered that the Qur'an be written into a single codex (mushaf) with the consensus of the Companions (al-Sahabah), and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan completed that excellence by copying the Qur'an into codices and sending them to the regions of Islam. The Messenger of Allah had also appointed the People of the Suffah (Ahl al-Suffah) to devote themselves to memorizing the Qur'an.

What has become clear from tracing the biography of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is that he would hasten to convey the Qur'an when it was revealed. If it was revealed to him at night, he would inform the people of it at the dawn prayer. In the hadith of 'Umar, the Messenger of Allah said: "A surah was revealed to me last night which is more beloved to me than everything upon which the sun rises," then he recited ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1]. In the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik concerning his staying behind from the expedition of Tabuk: "So Allah revealed our repentance to His Prophet when the last third of the night remained, while the Messenger of Allah was with Umm Salamah. He said: 'O Umm Salamah, Ka'b ibn Malik has been forgiven.' She said: 'Shall I not send to him to give him the good news?' He said: 'If you do, the people will crowd upon you and keep you from sleep for the rest of the night.' Until, when the Messenger of Allah prayed the dawn prayer, he announced the forgiveness of Allah upon us."

In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: the surah of al-An'am was revealed to the Messenger of Allah all at once in Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah called the scribes, and they wrote it down that same night.

In the use of the second-person pronoun in His saying ﴿to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68] there is a great allusion to honoring the Messenger (ﷺ) with the rank of intermediary between Allah and the people, since He made the sending down to him and did not say "to you" (plural) or "to them", as He said in the verse of Al 'Imran: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 199], and His saying ﴿so that you may clarify to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44].

[p. 260]

In linking the sending down to being from the Lord, there is an honoring of what is sent down.

The use of the term "Lord" (al-Rabb) here rather than the Name of Majesty (Allah) is because the reminder that He is his Lord carries a meaning of honor for him, and a meaning of performing what He wished to convey, such as hastening, spreading it, urging its acceptance, and acting upon what is in it.

On all the aspects mentioned above, the verse indicates that the Messenger is commanded to convey all that is revealed to him, such that no one may suppose that the Messenger of Allah had withheld any part of the revelation without conveying it. For if he had left any part of it unconveyed, that would be among what was revealed to him and whose conveying had not occurred. Since this verse is among the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an, we know that among its most important purposes is that Allah intended to cut off the speculation of those who might claim that the Messenger had kept back something he did not convey, or that he had singled out some people with conveying a part of the revelation which he did not convey to the people in general. So this is the most decisive verse for refuting the claim of the Rafidah (Rafidites) that the Qur'an is more than what is in the codex compiled by Abu Bakr and copied by 'Uthman, and that the Messenger of Allah specifically entrusted 'Ali ibn Abi Talib with much of the Qur'an, and that he bequeathed it to his sons, and that it amounts to a camel's load, and that today it is stored with the infallible Imam, whom some of the Shi'ah call the Awaited Mahdi and the Successor (al-Wasi).

[p. 261]

These misconceptions had seized the minds of some of the Shi'a-leaning people toward 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) during his lifetime, and this prompted some people to ask him about it. Al-Bukhari narrated that Abu Juhayfah asked 'Ali: "Do you have anything that is not in the Qur'an and is not held by the people?" He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul, we have nothing except what is in the Qur'an, except an understanding given to a man regarding the Book of Allah, and what is in this sheet." I said: "And what is in the sheet?" He said: "The blood-money (al-'aql), the freeing of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever."

The hadith of Masruq from 'A'ishah, which we will mention, indicates that this notion had appeared among the common people in her time. The Messenger may single out some people to explain certain rulings that are not part of the Qur'an sent down to him, for a need that called for such specification, just as he wrote to 'Ali explaining the blood-money, the freeing of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever, because at that time he was a judge in Yemen. Likewise he wrote to 'Amr ibn Hazm the book on the nisab of zakat, because he had sent him for that purpose. This does not contradict the command to convey, because that is an explanation of what was sent down, and not the very same thing that was sent down. Moreover, he did not intend by it to restrict it to his own knowledge; rather, he may inform of it those whose need to act upon it calls for it. Furthermore, when he commanded those who heard his statement to preserve it and to convey it as they heard it, and commanded that the present convey it to the absent, the purpose of conveying was achieved. As for his leaving some of the revelation exclusively with one person, and that the one entrusted with it conceals it from the people, then God forbid that.

He may also single out someone with knowledge that does not pertain to matters of legislation, a secret he confides to some of his Companions, as he confided to Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her) that he would die on that day, and that she would be the first of his family to join him. He confided to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) that Allah had permitted him to emigrate. He confided to Hudhayfah the report of the strife of those who rebelled against 'Uthman, and Hudhayfah in turn related that to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. As for what is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, that he said: "I memorized two receptacles of knowledge from the Messenger of Allah. As for one of them, I disseminated it; as for the other, if I disseminated it, this throat of mine would be cut."

Because of this, we are certain that the writing which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to write for the people during his final illness, and then set aside, was not concerned with legislation. For if it had been, he would not have set it aside, and Allah says to him: "O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord." Al-Bukhari narrated from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said to Masruq: "Whoever tells you three things has lied: whoever tells you that Muhammad concealed anything of what was sent down to him has lied, and Allah says: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾," and so on in the hadith.

As for His saying ﴿and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾: the condition is introduced with "in" (إن), which in Arabic usage is typically used when the occurrence of the condition is not certain. Failure to convey is not presumed of Muhammad (ﷺ); this condition is posited only so that the answer can be built upon it, namely His saying ﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾, in order to startle those who hoped that the Messenger of Allah would remain silent about the recitation of the Qur'an that exposed their disgraces, namely the Jews and the hypocrites, and to rebuke those whom Allah knew would fabricate, claiming that a great deal of the Qur'an had not been conveyed by the Messenger of Allah to the Ummah.

The meaning of "if you do not" (لم تفعل) is: if you do not do that, namely conveying what has been sent down to you. This is a common ellipsis in their speech; they say "if you do" (فإن فعلت) or "if you do not" (فإن لم تفعل). Allah says: ﴿And do not call upon other than Allah what neither benefits you nor harms you; for if you do, then you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [Yunus: 106], meaning: if you call upon what does not benefit you. They omit the object of "you did" and "you did not do" because what precedes it indicates it. Allah also says: ﴿But if you do not and you will never do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24] in Surat al-Baqarah. This is among the expressions that have become like a proverb, so it is used only in limited variation, and the authorities of usage did not address it.

The meaning of the answer being consequent upon this condition is that if you do not convey all that has been sent down to you, and you leave out part of it, you would be one who has not conveyed the Message, because concealing part is like concealing all in the attribute of non-conveyance. Also, what is concealed cannot be known: its concealment may cause the loss of some benefits of what was conveyed. The difference between the condition and its answer has become clear in a way that removes the need to interpret the building of the answer upon the condition, since the condition is: "if you do not convey what has been sent down," and the consequent is: "you have not conveyed the Message." That suffices for the validity of building the answer upon the condition without the need for what they interpreted, as found in al-Kashshaf and elsewhere. Then it is known from this condition that such a state is not befitting for the Messengers, and so it follows that the Messenger does not conceal anything of what he was sent with. The benefit of opening the address with "O Messenger" (يا أيها الرسول) is to point to the basis for the subsequent statement, and the benefit of concluding it with His saying ﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾ is likewise evident.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, and Abu Ja'far read ﴿risalatahu﴾ in the plural form (رسالاته). The rest read ﴿risalatahu﴾ in the singular (رسالته). The intended meaning is the genus, so in the context of negation it is the same whether the singular or the plural is used. The claim of some scholars of meanings that the generality of the singular noun is more comprehensive than the generality of the plural, and that a phrase such as "there are no men in the house" (لا رجال في الدار) is true whether there are two men or one man in it, in contrast to "there is no man in the house" (لا رجل في الدار), is not correct. It appears that the plural reading is more explicit, because the plural noun in a construct state is among the forms of generality and does not allow the meaning of a specific known referent, whereas the singular noun in a construct state allows both the genus and a specific referent. There is no doubt that negating a term that does not admit a specific referent is more definite in the generality of the negation; but the context has clarified the intended meaning.

His saying ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ begins with the divine name (Allah) to give it emphasis, because the addressee and the hearers would be expecting, following the command to convey everything that was sent down to him, that he would encounter hardship and a pack of enemies against him. So He began His reassurance with the mention of the name of Allah, since the meaning is: this is your duty, but as for our part, Allah will protect you. Thus placing the divine name at the front here serves in place of the use of "as for" (أما). Moreover, al-Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir has mentioned in the chapters on fronting (التقديم) in Dala'il al-I'jaz that among the things in which fronting the subject over a verbal predicate is good, and where promise and guarantee are frequent, is that such fronting negates any doubt on the part of the one being promised about the completeness of the promise and its fulfillment; for such a person is among those most in need of emphasis, like a man saying: "I will suffice you; I will take care of this matter." End of quote. From the same, Allah says, relating the words of Yusuf: ﴿And I am its guarantor﴾ [Yusuf: 72]. So His saying ﴿Allah will protect you from the people﴾ carries this meaning as well. Here "protection" (العصمة) means safeguarding and shielding from the plots of his enemies.

Here "the people" (الناس) in the verse refers to the disbelievers among the Jews, the hypocrites, and the polytheists, because protection in the sense of shielding implies a fear for him, and one fears for him only from his enemies, not from his beloved ones; and there is no enemy of his Messenger among the believers. So the intended protection is from the assassination attempts of the polytheists, because that is what used to concern the Prophet (ﷺ); for if that had happened, the guidance that the Prophet loved for the people would have been disrupted, since he was eager for their guidance. Accordingly, when the Messenger of Allah presented himself to the tribes at the beginning of his mission, he would say to them: "That you protect me until I explain from Allah what He has sent me with, or until I convey the messages of my Lord." As for harm and injury beyond that, it is among what befell the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that he might be among those harmed for the sake of Allah: the polytheists pelted him with stones until they drew blood, and his face was wounded. This protection that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was promised has been repeated in the Qur'an, as in His saying ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137], and outside the Qur'an. There came in some reports that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while in Makkah, informed that Allah had protected him from the polytheists. And it came in the Sahih from 'A'ishah that "the Messenger of Allah was guarded in Madinah, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Hudhayfah stood guard over him one night; and the Messenger of Allah put his head out of a tent and said to them: 'Go back to your places, for Allah has protected me.'" And "he said, in the Battle of Dhat al-Riqa' in the sixth year, to the Bedouin Ghawrath ibn al-Harith, who found the Messenger of Allah asleep under the shade of a tree and found his sword hanging, so he drew it and said to the Messenger: 'Who will protect you from me?' He said: 'Allah.' Then the sword fell from the Bedouin's hand." All of that occurred before the time of the revelation of this verse. Those who made some of that the cause of the revelation of this verse have confused matters.

So this verse is an affirmation of the promise, a perpetuation of it, and that it does not change with the changing forms of enemies.

Then He followed it with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾, to make clear that the intended "people" are their disbelievers, and to point out that the cause of their not being guided is their disbelief. Here "guidance" (الهداية) means making their actions upright and completing their aims; so it is a promise to His Messenger that his enemies will continue to be frustrated and will not find a way to scheme against the Messenger and the believers, as an act of kindness from Him, exalted is He. The intended meaning is not guidance in religion, because the context is not suitable for that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 68:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord." And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people.﴾

This command which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was ordered to say to the People of the Scripture is among the things with which Allah strengthened him in conveying (his message), by His saying ﴿Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. The Messenger of Allah used to love to win over the People of the Scripture (ta'alluf), and perhaps it was difficult for him to confront them with such a statement, but Allah speaks the truth.

It is possible that the clause ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture"﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿Convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], and it is possible that it is a fresh independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) occasioned by His saying ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67].

By "the People of the Scripture" is meant both the Jews and the Christians together. As for the Jews, it is because they are commanded to uphold those rulings of the Torah that were not abrogated, to believe in the Gospel until the time of the Muhammadan mission, and to uphold the rulings of the Qur'an, which is the guardian (muhaymin) over the whole Scripture. As for the Christians, it is because they turned away from the Gospel's glad tidings of the coming of the Messenger after 'Isa, peace be upon them both.

The meaning of ﴿you are not upon anything﴾ is the negation that they possess any attribute of religiosity and piety, because the Messenger's address is only concerned with matters of religion, guidance and piety. So there occurs here an ellipsis of the qualifier of "anything", which the context indicates, in the manner of His saying Exalted is He ﴿So I wished to damage it, for there was behind them a king who seizes every boat by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every good boat, or every boat not defective.

"Shay'" (thing) is a name for every existent, so it is a noun extremely broad in indefiniteness, applying to the little and the much, and its meaning is specified by the context or by indications. Here the intended sense is "something of the matters of the Scripture." Since it occurs in the context of negation in this verse, what is derived is the negation that they have even the least share of religion and piety, so long as they have not reached the goal that was mentioned, which is that they uphold the Torah, the Gospel and the Qur'an. The intended meaning is the negation that they have any share worthy of regard before Allah. A negation of this kind, on the basis of "not counting," is common in speech. 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

"Indeed I was in war a man of defense, yet I was not given anything sufficient, and I was not prevented."

That is, I was not given anything sufficient, as indicated by his saying: "and I was not prevented." And they say: "This is nothing," although it is certainly a thing and is pointed to, but they mean that it is not counted as worthy. From this is what occurred in the authentic hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about soothsayers (kuhhan), and he said: "They are nothing." The negation in the sense of "not counting" resembles the earlier negation in His saying ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], that is, you have not conveyed it in a manner counted worthy before Allah.

The purpose of the verse is only the upholding of the Torah and the Gospel when the Qur'an comes, by acknowledging what is in the Torah and the Gospel of the good news of Muhammad ﷺ, so that they may believe in him and in what was revealed to him.

This verse has also indicated the extent to which the Jews went in turning away from guidance, for they had suspended the upholding of the Torah for ages before 'Isa, and suspended the upholding of the Gospel when they denied it and denied the one who brought it, then they denied the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, so they did not uphold what was revealed to them from their Lord. The discussion of upholding the Torah and the Gospel has already passed at His saying earlier ﴿And if only they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66], etc.

This verse has also refuted the claims of the Jews that they were upon adherence to the Torah, and they used to claim that they were upon guidance so long as they adhered to the Torah and did not adhere to anything other than it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that "they came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Do you not acknowledge that the Torah is true?' He said: '(Yes).' They said: 'Then we believe in it and do not believe in what is other than it.'" So this verse was revealed. But there is no strong chain for this.

Some of the Christians also said to the Messenger ﷺ, regarding their adherence to the Gospel, something like the saying of some of the Jews, as in the story of the conversion of 'Adi ibn Hatim, and as in the disputation of some of the delegation of Najran.

As for His saying ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief﴾, that is, of the People of the Scripture, and this is either by the stirring of envy at the coming of this religion and the descent of the Qur'an abrogating their religion, or by what is in some verses of the Qur'an of thunderbolts against them and refutation of their claims. Many of them, whenever they mention Islam, even in historical and civilizational topics, have continued to rage against the civilization of Islam, to distort facts, and to burst with rage and obstinacy, to the point that you see the scholar who is acknowledged among them diminishing himself and sinking into the depths of foolishness and ignorance, except for a few who have made equity their motto and kept far from being accused of misunderstanding out of caution and wariness.

Allah has named what obstructs them of the bone in their throats regarding this religion "transgression," because transgression is the extremity of wrongdoing and the plunging into obstinacy with disregard for the blame of those of certainty who blame them.

Allah consoled His Messenger ﷺ with His saying ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾. The fa' here is fa' al-fasihah, to complete the consolation, because the Messenger's mercy toward creation saddens him over what they have reached of increased transgression and disbelief. So the fa' of explanation draws attention to the fact that they reached what they reached only because of envy of the Messenger, and it is therefore fitting that he not grieve for them. Al-asa means grief and sorrow, and its verb is like fariha.

The word "people" (qawm) is mentioned and followed by the description "the disbelievers," to indicate that by "the disbelievers" is meant those for whom disbelief has become a disposition and an attribute by which their peoplehood is constituted. Had He not mentioned "the people" and said ﴿do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾, it would have been like a title for them, not implying a description, and so it would have included those in whom disbelief was not firmly rooted, but who are rather in bewilderment and hesitation, whose faith is hoped for.

[p. 268]

The position of this verse is subtle, its meaning is even more subtle, and its grammatical analysis (i'rab) follows from the subtlety of both.

Its position is more subtle than that of its counterpart earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. What was explained there does not suffice without explaining what belongs specifically to the position of this verse. Its meaning is also more precise than the meaning of its counterpart, following the precision of its position.

Its grammatical analysis becomes complicated because of the word (wa-al-Sabi'un) being in the nominative case by the waw, although in the apparent sense of the speech it is coordinated with the subject of inna.

[p. 269 precedes this part? No: the page break follows.]

It is therefore incumbent upon us to give it an explanation that we have not previously given for its counterpart. Let us begin with its position, for it is the core of its meaning.

Know that this sentence may be a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), arising from an assumed question that occurs to the listener after His saying: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, you have no standing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:68). So a questioner asks about the condition of those among the People of the Book who passed away before the coming of Islam: were they upon something or not upon anything, and did following their religion benefit them in that time? Thus His saying ﴿Indeed those who believed and those who were Jews﴾ and so on came as an answer to this presumed question.

By ﴿those who believed﴾ is meant those who believe in God and in Muhammad (ﷺ), that is, the Muslims. The intended subject of the information is those who were Jews, the Sabians and the Christians. The mention of those who believed is for the sake of giving them attention, which we will explain shortly.

It is also possible that this sentence is a confirmation of the sentence ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and been mindful of God﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:65) and so on. After that sentence was followed by what was followed by it of sentences, the speech returned to convey the meaning of that sentence, as an emphasis of the promise, a connective for the coherence of the speech, and so that the Sabians would be joined to the People of the Book, and so that the concern with mentioning the condition of the Muslims in the gardens of bliss would become evident.

Thus the opening with mention of those who believed at the head of those enumerated is an incorporation (idmaj, i.e., weaving one theme into another) to give honour to the Muslims on this occasion, because the Muslims are the excellent example in the perfection of faith and in guarding against delusion and against the infiltration of avenues of polytheism into their beliefs, as the Prophet (ﷺ) gave good news of this in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage when he said: "Indeed, Satan has despaired of being worshipped in your land here."
