So the Muslims, because they are the unique ones in faith in God and the Last Day and in righteous deeds, came first in this virtue.

As for the meaning of the verse, its opening with the particle inna here serves to give emphasis to the information, since the context is free of any intent to refute denial, or to address hesitation regarding the ruling, or to treat one who is not hesitant as if he were hesitant.

[p. 270 — the text continues]

Commentators have been perplexed about the statement about all those mentioned with His saying ﴿whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾, since among those mentioned are the believers, and is there any faith except in God and the Last Day? Commentators have taken various approaches to its interpretation: it has been said that by "those who believed" is meant those who believed with their tongues but not their hearts, namely the hypocrites. It has been said that by "whoever believes" is meant whoever persisted in his faith and did not apostatize. And it has been said other than this.

In my view, the correct position is that by "those who believed" is meant the bearers of the attribute known as faith, with which the Muslims are known, and this cannot be except through the heart and the tongue, because this statement is a promise of God's recompense, and so it refers to God's knowledge, and God knows the true believer from the one who only displays faith hypocritically.

What I see is that the predicate of inna should be taken as omitted. Omission of the predicate of inna is found in eloquent speech, not infrequently, as Sibawayh mentioned in his book. The predicate is indicated by what follows it, namely His saying ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:274) and so on. And His saying "and those who were Jews" is a coordination of one sentence with another, so "those who were Jews" is made the subject (mubtada'), and for this reason the thing coordinated with it, namely (wa-al-Sabi'un), is rightly in the nominative. This is preferable to making (wa-al-Sabi'un) the beginning of the sentence and positing a predicate for it, i.e., "and the Sabians likewise," as most have held, because that leads to the coordinated items differing in ruling and being scattered, although it is possible to avoid that. His saying "whoever believes in God" is then a second subject, and "whoever" (man) is a relative pronoun, and the link connecting the sentence to what precedes it is omitted, i.e., "whoever of them believes," and the sentence ﴿for them is their reward﴾ is the predicate of the relative "whoever." Its connection with fa' (then/so) is because the relative pronoun resembles the conditional. This is common in speech, as in God's saying ﴿Indeed, those who afflicted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent, for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ (Al-Buruj 85:10) and so on. The presence of the fa' there determines that it is a predicate of the relative "whoever," and the predicate of inna is not as in the reverse of the saying of Dabi' ibn al-Harith:

"Whoever has made his abode in Medina tonight,
then I and Qabbar therein are indeed strangers."

For the presence of the lam of emphasis in His saying "indeed strangers" (la-gharib) determines that it is the predicate of inna, and there is a predicate for Qabbar that is omitted. So God's saying (wa-al-Sabi'un) should not be compared with it.

The meaning of ﴿whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾ is: whoever believes and persists, and they are those who did not alter their religions by associating partners with God or by denying resurrection. For many Jews mixed matters of polytheism into their religion and worshipped gods, as the Torah itself says. Among them were those who made Ezra a son of God. And the Christians deified Jesus and worshipped him. And the Sabians worshipped the stars after having been upon a religion that had a scripture. The explanation of their religion has already passed in the commentary on the counterpart of this verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

Then the Jews and Christians introduced into their belief a delusion about their salvation from the punishment of the Hereafter, by saying ﴿We are the sons of God and His beloved﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:18), and their saying ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:80), and the saying of the Christians that Jesus has expiated the sins of mankind by what he bore of the punishment of mockery, humiliation, crucifixion and killing. Thus they became in the position of one who does not believe in the Last Day, because they nullified recompense, which is the wisdom for which resurrection was decreed.

The majority of exegetes made His saying (wa-al-Sabi'un) a subject, and they regarded it as fronted from a delayed position, and posited for it an omitted predicate, since the predicate of inna indicates it. The original arrangement of the wording is: "Indeed those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians—for them is their reward and so on—and the Sabians likewise." They treated it like the saying of Dabi' ibn al-Harith:

"Indeed I and Qayyar therein are strangers."

Some exegetes posited other estimates, which al-Alusi carried to five.

What we have followed is clearer, more in line with the wording's structure, and more fitting to the meaning of this verse.

Moreover, what must be held with certainty is that this wording was thus revealed, and thus the Prophet (ﷺ) pronounced it, and thus the Muslims received it from him and recited it, and it was written in the codices, and they were pure Arabs. So it became for us a basis from which we learn one of the Arabs' patterns in the use of coordination, even if this usage is not common; yet it has a place in eloquence and conciseness. This is because it is common in speech that when a sentence is emphasized with the particle inna, with its subject and predicate given, and one wishes to coordinate with its subject a conjunct that is unusual in that ruling, the unusual conjunct is brought in the nominative, so as to indicate that they intended the coordination of sentences and not the coordination of single words, so that the listener would supply a predicate according to the context of the speech. Among this is God's saying ﴿that God is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾ (Al-Tawbah 9:3), that is, "and His Messenger likewise," for his disavowal of them while being of their kin and in-law relation is something strange, so that it becomes evident that the bond of religion is greater than all those other bonds. Likewise this conjunct here: since the Sabians were further from guidance than the Jews and Christians in the period of ignorance before the coming of Islam, because they had committed themselves to worshipping the stars, and yet salvation is due to them if they believe in God and the Last Day and do righteous deeds, the bringing of their name in the nominative served as an alert to this.

However, following the usual pattern would require that this conjunct not be brought in the nominative until after inna has completed its predicate. Rather, in the speech of the Arabs the subject intended for this ruling is usually placed later. As for fronting it, as in this verse, it may seem to the observer to contradict the purpose for which the grammatical form was changed. Yet this too is a rare usage, namely combining the demands of two states: indicating the strangeness of the one spoken of in this ruling, and alerting to the hastening of informing about this predicate, for the Sabians nearly despair of this ruling, or someone who hears the ruling about the Muslims and Jews despairs of them. So He alerted everyone that God's pardon is great and cannot be restricted in encompassing them. This is the reason for both the fronting and the nominative. Had it not been fronted, this consideration would not have been achieved; just as, had it not been put in the nominative, it would have become a conjunct of the subject of inna, and its coordination would not have been a coordination of sentences.

The Sabians are mentioned in Surat al-Hajj fronted before the Christians and in the accusative, so there the demand of one state was realized, namely the haste to inform about the inclusion of the decisive judgment among them and that before God's justice they are equal to others.

Then He concluded all of this with His saying "and does righteous deeds," which is the principal aim of connecting safety from fear and grief to it. It is a condition on all those mentioned, both Muslims and others. The first of the righteous deeds is affirming the Messenger and believing in the Qur'an, then comes obedience to the commands and avoidance of the prohibitions, as God said ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ (Al-Balad 90:12) up to His saying ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ (Al-Balad 90:17).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 70:

﴿Indeed, We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers. Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a party [of them] they denied, and a party they killed.﴾

This is a resumption (istinaf) by which the discourse returns to the condition of the Jews and their audacity toward God and His messengers. It is an allusion to despair of their guidance through what Muhammad ﷺ brought, and to the fact that their confrontation with his call is not something novel from them; rather, it is their established pattern, generation after generation.

The discussion of the covenant taken from the Jews has already preceded more than once. The first instance is in Surat al-Baqarah.

The messengers who were sent to them are Musa, Harun, and those who came after them, such as Yusha' ibn Nun, Isha'ya (Isaiah), Irmiya (Jeremiah), Hizqiyal (Ezekiel), Dawud, and 'Isa. Thus the word "messengers" (rusul) here means the prophets (anbiya'): those among them who came with a law (shar') and a scripture, such as Musa, Dawud, and 'Isa, and those who came to reinforce the law and clarify it, such as Yusha', Isha'ya, and Irmiya.

The application of the term "messenger" (rasul) to a prophet who did not bring a separate law is common in the Qur'an, as has preceded. Since He mentioned that they killed a party of the messengers, the interpretation of "messengers" as "prophets" is necessitated, for they only killed prophets, not messengers.

As for His saying ﴿every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, a party they denied﴾ and so on, "kullama" (every time) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyyah), because it indicates the totality of the times of the messengers' coming to them; so it indicates the totality of the messengers, following the totality of the times of their coming, since the totality of the times of the existence of a thing necessitates the totality of its individuals. Thus "ma" is a verbal-temporal particle (zarfiyyah masdariyyah) indicating time.

"Kull" is in the accusative as a substitute for the time, because it is annexed to the indefinite time-noun, which is the temporal "ma" (ma al-zarfiyyah al-masdariyyah). The meaning is: at every time of the messengers' coming to them, they denied [some] and kill [others]. "Kullama" is connected to the two verbs, "kadhdhabu" and "yaqtulun," by the grammatical device of tanazu' (contention of governors).

Placing "kullama" before its governing verb is a common usage that almost never varies, because by placing it first they intend to give it importance, so that it becomes clear that it is the focal point toward which the whole sentence is directed. The continuation of this conduct of theirs with all the messengers at all times is evidence that denial and killing had become fixed dispositions (sajiyyatan) for them that do not fail, since they did not consider the state of one messenger over another, nor one time over another; and this is more manifest in the atrocity of their condition, which is the aim here.

By this placement, the temporal "kullama" takes on the meaning of a conditional, so its governing verb occupies the position of its apodosis, just as conditional nouns come first before their verbs and apodoses, as in ﴿wherever you may be, death will overtake you﴾. However, "kullama" has not been heard followed by a jussive, and therefore it is not counted among the conditional nouns, because "kull" is far from the meaning of conditionality. The truth is that applying the term "conditional" to it in the speech of some grammarians is a loose usage. Sahib al-Kashshaf applied it in this verse, because he did not find for it a lexical cause requiring its placement first, unlike what is in His saying the Exalted ﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87] in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His saying ﴿Is it that whenever they made a covenant, a party of them cast it aside?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 100] in that same surah; for the placement in these two is due to their being directly preceded by the interrogative hamza, as we have mentioned there, although al-Kashshaf was silent about them because their matter was evident in those two verses.

The better view is that the clause ﴿a party they denied﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ("ilayhim"), because it is connected to a pronoun agreeing with the one it qualifies, and because the purpose of the statement is to portray in horrifying terms the condition of the Children of Israel in their ill treatment of their guides; and this is achieved only by considering the addressees in this state with their messengers. The clause "a party they denied" and what precedes it from its complement is not a resumption, since the intent is not to inform that God sent messengers to them, but rather to convey the meaning of this circumstance.

By this it becomes clear to you that the division in His saying ﴿a party they denied and a party they kill﴾ does not refer to "a messenger" in His saying ﴿every time a messenger came to them﴾, but rather to "rusulan" (messengers); because we have considered His saying ﴿every time a messenger came to them﴾ as preceded by a postponement. The meaning is: "And We sent to them messengers, of whom they denied a party and killed a party, every time a messenger of the messengers came to them." By this we dispense with the artifices and estimations in the structure of the verse, which is arranged with the most eloquent forms of brevity and the clearest meanings.

His saying ﴿with what their souls did not desire﴾, i.e., with what they do not love. It is said: "hawiya yahwa," meaning "to love," and his soul inclined toward being involved with something. The purpose of sending the messengers is to restrain souls from much of their desire, which causes them corruption in the present and loss in the future; were it not for this, people would be left to what they desire. Thus the laws necessarily include much restraint of souls from their desires. When the Children of Israel were described as denying the messengers and killing them when they came to them with what opposes their desire, we know that no messenger who came to them was free of one of two matters, or both: denial and killing; and this is derived from ﴿every time a messenger came to them﴾. Thus nothing remains for His saying ﴿with what their souls did not desire﴾ except to indicate the increase in the atrocity of their condition: that they deny the messengers or kill them in circumstances where they could not find for themselves an excuse, such as being burdened with a heavy hardship, or the occurrence of some turmoil, or for the sake of clinging to a religion they refuse to abandon, as the pagans of the Arabs did at the coming of Islam; rather, it is merely for opposing the desire of their souls after the covenant had been taken from them and they had accepted it, so that by their rebellion the benefit of legislation and the benefit of the nation's obedience to its guides are nullified.

This is a great teaching from the Qur'an: that it is the right of nations to proceed along the path of guidance by their scholars and guides; and that if they seek to compel their scholars and guides to accompany their desires, such that they disobey them when they call to what opposes the desire of the peoples, then ruin has befallen them just as it befell the Children of Israel, for in that is a reversal of realities and an attempt to make the follower a leader and the led a follower; and that the leaders of nations, their scholars and their sincere advisers, if they accompany nations in this disposition, become deceivers toward them, the benefit of their knowledge and wisdom vanishes, and what is guarded is mixed with what is neglected, and the rope with the rope-cutter. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever God entrusts with a flock and he deceives it, will not smell the fragrance of Paradise." Thus the pagans of the Arabs are closer to being excused, because they confronted the Messenger from the very first moment with their saying: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community, and indeed we are following in their footsteps, guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22], and the people of Shu'ayb said: ﴿Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped?﴾ [Hud: 87]. Unlike the Jews, who believed in their messengers at the outset and then turned against them with denial and killing when they bade them toward what was good for them, which they did not desire.

The fronting of the object in His saying "fariqan kadhdhabu" is merely for the sake of emphasis on the detail, because the discourse is directed toward detailing the states of the messengers of the Children of Israel in terms of what they encountered from their people; and because in fronting the object of "yaqtulun" there is observance of the verse-ending (fasilah), so the object of "kadhdhabu" was fronted so that the two objects would be on a single rhythm.

In His saying "yaqtulun" the present tense form is used to narrate a past state, in order to bring that horrifying condition vividly to mind, for emphasis in marveling at the vileness of its doers.

All the pronouns refer back to the Children of Israel, considering them as a nation whose generations succeed one another, and in which similar characters and followed customs became firmly rooted, such that the later among them is upon what the earlier was upon; therefore the actions occurring in different eras are attributed to their pronouns despite the differing agents, for those who killed some of the prophets are a party other than those who were limited to denial.

[Page 276]

It is coordinated with His saying "they denied" and "they kill," to show the corruption of their belief, from which their corrupt deeds arise. That is, they committed the atrocities they committed deliberately and through delusion, not from a slip or a sudden outburst of the soul that they might later repent of and turn back from. The pronouns in the verse refer back to the pronouns in the earlier "they denied" and "they kill." And they supposed that their deed would bring them no fitna (trial, affliction).

Fitna is the disorder of people's conditions and the upheaval of their order because of harms and successive calamities. Its meaning has already been examined under His saying ﴿Indeed, we are only a fitna﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:102] in Surat al-Baqarah. It may be a punishment from God upon people in recompense for their evil deeds, or a purification of the sincere among their faith, so that their ranks are raised thereby: ﴿Indeed, those who afflicted the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj 85:10], and so on. The Qur'an called Harut and Marut a fitna, the Prophet ﷺ called the Dajjal a fitna, and the Qur'an called the slips of Satan a fitna: ﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾ [al-A'raf 7:27]. Thus the meaning of testing is inherent in it.

The meaning is: they supposed that God would not afflict them with any fitna in this world in recompense for how they treated their prophets. The adverbial phrase "there" (hunālika) is an implied complement indicated by the context; that is, they supposed that no calamities would befall them in this world, so they felt safe from the punishment of God in this world, after they had made light of the punishment of the Hereafter. They imagined that they would be saved from it because they were the sons of God and His beloved, and that the Fire would touch them only for a number of days.

So among the marvels of the Qur'an's concision is that it alludes to the corruption of their belief concerning the recompense of the Hereafter, that they had cast the thought of it behind their backs, that they did not fear God when committing abominations, and to the gravity of their heedlessness of the fitna of this world, and that they were astray in both matters.

His saying ﴿they supposed that there would be no fitna﴾ indicates that had they not supposed this, they would have refrained, because they were more eager for the safety of this world than for safety in the Hereafter, owing to the decline of their faith and the weakness of their certainty.

This is the condition of nations when abandonment (khudhlān) overtakes them: their belief becomes corrupt, their faith becomes mixed, and their concern becomes confined to managing their immediate affairs. When they suppose that the affairs of this life are in order, they close their eyes to the Hereafter, seeking safety without its causes. So they lose the everlasting success and cling to the immediate success, and they do evil, and the immediate punishment of fitna and the deferred punishment befall them.

The expression "they became blind and deaf" (ʿamū wa-ṣammū) is used figuratively (istiʿārah) for turning away from the proofs of guidance brought by their messengers and books, because blindness and deafness lead to going astray from the path and to being unable to benefit from what is beneficial. The combination of blindness and deafness is a combination, in the metaphor, of the kinds of deprivation of benefit from the most beneficial thing. When turning away from that occurs, desire overcomes souls, because being drawn toward it is innate, so avoiding it needs a restraining force. When the restraining force is absent, evil conduct comes. For this reason, His saying "they became blind and deaf" is also intended in its implicative sense (kināyah), namely that they did evil deeds and corrupted. Therefore it was proper for Him to join to it His saying ﴿then God turned to them in forgiveness﴾. This intended meaning is confirmed by His saying at the close of the verse ﴿and God is Seeing of what they do﴾.

His saying ﴿then God turned to them in forgiveness﴾ means: after that misguidance, and turning away from right guidance, and what followed from it of evil conduct and corruption on earth.

From His saying ﴿that there would be no fitna﴾ and His saying ﴿then God turned to them in forgiveness﴾ it is understood that a fitna befell them after that blindness and deafness, and that its consequences were a punishment for them, and that when God turned to them in forgiveness He lifted the fitna from them. ﴿Then they became blind and deaf again﴾, that is, they returned to their former misguidance and their blameworthy conduct, because they persisted in supposing that there would be no fitna, so another fitna befell them.

The statement stopped at this second blindness and deafness, and it is not mentioned that God turned to them in forgiveness after it. This indicates that they turned away from the truth with great severity a second time, so a fitna befell them after which God did not turn to them in forgiveness.

It is certain that this refers to two great events from the history of the Children of Israel after Moses, peace be upon him. The most evident is the Babylonian Captivity, when God empowered over them Bukhtunassar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Assyria, who entered Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) several times, in 606, 598 and 588 BCE. In the third of these he came upon the city of Urshalim (Jerusalem), burned it, burned the Temple, and carried all the Children of Israel captive to Babylon. The turning of God toward them was manifested when Cyrus (Kurash), king of Persia, defeated the Assyrians and took control of Babylon in 530 BCE, and the Jews were permitted to return to their lands and rebuild them, so they returned and built their sanctuary.

[Page 278]

The second event is the destruction that occurred in the time of Titus (Titus), the Roman commander, who was the son of the Roman Emperor Vespasian (Vespasianus). He besieged Jerusalem until the Jews were forced to eat hides and some of them ate others from hunger. He killed a million men and took ninety-seven thousand captive, according to what is said, with exaggeration in that, and this was in 69 CE. Then the Roman Emperor Hadrian (Adrianus) pursued them from 117 to 138 CE, destroyed the city, made it a wasteland, and mixed its soil with salt. That was the end of the Jewish state and their city, and their dispersion over the earth.

The Qur'an has alluded to these two events in His saying ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book that you will surely cause corruption in the earth twice and you will surely become arrogant with great arrogance﴾ [al-Isra' 17:4]. ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they roamed through the homes, and it was a promise fulfilled﴾ [17:5]. ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them and provided you with wealth and sons and made you more numerous in manpower﴾ [17:6]. ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves, and if you do evil, it is for them. So when the promise of the Hereafter came, to sadden your faces and to enter the sanctuary as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had overcome with complete destruction﴾ [17:7]. ﴿Perhaps your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾ [17:8]. This is what al-Qaffal (al-Qaffal) chose. In the verse there are other opinions, which al-Fakhr (al-Razi) examined at length.

The particle "then" (thumma) indicates the lateness of the two verbs it conjoins relative to the two verbs they are conjoined to, and that there were two blindnesses and two deafnesses in two times, one earlier and one later. Nevertheless, the pronouns attached to the two conjoined verbs were the same as the pronouns attached to the two verbs they were conjoined to. What justified this is that the purpose is to show the recurrence of acts across ages and to claim that the agent is one, because that is the way of reports and attributes ascribed to nations and recorded against them, the inheritance of dispositions among them, good or bad. It is known that those who became blind and deaf the second time were not the same as those who became blind and deaf the first time, but because they were successors of predecessors, and because they had passed on their characters to their sons, they were treated as one thing, like the saying "the sons of so-and-so have an inheritance together with the sons of so-and-so."

His saying "many of them" (kathīrun minhum) is a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in His saying ﴿then they became blind and deaf﴾. It is intended to single out the people of virtue and righteousness among them in every age, to declare that they are innocent of what their common people were upon, proclaiming the truth and praising virtue. Since the referent of the last two pronouns in "then they became blind and deaf" is the same as the referent of the first two pronouns in "they became blind and deaf," the substitution from the last two pronouns, which conveys a specification of their generality, also conveys a specification of the generality of the two pronouns before them, by the rule of parity among pronouns, since the pronouns of one nation are treated as a single unit. Their referent is the phrase "Children of Israel." It is necessary that no misguided nation is devoid in every generation of righteous people among them. Among the later ones were men like Abdullah ibn Salam, and among the earlier ones were Yusha' (Joshua) and Kalib (Caleb), concerning whom God said: ﴿Two men of those who feared, on whom God had bestowed His favor, said: "Enter upon them through the gate"﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:23].

His saying ﴿and God is Seeing of what they do﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl). "Seeing" (baṣīr) is an intensive form of "one who sees," like "wise" (ḥakīm) in the sense of "one who makes firm." Here it means the Knower of everything that occurs in their actions which people are capable of seeing, whether what people saw of them or what they did not see. The purpose of this statement is its necessary implication, namely warning and reminding that nothing is hidden from God. It is therefore a threat against them for what they committed after God had turned to them in forgiveness.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read "an lā takūna" with the nūn of takūna vowelled with a fatḥah, taking "an" as a particle of the infinitive that governs the verb in the subjunctive. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it with a ḍammah on the nūn, taking "an" as the light form (mukhaffafah) of "anna," sister of "inna," which has a kasrah on its hamzah. When "anna" is lightened, its usual governance is cancelled and it is followed by a full sentence. Some grammarians claimed that even so it still governs, that its subject is obligatorily omitted, and that its predicate must be a sentence. This is an assumption for which there is no proof. Some went further and claimed that its omitted subject is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). This too is an assumption upon an assumption, and it is not in the nature of the pronoun of the matter to be omitted, since it is introduced for emphasis. Moreover, its non-appearance in any usage refutes the claim that it is to be supposed.

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." But the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord. Indeed, whoever associates partners with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise, and his refuge is the Fire. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers."﴾.

This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i, a new sentence that opens a fresh topic), serving to refute what the Christians hold, and it follows on naturally from the refutation of what the Jews hold.

This statement has already been discussed just above, in the parallel verse ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." Say: "Who then can prevent Allah in anything?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17], and in regard to the groups of Christians to whom this saying is attributed.

The waw in His words ﴿But the Messiah said﴾ is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal). The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿those who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah"﴾. That is, they said this while the Messiah was calling the Children of Israel to the fact that Allah is his Lord and their Lord. In other words, there is no excuse for them: they say that Allah has become united with the Messiah, while the Messiah whom they claim to believe in, and to whom they attribute this, has refuted them. This is because his saying "my Lord and your Lord" contradicts their saying "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah", since one who is a lord cannot be a servant of a lord, and that is what the word "my Lord" implies; and because there cannot be another god alongside Allah, and that is what the words "and your Lord" imply. For this reason, the clause ﴿Indeed, whoever associates partners with Allah, Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾ follows it. Accordingly, this clause may be a quotation of a statement issued by 'Isa, peace be upon him, in which case it serves as a justification (ta'lil) for the command to worship Allah. The use of "inna" (indeed) in this position takes the place of the resumptive fa' (fa' al-tafri', "so" or "therefore") and expresses causation. Its quotation also carries an implicit allusion (ta'rid) that their saying this has led them into associationism (shirk), even though they think they have avoided it out of fear of falling into what he warned against.

[p. 281]

the Messiah, because those who said "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah" intended a union with Allah, and that He is the very same as him. This is the saying of the Ya'aqibah (Jacobites), as mentioned just above and in Surat al-Nisa'. That is undoubtedly associationism, and indeed it is worse, because they associated with Allah another and mixed him with Him. Thus they fell into associationism, even though they aimed to avoid multiplicity of gods. Allah has nullified their saying completely, by the testimony of the words of the one to whom they attributed divinity.

If the clause is part of the speech of Allah the Exalted, then it is a concluding generalization (tadhyil), serving to confirm their disbelief, to add emphasis to the alerting of the invalidity of their belief, and as an allusion to them, that they have associated others with Allah while intending monotheism.

The pronoun attached to "inna" is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), which indicates concern with the predicate that follows it. The meaning of ﴿Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾ is that He prevented him from it, that is, from dwelling in it.

Al-ma'wa is the place to which a thing resorts, that is, to which it returns.

The clause ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ may also be a statement of the Messiah, peace be upon him, on the assumption that his words ﴿Indeed, whoever associates partners with Allah﴾ are part of his speech. It may also be a statement of Allah the Exalted, as a concluding generalization of the Messiah's speech on that assumption, or a concluding generalization of Allah's speech on the other assumption. What is meant by "the wrongdoers" is the associators, since associationism is indeed a great wrong; that is, the associators have no helpers who could support them to rescue them from the torment of the Fire.

Thus the implied sense is: "And his refuge is the Fire, inevitably, and he has no hope of escaping from it through any helper." Therefore, it is all the more certain that he will not escape without a helper.

[p. 282]

This is a new sentence (istiʾnaf) intended to move on to refuting another doctrine among the doctrines of the Christian sects: the doctrine of the Melkites (al-Malkaniyya), who are called the Jathaliqiyya (Catholics), and on which most of the Christian sects across the whole earth agree. Its explanation has already been given at His words, ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say, "Three"﴾ [al-Nisa larr: 171] in Surat al-Nisa, and His words there, ﴿and do not say, "Three"﴾ [al-Nisa: 171], include a refutation of all the Christian sects. By qalu ("they said") is meant "they believed and then said," because it is the nature of speech to proceed from belief, and this has already been explained.

The meaning of their words, "Indeed Allah is the third of three," is that what people know as Allah is a composite of three things, and that the one who deserves the name is one of those three things. They expressed these three by the term aqanim (hypostases), and they are: the hypostasis of existence, which is the Essence called Allah, and which they also call the Father; the hypostasis of knowledge, which they also call the Son, and which is the one that united with Jesus, so that Jesus thereby became God; and the hypostasis of life, which they call the Holy Spirit. Most of them, and among them the Rakusiyya, a sect of Arab Christians, say that when it (the Word) united with Mary at the time of her carrying it, it (the Word) was made the Word, and Mary also became divine. For this reason they differed over whether she is the Mother of the Word or the Mother of Allah.

So His words "third of three" mean "one of those three," because the Arabs form from the numeral, from two to ten, a form of the active participle (fa'il) construed with the numeral from which it is derived, to indicate that it is a part of that number, as in thani ithnayn ("second of two"). If they intended that the one for whom the pattern fa'il is derived is the one who completes the number, they would construe the pattern fa'il with the numeral that is higher than it, and say: rabiʿ thalatha ("fourth of three"), that is, one who makes the three four.

His words, ﴿And there is no god except One God﴾, are conjoined to the clause "they have certainly disbelieved," to state the truth of belief after mentioning false belief.

It is also permissible to make the clause a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in qalu, meaning: they said this statement while it was contrary to reality. In that case it serves as a reason for their disbelief in their saying that. The meaning on both readings is a negation, of the true God, that He could be other than one. The (min) here is for emphasizing the generality of the negation, so the negation by (ma) with which it is combined becomes equivalent to the negation by (la) of genus, in indicating the negation of the genus explicitly.

[p. 283]

Here he departed from negation by la of exoneration (al-tabri'a), and did not say, "There is no god except one God," but said, ﴿And there is no god except One God﴾, out of concern to display the particle (min), which, after negation, indicates the confirmation of the negation. For the negation by the particle (la) conveys negation of the genus only by implying the particle (min). When greater emphasis on negation was intended here, the negating particle (ma) was used and (min) was made explicit after it. This is something none of the exegetes has addressed.

His words, "except One God," indicate that the attribute of divinity is restricted to one, so the trinity attributed to them is negated. As for determining who this One is, its determination is not intended here, because the aim is to refute the doctrine of the Trinity. When the Trinity is refuted and the oneness is established, it is necessarily determined that this One is Allah, the Exalted, since His divinity is agreed upon. When the divinity of others alongside Him is negated, divinity becomes purely His. Thus His words here, ﴿And there is no god except One God﴾, are equivalent to His words in Surat Al 'Imran, ﴿And there is no god except One God﴾, except that the mention of the name of Allah occurred earlier here, and the saying of the deniers, "He is the third of three," occurred earlier, so the affirmation of oneness dispenses with specifying Him. For this reason He explicitly specified the One God in Surat Al 'Imran in His words, ﴿And there is no god except God﴾, since the context required specifying that divinity is restricted to Allah, the Exalted, and not to Jesus, and there was no mention in it of a plurality of gods.

His words, ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say, a painful punishment will surely touch those of them who disbelieve﴾, are conjoined to the clause ﴿Those who said, "Indeed Allah is the third of three," have certainly disbelieved﴾. That is, they have certainly disbelieved with a disbelief such that, if they do not desist from it, a painful punishment will befall them. The meaning of ʿamma yaqulun ("from what they say") is "from their statement mentioned just before," which is, "Indeed Allah is the third of three." He used the present tense (al-mudari') because it is appropriate to desisting, since desisting is only from something ongoing, just as His saying "they said" is appropriate to His saying "has disbelieved," because the disbelief occurred through their saying that from a past time onward.

The meaning of ʿamma yaqulun ("from what they say") is "from what they believe," because if they desisted from speaking with the tongue but concealed the belief in it, that would not benefit them. Since it is the nature of speech to proceed only from belief, it is suitable to be a metonymy (kinaya) for belief alongside its explicit meaning.

He emphasized the threat with the oath particle in His words, ﴿la-yamassanna﴾, in response to their belief that the Fire would not touch them, because the crucifixion of Jesus was an expiation for the sins of the children of Adam.

[p. 284]

The word massa ("touch") is a figurative usage (majaz) for "befall," because the literal meaning of touching is placing the hand upon a body, so it is used for befalling by the common element of contact, as in His words, ﴿And those who denied Our signs, the punishment will touch them because they used to defy﴾ [al-An'am: 49]. It thus indicates the general sense of befalling without restriction to severity or weakness. Severity or weakness is determined only by context, such as the word "painful" here, and as His words ﴿because they used to defy﴾ [al-An'am: 49] in the other verse. Yazid ibn al-Hakam al-Kilabi, one of the poets of the Hamasa, said:

"We touched upon some of the fathers, a thing, and all of us
toward a lineage among his people, not lowered."

That is, we traced the origins of our fathers.

The intended meaning of "those who disbelieved" is the very same as the intended meaning of "those who said, 'Indeed Allah is the third of three.'" He departed from expressing them by a pronoun to the relative clause that establishes the meaning of their disbelief mentioned just before in His words, "Those who said..." etc., in order to repeat the recording of their disbelief, and so that the relative pronoun would point to the cause of the ruling reported about them. On this basis, His words "of them" (minhum) attached to "those who disbelieved" are intended as a precaution, lest the hearer suppose that this is a threat to other disbelievers.

When Allah threatened them, He followed the threat with encouragement to guidance, saying, ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾. Repentance (tawba) is abandoning what one is upon in the future and returning to the correct belief. Seeking forgiveness (istighfar) is asking for forgiveness of what has passed from them in the past, and regret for what has been neglected from them of bad belief.

His words, ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, are a concluding statement (tadhyil) containing praise of Allah, that He forgives whoever repents and seeks forgiveness for what has passed from him, because "Forgiving" and "Merciful" are among the forms of intensification (mubalagha), indicating intensity of forgiveness and intensity of mercy. It is thus a promise that if they repent and seek His forgiveness, He will lift the punishment from them by His mercy and pardon what has passed from them by His forgiveness.

[p. 282]

[Page 285]

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) clarifying the true description of the Messiah and of his mother, in addition to refuting the belief of the Christians in the divinity of the Messiah and of his mother. It is known that their saying "God is the third of three" meant the divinity of the Messiah, and this is the belief of all Christians. A sect of Christians, called the Rukusiyya, branched off. They are a Christian group of Sabian character who held the divinity of Jesus and the divinity of his mother. Had that not been their belief, the description of Mary would not have been mentioned, nor would her humanity have been argued from the fact that they both ate food.

So His saying ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, is only a messenger﴾ is a restriction (qasr) of the subject to an attribute, and it is a relative restriction (qasr idafi). That is, the Messiah is restricted to the attribute of messengership and does not go beyond it to anything else, such as divinity. The restriction is therefore a reversing restriction (qasr qalb), to reject the belief of the Christians that he is God.

His saying ﴿Messengers had passed away before him﴾ is a qualifier of "messenger," meant to show that he is equal to the other messengers who passed before him, and that he is not unprecedented in this attribute, nor is he distinguished in the attribute of messengership by a particularity not found in others. So there is no basis for those who claimed divinity for him, since he brought nothing beyond what the messengers brought. The miracles that occurred at his hands were like those that occurred at the hands of messengers before him, even though their characteristics differ. They are equal in being departures from custom, and none of them is more wondrous than another. Thus his raising of the dead was not truly such as to suggest his divinity. In this there is a rebuke of the folly of the people who argued for his divinity from his raising of the dead animals, for Moses turned a staff, which is inanimate, into a serpent.

The clause ﴿and his mother was a truthful woman﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, is only a messenger﴾. The purpose of describing her as a truthful woman (siddiqa) is to negate that she has any attribute higher than this, namely the attribute of divinity, because the context is the refutation of the saying of those who said "God is the third of three," since they made Mary the third hypostasis (uqnum). This is what the author of al-Kashshaf indicated when he said: "That is, his mother was only a truthful woman." Yet the clause does not contain a formula of exclusion. Al-'Allama al-Taftazani, in his commentary on al-Kashshaf, explained it by saying: "The exclusion to which he pointed is derived from the context and the coordination," that is, from the combination of the two matters. There is an objection to al-Taftazani's saying "and the coordination."

Al-Siddiqa is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha), like shirrib and missik, which intensify drinking and holding. It is also like the epithet of Imru' al-Qays, "al-Malik al-Dilil" (the king who went astray), because he did not find the way to recover his father's kingdom. The basic form of this pattern is that it is derived from the unaugmented triliteral root. So the meaning is an intensification in describing her as truthful, that is, truthful in the promise of her Lord, which is the covenant of faith, and truthful in her word to people. Likewise Isma'il, peace be upon him, was described with this in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il; he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54]. Yusuf was also given the epithet al-Siddiq, because he was true to his Lord's promise in refraining from forbidden things despite the full availability of their means. It has been said that what is meant here is describing her with intensity in affirmation, in reference to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]. Likewise Abu Bakr was given the epithet al-Siddiq because he was the first to affirm the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he who brought the truth and affirmed it﴾ [al-Zumar: 33]. In that case it is derived from the augmented form.

His saying ﴿they both used to eat food﴾ is a clause that stands in the position of an argument for the implication of the restriction, which is the negation of divinity for the Messiah and his mother. For this reason it is separated from the preceding clause, because the proof stands in the place of an explanation. He argued for their humanity by establishing an attribute of human beings, namely eating food. This attribute was chosen from among many attributes because it is apparent and clear to people, and because the Gospels establish it. The Gospels establish that Mary ate from the fruit of the palm tree at the time of her labor, and that Jesus ate with the disciples on the day of Passover, bread and wine. In the Gospel of Luke, chapter 22: "And he said to them, I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I say to you, I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God." And in the morning, when he was returning to the city, he was hungry.

His saying ﴿See how We make the signs clear to them﴾ is a resumptive statement expressing wonder at the state of those who claimed divinity for Jesus. The address is intended for an unspecified person, namely everyone who heard the preceding proofs. The command to look (al-nazar) is used in place of the command to know (al-'ilm), by way of likening knowledge to sight in clarity and manifestness, and similar instances have already been mentioned. This conveys the meaning of wonder. It is also possible that the address is to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and what is meant is him and the people of the Qur'an.

Kayfa is an interrogative noun suspending the verb "look" from acting on two objects. It is in the position of the direct object of "look," and the meaning is: look at the answer to this question. Together with the interrogation, wonder is intended by way of metonymy, that is: look at that and you will find your answer, that it is a great clarity at which the observer wonders because of its manifestness.

Al-Ayat is the plural of ayah, which is a sign of the existence of the sought object. It is borrowed for proof and demonstration, by likening the proof to the sought place, in the manner of metaphor by allusion (al-makniyya). Attributing signs to it is an imaginative representation (takhyil), likened to the signposts of a road that indicate the sought place.

His saying ﴿Then look how they are turned away﴾: "then" (thumma) here indicates ranked sequence, and the intended meaning is that reflection on the manifestation of the proofs requires moving from wonder at the clarity of the explanation to a more wondrous matter, namely their turning away from the truth despite its clarity.

Yu'faknun means they are turned away (yusrafun). It is said: afakahu, from the pattern of daraba, meaning he turned him away from the thing.

And anna is an interrogative noun used with the meaning of "from where" and also with the meaning of "how." Here it may mean "how," as in al-Kashshaf, and in that case He changed from repeating "kayfa" for variety. It may also mean "from where," and the meaning is wonder at how the turning away from the correct belief could reach them after that explanation, which is so thoroughly clear that it is itself a cause for wonder at its clarity. The second verb "look" is suspended by "anna" from acting, and the complement of "yu'faknun" is omitted for brevity, since it is evident that they are turned away from the truth that the signs made clear to them.

[Page 288]

﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah, that which possesses for you neither harm nor benefit? And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

Since the preceding speech followed the manner of addressing an unspecified audience, the clause ﴿Say: Do you worship, besides Allah…﴾ and what follows is resumed speech, commanding the Messenger to convey to them what they were intended by it.

The apparent meaning is that ﴿Do you worship﴾ is addressed to all who worship something besides Allah among the polytheists and the Christians. The interrogative is for reproach and rebuke, used figuratively.

The meaning of ﴿besides Allah﴾ is "other than Allah." Here min (from) is for emphasis, and dūna (besides) is a noun meaning "other than," so it is synonymous with siwā (other than). The sense is: "Do you worship an object of worship that is other than Allah?", that is, "Do you associate with Allah, in divinity, something other than Him?" The meaning is not "Do you worship an object of worship while abandoning the worship of Allah." Refer to what we explained at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿And do not revile those who call upon other than Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 108] in Surat al-An'am. Thus, all those addressed were worshipping Allah while also associating with Him something else in worship, including those who said that Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary. They did not worship the Messiah except because they claimed that Allah had indwelt in him, so they were worshipping Allah in him. Therefore this address encompasses the polytheists of the Arabs and all the Christians of the Arabs.

For this reason, mā (what) is used as the relative pronoun rather than man (who), because most of what is worshipped besides Allah consists of things that do not understand, and mā predominates for what does not understand. If by ﴿that which does not possess﴾ were meant ʿĪsā and his mother, as in al-Kashshāf and others, and the address were restricted to the Christians, then expressing it with mā would be correct, because it is used in the manner of man, and it occurs so frequently in speech that it is common under interpretation. However, expressing it with man may be more apparent.

The meaning of "does not possess harm" is "is not able over it." The literal meaning of milk (possession) is being empowered to dispose of something without opposition. Then it was applied to the ability to dispose of things without weakness, as Qays ibn al-Khatim said:

"I held it in my hand, and it burst its seam;
one standing before it sees what lies behind it."

Page 289

His hand is undoubtedly owned by him, but he meant that he had complete control over his hand, so he thrust the spear with a mighty thrust in which his hand did not fail him. From this usage arose the application of milk in the sense of strong and enduring ability, by way of the figurative metonymy (al-majāz al-mursal), as occurs in this verse and its counterparts: ﴿They do not possess for themselves harm or benefit, nor do they possess death or life or resurrection﴾; ﴿Say: I do not possess for myself harm or benefit﴾ [Yunus: 49]; ﴿Indeed, those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you provision﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 17]. In these, the verb of possession is connected to meanings rather than to objects and entities, and this is not possible except by taking milk to mean strong ability. Do you not see the coordination of one negation upon another negation of possession, in ascending order, in His saying: ﴿And they worship besides Allah what does not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth at all, and they are not able﴾ [al-Naḥl: 73] in Surat al-Naḥl? Another usage has already been mentioned just above, in His saying: ﴿Say: Who then could prevent Allah from anything if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 17].

He put harm before benefit because souls are more eager to ward off harm than to attract benefit. So the greatest thing that drives them to worship idols is that they seek by them to repel harms through victory over enemies and through avoiding inflicting harm upon their worshippers.

The argument that their objects of worship do not possess harm or benefit is shown by the harms that befall them and the benefits that fail to reach them.

The clause ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is restricted, by means of the definiteness of the two components and the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), to being the cause of aid and succor in both states of asking and the manifestation of the condition, upon Allah, exalted is He, as a restriction of claim in the sense of perfection. That is: none hears every supplication and knows every need except Allah, exalted is He; neither ʿĪsā nor anyone else worshipped besides Allah.

Thus the waw in His saying ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is the waw of the circumstantial clause. The placement of this clause establishes the nullification of their worship of ʿĪsā and Maryam by three methods: the method of restriction (qaṣr), the method of the separating pronoun, and the method of the circumstantial clause, in terms of what it conveys of the concept of contrary implication (mafhūm mukhālafa).

[Page 290]

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, do not go to excess in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of a people who had already gone astray before and led many astray, and who strayed from the even path.﴾

The address is to the People of the Scripture in general, both Jews and Christians, and the explanation of its like has already passed at the end of Surat an-Nisa'.

Al-ghuluww (excess) is a verbal noun from ghalā fī al-amr, meaning he exceeded its well-known limit. Thus ghuluww is an increase in an action beyond what is customary, according to reason, custom, or the Law.

His saying ghayr al-haqq (beyond the truth) is in the accusative as a substitute for an absolute object of the verb taghlū, meaning ghuluwwan ghayra al-haqq. Ghayr al-haqq is falsehood (al-batil). He turned away from saying bāṭilan to ghayr al-haqq because of the disparagement of the described party implied in describing it as "other than the truth." The meaning is that it opposes the known truth, and so it is blameworthy, since the truth is praiseworthy and what is other than it is blameworthy. It is also intended that it opposes what is correct, excluding the excess that is not harmful, such as exaggerated praise of a righteous deed without exceeding what the Law requires. This is indicated by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O People of the Scripture, do not go to excess in your religion, and do not say about God except the truth﴾ [an-Nisa': 171] in Surat an-Nisa'. Among the excess of the Jews is their exceeding the limit in adhering to the law of the Torah after the mission of 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Among the excess of the Christians is the claim of the divinity of 'Isa and their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ). Among the excess that is not false is that which is like increasing the washing in ablution beyond three washings, which is disliked.

His saying ﴿and do not follow the desires of a people who had already gone astray before﴾ is conjoined to the prohibition of excess. It is a conjunction of the general in one respect to the specific in another respect, and in it lies the benefit of conjoining the general to the specific and the specific to the general. This is a prohibition addressed to the present People of the Scripture against following the teachings of their extremist rabbis and monks, who misunderstood the Law out of desires that oppose the evidence. Therefore their excess was called desires, because they are such in reality, even if the addressees do not know that they are desires; so they went astray and called others to their error.

[Page 291]

So they led many astray, such as Qiyafa (Caiaphas), the Jewish rabbi who declared 'Isa to be a disbeliever and ruled that he should be killed, and such as al-Majma' al-Malakani (the Melkite Council), which recorded the doctrine of the Trinity.

His saying (min qabl) means "from before you" (min qablikum). In the speech of the Arabs, it is common to omit what qabl and ba'd and ghayr and ḥasb and dūn and the names of directions are attached to. In that case these nouns are often built on ḍamm, and it is rare for them to be inflected unless they are made indefinite. The grammarians explained the inflectional state of these nouns when they are not made indefinite by saying that it is according to the presumed wording of the omitted genitive, to distinguish between their common built state and their rare inflected state. This reveals a subtle secret of the mysteries of the language.

His saying ﴿and they strayed from the even path﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿they had already gone astray before﴾, so this is another straying. It is therefore determined that the even path (sawā' al-sabīl) from which they strayed is Islam.

Sawā' means the straight, and it has been used metaphorically for the clear truth. That is, they had gone astray in their religion before the coming of Islam, and they strayed from Islam after that.

It has also been said that the address in His saying "O People of the Scripture" is specifically to the Christians, because it came after a debate with the Christians; that the excess intended is the Trinity; and that the people who had gone astray before are the Jews. The meaning of the prohibition against following their desires is a prohibition against doing the like of what they did, such that when the addressees reflect they find themselves having followed them, even if they did not intend to follow them. Thus the speech is a warning to the Christians against behaving in their religion in a manner similar to the conduct of the Jews, because the Christians hate the Jews and know that they are in error.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 78–79:

﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud (David) and Isa (Jesus) son of Maryam. That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾ ﴿They used not to prevent one another from any wrongdoing they committed. Evil indeed was what they used to do.﴾

Page 292

The clause "lu'ina" (was cursed) is a resumptive clause (mustanafah) of initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), containing an elegant transition (takhallus) to specify the Jews for condemnation, to the exclusion of the Christians. It is a declarative clause (khabariyyah) suited to the clause ﴿they have certainly strayed before﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 77], functioning relative to it as evidence, since it contains an argument against the Jews from what is in their own books and from what is in the books of the Christians. The intended purpose is to establish that misguidance persists among them, for the span between Dawud and Isa is more than a thousand years.

The "ʿala" (upon) in His saying ﴿upon the tongue of Dawud﴾ is for figurative elevation (isti'la' majazi) used to express firm attachment (tamakkun al-mulabasah). It is therefore a subordinate metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah) for the meaning of the bā' of attachment, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5], intending by it an emphasis on attachment. That is, they were cursed by the tongue of Dawud, i.e., by his speech which was attached to his tongue. It occurs in the Book of Kings and in the Book of Psalms that David cursed those who alter the religion, and in Psalm fifty-three there occurs: "God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, that did seek God. They are all gone aside, they are altogether become filthy," then he said: "I have put them to shame, because God has rejected them; would that the salvation of Israel came out of Zion." And in Psalm 109: "For the mouth of the wicked is opened against me; they have spoken against me with a lying tongue. They compassed me about also with words of hatred; and fought against me without a cause," then he said: "They look upon me and shake their heads." Then he said: "Let them curse, but bless thou; when they arise, let them be ashamed, but let thy servant rejoice." That is because the Children of Israel had rebelled against Dawud together with his son Absalom. Likewise their cursing upon the tongue of Isa is repeated in the Gospels.

"Dhalika" (that) is a demonstrative referring to the curse derived from "lu'ina" or to the preceding speech by way of interpreting it as "the mentioned."

The clause is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani); as if a questioner asks about the cause of this curse, and he is answered that it is due to their disobedience and transgression, i.e., it was not without cause. The demonstrative noun together with the bā' of causation, and its occurrence in answer to an implied question, together convey the sense of restriction (qasr), i.e., their cursing is only because of their disobedience, as indicated in the Kashshaf; there is no restrictive particle in the speech, so the restriction is derived from the combination of the three elements. This subtlety is among the gems of the author of the Kashshaf. The purpose of the restriction is that people should not go astray in ascribing the cause of the curse, for they might attribute it to other causes, in the habit of the misguided who concern themselves with trivialities and neglect the essentials, because awareness of the causes of punishment is the first degree of success. The likeness of this is that of foolish people who are afflicted with stubborn illnesses and attribute them to the touch of jinn or to an evil eye that struck them, and turn away from the ailments and their causes, so they do not treat them with their remedy.

Page 293

The "ma" in His saying "bima 'asaw" (because they disobeyed) is verbal-masdarial, i.e., "with their disobedience and their being transgressors." He departed from expressing with the two verbal nouns to expressing with the two verbs with "ma" of the masdar, so that the verbs convey the meaning of the renewal of disobedience and the continuity of transgression on their part; and so that the past form indicates that this is an ancient matter among them, and the present form indicates that it recurs repeatedly. Disobedience is the violation of God's commands, and transgression is harming the prophets. He expressed the disobedience side with the past tense because it has become established and does not admit increase, and he expressed the transgression side with the present tense because it is continuous; for they transgressed against Muhammad (ﷺ) through denial, hypocrisy, and attempts at murder and plotting.

The clause ﴿They used not to prevent one another from any wrongdoing they committed﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption, an answer to a question arising from His saying ﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾, namely, how could a nation all of which colluded in disobedience and transgression be? So He said ﴿They used not to prevent one another from any wrongdoing they committed﴾. This is because the nature of wrongdoings is that one or a small group initiates them; then, when they find no one to change them, they multiply in them, and they spread, and the common people follow one another in them until they become universal and their being wrongdoings is forgotten, so people do not guide themselves to abandoning them and repenting of them, and thus the curse of God befalls them. Al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud related from several chains, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, in similar wording, that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A man from the Children of Israel would meet another man when he saw him committing a sin, and say: 'O such-and-such, fear God and leave off what you are doing.' Then he would meet him the next day, and that would not prevent him from being his table-companion, his associate, and his partner. When they did that, God struck their hearts, one against another, and cursed them upon the tongue of Dawud and Isa son of Maryam." Then he recited: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed﴾ until His saying ﴿are defiantly disobedient﴾. Then he said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, you must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and you must take the hand of the oppressor and turn him toward the truth, or God will surely strike your hearts, one against another, or He will surely curse you as He cursed them."

Page 294

He applied the reciprocal form "tanahaw" (prevent one another) to the forbidding of some of them by others, with regard to the totality of the community, and that the one who forbids among them the doer of wrongdoing is in a position to be forbidden by the one forbidden when he himself commits a wrongdoing, so that reciprocal prohibition is achieved thereby. The reciprocity is thus assumed and not literal, and the indicator is the generality of the pronoun in His saying "fa'aluhu" (they did it), for a wrongdoing is committed by some of them while the rest remain silent about it; and perhaps another of them commits another wrongdoing and the one who had committed a wrongdoing before remains silent about it, and so on; thus they accommodate themselves.

By "what they used to do" is meant their abandonment of mutual prohibition.

He applied the verb form "yaf'aluna" (used to do) to the abandonment of mutual prohibition in His saying ﴿Evil indeed was what they used to do﴾, even though it is an abandonment, because silence regarding wrongdoing is never free of showing approval of it and participation in it.

In this there is evidence for those among the leading scholars of kalam of the Ash'ariyyah who hold that there is no obligation (taklif) except with an act, and that what is obligated in the prohibition is an act, namely cessation (intiha'), that is restraint (kaff), and restraint is an act; and God has here named abandonment an act. He emphasized the verb of blame by introducing the oath particle upon it, for the sake of intensifying its condemnation.

﴿You see many of them befriending those who disbelieve. This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic) in which the condition of a group of Jews who lived at the time of the Messenger ﷺ is mentioned. They displayed Islam, and they were the majority of the hypocrites (munafiqun). This is indicated by His saying ﴿who befriend those who disbelieve﴾, because this would only be surprising if it came from those who had outwardly embraced Islam. Thus this is a transition to describe the vileness of the hypocrites. The seeing in His saying ﴿tara﴾ (you see) is visual seeing, and the address is to the Messenger. By ﴿many of them﴾ is meant many of the Jews of Madinah, as indicated by the context of His saying ﴿you see﴾. This is because many Jews in Madinah displayed Islam out of hypocrisy, given that all the people of Madinah from the Aws and the Khazraj had embraced Islam. The Jews therefore felt isolated among them, so they feigned Islam in order to become spies for the Jews of Khaybar, Qurayzah and al-Nadir.

The meaning of ﴿yatawallawn﴾ (they befriend) is ﴿yattakhidhunahum awliya'﴾ (they take them as allies). By ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is meant the polytheists of Makkah and the Bedouins around Madinah who remained upon polytheism. Among these Jews was Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the chief of the Jews, for he was allied with the people of Makkah and used to incite them to attack Madinah. It has already been stated that they are the ones intended in His exalted saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who believe in idols and false deities and say of those who disbelieve, "These are better guided than those who have believed as to the way"?﴾ [al-Nisa': 51].

As for His saying ﴿that Allah has become angry with them﴾: the (an) here is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), which has entered upon a past-tense verb, and this is permissible, as in the Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari), like His saying ﴿Had We not made you firm﴾ [al-Isra': 74]. The verbal noun derived from it is the specified object of blame (al-makhsus bi'l-dhamm). The estimated construction is: "Evil is what their souls have put forward for them: the anger of Allah upon them," so the anger of Allah is blameworthy. This specified object indicates that Allah became angry with them with a particular anger because of their befriending those who disbelieve, and this is not explicitly stated in the speech; this is therefore an instance of concise omission (ijaz al-hadhf). You may also take the meaning of the anger of Allah to be the curse mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 78]. That this is among what their souls have put forward is known from the preceding speech.

As for His saying ﴿Had they believed in Allah and the Prophet﴾ etc.: the waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), relating to His saying ﴿you see many of them﴾, taking into account that those intended are those who outwardly displayed Islam, as indicated by what preceded. So the meaning is: had they believed with sincere faith, they would not have taken the polytheists as allies. By the Prophet is meant Muhammad ﷺ, and by what was revealed to him is meant the Qur'an. This is because the Prophet forbade the believers from befriending the polytheists, and the Qur'an forbade this in more than one verse. This has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies rather than the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]. He has made their befriending of the polytheists a sign of their not believing, through the method of the conditional exceptive syllogism (qiyas istithna'i), because the polytheists are enemies of the Messenger, so befriending them is a sign of not believing in him. This has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 82–84 (part 2 of 2):

By "those who bear witness" (al-shahidin) is meant those who witnessed the sending of the Messengers and affirmed them. This is a great virtue that was attained only in the times when the call of the Messengers first began, and is not attained after this time. That virtue lies in being the first to affirm the Messengers at the time of their sending, when people deny them at the outset, as Waraqah said: "Would that I were a young man when your people drive you out." That is, [it is] a denial on their part. Or they meant: "Then write us down with those who bear witness," namely those whom Jesus, peace be upon him, informed of the sending of the Messenger who would come after him, so that they would be a testimony to his coming and a testimony to the truthfulness of Jesus. In the Gospel of Matthew, verse 24, [there is a statement] from Jesus: "And many false prophets shall rise and shall deceive many. But he who endures to the end, he shall be saved, and shall obtain the glad tidings of the kingdom. This gospel of the kingdom shall be preached as a testimony to all nations." And in the Gospel of John, verse 15, [there is a statement] from Jesus: "But when the Comforter comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me; and you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning." The words "the truth" and "those who bear witness" in this verse have a position that no other words can fill, because they point to what is in the glad tidings of Jesus, peace be upon him.

As for His saying ﴿And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth﴾, it is from their saying, and it is possible that they say it within themselves when hesitation occurs to them regarding turning away from their former religion and entering Islam. That hesitation befalls the believer when he intends to abandon his belief, and it is what is called (al-nazar) "reflection." It is also possible that they say it to one among their own community or brethren who opposes them and casts doubt on what they have resolved upon. And it is possible that they say it to one of the Jews or others who reproaches them that they have not been steadfast in their religion. It has been said that the Jews reproached the group who embraced Islam, if the report of their conversion is sound. The discussion of the construction (ma lana la naf'al) has already been presented at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of God?﴾ [al-Nisa': 75] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The clause "and we hope" (wa natma') may be coordinated with the clause ﴿why should we not believe﴾. It is also possible that the waw is for circumstance (al-hal), meaning: how can we abandon belief in the truth when we previously hoped that our Lord would make us among the righteous people, like the disciples (al-Hawariyyun)? So how can we let slip the means of attaining this noble distinction that has presented itself to us? It is not correct to make it coordinated with the clause "we believe," lest it become governed by the negation, since the meaning would not be "why do we not hope," because hope for good is not hesitated about, nor is one blamed for it, such that its bearer would need to argue for himself with "why should we not do it."

In the Gospel of Matthew, verse 24, [there is a statement] from Jesus: "And many false prophets shall rise and shall deceive many. But he who endures to the end, he shall be saved, and shall obtain the glad tidings of the kingdom. This gospel of the kingdom shall be preached as a testimony to all nations." And in the Gospel of John, verse 15, [there is a statement] from Jesus: "But when the Comforter comes, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me; and you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning." The words "the truth" and "those who bear witness" in this verse have a position that no other words can fill, because they point to what is in the glad tidings of Jesus, peace be upon him.

As for His saying ﴿And why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth﴾, it is from their saying, and it is possible that they say it within themselves when hesitation occurs to them regarding turning away from their former religion and entering Islam. That hesitation befalls the believer when he intends to abandon his belief, and it is what is called (al-nazar) "reflection." It is also possible that they say it to one among their own community or brethren who opposes them and casts doubt on what they have resolved upon. And it is possible that they say it to one of the Jews or others who reproaches them that they have not been steadfast in their religion. It has been said that the Jews reproached the group who embraced Islam, if the report of their conversion is sound. The discussion of the construction (ma lana la naf'al) has already been presented at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of God?﴾ [al-Nisa': 75] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The clause "and we hope" (wa natma') may be coordinated with the clause ﴿why should we not believe﴾. It is also possible that the waw is for circumstance (al-hal), meaning: how can we abandon belief in the truth when we previously hoped that our Lord would make us among the righteous people, like the disciples (al-Hawariyyun)? So how can we let slip the means of attaining this noble distinction that has presented itself to us? It is not correct to make it coordinated with the clause "we believe," lest it become governed by the negation, since the meaning would not be "why do we not hope," because hope for good is not hesitated about, nor is one blamed for it, such that its bearer would need to argue for himself with "why should we not do it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 82–84 (part 1 of 2):

Page 5
﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believe to be the Jews and those who associated partners (with God). And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward those who believe to be those who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests (qissisin) and monks, and because they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized.
