A summation (fadhlaka) of what preceded, concerning the reception that the Jews and Christians gave to the call of Islam, from opposition, with variation in it between the two groups. God censured, from the conditions of the Jews, that by which their enmity toward Islam is known, when He said: ﴿But it will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief, what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], and He repeated it twice, and He said: ﴿You see many of them allying themselves with those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 80], and He said: ﴿And when they come to you, they say, "We believe," and they had entered with disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 61]. Thus their duplicity in harming the Muslims and hurting them is known. He mentioned from the conditions of the Christians what censured their doctrine, but He did not relate from them what expresses their enmity toward the Muslims. He had forbidden the Muslims from taking both groups as allies in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 51], the verse. So His saying ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity﴾, the verse, came as a summation of what the hearts of both groups conceal toward the Muslims, and for this reason it was separated and not joined by a conjunction.

The lam in "latajidanna" is the lam of oath, intended for emphasis, and the nun of emphasis increased it in emphasis.

Page 6
The finding (wijdan) here is a finding of the heart, and it is among the verbs of knowledge, and for this reason it is transitive to two objects. It has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96], in Surat al-Baqarah.

"'Adawatan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the relation of "ashadd" to "al-nas," and similarly "mawaddatan" is in the accusative.

He mentioned the polytheists along with the Jews because of the occasion of the gathering of the two groups upon enmity toward the Muslims, for hatred of Islam has united the Jews and the polytheists. The Jews, out of envy at prophethood coming from other than them, and the polytheists, out of envy that the Muslims preceded them in being guided to the true religion and in rejecting falsehood.

His saying ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection﴾ means the nearest of people in affection toward those who believe, that is, the nearest of people among the adherents of religions opposed to Islam. These are two extremes in the treatment of the Muslims. Between the two extremes are groups varying in their hatred of the Muslims, such as the Magians, the Sabians, the worshippers of idols, and the Mu'attilah.

What is meant by the Christians here is undoubtedly those who remain upon the religion of Christianity, because of His saying ﴿nearest in affection toward those who believe﴾. As for those among the Christians who believed, they have become among the Muslims.

The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ has already preceded in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And from those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 14]. The intent of it there was to establish the proof against them, that they had committed themselves to be helpers of God, ﴿The disciples said, "We are the helpers of God"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52], as was mentioned in the explanation of its parallel. So the intent here is to remind them of the content of this title, so that they may increase in the affection of the Muslims and follow the religion of Islam.

His saying "dhalika" (that) is a reference to the preceding statement, which is that they are nearer in affection toward those who believe.

The ba' in His saying ﴿bi-anna minhum qissisin﴾ is the ba' of causation, and it conveys the meaning of the lam of causation. The pronoun in His saying "minhum" refers to the Christians.

"Al-qissisun" is the sound plural of "qissis," on the pattern of "sijin." It is said "qassa" with a fatha on the qaf and a shadda on the sin, and he is a scholar of the religion of Christianity. Qutrub said: it is in the language of the Romans. This is among what has an agreement between the two languages.

"Al-Ruhban" here is the plural of "rahib," like "rukban," the plural of "rakib," and "fursan," the plural of "faris," and it is not analogous as a plural of an adjective on the pattern fa'il. The rahib among the Christians is one who isolates himself in a monastery or a hermitage for worship. Al-Raghib said: "al-Ruhban" may be singular and plural; whoever makes it singular pluralizes it as "rahabin" and "rahabina." This is related from al-Farra'. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention in al-Asas that "Ruhban" may be singular. Its application to the singular is in a verse which Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

"Had she seen a monk of a monastery in the mountain, the monk would have descended running and slipping."

The existence of the priests and monks among them was a cause of their affection drawing near to the believers, because of what is well known among the Arabs of the good character of priests and monks, their humility and their tolerance. They were spread in many regions of the lands of the Arabs, building monasteries, hermitages and churches, and most of them were from the Arabs of Syria, whom the call of Christianity reached by way of the Romans. The Arabs knew them for asceticism and peaceableness with people, and this was frequent in the speech of their poets. Al-Nabigha said:

"Were she to appear to a white-haired monk, a celibate who worships God, who dedicates himself to worship,
We would be astonished at her radiance and the sweetness of her speech, and we would think him rightly guided, though he is not guided."

The existence of these people among them, and their being the leaders of their religion, is among what would be a cause of the goodness of the morals of the people of their community. "Al-istikbar": the sin and ta' in it are for intensification. It is applied to haughtiness and self-exaltation, and it is applied to obstinacy and aversion to the truth, and these two are mutually implicative. So the intent of His saying "la yastakbirun" is that they are humble and fair.

Page 8
The pronoun in ﴿wa-annahum la yastakbirun﴾ may refer to what the pronoun of "bi-anna minhum" referred to, that is, "and that those who say, 'We are Christians' are not arrogant," so it would have affirmed humility for all the people of the religion of Christianity in that age. The Christians of the Arabs were adorned with noble qualities of character. Al-Nabigha said praising the family of al-Nu'man al-Ghassani, and they were Christians:

"Their majesty is from God, and their religion is upright; they hope for nothing but good outcomes.
They do not reckon good to have no evil after it, nor do they reckon evil to be an inevitable blow."

The apparent sense of His saying ﴿those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ is that this moral quality is a description of all Christians insofar as they are Christians, so the relative clause must be taken in customary generality, meaning the Christians of the Arabs, for their following Christianity, despite their weakness in it, added to their Arab noble qualities noble religious qualities, as Zuhayr, Labid, Waraqah ibn Nawfal and their like were.

The pronoun in ﴿wa-annahum la yastakbirun﴾ refers to ﴿qissisin wa-ruhbanan﴾ because it is nearer in mention, and this is indicated by the repetition of His saying "wa-annahum," so as to be a hint at the change of style in the return of the pronoun, and so that the plural pronouns from His saying "wa-idha sami'u" to His saying "fa-athabahumu Allahu" follow the pronoun of ﴿wa-annahum la yastakbirun﴾.

The indicator for turning similar pronouns to two different referents is the context of the speech. Its like occurs in pronouns, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And they cultivated it more than they cultivated it﴾ [al-Rum: 9]. The pronoun of subject in the first "'amaruha" refers to something other than the pronoun of subject in the second "'amaruha." And like the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"We returned, and had we not been, the multitude of them would have surrounded the Muslims, and they would have seized what they had gathered."

He intends by the pronoun of "ahrazu" the group of polytheists, and by the pronoun of "jamma'u" the group of Muslims.

This is supported by what al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and many of the exegetes related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others: that the ones meant in this verse were eight of the Christians of Syria who were in the land of Abyssinia and came to Medina with sixty-two monks from Abyssinia, companions of the Muslims who returned from their emigration to Abyssinia, and they heard the Qur'an and embraced Islam. They were Bahira the monk, Idris, Ashraf, Abraha, Thumama, Qutham, Duraid, and Ayman, that is, of those who are good in Arabic so that they could understand the Qur'an upon hearing it. This delegation arrived in Medina with those who returned from the emigrants to Abyssinia, in the seventh year, so the reference to them in this verse was a reminder of their virtue. It is among the last of what was revealed. No specific named group of Christians is known to have embraced Islam in the time of the Messenger ﷺ, but perhaps God informed His Messenger of a group of Christians who believed in Muhammad ﷺ in their hearts, but did not manage to meet him or to manifest their faith, and the portion of the Law that reached them was only a little, which they held to, and they did not know the requirement of manifesting the faith called Islam. The condition of these resembles the condition of one to whom the call has not reached, because the reaching of the call varies in degrees. Perhaps among these were some who were in the land of Abyssinia or in Yemen. There is no doubt that the Negus (Ashama) was among them, and the Prophet ﷺ informed of him that he was in this state.

The intent is that the nation in which there are the likes of these will be near to the affection of the Muslims.

The Messenger is Muhammad ﷺ, as is predominant in his usage in the Qur'an. What was revealed to him is the Qur'an.

The address in His saying ﴿you see their eyes﴾ is to the Prophet ﷺ, if he had seen among them one with this description, or it is an address to everyone who is capable of seeing. It is thus an address to an unspecified person so that it includes everyone who is addressed.

His saying ﴿overflowing with tears﴾ means the tears overflow from them, because the true sense of overflow is to be attributed to a liquid exceeding its container so that it flows outside of it. It is said: the water overflowed, when it exceeded its vessel. And the tears overflowed when they exceeded what is held in the eye.

Overflow may be attributed to the container by way of metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli), so it is said: the valley overflowed, meaning its water overflowed, as it is said: the valley flowed, meaning its water flowed. In a hadith: "and a man who remembered God in solitude, and his eyes overflowed." They may join this attribution with a specification that serves as an indicator of the metaphorical attribution, so they say: his eye overflowed with tears, by transferring the attribution, called the specification of the relation, that is, the indicator of the metaphorical relation. As for what is in this verse, its treatment according to the view of the grammarians of Basra prevents "min" attached to the tears from being the explanatory "min" by which the specification is put in the genitive, because that is impossible in their view for the specification of relation. So the verse is woven in the pattern of inversion for intensification: the customary speech of people, "the tears overflowed from the eye of so-and-so," was inverted, and it was said: ﴿their eyes overflow with tears﴾, so the particle "min" is a particle of origin.

If it is treated according to the view of the grammarians of Kufa, "min" is explanatory and governs the specification, and the definiteness of "al-dam'" is definiteness of the genus, like "tibta al-nafs."

The "min" in His saying "mimma 'arafu" is causal, that is, the cause of its overflowing is what they recognized upon hearing the Qur'an, that it is the truth promised. So "min" stands in the place of the object of purpose, as in His saying: ﴿They turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears from grief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92], that is, their eyes overflowed out of the agitation of joy, by their attending the scene of the confirmation of Jesus in what he gave good news of, and by their attending the Messenger promised, so they attained the two virtues. The "min" in His saying

"min al-haqq" is explanatory, that is, "of what they recognized," which is the particular truth. Or it is partitive, that is, of what they recognized, which is the Prophet promised, whose report is among the totality of the truth that Jesus and the prophets before him brought.

The clause "yaqulun" is a circumstantial clause, that is, their eyes overflow while they are saying this. This saying may be openly, and it may be in their private whispering.

It has been said that the Jews reproached the group who embraced Islam, if the report of their conversion is sound. The discussion of the construction (ma lana la naf'al) has already been presented at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And why should you not fight in the way of God?﴾ [al-Nisa': 75] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The clause "and we hope" (wa natma') may be coordinated with the clause ﴿why should we not believe﴾. This is a consequence of His saying ﴿They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so write us down among the witnesses"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83], through to the end of the verse.

The meaning of *athabahum* is that He gave them the reward (*thawab*). This has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿Surely a reward from Allah is better﴾ [al-Baqarah: 103], in Surah al-Baqarah.

The *ba'* in His saying ﴿bima qalu﴾ ("for what they said") indicates causation (*li-al-sababiyyah*). By "saying" is meant the truthful saying, which is that which corresponds to reality, that is, the saying which corresponds to the belief of the heart. What they said is what was related by His saying, ﴿They say, "Our Lord, we have believed, so write us down among the witnesses"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83], and so on. *Athaba* takes two objects by the pattern of *a'ta* (to give), so *jannat* ("gardens") is its second object, which is the one given to them. The demonstrative in His saying, ﴿And that is the recompense of the good-doers﴾, refers to the reward derived from *athabahum*. You may also take the demonstrative to refer to what was mentioned, namely the gardens, the rivers within them, and their remaining in them forever. A parallel to this was discussed at His saying in Surah al-Baqarah, ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 86:

Page 13

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

This is a completion and a safeguard (tatmim wa ihtiras), meaning: those who disbelieved among the Christians and denied the Qur'an are the opposite of those whom Allah rewarded with gardens beneath which rivers flow.

And ashab al-Jahim (the companions of the Blazing Fire) means those who are constantly bound to it. Al-Jahim is Jahannam (Hellfire), and the origin of al-Jahim is a great fire placed in a pit so that its blaze endures. It is said: "nar jahmah" (a fire of intense flame), meaning one that is very fierce in its blaze. One of the Tayy poets from the Jahiliyyah, among the poets of al-Hamasah, said:

"We confined the Banu Jadilah in a fire of war, a blazing fire of kindling."

[Page 14]

This is a fresh (isti'naf ibtida'i, a resumptive new sentence) address to the believers with legislative rulings. It follows in a sequence of consequence (tafri') and comes as a complement to what preceded it, namely the praise of the priests and monks (qissisin wa-ruhban). Since it was their custom to go to extremes in asceticism (zuhd, renunciation of worldly pleasures), they introduced monasticism (rahbaniyya, the monastic way of life) by abstaining from marriage, from eating meat, and from many good things such as using oil for anointing, enjoying a comfortable state, and wearing fine clothing. Allah alerted the believers that praising the monks and priests for their virtues does not require approving of all their monastic practices. It happened that some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had their souls aspire to limit their attachment to the delights of life, imitating their master, the leader of the ascetics (ﷺ).

al-Tabari and al-Wahidi narrated that "a group competed in asceticism. One of them said: 'As for me, I will stand in prayer all night and not sleep.' The other said: 'As for me, I will fast by day.' Another said: 'As for me, I will not approach women.' News of them reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he sent for them and said: 'Did I not hear that you said such-and-such?' They said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, we intended only good.' He said: 'But I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, and I approach women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.' Then this verse was revealed." The meaning of this is in the Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim from Anas ibn Malik, but it does not state that this was the occasion of revelation of this verse.

It was also narrated that "some people among them, namely Abu Bakr, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Dharr, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, Salman al-Farisi, and Ma'qil ibn Muqarrin, gathered in the house of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and agreed to abandon worldly occupations, leave off women, and become monks. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, spoke to them with severity, and then said: 'Those before you were destroyed only through severity. They were strict upon themselves, so Allah was strict upon them. Those are their remnants in the dwellings and the monasteries.'" Then this verse was revealed concerning them. This report implies that this gathering took place at the beginning of the period of the Hijra, because 'Uthman ibn Maz'un did not have a house in Medina, and the Prophet (ﷺ) housed him in the house of Umm al-'Ala al-Ansariyya, who is said to have been the wife of Zayd ibn Thabit. 'Uthman ibn Maz'un died in the second year of the Hijra.

In another narration: "some people said, 'The Christians have forbidden themselves certain things, so we will forbid ourselves some good things.' Some of them forbade themselves eating meat, some sleep, and some women, and they bound themselves to that by oaths they swore to abandon what they had committed to abandon. Then this verse was revealed."

These reports, which corroborate one another, about the inclination of some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward excessive asceticism, are also found in the Sahih, such as the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "The Messenger of Allah said to me: 'Have I not been informed that you stand in prayer all night and fast by day?' I said: 'Indeed, I do that.' He said: 'If you do that, your eyes will become sunken and your soul will become weary. Your soul has a right over you, and your family has a right over you. So fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep.'" And the hadith of Salman with Abu al-Darda: "Salman visited Abu al-Darda, and Abu al-Darda prepared food and said to Salman, 'Eat, for I am fasting.' When night came, Abu al-Darda went to stand in prayer, and Salman said, 'Sleep.' So he slept. Then he went to stand in prayer again, and Salman said, 'Sleep.' So he slept. When it was the last part of the night, Salman said, 'Stand up now.' Then Salman said: 'Your Lord has a right over you, your soul has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give every possessor of a right his right.' So he came to the Prophet and mentioned that to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Salman has spoken the truth.'" And in the authentic hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "As for me, I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me."

The prohibition is only the forbidding of these things upon oneself. As for abstaining from partaking of some of these things at some times, without binding oneself to it, and with the intention of training the soul to be patient with deprivation when one does not have them, there is no harm in it to the extent needed for disciplining the soul. Likewise, turning away from many good things in order to aspire to what is higher, such as worship or occupation with beneficial work, is the highest form of asceticism. This was the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), especially among his Companions. It is a state suited to his rank and not suited to some levels of people, so aspiring to it is hardship. Yet he (ﷺ) used to partake of good things without eagerness or aspiration, and partaking of them is thankfulness to Allah the Exalted, as was related in the story of Abu al-Dahdah when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and 'Umar came to his orchard and he fed them and gave them drink. It is also reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he was invited to a meal, and with him were Farqad al-Sabakhi and his companions. They sat at a table on which were various kinds of food: fattened chicken and faluzaj (a sweet). Farqad withdrew to one side. Al-Hasan asked him: "Are you fasting?" He said: "No, but I dislike these varieties, because I cannot fulfill their thanks." Al-Hasan said to him: "Do you drink cold water?" He said: "Yes." Al-Hasan said: "Indeed, Allah's blessing in cold water is greater than His blessing in faluzaj."

The purpose of the prohibition is not merely that one utters the word of prohibition, but that one leaves it, out of strictness upon oneself, whether one pronounces the prohibition or does not pronounce it.

Because of this prohibition, this (self-imposed) prohibition is regarded as void (laghw) in Islam. It does not bind its maker in all things for which Islam has not provided a means of prohibition. That covers every case except the prohibition of a wife. For this reason, Malik said regarding one who prohibits upon himself some of what is lawful, or generalizes it, saying, "What is lawful is unlawful for me": there is nothing in anything lawful (that becomes binding) except the wife, for she becomes unlawful to him, like the irrevocable divorce (al-batt), unless he intends to remove the wife before pronouncing the formula of prohibition, or removes her by the wording of an exception (istithna') after pronouncing the formula of prohibition, according to the ruling of exception in an oath. Its basis is that the bond of marriage is subject to prohibition in law in some circumstances, so binding oneself to prohibition applies to it specifically. For if one prohibits the wife alone, she becomes unlawful; likewise, if a general expression includes her. al-Shafi'i agreed with him. Abu Hanifa said: whoever prohibits upon himself something lawful, it becomes unlawful for him to partake of it unless he expiates with the expiation of an oath; if he expiates, it becomes lawful for him, except the wife. Masruq and Abu Salama held that the prohibition does not bind regarding the wife or others.

In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾, there is an admonition to the jurists of the Community to be cautious in declaring something unlawful for which no proof of its prohibition has been established, or whose proof does not reach the strength of the proof of the prohibition in this verse.

Furthermore, the people of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) had forbidden things upon themselves, as Surat al-An'am includes. Allah nullified that by His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-A'raf: 32], and His saying: ﴿Those have lost who killed their children foolishly without knowledge and forbade what Allah had provided for them, fabricating against Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 140], and His saying: ﴿Say: Has He forbidden the two males or the two females?﴾ [al-An'am: 143], up to His saying: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah to mislead people without knowledge?﴾ [al-An'am: 144], and other verses. Many Arabs had entered Islam all at once after the conquest of Mecca, as Allah described them by His saying: ﴿They enter the religion of Allah in multitudes﴾ [al-Nasr: 2]. The shortness of time and the vastness of the land prevented the firm establishment of the laws of Islam among them, so they were in need of refraining from many widespread matters among them during the period of the revelation of this sura, which was the days of the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada') and what preceded it and what followed it.

The clause ﴿and do not transgress﴾ is an interjected clause (mu'tarida) because forbidding good things is a transgression upon what Allah has legislated. Thus the waw is an interjectional waw (waw i'tiradiyya). Because of the generality within this prohibition, the clause serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil).

The word i'tida' (transgression) is an ifti'al form of 'adw, meaning injustice. Its mention in contrast to forbidding good things indicates that the intended meaning is a prohibition against exceeding the permitted limit of what is legislated, as He said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqara: 229]. When He prohibited forbidding what is lawful, He followed it with a prohibition against declaring unlawful what is forbidden, and that is by transgressing upon the rights of people, which is the gravest transgression, or upon the rights of Allah the Exalted in His commands and prohibitions without the rights of people, such as eating pork or carrion. The transgression in the context of the prohibition generalizes all its kinds of what the Jahiliyya practiced of aggression. The greatest of it is aggression against the weak, such as burying daughters alive (wa'd), consuming the property of orphans, and preventing the unmarried women from marrying (adl al-ayama), and other such things.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyil) for the preceding clause, as a warning against every transgression.

His saying ﴿and eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾ is an emphasis of the prohibition against forbidding good things, and it is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon His saying ﴿Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾. That is, Allah has granted you latitude with the lawful, so do not transgress it into the unlawful, for then you would be ungrateful for the blessing, nor should you leave it by prohibition, for then you would turn away from the blessing.

Eating alone is specified because most of what people have forbidden themselves is food. It seems that Allah alludes to them that attending to important matters is better than being preoccupied with eating, as He said: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 93], and so on. By this, He nullified what existed in previous laws of excessive concern with the rulings on food. In this there is an admonition to this Community.

His saying ﴿and fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾ came with the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) to hint at the reason for the command to piety, that is: because it is the nature of faith to require piety. So when you have believed in Allah and been guided to faith, then perfect it with piety.

It is narrated that al-Hasan al-Basri met al-Farazdaq at a funeral, and they were at the grave. Al-Hasan said to al-Farazdaq: "What have you prepared for this?" meaning the grave. al-Farazdaq said: "The testimony that there is no god but Allah, for so many years." Al-Hasan said: "That is the pillar, so where are the tent-ropes (al-itnab)?"

[Page 14]

This is a fresh (isti'naf ibtida'i, a resumptive new sentence) address to the believers with legislative rulings. It follows in a sequence of consequence (tafri') and comes as a complement to what preceded it, namely the praise of the priests and monks (qissisin wa-ruhban). Since it was their custom to go to extremes in asceticism (zuhd, renunciation of worldly pleasures), they introduced monasticism (rahbaniyya, the monastic way of life) by abstaining from marriage, from eating meat, and from many good things such as using oil for anointing, enjoying a comfortable state, and wearing fine clothing. Allah alerted the believers that praising the monks and priests for their virtues does not require approving of all their monastic practices. It happened that some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had their souls aspire to limit their attachment to the delights of life, imitating their master, the leader of the ascetics (ﷺ).

al-Tabari and al-Wahidi narrated that "a group competed in asceticism. One of them said: 'As for me, I will stand in prayer all night and not sleep.' The other said: 'As for me, I will fast by day.' Another said: 'As for me, I will not approach women.' News of them reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he sent for them and said: 'Did I not hear that you said such-and-such?' They said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah, we intended only good.' He said: 'But I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, and I approach women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.' Then this verse was revealed." The meaning of this is in the Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim from Anas ibn Malik, but it does not state that this was the occasion of revelation of this verse.

It was also narrated that "some people among them, namely Abu Bakr, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Dharr, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, Salman al-Farisi, and Ma'qil ibn Muqarrin, gathered in the house of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and agreed to abandon worldly occupations, leave off women, and become monks. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, spoke to them with severity, and then said: 'Those before you were destroyed only through severity. They were strict upon themselves, so Allah was strict upon them. Those are their remnants in the dwellings and the monasteries.'" Then this verse was revealed concerning them. This report implies that this gathering took place at the beginning of the period of the Hijra, because 'Uthman ibn Maz'un did not have a house in Medina, and the Prophet (ﷺ) housed him in the house of Umm al-'Ala al-Ansariyya, who is said to have been the wife of Zayd ibn Thabit. 'Uthman ibn Maz'un died in the second year of the Hijra.

In another narration: "some people said, 'The Christians have forbidden themselves certain things, so we will forbid ourselves some good things.' Some of them forbade themselves eating meat, some sleep, and some women, and they bound themselves to that by oaths they swore to abandon what they had committed to abandon. Then this verse was revealed."

These reports, which corroborate one another, about the inclination of some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward excessive asceticism, are also found in the Sahih, such as the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "The Messenger of Allah said to me: 'Have I not been informed that you stand in prayer all night and fast by day?' I said: 'Indeed, I do that.' He said: 'If you do that, your eyes will become sunken and your soul will become weary. Your soul has a right over you, and your family has a right over you. So fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep.'" And the hadith of Salman with Abu al-Darda: "Salman visited Abu al-Darda, and Abu al-Darda prepared food and said to Salman, 'Eat, for I am fasting.' When night came, Abu al-Darda went to stand in prayer, and Salman said, 'Sleep.' So he slept. Then he went to stand in prayer again, and Salman said, 'Sleep.' So he slept. When it was the last part of the night, Salman said, 'Stand up now.' Then Salman said: 'Your Lord has a right over you, your soul has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give every possessor of a right his right.' So he came to the Prophet and mentioned that to him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Salman has spoken the truth.'" And in the authentic hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "As for me, I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me."

The prohibition is only the forbidding of these things upon oneself. As for abstaining from partaking of some of these things at some times, without binding oneself to it, and with the intention of training the soul to be patient with deprivation when one does not have them, there is no harm in it to the extent needed for disciplining the soul. Likewise, turning away from many good things in order to aspire to what is higher, such as worship or occupation with beneficial work, is the highest form of asceticism. This was the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), especially among his Companions. It is a state suited to his rank and not suited to some levels of people, so aspiring to it is hardship. Yet he (ﷺ) used to partake of good things without eagerness or aspiration, and partaking of them is thankfulness to Allah the Exalted, as was related in the story of Abu al-Dahdah when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and 'Umar came to his orchard and he fed them and gave them drink. It is also reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he was invited to a meal, and with him were Farqad al-Sabakhi and his companions. They sat at a table on which were various kinds of food: fattened chicken and faluzaj (a sweet). Farqad withdrew to one side. Al-Hasan asked him: "Are you fasting?" He said: "No, but I dislike these varieties, because I cannot fulfill their thanks." Al-Hasan said to him: "Do you drink cold water?" He said: "Yes." Al-Hasan said: "Indeed, Allah's blessing in cold water is greater than His blessing in faluzaj."

The purpose of the prohibition is not merely that one utters the word of prohibition, but that one leaves it, out of strictness upon oneself, whether one pronounces the prohibition or does not pronounce it.

Because of this prohibition, this (self-imposed) prohibition is regarded as void (laghw) in Islam. It does not bind its maker in all things for which Islam has not provided a means of prohibition. That covers every case except the prohibition of a wife. For this reason, Malik said regarding one who prohibits upon himself some of what is lawful, or generalizes it, saying, "What is lawful is unlawful for me": there is nothing in anything lawful (that becomes binding) except the wife, for she becomes unlawful to him, like the irrevocable divorce (al-batt), unless he intends to remove the wife before pronouncing the formula of prohibition, or removes her by the wording of an exception (istithna') after pronouncing the formula of prohibition, according to the ruling of exception in an oath. Its basis is that the bond of marriage is subject to prohibition in law in some circumstances, so binding oneself to prohibition applies to it specifically. For if one prohibits the wife alone, she becomes unlawful; likewise, if a general expression includes her. al-Shafi'i agreed with him. Abu Hanifa said: whoever prohibits upon himself something lawful, it becomes unlawful for him to partake of it unless he expiates with the expiation of an oath; if he expiates, it becomes lawful for him, except the wife. Masruq and Abu Salama held that the prohibition does not bind regarding the wife or others.

In His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾, there is an admonition to the jurists of the Community to be cautious in declaring something unlawful for which no proof of its prohibition has been established, or whose proof does not reach the strength of the proof of the prohibition in this verse.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 89:**

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what you have bound with oaths. Its expiation is feeding ten needy people from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you swear. And guard your oaths. Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses that you may be grateful.﴾

This is an initial resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a new sentence beginning a fresh topic), occasioned by His saying ﴿Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 87), because prohibition most often occurs through firmly resolved oaths, or through oaths that come to the tongue for the purpose of emphasizing speech, as when one says: "By Allah, I will not eat such-and-such." Or [oaths] that occur because of anger. It has been said that it was revealed together with the preceding verse, so there is no need to show a connection by mentioning this after what came before it.

Al-Tabari and al-Wahidi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when the words of the Exalted ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 87) were revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them from what they had resolved upon of that, as was mentioned just before, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, how should we deal with our oaths that we have sworn to them?" So Allah revealed ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths﴾, [and the rest of] the verse.

[Page 19]

So Allah prescribed the expiation (*kaffarah*, the act of atonement that covers and removes the consequence of an oath broken). The discussion of the like of the opening of this verse has already passed in surah al-Baqarah, and the disagreement about the meaning of idle oath (*laghw al-yamin*) has already passed. Nothing of that is in the occasion of revelation of the verse ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 87), nor in considering what those whose case that verse concerns resolved upon to be among idle oaths. Thus the interpretation of what al-Tabari and al-Wahidi narrated concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse is that the incident of those who forbade upon themselves some of the good things was attached to the ruling on idle oaths, in the concession granted to them to release themselves from their oaths.

His saying ﴿with what you have bound with oaths﴾ means: what you intended by the oath. It explains the general statement in surah al-Baqarah ﴿with what your hearts have earned﴾ (al-Baqarah: 225).

The majority read *'aqqadtum* (عَقَّدتُّمُ) with a doubled *qaf*. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Khalaf, read it with a single *qaf* (عَقَدتُّمُ). Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir read (*'aqadtum*, عاقَدْتُمُ) with an *alif* after the *ayn*, from the pattern of *mufa'alah*. As for (*'aqqadtum*) with the doubling, it conveys intensification of the verb *'aqada*, and likewise the reading (*'aqadtum*) because the *mufa'alah* in it is not in its proper sense, so its purpose is intensification, like *'afahu Allah* (God grant him well-being). As for the reading with a single *qaf*, the root *'aqd* (binding) is sufficient to convey firmness. The intended meaning is that the holding to account occurs with the intention of binding oneself by the oath. Thus the expression of binding oneself firmly has three verbs in the speech of the Arabs: *'aqada* (the unemphasized form), *'aqqada* (the emphasized form), and *'aqada* (the form with *alif*).

His saying ﴿That is the expiation of your oaths﴾ refers back to what has been mentioned, for added clarity.

The word *kaffarah* is an intensive form of *kafara*, which means "to cover" and "to remove." The root meaning of *kafr* (with the *kaf* vowelled with a fatha) is covering.

Two indicators of intensification have come in it, namely the doubling and the added *ta'* (ة), like the *ta'* in *nassabah* and *allamah*. The Arabs often combine the two.

His saying ﴿when you swear﴾ means: when you swear and intend to release yourselves from what you have sworn to.

[Page 20]

The implication of this is from the implication of necessity (*dalalat al-iqtida'*, the meaning that a sentence requires in order to be sensible), because it is evident that the expiation is not for the utterance of the oath itself, but for not acting upon the oath, since the meaning of expiation requires that a sin has occurred, and that is the sin of breaking the oath (*hinth*).

It is reported from al-Shafi'i that he cited His saying ﴿the expiation of your oaths when you swear﴾ as evidence for the permissibility of paying the expiation before the breaking of the oath occurs. It is possible that he took the apparent sense of the annexation of *kaffarah* to *aymanikum* (your oaths), and it is possible that he meant that the swearing is the cause of the cause, so when the swearer resolves not to act upon his oath after having sworn, it is permissible for him to make expiation before breaking it, because this is from advancing the compensation, and there is no harm in it. I do not think he meant anything other than this. His intention was not that mere swearing is what necessitates expiation. Since there is certainly an implication in the speech, there is no basis for citing the wording of the verse as evidence for the validity of paying expiation in advance. The origin of this ruling is the view of Malik on the permissibility of paying expiation before breaking the oath when one has resolved to break it, and he did not cite the verse as evidence. Al-Shafi'i cited it as support for the Sunnah. Paying expiation after breaking the oath is preferable.

He (Allah) followed the concession that He granted people, namely not holding them accountable for idle oaths, by saying ﴿and guard your oaths﴾. So He commanded seeking righteousness when there is no hardship in it and no harm to others, because in righteousness there is the glorification of the name of Allah the Exalted. We have already mentioned in surah al-Baqarah that their customary practice was to swear when they wanted to confirm a report, or to compel themselves to an action they had resolved upon, lest they regret their resolution. So His saying ﴿and guard your oaths﴾ was a rebuke to them against that foolish custom. This command entails a command to swear little, lest the swearer expose himself to breaking his oath. The expiation is nothing but an exit from sin. Allah the Exalted said to Ayyub (peace be upon him) ﴿Take in your hand a bundle [of grass] and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾ (Sad: 44). So He exempted him from breaking the oath by a ruling specific to him.

The clause ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*, a summarizing addition). The meaning of "thus" is: as with this clarification, Allah makes clear. That is the custom of His law, that it be clear. The discussion of its like has already passed in His saying the Exalted ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ (al-Baqarah: 143) in surah al-Baqarah.

[Page 21]

The discussion of the meaning of ﴿that you may be grateful﴾ has already passed at His saying the Exalted ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah: 21) in surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 90–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ ﴿Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾

This is a resumed address to the believers, following the preceding address, so that its content is strung on the same thread on which the content of the previous address was strung, namely His saying (and do not transgress), which points out that just as Allah forbade the declaring unlawful of what is permitted, He also forbade making lawful what is unlawful; and that when Allah made the good things lawful, He forbade the corrupt things that lead to harms. For intoxicants were regarded as good by the people, and Allah the Exalted has said ﴿And from the fruits of palm trees and grapes you take from them intoxicant and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]. Gambling was a means of feeding meat to those who could not afford it. So this verse serves as a safeguard against what the statement ﴿Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87] might be misinterpreted to mean.

It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah that the most reliable of the views of our scholars is that the prohibition of intoxicants came in stages, three times. The first was when the verse ﴿They ask you about intoxicants and gambling. Say, "In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people; but their sin is greater than their benefit."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] was revealed. This contains a prohibition that is not decisive, so some people who were more God-fearing abandoned drinking intoxicants. Then 'Umar said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient explanation regarding intoxicants." Then the verse of Surat al-Nisa' was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], so the Muslims avoided drinking it at the times when it was thought the intoxication would remain until the time of prayer. 'Umar said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient explanation regarding intoxicants."
Page 22
Then this verse was revealed. 'Umar said: "We have ceased."

It is well known that intoxicants were prohibited in the third year after the Hijrah, after the battle of Uhud. Thus this verse was revealed before Surat al-'Uqud and was placed here afterwards in its current position. It is narrated that this verse was revealed because of a quarrel that took place between Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and a man from the Ansar. Muslim related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I came upon a group of the Ansar, and they said: 'Come, we will feed you and give you wine to drink,' and that was before intoxicants were prohibited. So I went to them in a garden enclosure, and there was a roasted camel's head and a skin of wine. I ate and drank with them, and I mentioned the Ansar and the Emigrants in their presence, and I said: 'The Emigrants are better than the Ansar.' A man from the Ansar took the jawbone of a camel and struck me with it, wounding my nose. So I went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him, and Allah the Exalted revealed concerning me: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾." Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] and ﴿They ask you about intoxicants and gambling. Say, 'In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] were abrogated in al-Ma'idah by ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan﴾."

Therefore this prohibition was of utmost concern to the Lawgiver, who advanced it to the nation by explaining its causes, out of gentleness toward them and to make them comfortable. So He began with the verse of Surat al-Baqarah, and He did not belittle them for what they were engaging in; rather, He informed them of their excuse in His saying ﴿In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people; but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. Then with the verse of Surat al-Nisa', then He followed it with prohibition through the verse of Surat al-Ma'idah, thus confining their matter to being "defilement from the work of Satan," and He hoped for them success in avoiding them by His saying "so that you may be successful." He stirred up what is in natures of hatred for Satan by His saying ﴿Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred﴾. Then He said ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, using the interrogative to depict the state of those addressed as the state of one to whom the speaker has explained the reality of something and then tested the extent of that explanation's effect on his soul.

The form "Are you going to do such-and-such?" (hal anta fa'il kadha) is used to urge an action in a context of delay, which al-Zamakhshari pointed out in al-Kashshaf at His saying Most High ﴿And it is said to the people, "Are you assembled?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 39] in Surat al-Shu'ara'. He said: "From it is the saying of Ta'abbata Sharran:
Are you one who sends a dinar for our need, or 'Abd Rabb, brother of 'Awn ibn Mikhraq?
Dinar is the name of a man, and likewise 'Abd Rabb. And His saying 'brother of 'Awn' or 'Awf' is a vocative, meaning 'O brother of 'Awn.'" So the prohibition of intoxicants was already established before the revelation of this surah, for the delegation of 'Abd al-Qays came before the conquest of Makkah in the year eight, and among what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ instructed them was not to make nabidh in the hantam, the naqir, the muzaffat, or the dubba', because these vessels cause fermentation to proceed quickly in their nabidh.

What is meant by "stone altars" here is worship of stone altars. What is meant by "divining arrows" is seeking decisions through them, because their conjunction with gambling requires that the arrows be other than gambling.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The mention of stone altars and divining arrows alongside intoxicants and gambling is intended to emphasize the prohibition of intoxicants and gambling." The discussion of intoxicants and gambling has already occurred at the verse in Surat al-Baqarah, and the discussion of stone altars has occurred at His saying Most High ﴿and what is slaughtered on the stone altars﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and the discussion of divining arrows at His saying ﴿and that you seek decision by divining arrows﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] at the beginning of this surah. In this verse He emphasized the prohibition of what is slaughtered on stone altars and the prohibition of seeking decisions through divining arrows, which is the prohibition mentioned at the beginning of the surah and established in Islam from the beginning of the Prophethood.

What is meant by these four things here is engaging in them, each according to how it is engaged in: drinking, gambling, slaughtering, and seeking decisions.

The restriction derived from "innama" is the restriction of a described thing to an attribute: that these four mentioned things are confined to the attribute of defilement and do not go beyond it to anything else. It is a claimed restriction, for the sake of emphasis on disregarding any attributes of these four other than the attribute of defilement. Do you not see that Allah said in Surat al-Baqarah concerning intoxicants and gambling ﴿In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], thereby affirming for them sin, which is an attribute equal to defilement in the view of the Sharia, since sin requires distance from engaging with them, like defilement does. And He affirmed for them benefit, which is an attribute equal to the opposite of defilement in the view of the Sharia, since benefit entails people's eagerness to engage in them. Thus it is valid that intoxicants and gambling have two attributes. In the verse of al-Ma'idah He restricted them to what equals one of those two attributes, namely defilement. So it is only a claimed restriction, pointing to what is in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying ﴿and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. For when He alerted us to the preponderance of sin over benefit in them, He also alerted us to the refutation of the benefit in them in face of the sin in them, until it is as if they were purely characterized by "in them is sin." So it is valid in Surat al-Ma'idah to say about them what conveys the confinement of them to being "in them is sin," that is, the confinement of them to the attribute of being in this container, like the confinement in His saying ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 113], meaning their reckoning is restricted to being upon my Lord, that is, their reckoning is confined to the meaning of this particle. This is what is expressed by the phrase "defilement."

Rijs (defilement) is the filth that is loathsome and detestable among visible matters, and it is also applied to inward blameworthy qualities, as in His saying ﴿As for those in whose hearts is disease, it adds to them defilement upon their defilement﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], and His saying ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the defilement, O people of the household﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. What is meant by it here is that which is corrupt in souls and in the consideration of the Sharia. It is a noun of genus, so predicating it of something is like predicating a verbal noun, which conveys emphasis in the attribution of it, to the extent that this described thing is as if it were the very defilement. For this reason "rijs" is used in the singular although it is a predicate about multiple things, because it functions like a predicate with a verbal noun.

The meaning of "they are from the work of Satan" is that engaging in them, by what they are engaged in for their sake, is due to his enticing people to engage in them; so it is as if he himself performed and engaged in them. In this there is an aversion for those who engage in them, that they are doing the work of Satan, so he is a devil. And this is something souls reject.
Page 25

The fa' in "fa-ijtanibuhu" is for consequence, and the fitness of this consequence has become apparent after mention of what necessitates aversion from them. The pronoun in the accusative "ijtanibuhu" refers to "rijs," which encompasses the four. "So that you may be successful" is a hope for them to succeed upon avoiding these prohibited things, provided they have not persisted in other prohibited things. The discussion of its counterpart has already been given at His saying Most High ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. I have explained what I have chosen regarding the meaning of "la'alla," and it is the consistent meaning across all its usages; as for the other meanings by which some interpreted "la'alla" in the verse of Surat al-Baqarah, some of them do not apply in this verse, so reflect upon it.

Avoiding the things mentioned means avoiding engaging in them in respect of the corruptions they are aimed at, according to the differences in their states: so avoiding intoxicants is avoiding drinking them; avoiding gambling is avoiding gambling with it; avoiding stone altars is avoiding slaughtering upon them; avoiding divining arrows is avoiding seeking decisions by them and consulting them. Not included in this avoidance is avoiding touching them or showing them to people for the need for that, such as considering some of their states in distillation and the like, or to know their forms, or to preserve them as relics of history, or leaving wine during its fermentation for one who pressed grapes to make vinegar from it, according to a detailed discussion and disagreement regarding some of that.

As for avoiding touching intoxicants and regarding them as impure for one whose body or garment is smeared with them, this is among the matters on which the people of knowledge differ. Among them are those who understood "rijs" in the verse regarding intoxicants in both its senses, the figurative and the literal, and so they regarded intoxicants as impure in substance, requiring washing as impurity requires washing, taking the word "rijs" to encompass all that it may bear. This is the view of Malik. They did not say this about the arrows of gambling, nor about the stones of the stone altars, nor about divining arrows, and the distinction between these three and intoxicants has no basis from the standpoint of reasoning. There is nothing in the narrated reports that can be used as proof for the impurity of intoxicants. Perhaps the fluidity of intoxicants is what brought its resemblance close to impure substances, so when it was described as "rijs" it was understood in its particular case in both its senses. As for what was narrated in the hadith of Anas that many of

[Page 26]

The Companions poured out the wine jars when the prohibition of drinking it was announced. This was an extreme display of disavowal of wine and of erasing its trace before turning to consider anything else. Do you not see that some of them broke its jars, yet no one held that a vessel containing something impure must be broken? Moreover, they did this without having been commanded to do it by the Messenger (ﷺ).

Some scholars held that the substance of wine is not impure (najis). This is the view of Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Muzani among the companions of al-Shafi'i, and many of the Baghdadi Malikis and the Qayrawanis, among them Sa'id ibn al-Haddad al-Qayrawani. Sa'id ibn al-Haddad argued for its purity by saying that wine was poured out in the streets of Medina, and if it were impure they would have been forbidden to do so, since a prohibition has been reported against spilling impurities in the streets. Ibn al-Faras reported from Ibn Lubaba that he upheld the view, from within the school, that the substance of wine is pure.

I say: What reflection requires is that wine is not impure in its essence, and that the context of the verse is far from aiming at the impurity of its substance. The intent is rather that it is a moral impurity (rijs ma'nawi). This is why He described it as being "from the work of Satan," and He explained this afterwards by saying: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred between you﴾. Moreover, impurity (najasa) is grounded in filth and foulness, and wine is not like that. The early generation (al-salaf) only avoided approaching it in order to establish its repugnance in souls.

The clause ﴿Satan only wants﴾ explains that these are from the work of Satan. Here "yurid" means "yuhibb" (wants/loves). The meaning of irada as mahabba (love) has already been explained at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who purchase error and want you to stray from the way?﴾ [al-Nisa': 44] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The discussion of enmity and hatred has already been given at His saying: ﴿And We put among them enmity and hatred﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 64] in this surah.

His saying ﴿in wine and gambling﴾ means in indulging in them, following the common usage of attributing rulings to the essences themselves. That is, by what arises from drinking wine: stirring up quarrels, and proceeding to crimes; and what occurs in gambling: envy toward the winner, anger and regret for the loser, and what results from that: ill omen, abuse and beating. Furthermore, the mere arising of enmity and hatred among the Muslims is a great corruption, because God willed that the believers be brothers, since the affairs of a community cannot be upright when hatred prevails among its members. In a hadith: "Do not hate one another, do not envy one another, and be servants of God as brothers."

The "fi" in ﴿in wine and gambling﴾ is either causal (sababiyya) or a figurative locative (zarfiyya), meaning: in the gatherings of indulging in them.

As for the prevention from the remembrance of God and from the prayer, it is because of the loss of reason that wine causes, and the squandering of time that gambling involves through repeated return in pursuit of gain.

These are four causes, each of which requires prohibition, so it is no wonder that their combination requires an intensified prohibition. Whatever shares its attributes is added to wine: whatever causes enmity, hatred, and prevention from the remembrance of God and the prayer. Added to gambling is whatever shares with it in causing enmity, hatred, and prevention from the remembrance of God and the prayer, and this includes all kinds of gambling. As for play without gambling, such as chess without wagering, it is less than gambling, because it rarely prevents from the remembrance of God and the prayer, and because it does not usually cause enmity and hatred. Its rulings therefore fall under other evidences.

The remembrance intended in His saying ﴿from the remembrance of God﴾ may be verbal remembrance, in which case what is meant is the Qur'an and the speech of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in which lies their benefit and guidance, because it contains the explanation of the rulings they need. So when they immerse themselves in drinking wine and gambling, they absent themselves from the Messenger's gatherings, from hearing his sermons, and from meeting his companions who were constantly with him. Thus they do not hear the remembrance, nor receive it from the mouths of those who hear it, and they remain ignorant of much of it, including what the responsible person is obliged to know. Therefore, whatever prevents from this is a great corruption that deserves to have its indulgence forbidden. It may also be that what is meant is the remembrance of the heart, which is recalling what God has commanded and forbidden, for remembering that is the remembrance of God, as in the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: "Better than the remembrance of God with the tongue is the remembrance of God at His command and His prohibition." So whatever prevents from recalling God's command and prohibition is a means to falling into disobedience of the command and to plunging into the prohibition. The remembrance in this verse does not mean verbal remembrance of God, because none of it is obligatory except what is among the pillars of the prayer, and that is dispensed with by His saying "and from the prayer."

His saying ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ The fa' is a consequence of His saying ﴿Satan only wants﴾ and the rest of the verse. What has become apparent of the corruptions of wine and gambling is sufficient for people to desist from them, so there is no need to repeat the prohibition. Instead, the prohibition is dispensed with by asking them about the extent of the effect of this explanation upon their souls, elevating them to the station of the discerning and knowing. Had He, after this whole explanation, prohibited them from indulging in them, He would have placed them in the rank of the foolish. In this question lies a marvelous subtlety of address that reaches the limit of inimitability.

For this reason the interrogative with "hal" was chosen, whose original meaning is "qad." It frequently occurs in the scope of the interrogative hamza, so they dispensed with mentioning the hamza and used "hal" instead. It is thus an interrogative that affirms the establishing of the predicate being asked about, namely "antum muntahun" (you are desisting), without the hamza, since it was not said "a-tantahun" (do you desist?). This is in contrast to the context of His saying ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others; will you be patient?﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. The clause after "hal" was made nominal because it indicates the stability of the predicate, for greater affirmation of the realization of what is being asked about. So the interrogative here is used in its literal sense, and with it its figurative (kinaya) meaning is intended, namely a warning against the non-occurrence of what is asked about. For this reason it is reported that 'Umar, when he heard the verse, said: "We have desisted, we have desisted." It is known to the eloquent listeners that the interrogative in such a context is not free of implication. As for what is reported from 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib, his saying: "Surely God, exalted is He, said ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, so we said: No." If that is correctly reported from him, I doubt its soundness; it is an error of understanding or interpretation. Some of the early generation diverged, and reports are transmitted from them of persisting in drinking wine, whose authenticity is not known. If they are authentic, their meaning is that they interpreted His saying ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ as a non-definitive prohibition, and this did not last long among them.

It is said that Qudama ibn Maz'un, one of those who attended Badr, was appointed by 'Umar over Bahrain. Abu Hurayra and al-Jarud testified against him that he had drunk wine, and al-Jarud denied it, but the testimony was completed against him by a man and a woman. When 'Umar wanted to carry out the legal punishment upon him, Qudama said: "If I had drunk it as they claim, it would not be lawful for you to flog me." 'Umar said: "No." He said: "Because God says ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, when they fear God, believe and do good deeds﴾." 'Umar said to him: "You have erred in interpretation; when you fear God you avoid what He has forbidden to you."

It is also reported that Wahshi used to drink wine after his conversion to Islam, and that a group of Muslims from the people of Syria drank wine in the time of 'Umar, and interpreted the prohibition by reciting His saying ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, and that 'Umar consulted 'Ali concerning them, and they agreed that they should be asked to repent, or else be killed. There is also doubt about the soundness of this.

In the books of reports it is mentioned that 'Uyayna ibn Hisn stayed with 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib in the quarter of Banu Zubayd in Kufa, and 'Amr served him wine. 'Uyayna said: "Has God not forbidden it?" 'Amr said: "Are you older in years or am I?" 'Uyayna said: "You are." He said: "Are you earlier in Islam or am I?" He said: "You are." He said: "Indeed I have read what is between the two covers (of the Qur'an). By God, I have found no prohibition of it except that God said ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, and we said: No." So he spent the night with him, and they drank together and reveled. When 'Uyayna wanted to leave, 'Uyayna ibn Hisn said:

May you be rewarded, Abu Thawr, with the reward of generosity,
For you are a fine youth, both the visitor and the host.
You hosted and honored the hospitality, and you gave us
A greeting of knowledge that was not known before.
You said: "It is lawful for us to pass around a drink
Like the color of the lightning's flash while the night is dark."
And you presented in it an Arabic proof
That returns to fairness whoever is not fair.
And you, by God, Lord of the Throne, are for us an example
When the one who burdens himself keeps us from drinking it.
We say: Abu Thawr made its drink lawful,
But the word of Abu Thawr is firmer and more knowing.

The complement of "muntahun" is omitted because it is evident, the estimated sense being: "So will you not desist from them?" That is, from wine and gambling, because the consequence of this interrogative from His saying ﴿Satan only wants﴾ specifies that these two are what is meant by desisting.

The verse is restricted to clarifying the corruptions of drinking wine and engaging in gambling, without clarifying the corruption in the worship of idols (ansab) and divination by arrows (istiqsam bil-azlam). This is because the Muslims' abandonment of those two had already been established before this verse, from the time of entering Islam, since they are among the marks of the beliefs of polytheism. Also, the souls do not have anything that resists the legal restraint against them, unlike wine and gambling, for the pleasures they contain that drive souls toward indulging in them may resist the legal restraint. Therefore the prohibition of them was emphasized more strongly than the prohibition of idols and arrows.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 90–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ ﴿Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾

This is a resumed address to the believers, following the preceding address, so that its content is strung on the same thread on which the content of the previous address was strung, namely His saying (and do not transgress), which points out that just as Allah forbade the declaring unlawful of what is permitted, He also forbade making lawful what is unlawful; and that when Allah made the good things lawful, He forbade the corrupt things that lead to harms. For intoxicants were regarded as good by the people, and Allah the Exalted has said ﴿And from the fruits of palm trees and grapes you take from them intoxicant and good provision﴾ [al-Nahl: 67]. Gambling was a means of feeding meat to those who could not afford it. So this verse serves as a safeguard against what the statement ﴿Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87] might be misinterpreted to mean.

It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah that the most reliable of the views of our scholars is that the prohibition of intoxicants came in stages, three times. The first was when the verse ﴿They ask you about intoxicants and gambling. Say, "In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people; but their sin is greater than their benefit."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] was revealed. This contains a prohibition that is not decisive, so some people who were more God-fearing abandoned drinking intoxicants. Then 'Umar said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient explanation regarding intoxicants." Then the verse of Surat al-Nisa' was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying﴾ [al-Nisa': 43], so the Muslims avoided drinking it at the times when it was thought the intoxication would remain until the time of prayer. 'Umar said: "O Allah, make clear to us a sufficient explanation regarding intoxicants."

Then this verse was revealed. 'Umar said: "We have ceased."

It is well known that intoxicants were prohibited in the third year after the Hijrah, after the battle of Uhud. Thus this verse was revealed before Surat al-'Uqud and was placed here afterwards in its current position. It is narrated that this verse was revealed because of a quarrel that took place between Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and a man from the Ansar. Muslim related from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: "I came upon a group of the Ansar, and they said: 'Come, we will feed you and give you wine to drink,' and that was before intoxicants were prohibited. So I went to them in a garden enclosure, and there was a roasted camel's head and a skin of wine. I ate and drank with them, and I mentioned the Ansar and the Emigrants in their presence, and I said: 'The Emigrants are better than the Ansar.' A man from the Ansar took the jawbone of a camel and struck me with it, wounding my nose. So I went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him, and Allah the Exalted revealed concerning me: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾." Abu Dawud related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] and ﴿They ask you about intoxicants and gambling. Say, 'In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] were abrogated in al-Ma'idah by ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan﴾."

Therefore this prohibition was of utmost concern to the Lawgiver, who advanced it to the nation by explaining its causes, out of gentleness toward them and to make them comfortable. So He began with the verse of Surat al-Baqarah, and He did not belittle them for what they were engaging in; rather, He informed them of their excuse in His saying ﴿In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people; but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. Then with the verse of Surat al-Nisa', then He followed it with prohibition through the verse of Surat al-Ma'idah, thus confining their matter to being "defilement from the work of Satan," and He hoped for them success in avoiding them by His saying "so that you may be successful." He stirred up what is in natures of hatred for Satan by His saying ﴿Satan only wants to cause between you animosity and hatred﴾. Then He said ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, using the interrogative to depict the state of those addressed as the state of one to whom the speaker has explained the reality of something and then tested the extent of that explanation's effect on his soul.

The form "Are you going to do such-and-such?" (hal anta fa'il kadha) is used to urge an action in a context of delay, which al-Zamakhshari pointed out in al-Kashshaf at His saying Most High ﴿And it is said to the people, "Are you assembled?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 39] in Surat al-Shu'ara'. He said: "From it is the saying of Ta'abbata Sharran:
Are you one who sends a dinar for our need, or 'Abd Rabb, brother of 'Awn ibn Mikhraq?
Dinar is the name of a man, and likewise 'Abd Rabb. And His saying 'brother of 'Awn' or 'Awf' is a vocative, meaning 'O brother of 'Awn.'" So the prohibition of intoxicants was already established before the revelation of this surah, for the delegation of 'Abd al-Qays came before the conquest of Makkah in the year eight, and among what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ instructed them was not to make nabidh in the hantam, the naqir, the muzaffat, or the dubba', because these vessels cause fermentation to proceed quickly in their nabidh.

What is meant by "stone altars" here is worship of stone altars. What is meant by "divining arrows" is seeking decisions through them, because their conjunction with gambling requires that the arrows be other than gambling.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The mention of stone altars and divining arrows alongside intoxicants and gambling is intended to emphasize the prohibition of intoxicants and gambling." In this verse He emphasized the prohibition of what is slaughtered on stone altars and the prohibition of seeking decisions through divining arrows, which is the prohibition mentioned at the beginning of the surah and established in Islam from the beginning of the Prophethood.

Moreover, they did this without having been commanded to do it by the Messenger (ﷺ).

Some scholars held that the substance of wine is not impure (najis). This is the view of Rabi'a ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Muzani among the companions of al-Shafi'i, and many of the Baghdadi Malikis and the Qayrawanis, among them Sa'id ibn al-Haddad al-Qayrawani. Sa'id ibn al-Haddad argued for its purity by saying that wine was poured out in the streets of Medina, and if it were impure they would have been forbidden to do so, since a prohibition has been reported against spilling impurities in the streets. Ibn al-Faras reported from Ibn Lubaba that he upheld the view, from within the school, that the substance of wine is pure.

I say: What reflection requires is that wine is not impure in its essence, and that the context of the verse is far from aiming at the impurity of its substance. The intent is rather that it is a moral impurity (rijs ma'nawi). This is why He described it as being "from the work of Satan," and He explained this afterwards by saying: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred between you﴾. Moreover, impurity (najasa) is grounded in filth and foulness, and wine is not like that. The early generation (al-salaf) only avoided approaching it in order to establish its repugnance in souls.

The clause ﴿Satan only wants﴾ explains that these are from the work of Satan. Here "yurid" means "yuhibb" (wants/loves). The meaning of irada as mahabba (love) has already been explained at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, who purchase error and want you to stray from the way?﴾ [al-Nisa': 44] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The discussion of enmity and hatred has already been given at His saying: ﴿And We put among them enmity and hatred﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 64] in this surah.

His saying ﴿in wine and gambling﴾ means in indulging in them, following the common usage of attributing rulings to the essences themselves. That is, by what arises from drinking wine: stirring up quarrels, and proceeding to crimes; and what occurs in gambling: envy toward the winner, anger and regret for the loser, and what results from that: ill omen, abuse and beating. Furthermore, the mere arising of enmity and hatred among the Muslims is a great corruption, because God willed that the believers be brothers, since the affairs of a community cannot be upright when hatred prevails among its members. In a hadith: "Do not hate one another, do not envy one another, and be servants of God as brothers."

The "fi" in ﴿in wine and gambling﴾ is either causal (sababiyya) or a figurative locative (zarfiyya), meaning: in the gatherings of indulging in them.

As for the prevention from the remembrance of God and from the prayer, it is because of the loss of reason that wine causes, and the squandering of time that gambling involves through repeated return in pursuit of gain.

These are four causes, each of which requires prohibition, so it is no wonder that their combination requires an intensified prohibition. Whatever shares its attributes is added to wine: whatever causes enmity, hatred, and prevention from the remembrance of God and the prayer. Added to gambling is whatever shares with it in causing enmity, hatred, and prevention from the remembrance of God and the prayer, and this includes all kinds of gambling. As for play without gambling, such as chess without wagering, it is less than gambling, because it rarely prevents from the remembrance of God and the prayer, and because it does not usually cause enmity and hatred. Its rulings therefore fall under other evidences.

The remembrance intended in His saying ﴿from the remembrance of God﴾ may be verbal remembrance, in which case what is meant is the Qur'an and the speech of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in which lies their benefit and guidance, because it contains the explanation of the rulings they need. So when they immerse themselves in drinking wine and gambling, they absent themselves from the Messenger's gatherings, from hearing his sermons, and from meeting his companions who were constantly with him. Thus they do not hear the remembrance, nor receive it from the mouths of those who hear it, and they remain ignorant of much of it, including what the responsible person is obliged to know. Therefore, whatever prevents from this is a great corruption that deserves to have its indulgence forbidden. It may also be that what is meant is the remembrance of the heart, which is recalling what God has commanded and forbidden, for remembering that is the remembrance of God, as in the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: "Better than the remembrance of God with the tongue is the remembrance of God at His command and His prohibition."
