So whatever prevents from recalling God's command and prohibition is a means to falling into disobedience of the command and to plunging into the prohibition. The remembrance in this verse does not mean verbal remembrance of God, because none of it is obligatory except what is among the pillars of the prayer, and that is dispensed with by His saying "and from the prayer."

His saying ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ The fa' is a consequence of His saying ﴿Satan only wants﴾ and the rest of the verse. What has become apparent of the corruptions of wine and gambling is sufficient for people to desist from them, so there is no need to repeat the prohibition. Instead, the prohibition is dispensed with by asking them about the extent of the effect of this explanation upon their souls, elevating them to the station of the discerning and knowing. Had He, after this whole explanation, prohibited them from indulging in them, He would have placed them in the rank of the foolish. In this question lies a marvelous subtlety of address that reaches the limit of inimitability.

For this reason the interrogative with "hal" was chosen, whose original meaning is "qad." It frequently occurs in the scope of the interrogative hamza, so they dispensed with mentioning the hamza and used "hal" instead. It is thus an interrogative that affirms the establishing of the predicate being asked about, namely "antum muntahun" (you are desisting), without the hamza, since it was not said "a-tantahun" (do you desist?). This is in contrast to the context of His saying ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others; will you be patient?﴾ [al-Furqan: 20]. The clause after "hal" was made nominal because it indicates the stability of the predicate, for greater affirmation of the realization of what is being asked about. So the interrogative here is used in its literal sense, and with it its figurative (kinaya) meaning is intended, namely a warning against the non-occurrence of what is asked about. For this reason it is reported that 'Umar, when he heard the verse, said: "We have desisted, we have desisted." It is known to the eloquent listeners that the interrogative in such a context is not free of implication. As for what is reported from 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib, his saying: "Surely God, exalted is He, said ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, so we said: No." If that is correctly reported from him, I doubt its soundness; it is an error of understanding or interpretation. Some of the early generation diverged, and reports are transmitted from them of persisting in drinking wine, whose authenticity is not known. If they are authentic, their meaning is that they interpreted His saying ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ as a non-definitive prohibition, and this did not last long among them.

It is said that Qudama ibn Maz'un, one of those who attended Badr, was appointed by 'Umar over Bahrain. Abu Hurayra and al-Jarud testified against him that he had drunk wine, and al-Jarud denied it, but the testimony was completed against him by a man and a woman. When 'Umar wanted to carry out the legal punishment upon him, Qudama said: "If I had drunk it as they claim, it would not be lawful for you to flog me." 'Umar said: "No." He said: "Because God says ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, when they fear God, believe and do good deeds﴾." 'Umar said to him: "You have erred in interpretation; when you fear God you avoid what He has forbidden to you."

It is also reported that Wahshi used to drink wine after his conversion to Islam, and that a group of Muslims from the people of Syria drank wine in the time of 'Umar, and interpreted the prohibition by reciting His saying ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, and that 'Umar consulted 'Ali concerning them, and they agreed that they should be asked to repent, or else be killed. There is also doubt about the soundness of this.

In the books of reports it is mentioned that 'Uyayna ibn Hisn stayed with 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib in the quarter of Banu Zubayd in Kufa, and 'Amr served him wine. 'Uyayna said: "Has God not forbidden it?" 'Amr said: "Are you older in years or am I?" 'Uyayna said: "You are." He said: "Are you earlier in Islam or am I?" He said: "You are." He said: "Indeed I have read what is between the two covers (of the Qur'an). By God, I have found no prohibition of it except that God said ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, and we said: No." So he spent the night with him, and they drank together and reveled. When 'Uyayna wanted to leave, 'Uyayna ibn Hisn said:

May you be rewarded, Abu Thawr, with the reward of generosity,
For you are a fine youth, both the visitor and the host.
You hosted and honored the hospitality, and you gave us
A greeting of knowledge that was not known before.
You said: "It is lawful for us to pass around a drink
Like the color of the lightning's flash while the night is dark."
And you presented in it an Arabic proof
That returns to fairness whoever is not fair.
And you, by God, Lord of the Throne, are for us an example
When the one who burdens himself keeps us from drinking it.
We say: Abu Thawr made its drink lawful,
But the word of Abu Thawr is firmer and more knowing.

The complement of "muntahun" is omitted because it is evident, the estimated sense being: "So will you not desist from them?" That is, from wine and gambling, because the consequence of this interrogative from His saying ﴿Satan only wants﴾ specifies that these two are what is meant by desisting.

The verse is restricted to clarifying the corruptions of drinking wine and engaging in gambling, without clarifying the corruption in the worship of idols (ansab) and divination by arrows (istiqsam bil-azlam). This is because the Muslims' abandonment of those two had already been established before this verse, from the time of entering Islam, since they are among the marks of the beliefs of polytheism. Also, the souls do not have anything that resists the legal restraint against them, unlike wine and gambling, for the pleasures they contain that drive souls toward indulging in them may resist the legal restraint. Therefore the prohibition of them was emphasized more strongly than the prohibition of idols and arrows.

The clause "and obey God and obey the Messenger" is conjoined to the clause "So will you not desist?" (﴿فَهَلْ أنْتُمْ مُنْتَهُونَ﴾ [5:91]), and it serves as a concluding summary (tadhyil), because obedience to God and His Messenger encompasses abstaining from wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows, and encompasses other forms of compliance and avoidance besides these. "And obey" is repeated to give emphasis to the command to obey. "And beware" is conjoined to "obey," meaning "and be on guard." The object of "beware" is omitted so that the verb is treated as intransitive, because the intended sense is to be engaged in caution regarding matters of religion, that is, caution against falling into what God and His Messenger reject. This is more eloquent than saying "beware of them both," because an intransitive verb's meaning approaches that of verbs of disposition, which is why its active participle follows the pattern fa'il (ism al-fa'il, the active participle), as in fariha (joyful) and nahima (greedy).

His words ﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّيْتُمْ﴾ ("But if you turn away") are a consequence (tafri') of "obey" and "beware." "Turning away" (tawalli) here is a metaphor (isti'ara) for disobedience. Disobedience is likened to withdrawing from and leaving the position in which the disobedient person stood, with the common element being separation and departure. For the same reason, the term "turning back" (idbar) is also applied to it. Thus, in the hadith of Ibn Sayyad: "If you turn back, God will surely strike you down," meaning, "If you turn away from Islam."

His words ﴿فاعْلَمُوا﴾ ("then know") are the answer to the conditional, considered in terms of the implication of its meaning. The meaning is: if you turn away from obeying the Messenger, then know that your turning away does not harm the Messenger, because his duty is only to convey (the message). That is, your turning away harms only yourselves. Were it not for this implied meaning of the answer, the connection between turning away and their knowledge that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was commanded only to convey would not be coherent. The mention of the verb "know" serves to draw attention to the importance of the information, as we explained at His words ﴿واتَّقُوا اللَّهَ واعْلَمُوا أنَّكم مُلاقُوهُ﴾ ("Fear God and know that you will meet Him") [2:223] in Surat al-Baqara.

The word ﴿أنَّما﴾ with a fatha on the hamza restricts meaning (husr, exclusivity), just as "innama" with a kasra on the hamza does. Since the kasra form is agreed to express restriction, the fatha form also expresses restriction, because it is a derivative of the kasra form and is its sister. There should be no lingering disagreement with those who denied that it expresses restriction. The meaning is that his task is restricted to conveying the message and does not extend to the ability to guide those to whom it is conveyed.

Attributing the Messenger to the Divine Name (ḍamīr al-jalāla) glorifies the side of this message and establishes the excuse of the Messenger in conveying it: he is a messenger from the One capable of all things. Had his Sender willed, He would have guided those to whom he was sent. So if they do not become guided, that is not due to any shortcoming on the part of the Messenger.

Describing the conveyance as ﴿الْمُبِينُ﴾ ("clear") is an exhaustive affirmation of the Messenger's excuse, and of the warning given to those who turn away from compliance, after the message has become clear, sufficient, and supported by compelling proof.

[32]

This verse clarifies an ambiguity in understanding the verse before it. Some Muslims thought that drinking wine before this verse was revealed was tainted with sin, because God had described wine and what was mentioned with it as "an abomination from the work of Satan." The occasion of revelation of this verse is what is in the Two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from Anas ibn Malik, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and Ibn 'Abbas, that when the prohibition of wine was revealed, some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What about our companions who died while they were drinking wine?" or he said, "while it was in their bellies," and who ate gambling (al-maysir) [meat obtained through gambling]. So God revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, and the verse. In the Tafsir of al-Fakhr (al-Razi), Abu Bakr al-Asamm narrated that when the prohibition of wine was revealed, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: "O Messenger of God, what about our brothers who died after drinking wine and committing gambling? And what about those absent from us in the lands, who do not know that God has prohibited wine, and they are eating it?" So God revealed these verses.

It may appear at first glance that the state of those who died before the prohibition of wine is not something the Companions would need to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about, since God does not hold anyone accountable for an act that was not forbidden before it was done, and He does not hold anyone accountable for committing it until he has come to know of the prohibition. The answer is that the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were very cautious about anything that diminishes reward, and eager for complete uprightness. When it was revealed about wine and gambling that they are an abomination from the work of Satan, they feared that Satan might have a share in those who drank wine, ate [the meat obtained through] gambling, and died before giving it up, or died while the wine was in their bodies, mixing with their flesh. So they could not restrain themselves from asking the Prophet (ﷺ) about their condition, out of their intense concern for their brothers. This is like how 'Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum asked when God's saying was revealed: ﴿Not equal are those who sit [at home] among the believers﴾ [al-Nisa: 95] and ﴿and those who strive in the way of God with their wealth and their lives﴾ [al-Nisa: 95]. He said: "O Messenger of God, what then of me, for I am blind and cannot see?" So God revealed: ﴿other than those with a [legitimate] excuse﴾ [al-Nisa: 95]. Likewise what occurred when the qiblah was changed from facing Bayt al-Maqdis to facing the Ka'bah: some people said, "What about our brothers who died while facing Bayt al-Maqdis?" So God, exalted is He, revealed

[33]
﴿And God would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning your prayer. So the purpose of the question was to seek certainty in understanding, and not to go beyond receiving [knowledge] from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in matters of their religion.

The negation of blame (junah) means the negation of sin and disobedience. "Ma" (what) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah). "Ta'imu" (they ate) is the relative clause (silah). The returning pronoun of the relative clause is omitted. "Ma" is not a verbal-infinitive particle (masdariyyah), because the intended meaning is pardon for something they ate, which is known from the question. Thus the linking of the temporal sense of "ma ta'imu" to "junah" is according to the estimate: "in the eating of what they ate."

The original meaning of "ta'imu" is that it means "akalu" (they ate). God says: ﴿And when you have eaten, disperse﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. The essential meaning of "ta'm" is eating, and the thing eaten is "ta'am" (food). Drink is not part of food, but is other than it; therefore it is conjoined in God's saying: ﴿Look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259]. What supports this is the exception made for edibles in God's saying: ﴿Say, I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be carrion, or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure, or [it is] a defiant sin, [over] which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾ [al-An'am: 145]. It is also said: "tami'a" means "adhaqa" (to make taste), and its verbal noun is "al-tu'm" with a damma on the ta'. They considered it derived from "al-ta'm," which is the sense of taste. The saying of God has already been mentioned: ﴿And whoever does not taste it, he is not of me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249], meaning, whoever does not taste it, by the indication of His saying "except one who scoops with his hand." It is also said: "I found in the water the taste of dust." And it is said: "the taste of the water changed," meaning it became foul. So among the eloquence of the Qur'an is the use of the verb "ta'imu" here, because the intention is to negate responsibility from those who drank wine and ate the meat [obtained through] gambling before the revelation of the verse prohibiting them. The word is used in both its meanings, that is, in its literal and metaphorical senses, or it is of the style of "taghlib" (prevalence of one term over another).

Since He expressed it with the past tense form in His saying "ta'imu," "idha" must be a temporal adverb of the past. This is according to the more correct of the two opinions of the grammarians, although it is well known that "idha" is a temporal adverb of the future. The truth is that "idha" can occur as a temporal adverb of the past. This is what Ibn Malik chose, and what Ibn Hisham followed in Mughni al-Labib. Its evidence is God's saying: ﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who, when they came to you to be provided with mounts [and you said, "I do not find any to carry you"]﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92], and His saying: ﴿And when they saw a transaction or diversion, they dispersed toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and many other verses. So the meaning is: there is no blame upon them, since they believed and were mindful [of God] (idh kanu amanu wa-ittaqaw). The meaning of the speech is interpreted as: there is no blame upon them, because they believed and were mindful [of God] regarding what was forbidden on that day. They only consumed wine and ate [meat obtained through] gambling before their prohibition.

This is the explanation of the verse, which follows what the majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin) have adopted, following what has come regarding the occasion of its revelation in the authentic hadiths.

Among the exegetes there are those who made the meaning of the verse unconnected to the verse on the prohibition of wine and gambling. I suppose they did not take into account what was narrated about its occasion of revelation, because they saw that the occasion of revelation does not restrict it to the particular case, but rather the general wording applies, according to what is correct, that the generality of the wording is not restricted by the particularity of the occasion. So they said: God lifted blame from the believers regarding whatever they eat of pleasant foods and lawful provisions, if they are mindful of what God has forbidden to them. That is, it is not righteousness to deprive oneself by forbidding the good things; rather righteousness is piety. This falls under the category of God's saying: ﴿It is not righteousness to enter houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189]. This interpretation was adopted in the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari), beginning with it.

On this view, the meaning of the verse is connected to the verse: ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things which God has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87]. It is then a new independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), because of the connection with what preceded regarding the prohibition of making unlawful for themselves the good things God has made lawful for them, by oath or vow to abstain.

Some claimed that this verse was revealed concerning the people who made meat unlawful for themselves and adopted the path of asceticism (tarahhub), among them 'Uthman ibn Maz'un. But it is not authentically established that this was the occasion of its revelation. On this interpretation, "ta'imu" is used in its well-known meaning, namely eating, and "idha" is used for the future, and the verb

[35]
"ta'imu" is an expression of the future with a past-tense form, by the indication of the word "idha," as in His saying: ﴿Then when He calls you with a single call from the earth, at once you will come out﴾ [al-Rum: 25].

What weakens this interpretation is that those who forbade good things to themselves did not restrict their prohibition to food and drink, but it includes clothing and women. Except that it may be said that the speech followed the consideration of what is most common in prohibition.

Al-Fakhr said: Some ignorant people claimed that God, exalted is He, when He made wine forbidden at the time it causes enmity and hatred and prevents remembrance of God and prayer, clarified in this verse that there is no blame upon one who ate it if no such harms result from it, but rather obedience, piety, and kindness to creation result from it. It is not possible to interpret it as referring to the condition of those who drank wine before the revelation of the verse of prohibition; for if that were the case, He would have said "there was no blame upon those who ate," as He mentioned in the verse about the change of the qiblah, when He said, "And God would not have caused your faith to be lost." There is no doubt that "idha" is for the future, not for the past. Al-Fakhr said: This view is rejected by the consensus (ijma') of the whole Community. As for their saying that "idha" is for the future, its answer is that the permissibility for the future relates to the time of the revelation of the verse concerning those who were absent.

Piety (taqwa) is the performance of what is commanded and the avoidance of what is prohibited. Therefore, the conjunction of "wa-'amilu al-salihat" (and did righteous deeds) with "ittaqaw" (were mindful) is a conjunction of the particular to the general, for the sake of emphasis on it, like His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. Also, avoiding what is prohibited is more immediately understood by the wording "taqwa," because it is derived from "tawaqqi" and "kaff" (restraint and abstaining).

As for the conjunction of "wa-amanu" (and believed) with "ittaqaw," it is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) to indicate that faith is the root of piety, like His saying: ﴿[It is] freeing a neck, or feeding on a day of severe hunger... then being among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 13–17]. The purpose of this conditional-like temporal clause is merely to draw attention to piety, faith, and righteous deeds, and it is not intended that the negation of blame for them is restricted to their being mindful, believing, and doing righteous deeds, because it is known that every act has an effect on its doing or on its abandonment. Since they had been believers before, and faith is a rational conviction that does not admit renewal, it becomes clear that the intended meaning of "wa-amanu" is: and they persisted in faith and did not nullify it by disbelief.

The clause ﴿then they were mindful and believed﴾ is a verbal emphasis of the clause ﴿when they are mindful and believe and do righteous deeds﴾, and it is joined with the particle "thumma" (then), which indicates a gradation of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), to indicate an increase in piety and the effects of faith, like the emphasis in His saying: ﴿No! They will [soon] know. Then again, no! They will [soon] know﴾ [al-Naba': 4–5]. For this reason he did not repeat "and did righteous deeds," because doing righteous deeds is included in piety.

As for the clause ﴿then they were mindful and did good﴾, it gives verbal emphasis to the clause "then they were mindful," and it indicates an ascent in piety by the indication of the particle "thumma" as a gradation of rank, together with the added quality of excellence (ihsan). The Prophet (ﷺ) explained excellence by his saying: "That you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." This necessarily includes faith, so the repetition of "and believed" is dispensed with here. The verb "and did good" includes doing good to Muslims, and it is in addition to piety, because among it is good that is not obligatory, and it is something that brings God's pleasure. For this reason He concluded it with His saying: ﴿And God loves the doers of good﴾.

The exegetes have taken various approaches to interpreting the repetition occurring in this verse, which have no evidence in the composition of the verse. Their basis is making the repetition in "then they were mindful" to mean that piety and faith differ according to time or according to states.

Some exegetes, in interpreting God's saying ﴿when they are mindful﴾ and what is conjoined with it, went in directions that arose from taking it as a restrictive condition for the negation of blame upon the fulfillment of the condition. Bringing them up would be lengthy.

It has been mentioned that some of the early generation (al-salaf) interpreted this verse as meaning a permission to drink wine for one who is mindful of God regarding what is counted [as lawful], and the wine was not a means to the forbidden things, nor to harming people. This is attributed to Qudamah ibn Maz'un, as was mentioned in the commentary on the verse prohibiting wine. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib did not accept this from him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 94:

﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and your spears can reach, so that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾

I do not think this verse is anything but an explanation of His saying at the beginning of the surah, ﴿not violating the sanctity of game while you are in the state of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage)﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 1], and a preparation for the ruling on killing game while in the state of ihram, and a preface to His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95]. What led to this preface was the context of mentioning the prohibited things: wine, gambling, and what is joined with them. So Allah addressed the believers by alerting them to a situation in which their greed may outrun their caution, and their desire may overcome their piety. This is a situation of trial and testing, in which the differences in their adherence to the commandments of Allah Most High become manifest in existence. This situation had not occurred at the time this verse was revealed, because His saying ﴿will surely test you﴾ is clearly in the future tense, since the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) does not enter upon the present tense in the answer to an oath except when it carries the meaning of the future. The apparent view is that the ruling on hitting game while in ihram or within the land of the Haram (the sacred precinct) had not yet been established by such a thing. It has been narrated from Muqatil that the Muslims, during the 'Umrah (lesser pilgrimage) of al-Hudaybiyyah, encountered a large amount of game on their route, which kept running into their baggage and tents. Some of them were in the state of ihram and some were not. They were able to catch it with their hands, and to hunt some of it with spears, and they had never seen game like this before. Their states differed in regard to daring to seize it. Some of them took it with their hands and struck it with their spears. Then this verse was revealed. Thus it may be that this verse was attached to Surat al-Ma'idah as an attachment, so that it would be a reminder to them in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, that they might beware of what had befallen them on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah. They were, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, in greater need of warning and clarification, because of the large number of Muslims in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage and the large number of Bedouins among them. This explains the meaning of His saying ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾, since the word (tanaluhu) indicates that this is within their capacity and with ease of taking.

The address is to the believers, and it is general (mujmal), which is clarified by His saying that follows it: ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95]. Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: The scholars differed regarding the one addressed by this verse on two views. One of them is that they are those not in the state of ihram, as said by Malik. The second is that they are those in the state of ihram, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and others. And he said in al-Qabas: Some people imagined that the meaning of the verse is the prohibition of game while in the state of ihram, and this is an intricate matter (u'dulah). Rather, what is meant is the trial in both states, that of being out of ihram and that of being in its sanctity.

The root of this disagreement is the consideration of whether the verse includes the ruling for what a non-muhrim hunts of the game of the Haram, and whether it does not include it, such that its ruling does not need another proof, or does need one. Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Ahkam: His saying ﴿will surely test you﴾ requires that the obligation is realized for the non-muhrim with what is conditioned for him regarding matters of game and what is conditioned for him regarding the manner of hunting. And all obligation is a trial, even if it varies in its paucity and abundance and differs in its weakness and strength. He means that His saying ﴿Allah will surely test you with something of game﴾ does not mean striking with a calamity, that is, the disaster of killing forbidden game, but rather it means that Allah will impose an obligation upon you through some states of game. This looks to the view that His saying, ﴿while you are in the state of ihram and in the sanctity of the Haram﴾, includes both the state of ihram and being within the Haram.

And His saying ﴿Allah will surely test you with something of game﴾ is a trial of obligation and prohibition, as indicated by its connection to a matter of what one does. So it is not like the trial in His saying ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 155]. Rather, He informed them of this in the manner of warning. So the report is used in its meaning and in what follows from its meaning, which is warning. It is necessary that this address was directed at them at a time when they were wavering between holding the game and eating it, and between observing the sanctity of ihram, since they were in ihram for 'Umrah at al-Hudaybiyyah and they had wavered about what they should do, that is, whether what the people were upon regarding the prohibition of hitting game for the one in ihram was valid in Islam or not valid. So the trial is in the future, because the realization of the meaning of trial occurs only after the prohibition and warning. The presence of the emphatic nun specifies the present tense for the future, so the future is the trial itself. As for the game, and the reaching of hands and spears, it is present.

Al-sayd (game): the thing hunted (al-masid), because His saying ﴿of game﴾ came as an explanation of His saying ﴿with something﴾. What was previously said about its counterpart in His saying ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 155] in Surat al-Baqarah suffices, so there is no need to discuss it again here, nor the word ﴿something﴾.

The indefiniteness of ﴿something﴾ here is for variety (al-tanwi'), not for belittling, contrary to al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him.

By His saying ﴿that your hands and your spears can reach﴾ He indicated the types of game, the small and the large. They used to seize chicks with their hands, and what is a means to seizing with the hands, such as nets, snares, and trained hunting animals, since all of that leads back to seizing by the hand. And they used to pursue the large ones on horseback with spears, as they did with wild donkeys and wild cattle. As in the hadith of Abu Qatadah, that he saw a wild donkey during the year of al-Hudaybiyyah while he was not in ihram. He mounted his horse, took his spear, and ran after the donkey, catching it and striking it with his spear, and brought it back, etc. And sometimes they hunted by shooting arrows from their bows, as in the hadith of al-Muwatta: "From Zayd al-Bahzi, that he went out with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ intending Makkah, and there was a gazelle crouching with an arrow in it..." the hadith. Some hunters would hide in a blind and hold their bow, and when the game passed by, they shot it with an arrow. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He specified spears for mention because they are the greatest means by which game is wounded.

It may be said: He omitted what is other than hands and other than spears, relying on the two extremes to dispense with the middle.

The clause ﴿that your hands can reach﴾ is an attribute of the game or a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. Its purpose is to exhaust the types of game, lest it be thought that the warning concerns only game that is wounded or killed, not game that is seized by hand, or picking up eggs or the like.

His saying ﴿so that Allah may make evident who fears Him unseen﴾ is a cause (illah) for His saying ﴿will surely test you﴾, because testing is examination, so its cause is that Allah may know from it who fears Him. The making of Allah's knowledge a cause of the trial is only in the sense of: so that it may become manifest to people who fears Allah from everyone whom Allah knows fears Him. So the knowledge of Allah is applied to its necessary consequence, which is the manifestation and distinction of that, because Allah's knowledge necessarily entails actual realization, since Allah's knowledge can only be in conformity with what is in reality, as we have explained more than once. Or it is meant by His saying "so that Allah may know" the transitive (tanjizi) relation of Allah's knowledge to the act of some of the accountable, based on affirming a transitive relation of the attribute of knowledge. This is the position that 'Abd al-Hakim adopted in the al-Risalah al-Khaqaniyyah.

It has been said: knowledge is applied to its relation to the known in external reality. It follows that the intention of this speaker is that this application was made to bring the meaning closer to the general understanding of the addressees. Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-Qabas: "so that Allah may know by witnessing what He knew unseen, of the obedience of those who obeyed and the transgression of those who transgressed, for He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, He knows the unseen first, then He creates the nonexistent and knows it by witnessing. The known changes but knowledge does not change."

The ba' (bi) is either for accompaniment (mulabasah) or for location (zarfiyyah), and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the nominative in ﴿yakhafuhu﴾ (fears Him).

Al-ghayb (the unseen) is the opposite of presence and the opposite of witnessing. It has already been discussed in His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 3] in one of its two aspects there. So the attachment of the prepositional phrase here to ﴿yakhafuhu﴾ is most apparently for mere disclosure, without intending specification or restriction, like His saying ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾ [Al-'Imran: 21]. That is, whoever fears Allah while being absent from Allah, that is, not witnessed by Him. And all of people's fear of Allah in this world is fear in the unseen. Allah Most High said: ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord in the unseen will have forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [Al-Mulk: 12].

The benefit of mentioning it is that it is praise of those who fear Allah. He praised them for true faith and the illumination of insight, for they feared Him without seeing His greatness, majesty, bounty, and reward, but they were certain of that through true inference. This is indicated by what is in the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi, a hadith in which the words are attributed to God in the first person): "They believed in Me without having seen Me, so how would it be if they saw Me?" Among the exegetes, some interpreted al-ghayb as "the world." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The apparent meaning is that the meaning of "in the unseen" is away from people, that is, in privacy. So whoever fears Allah refrains from hunting by himself. This means that the prepositional phrase is for restriction, that is, whoever fears Allah while being absent from the eyes of people, whose denunciation of him or whose prevention of him or whose taking him by the hand or whose hearing of him is feared. This looks to what they built upon: that the verse was revealed concerning game that came upon them during their journey in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, coming upon them in their baggage and tents, that is, they were able to seize it without a watcher. Or the game warned against may be similar to that game.

His saying ﴿And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment﴾ is an explicit statement of the warning that He had alluded to with His saying ﴿will surely test you﴾, since His saying ﴿will surely test you﴾ indicated that in this report there is a warning against an act to which the soul may quickly incline.

The reference by ﴿after that﴾ is to the warning derived from ﴿will surely test you﴾, that is, after what We have presented to you and given you excuse concerning it. Therefore the particle of consequence (fa' al-tafri') came after it. What is meant by transgression (i'tida') is transgression by hunting, and He called it transgression because it is a daring act upon something forbidden and a violation of the sanctity of ihram or of the Haram.

His saying ﴿then he will have a painful punishment﴾ means a severe retribution in the Hereafter for having dared against the Haram, or against ihram, or both, and for having opposed the warning of Allah Most High. This applies if he transgresses and does not make amends for his transgression by repentance or by expiation. Repentance is known from the foundations of Islam, and expiation is the compensation for the game, because the apparent view is that the compensation is an expiation for this transgression, as will come later. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: The painful punishment is that his belly and back are stretched out and he is beaten with whips and his clothes are stripped off, and this was the practice concerning it in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period). So the punishment is worldly harm, and this implies that this verse confirmed what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to do, and so the verse that follows it is an abrogation (naskh) of it. None of the jurists of Islam said this punishment, which indicates that it was annulled by what is in the following verse, and this is what the meaning of this verse coheres with the meaning of the verse after it. It is possible that the compensation is of the nature of guaranteeing destroyed property, and the sin of transgression remains, and it is what necessitates the painful punishment. According to the well-known interpretation, only repentance removes it, and according to what has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, the beating remains as discipline, but none of the jurists of Islam said this. The apparent view is that his spoils were taken by the poor of Makkah, such as the covers of the sacrificial camels and their sandals.

صفحة ٣٨
[Page 38 marker from source]

[Page 42]

﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram (ritual consecration). Whoever among you kills it intentionally, the compensation is an equivalent of what he killed from the livestock, judged by two just men among you, as an offering brought to the Kaabah, or an expiation of feeding needy persons, or the equivalent of that in fasting, so that he may taste the consequence of his deed. Allah has pardoned what is past. Whoever returns to it, Allah will take retribution from him, and Allah is Mighty, Owner of retribution.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new clause that begins a fresh topic) explaining the verse ﴿Allah will surely test you with something of the game﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:94), or it abrogates its ruling (naskh, the repeal of an earlier ruling by a later one), if that verse contained a ruling by which no action was taken. The meaning of ﴿and you are in ihram﴾ was discussed at the beginning of this surah.

Know that Allah has forbidden game in two circumstances: when the hunter is in ihram, and when the game is from the game of the sacred precinct (haram), even if the hunter is not in ihram. The wisdom in this is that Allah, exalted is He, magnified the status of the Kaabah from the time of Ibrahim (ﷺ)(peace be upon him), and commanded him to designate a sanctuary around it, just as kings used to designate a protected preserve (hima). So it was the House of Allah and its protected zone. The sanctuary of the House is made sacred to the utmost extent of what is considered sanctity and honor. Therefore Allah legislated a broad sanctuary for the House and made the House a place of security for people, and extended that security until it included the animals living within its sanctuary, so that people see the House as nothing but a refuge for whoever seeks protection in it and in its sanctuary. Al-Nabighah said:

"And the protector of the birds that seek refuge, whom the riders of Makkah stroke between al-Ghil and al-Sanad."

Thus the prohibition applies to the hunting of land animals. The hunting of sea creatures is not prohibited, because there is no sea or river within the area of the sanctuary. Then Allah forbade hunting to the one in ihram for hajj or 'umrah (the lesser pilgrimage), because hunting stirs up some of the creatures that are safe. The ihram also prevented those in it from fighting, and they were forbidden to fight during the sacred months, because these are the times of hajj and 'umrah. So the animal was linked in sanctity to the killing of a human being. Or it is because most people in ihram do not intend ihram until they reach the sanctuary, so most people do not hunt except the animals of the sanctuary.

[Page 43]

Game (sayd) is general to everything that is customarily hunted and killed, from quadrupeds and birds, for eating or for benefiting from some part of it. The wild beasts are all included with game. Ibn al-Faras said: wild beasts are called game even if they have not yet been hunted, just as one says "the rabbit is a bad catch (ramiyyah)" even if it has not yet been shot. Some of its generality is excluded for harmful animals, namely the harmful predators, venomous creatures, the mouse, and the birds of prey. The evidence for this exclusion is the Sunnah (the Prophetic practice and tradition).

The intention to kill is subordinate to the hunter's remembering that he is in ihram, and this is the scope of the verse. So if he forgot that he was in ihram, he is not intentional. And if he did not intend to kill it but it was hit, he is not intentional. There is no basis or evidence for those who interpret "intentionally" in the verse as intentionally killing while forgetting that he is in ihram.

As for His saying ﴿and you are in ihram﴾, ḥurum is the plural of ḥarām, meaning muḥrim (one in ihram), like the plural of qadhāl as quḍul. The muḥrim originally refers to one who has entered into ihram for hajj or 'umrah. The term muḥrim is also applied to one who is within the sanctuary. Al-Ra'i said:

"They killed the son of 'Affan, the caliph, while he was in the state of sanctity."

That is, while he was within the sacred precinct of Madinah. As for ihram for hajj and 'umrah, it is well known. As for being within the sanctuary, it means being in the place of the haram, either Makkah or Madinah. Al-Shafi'i added al-Ta'if to the sanctity of its game, but not to the obligation of compensation upon its hunter. As for the sanctuary of Makkah, hunting in it is forbidden by consensus, and there is compensation for hunting in it. As for the sanctuary of Madinah, hunting in it is forbidden, and there is no compensation for it. Al-Ta'if is similar to it according to al-Shafi'i.

The sanctuary of Makkah is known by boundaries from before Islam; it is the sanctuary that Ibrahim (ﷺ) (peace be upon him) made sacred, and markers were placed at its boundaries in the time of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. As for the sanctuary of Madinah, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Madinah is a sanctuary from such-and-such place between 'Ayr or 'a'ir (a mountain) to Thawr." It was said that Thawr is a mountain, and Thawr is not known except in Makkah. Al-Nawawi said: Most narrators in the Sahih of al-Bukhari mention 'Ayr, but as for Thawr, some of them alluded to it by saying "from 'Ayr to such-and-such," and some left a blank in its place, because they believed that the mention of Thawr here was an error. It was said that the correct reading is "to Uhud," as in Ahmad and al-Tabarani. It was also said that Thawr is a small mountain behind the mountain of Uhud.

As for His saying ﴿Whoever among you kills it﴾ and so on, "man" (man) is a conditional noun in the nominative as a subject, and "killed it" (qatalahu) is the conditional verb, and "among you" is a qualifier of the conditional noun, meaning: from among those who believe.

[Page 44]

The purpose of the phrase "among you" is something the exegetes have left aside without explaining. The apparent reason for mentioning this description is to nullify the practice of the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period), for whoever among them hit game in the sanctuary, they would beat him and strip him of his clothes, as was mentioned just before.

Making the ruling of compensation dependent on the occurrence of killing indicates that compensation is not obligatory unless he kills the game. If he wounds it or cuts off a limb of it without killing it, there is no compensation. It also indicates that the ruling is the same whether the killer eats the game or does not eat it, because the basis of the ruling is the killing.

His saying "intentionally" has excluded the one who errs in his hunting. The verse does not state a ruling for him, but it indicates that his ruling cannot be harsher than that of the intentional one. So it is possible that there is another lighter compensation for him, and it is possible that there is no compensation for him at all, and the Sunnah has clarified it. Al-Zuhri said: the Qur'an was revealed concerning intentional acts, and the Sunnah established that the forgetful and the erring must also expiate. Perhaps he meant by the Sunnah the practice from the time of Prophethood and the caliphs, which continued as the practice of the Companions. But there is no report on this from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Malik, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, and the majority of the jurists of the major cities said: intentional and mistaken hunting are equal in this. Malik gave weight to the meaning of compensation (ghurm), that is, he analogized it to the compensation for property, and intentional and mistaken acts are equal in compensation for property, so he treated them equally. This practice continued among the Companions.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam from the Malikis, Dawud al-Zahiri, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Salim ibn 'Abdullah, 'Ata', and Mujahid said: there is nothing for the forgetful. Similar was reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Mujahid, al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Juraij said: if he intentionally kills while forgetting his ihram, this is the scope of the verse, and he must pay compensation. As for one who intentionally kills while remembering his ihram, this is too grave a sin to be expiated, and his hajj is invalid, and his game is carrion that may not be eaten.

[Page 45]

Compensation (jaza') is a recompense for an action. Allah called it jaza' because it is a discipline and a punishment, except that it was legislated in the manner of expiations (kaffarat), like the expiation for killing and the expiation for zihar (a type of divorce formula). The purpose of it is not compensation for property, since the game is not something any person benefits from, such that its killer would pay to make up for what he destroyed. Rather, the game is the property of Allah, exalted is He. He permitted it outside of ihram and did not permit it to people while they are in ihram. So whoever transgresses against it in that state, Allah has imposed upon the transgressor a compensation, and He made it a compensation from which the weak among His servants benefit.

The fact that the purpose of the legislation in this is punishment is indicated by His saying right after it ﴿so that he may taste the consequence of his deed﴾. It was called jaza' and not kaffarah because equivalence was taken into account in it. It is measured by the equivalent of the act, so it was called jaza'. The concept of jaza' requires equivalence and correspondence, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿a fitting recompense﴾ (al-Naba' 78:26).

He informed that the compensation is the equivalent of what the hunter killed, and that equivalent is from the livestock. This is because game is either from quadrupeds or from birds. Most of the game of the Arabs was from quadrupeds, such as wild donkeys, wild cattle, the arwa (a wild goat), and gazelles. And from the winged animals, the ostrich and the wild goose. As for birds that fly in the air, their hunting is rare, because they are only caught with the mi'rad (a throwing stick), and the mi'rad rarely hits anything except the pigeons of Makkah and what is near them. So the equivalence of quadrupeds to livestock is easy. As for the equivalence of birds to livestock, it is approximate rather than exact. The ostrich is close to a cow or a camel, the wild goose is close to a young goat, and so on. What has no counterpart, like the sparrow, has a monetary value. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. Abu Hanifah and Abu Yusuf said: the equivalent is the monetary value in all that is hunted. The value according to Malik is food. Abu Hanifah said: it is dirhams. If the resort is to monetary value, then according to Malik the value is food that is given in charity, or one fasts for each mudd (a measure) of food for one day, and for a remainder of a mudd, a full day. Abu Hanifah said: he buys with the value a sacrificial animal if he wishes, and if he wishes he buys food, and if he wishes he fasts for each half sa' (a measure) for one day.

The scholars differed over whether the compensation may be less than what is accepted in sacrificial animals and offerings. Malik said: nothing less than a sheep or goat that has lost its milk teeth (thani) is acceptable, because Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿an offering brought to the Kaabah﴾. So what is not acceptable as an offering from livestock cannot be compensation. Therefore, whoever hits young game is given the choice between giving the least acceptable offering from livestock, or giving the value of what he hunted as food, and he does not give young livestock.

[Page 46]

Malik said in the Muwatta': "Whatever is ransomed, its young is like its adult." Similarly, the blood money for a free young person and a free adult is of the same value. Al-Shafi'i and some scholars of Madinah said: if the game is young, its compensation is what is closest to it of young livestock, based on what Malik reported in the Muwatta' from Abu al-Zubayr al-Makki that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab judged that for a rabbit one should give a young goat, and for a jerboa a young female goat weaned from its mother. The grandson Ibn Rushd said in Bidayat al-Mujtahid: "This is what was reported from 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, and Ibn Mas'ud." I say: nothing has been authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this. As for what 'Umar judged, perhaps Malik regarded it as an ijtihad (independent reasoning) of 'Umar, which he did not agree with, because the argument from His saying ﴿an offering brought to the Kaabah﴾ is clearer. This is from the indication of the implication (dalalat al-isharah). He saw in returning to food a matter of ease. Moreover, if the game has no counterpart among young livestock, such as a locust or a beetle, it would be necessary to return to food. So one should return to food when the game is smaller than what is equivalent to it among what is acceptable in offerings. It is strange that Ibn al-'Arabi said that al-Shafi'i's view is correct and is the choice of our scholars. I do not know whom he means by "our scholars," for I do not know of any Malikis who disagree with Malik on this. The same applies to birds as to young game, and to quadrupeds, and similarly for large animals such as the elephant and the giraffe, which return to food.

Since Allah called this a jaza' and made it equivalent to the game killed, He informed us that whoever repeatedly kills game while in ihram must pay compensation for each animal he killed, contrary to Dawud al-Zahiri. For two things of one kind are not equivalent to one thing of that kind, and because various kinds of things may be killed, so how could one thing of one kind be equivalent to all that he killed?

The majority of the readers recited ﴿fa-jaza'u mithli ma qatala﴾ with jaza' in construct to mithl. So jaza' is a verbal noun in place of the verb, and mithli ma qatala is the subject of the verbal noun, to which its verbal noun is attached. And ﴿min al-na'am﴾ is an explanation of the equivalent, not of what was killed. The intended meaning is: so the equivalent of what he killed from the livestock is due as compensation

[Page 47]

*ma qatalahu*, meaning he compensates for, or makes restitution for, what he killed. Attributing the recompense (*jaza'*) to the "like" (*mithl*) is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*). You may also take the *idafa* (construct) as explicative (*idafa bayaniyya*), so that the meaning is "a recompense which is the like of what he killed." An *idafa* may be used for even the slightest connection. A parallel is His saying ﴿Those will have a double recompense for what they did﴾ [Saba: 37]. This is an elegant construction on the pattern of His saying ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, then the freeing of a believing slave﴾ [al-Nisa: 92], meaning: then let him free a slave. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) considered it an *idafa* of a verbal noun (*masdar*) to its object, meaning: then let him be recompensed with the like of what he killed. This implies that the cattle (*ni'am*) is the thing compensated, not the compensation (*iwad*), because the compensation is governed by the verb *jaza* with the preposition *bi-*, while the thing compensated is governed directly. One says: "I compensated (*jazaytu*) what I destroyed with such-and-such a dirham," but one does not say, "I compensated such-and-such a dirham with what I destroyed." Therefore those who posited this reading were compelled to regard the word *mithl* (like) as superfluous (*muqhaman*). They compared it with the saying "Your like does not withhold," as Ibn 'Atiyya, a contemporary of al-Zamakhshari, said. Al-Zamakhshari remained silent and did not go into this matter. Al-Qutb affirmed the statement of *al-Kashshaf* on the necessity of regarding the word *mithl* as superfluous, and that the expression is figurative (*kinaya*), namely like His saying ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. Al-Taftazani likewise imposed this on him, and excused al-Zamakhshari's failure to state it explicitly by saying that al-Zamakhshari was concerned with explaining the recompense, not with explaining that the recompense for what he killed is due. This is a weak excuse. The correct view is that there is no need for this assumption at all. Al-Tabari dared to say that there is no justification for the *idafa* reading, which is an error on his part and a failure to recognise the varied forms of Arabic expression.

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, Yaʿqūb, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read ﴿fa-jazāʾun mithlu﴾ with *jazāʾun* nunated, and *mithlu* in the nominative. The meaning is: "So the recompense is a like," taking *jazāʾ* as a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (*ism al-maf'ul*), that is: "the thing to be recompensed with is a like of what the hunter killed."

His saying ﴿judged by two just men among you﴾ is a clause in the position of an adjective for *jazāʾ*, or an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnāf bayānī*), meaning: they judge the recompense, that is, determine it. The purpose is that not everyone can know the quality of equivalence between the game and the livestock, so God entrusted this matter to the two judges. The hunter must seek out someone in whom the qualities of justice (*ʿadāla*) and knowledge (*maʿrifa*) are established and refer the matter to them. Both are obliged to respond to what he asks of them, while they determine the like and give him the choice between giving the like, or food, or fasting. They also determine the quantity of food if he chooses it.

[Page 48]

Among the Companions, ʿUmar judged concerning the recompense for game together with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf; he judged together with Kaʿb ibn Mālik; Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ judged together with ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf; and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar judged together with Ibn Ṣafwān.

He described the two just men by His saying ﴿from among you﴾, that is, from among the Muslims, to warn against following what the people of the pre-Islamic age (*jahiliyya*) practised concerning hunting in the sanctuary (*ḥaram*), for they may claim a special knowledge of the recompense.

His saying ﴿as an offering (*hadyan*) reaching the Kaʿba﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from ﴿like what he killed﴾, or from the pronoun in *bihi*. The *hady* is that which is slaughtered or sacrificed at the place of sacrifice in Mecca. The place of sacrifice (*manḥar*) is Mina and al-Marwa. Since God called it *hady*, it has all the well-known rulings of the *hady*. The meaning of ﴿reaching the Kaʿba﴾ is that it is slaughtered or sacrificed within the sacred precinct (*ḥaram*) of the Kaʿba, and the intended meaning is not that it is slaughtered or sacrificed around the Kaʿba itself.

His saying ﴿or an expiation (*kaffāra*) of feeding the needy﴾ is coordinated with *jazāʾ* (recompense). He called the feeding an expiation because it is not a recompense, since the recompense is the compensation, and that involves equivalence. As for feeding, it does not match the game; it is rather an expiation by which the offence is covered. He stated the expiation in general terms and did not specify the quantity of food or the number of the needy. As for the quantity of food, it is left to the two judges. It is widespread among the Arabs that a *mudd* of food is the food of one man, and therefore Malik set it at one *mudd* for each needy person. This is the view of the majority of scholars. From Ibn ʿAbbās: the assessment of the feeding is that the recompense from the livestock is valued in dirhams, and then the dirhams are valued as food. As for the number of the needy, it is necessarily tied to the number of *mudds*. Malik said: "The best I have heard … in my view is that the game which was hit is valued, and one looks at how much food that price equals, and he feeds one *mudd* to each needy person." Among the scholars are those who fixed for each animal an equivalent quantity of food. From Ibn ʿAbbās: the gazelle is equated with feeding six needy persons, the deer (*ayyil*) with feeding twenty needy persons, and the wild ass with thirty. The best view is that this is left to the two judges.

The particle *aw* (or) in His saying ﴿or an expiation of feeding the needy﴾ and His saying ﴿or its equivalent (*ʿadl*) in fasting﴾ requires that the one who killed the game be given the choice among the three mentioned. Likewise, every command expressed with *aw* in the Qur'an is an obligation with choice (*wājib mukhayyar*). The view that there is choice is the view of the majority. Then it has been said: the choice belongs to the one who is judged against, not to the two judges; this is the view of the majority among those who hold the choice. It has been said: the choice belongs to the two judges. This was held by al-Thawri, and Ibn Abī Layla, and al-Ḥasan. Some scholars said that one does not move from the recompense to the food expiation except when unable to provide the recompense, and one does not move from the expiation to fasting except when unable to feed. So the ordering is sequential according to them. This is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar read ﴿expiation﴾ *kaffāratu* in the nominative without nunation, with a genitive following, *ṭaʿāmi masākīna*, just as they read ﴿recompense like what he killed﴾ [with the *idafa*]. Its reading may be either like the reading of the nominative and *idafa* in His saying ﴿fa-jazāʾu mithli mā qatala﴾, where *kaffāra* is taken as a verbal noun (*ism maṣdar*) replacing the verb and is added to its agent, meaning: the feeding of the needy expiates it; or it may be taken as an explicative *idafa*, meaning: an expiation consisting of food, as one says "a garment of silk" (*thawb khazz*). In that case *kaffāra* takes the meaning of what is expiated by, so that the explicative *idafa* is valid; the expiation is thus explained by food, meaning that there is no other expiation, for expiation takes place through various kinds. Al-Zamakhshari decided on this reading in *al-Kashshaf*, but it involves artificiality (*takalluf*). The rest read *kaffāratun* with nunation and *ṭaʿāmu* in the nominative, as a substitute (*badal*) for *kaffāratun*.

His saying ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ is coordinated with *kaffāra*, and the reference of *dhālika* (that) is to the food. *ʿAdl* with a fatha on the ʿayn is what equals a thing of a different kind. The original meaning of *ʿadl* is equality. Al-Rāghib said: it applies to what is perceived by insight, as here. As for *ʿidl* with a kasra on the ʿayn, it applies to sensible things such as weighed and measured goods. It has also been said that they are synonyms. The reference of *dhālika* is to ﴿food of the needy﴾. *Ṣiyāman* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*), because the word *ʿadl* contains the sense of estimation.

The verse left fasting in general terms just as it left food in general terms, and it is left to the judgement of the two judges. Malik and al-Shāfiʿī said: he fasts one day for each *mudd* of food. Abū Ḥanīfa said: one day for each two *mudds*. They differed concerning the maximum period of fasting. Malik and the majority said: it is not to be reduced below the number of *mudds* in days, even if it exceeds two months. Some scholars said: it does not exceed two months, because that is the highest of the expiations. From Ibn ʿAbbās: he fasts three days up to ten.

His saying ﴿so that he may taste (*li-yadhūqa*) the evil consequence of his deed﴾ is connected with *fa-jazāʾun* (so the recompense), and the *lām* is causal, meaning: that was made a recompense for his killing of the game, so that he may taste the evil consequence of his affair.

*Dhawq* (tasting) is used metaphorically for perceiving distress. The perception is likened to tasting a disagreeable flavour, as if they took into account the swiftness with which pain reaches perception. For this reason we do not regard it as a metonymy (*majāz mursal*) by the relation of generality, since there is no need to consider that relation, for distress is more evident than perception in general. This usage is considered important in their speech; therefore the use of *dhawq* for perceiving pains and pleasures became well known. In the Qur'an: ﴿Taste, for you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], ﴿They will not taste death therein﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56]. Abū Sufyān said on the day of Uḥud, addressing the corpse of Ḥamza: "Taste ʿUqqa!" The currency of this metaphor has nearly reached the level of a literal usage, so it was fine to build upon it another metaphor in His saying ﴿So God made them taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾ [al-Naḥl: 112].

*Wabāl* is evil and what is disliked when it is severe. *Wabīl* is strong in evil: ﴿So We seized him with a severe seizure﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16]. *Ṭaʿām wabīl* is food that is hard to digest, and *kalaʾ wabīl* and *mustawbil* is pasture which camels find unwholesome, that is, they find it harmful. Zuhayr said:

*"To pasture that is unwholesome and harmful."*

*Al-amr* means the affair and the act, that is, the affair of whoever killed the game intentionally. The meaning is: let him find the evil outcome of his act through what was imposed upon him of loss or of hardship.

God followed the threat with what He had accustomed the Muslims to of compassion, saying ﴿God has pardoned what is past﴾, that is, He has pardoned what you killed of game before this explanation. As for whoever returns to killing game while in the state of ihram, God will take vengeance upon him.

The vengeance is what was expressed earlier by *wabāl*, namely loss or hardship. It is thus understood that whenever he returns he is obliged to the recompense, the expiation or the fast. This is the view of the majority. From Ibn ʿAbbās, Shurayḥ, al-Nakhaʿī, Mujāhid and Jābir ibn Zayd: the one who kills intentionally is obliged to the recompense only once; if he returns, the punishment of vengeance in the Hereafter is due to him, and no recompense is accepted from him. This is an anomalous view.

The particle *fa* entered in His saying ﴿then God will take vengeance upon him﴾, although when the response to a conditional is a verb it is customary that the connecting *fa* not enter upon it, since it is sufficiently connected by the mere verbal link. The entry of *fa* is therefore against the usual pattern in their speech. It is most likely that they intend by it that the response clause is nominal in estimation, so they signal with the *fa* an omitted subject (*mubtada'*) of which the verb is the predicate, for the purpose of indicating exclusiveness or emphasis. The estimate is: "so it is God who takes vengeance upon him," for the purpose of exclusiveness, to stress the intensity of what he will suffer, as if he will not suffer anything else; or for the purpose of emphasis, that is, to stress the certainty of this vengeance. A parallel is His saying ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord fears neither diminution nor oppression﴾ [al-Jinn: 13], where the *fa* has dispensed with stating the subject, so emphasis is achieved together with brevity. This is the view of the verifiers (*muḥaqqiqūn*) with its justification. Among the grammarians some have said that the presence or absence of the *fa* in such cases is equal, and that it came against the usual pattern.

His saying ﴿and God is Mighty, Lord of retribution﴾ is a concluding phrase (*tadhyīl*). The Mighty is the One who has no need of a helper, and for this reason He is described as Lord of retribution, that is, because among His attributes is wisdom, and wisdom requires taking vengeance upon the corrupter, so that the outcomes of deeds accord with it.

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food, as a provision for you and for the travelers, but the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram. And fear God, to whom you will be gathered.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani) that arises from His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. That verse required the prohibition of killing game for the one in ihram and made the expiation for doing so an offering equivalent to what he killed of the livestock. The listener is therefore inclined to ask about the game of the sea, since catching it is not called "killing" in common usage, and there is no equivalent of it among livestock. Yet a doubt may arise: perhaps God intended "killing" in the sense of causing death, and by "the equivalent from livestock" He meant something close in size and quantity. So God made clear the ruling on the game of the sea and kept it permissible, because the game of the sea is not among the animals of the Sacred Precinct (haram), since no part of the land of the Haram contains a sea. We have already explained, at His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], that the basic wisdom behind the prohibition of game for the one in ihram is the preservation of the sanctity of the Ka'bah and its Haram.

[Page 52]

The meaning of ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾ is the continuation of its lawfulness, because it was lawful before the state of ihram. The address in "for you" is to those who have believed. Here "game" (al-sayd) is used in the sense of "what is hunted" (al-masid), so that the wording follows one consistent pattern in its occurrences in these verses. That is, "it is lawful for you to kill it," meaning to take it, from the sea.

The sea (al-bahr) includes rivers and valleys, because all of them are called "sea" in the Arabic language. God Most High has said: ﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet and palatable﴾ [Fatir: 12], and so on. The sweet water is nothing but the rivers, like the Tigris and the Euphrates. The game of the sea is every water-dwelling creature that is hunted in it, so that bringing it out from there is the cause of its death, whether soon or later. As for what lives both on land and in water, such as the frog and the turtle, it is not among the game of the sea, and there is no disagreement on this. As for the disagreement concerning what of the game of the sea may be eaten and what may not, among those who hold that some of it may not be eaten, this is not the place to mention it, because the verse does not establish the permissibility of eating the game of the sea. Rather, it draws attention to the fact that it is not forbidden during the state of ihram.

His saying "and its food" is conjoined to "the game of the sea." The pronoun refers to the sea, that is, "and the food of the sea." Its conjunction requires that it be different from the game. The meaning is: the gathering of its food, or the taking of its food. There has been disagreement about what is meant by its food. What has been transmitted from the leading Companions, may God be pleased with them, is that the food of the sea is what floats upon it of carrion, provided that the cause of its death was not the hunter's catching it. Among the scholars there are those who have reported, regarding the interpretation of "the food of the sea," views other than this, which do not fit the context of the verse. These are the ones who forbade eating what the sea casts up dead. What reported from the Messenger of God ﷺ refutes their view: he said concerning the sea, "Its water is pure and its carrion is lawful." There is also the hadith of Jabir concerning the fish called al-'Anbar, when they found it dead while they were on a military expedition; they ate from it, informed the Messenger of God, and the Messenger of God ﷺ also ate from it.

"As a provision" (matā'an) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). A provision (matā') is what one enjoys, and enjoyment (tamattu') is benefiting from what is pleasant and gladdening. The address in His saying ﴿as a provision for you﴾ is to those addressed in His saying ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾, considering that they are the ones who take the game, meaning: a provision for the hunters and for the travelers.

Al-sayyarah means the group traveling across the land for journey and trade. It is the feminine of sayyar, and the feminine form is used with regard to the group. God Most High has said: ﴿And a caravan came﴾ [Yusuf: 19]. The meaning is: it is lawful for you to hunt the game of the sea, which you enjoy by eating it, and which the travelers also enjoy; that is, you sell it to those who trade and bring it to the cities.

His saying ﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾ is an added emphasis on the prohibition of game, explicitly stating the implication of His saying ﴿do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. It also clarifies that the period of prohibition is the period during which they are in the state of ihram, that is, either in ihram or passing through the Sacred Precinct of Makkah. This also hints at reducing the duration of the prohibition, to ease the minds of the obligated by lightening it, and it hints at the favor of limiting its prohibition to that period. Had God willed, He would have forbidden it forever. In the Muwatta' it is related that 'Aishah said to 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr: "O son of my sister, it is only ten nights," meaning the duration of ihram; "so if something stirs in your soul, leave it," meaning eating the flesh of game.

He concluded this with His saying ﴿And fear God, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ In the use of the relative description and that clause, there is a reminder that the return is to God, so that people may increase whatever obedience they can for that encounter.

Al-hashr means gathering people in one place.

Here "game" (al-sayd) is intended in the sense of what is hunted (al-masid), as has already been stated.

The prohibition is connected to killing it, because of His saying before it: ﴿do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95]. Therefore His saying ﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in the state of ihram﴾ does not require the prohibition of eating land game for one in ihram if he buys it from a seller, or if a lawful man hands it to him, because it is known that the prohibition is connected to the act of the one in ihram killing it during the state of hunting. "The Messenger of God ﷺ ate from a wild donkey that Abu Qatadah had hunted," as in the hadith of the Muwatta' from Zayd ibn Aslam. "The Messenger of God ﷺ ordered the wild donkey that Zayd al-Buhzi had hunted to be divided among the companions while they were in ihram." This was the practice of the Companions, and it is the view. As for what is hunted for the sake of the one in ihram, it is established that "the Prophet ﷺ returned to al-Sa'b ibn Jaththamah a wild donkey that he had sent him as a gift, and said to him: 'We did not return it to you except that we are in the state of ihram.'" The jurists have differed about the implication of this abstention. It has been said: it is forbidden for one for whom the game was hunted to eat it, and no one else. This is the view of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, a group of the jurists of Madinah, and a narration from Malik, and it is the most apparent, because the apparent meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ words "We did not return it to you except that we are in the state of ihram" is that the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ alone, since he said "we did not return it," and he alone returned it. It has been said: it is forbidden for one in ihram to eat what was hunted for another person in ihram; this is the view of some people of Madinah and is the well-known view of Malik. It seems their basis for this is caution. It has been said: the one in ihram does not eat game that was hunted during the period of his ihram, but he may eat what was hunted before that. This is attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas. It has been said: it is permissible for the one in ihram to eat game absolutely, and God only forbade killing game; this is the view of Abu Hanifah. The conclusion is that abstaining from eating the game that was hunted for the sake of the one in ihram is established in the Sunnah by the hadith of al-Sa'b ibn Jaththamah, and it is open to interpretation, as you have known. The basis for abstention is prohibition, because if he had intended mere scrupulousness he would have said, "As for me, I do not eat it," as he said in the hadith of Khalid ibn al-Walid concerning the lizard.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 97 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah has made the Ka'ba, the Sacred House, a means of establishment (qiyaman) for the people, and the sacred month, and the offerings (al-hady) and the garlands (al-qala'id). That is so that you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), because it provides an answer to what may occur to the listener's mind when he asks about the wisdom behind the prohibition of hunting within the sanctuary (al-haram) and while in the state of ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage). The answer is that this is part of magnifying the status of the Ka'ba, for whose sake the land of the sanctuary was made sacred. It is also a reminder of Allah's blessing upon its inhabitants, through the security He established for them in its associated places and rites.

The verb ja'ala (made) is used in the sense of bringing into existence (al-ijad), in which case it takes one object, as in His saying ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ (6:1), in Surat al-An'am. It is also used in the sense of making something become (al-tasyir), in which case it takes two objects. Both meanings are suitable here, but the first is more apparent: Allah brought the Ka'ba into existence, that is, He commanded His friend (Khalil) Abraham to build it so that it would be a means of establishment for the people. Thus His saying qiyaman is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is a future-oriented circumstance (hal muqaddara): He brought it into existence intending that it would be a means of establishment. If ja'ala is understood in the sense of making something become, the meaning is that it already existed as a house of worship, and Allah made it a means of establishment for the people out of kindness toward its inhabitants and their descendants. In that case qiyaman is the second object of ja'ala. As for His saying al-Bayt al-Haram, it cannot be taken as an object.

Al-Ka'ba is a proper name for the house that Abraham, peace be upon him, built in Mecca by the command of Allah, the Exalted, to be a sign of monotheism (al-tawhid). This has been discussed earlier in the commentary on His saying ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah﴾ (3:96), in Surat Al 'Imran.

[p. 55]

Some have said that it is a proper noun derived from ka'b, which means a protrusion or elevation, and this is possible. It is also possible that they called every elevated structure a ka'ba, by analogy with the Sacred House, since it was the first house among them, and they were people of tents before it. Thus the house became an example by which every elevated thing is described.

As for the use of the name al-Ka'ba for the church (al-Qalis) built by the Abyssinians in San'a', which some Arabs called al-Ka'ba al-Yamaniyya (the Yemeni Ka'ba), and for the dome of Najran that the Christians of Najran erected for their worship, which al-A'sha referred to in his saying:

*So the Ka'ba of Najran is an obligation upon you, until you kneel your camel at its doors.*

This is by way of imitation and comparison, just as the Banu Hanifa named Musaylima "Rahman" (the Merciful).

His saying al-Bayt al-Haram is an explanatory apposition (bayan) for al-Ka'ba. Its purpose is to draw attention and to magnify, since the function of an explanatory element is to clarify what it explains, by being better known than it. Since the name al-Ka'ba is equivalent to al-Bayt al-Haram in referring to this house, the Qur'an used the latter to refer to the Ka'ba in His saying ﴿nor those heading to the Sacred House﴾ (5:2). Thus it is established that the mention of the apposition is for magnification, because an explanatory element comes for the same purposes for which a descriptive adjective (na't) comes: clarification, praise, and the like. The basis for this name's indicating magnification is that it contains an implicit sense of the description "sacred" (al-haram) before it became a name through common usage. The house is mentioned here because this described entity together with this description became a proper name, through common usage, for the Ka'ba.

Al-haram originally is a verbal noun from haruma, meaning "to be forbidden," and its verbal noun is al-haram, like al-salah from saluha. So describing something as haram is an intensification of its being forbidden.

The meaning of describing the house as haram is that it is protected from the hands of tyrants, so it is respected and greatly revered. This entails prohibiting injustices and indecencies from occurring within it. It has been previously noted, in the commentary on His saying ﴿not hunting game while you are in the state of ihram﴾ (5:1), in this surah, that one says "a man is muharram" (in the state of ihram), and in the commentary on His saying ﴿nor the sacred month﴾ (5:2) in it as well, that one says "a sacred month." So this description is understood according to what suits the entity it applies to. In every case it indicates that the thing is to be avoided. If avoiding it is for magnification or awe, then it is a description of praise. If avoiding it is for purity from it, then it is a description of blame, as when you say, "Wine is haram."

[p. 56]
