Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read qiyaman with an alif after the ya'. Ibn 'Amir read qiyamā (qiyaman with a shortened vowel) without an alif after the mim.

Al-qiyam originally is the verbal noun of qama, meaning to stand up straight on one's feet. It is used metaphorically for vigor, and from that usage it is used for managing and reforming, because one who undertakes an important task stands up to it. This was explained earlier in the commentary on His saying ﴿and establish prayer﴾ (2:3), in Surat al-Baqara. From this usage, the one who oversees the affairs of something and manages it is called qayyim 'alayhi or qa'im 'alayhi (one who is in charge of it). So qiyam here means righteousness and benefit. As for Ibn 'Amir's reading qiyama, it is the verbal noun of qama on the pattern fi'al with a kasra then a fatha, like shiba' (satiety). This was previously noted as one of two interpretations of His saying ﴿Do not give the foolish your property which Allah has made for you a means of sustenance (qiyaman)﴾ (4:5), in Surat al-Nisa'. Its waw was changed to ya' because of the strong affinity of ya' with kasra. This conversion is rare in verbal nouns of the pattern fi'al from hollow verbs with a waw middle radical.

Describing the Ka'ba with this verbal noun is an intensification, and it is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi), because when Allah made the Ka'ba a cause of legislated rulings that preceded it, and through it the righteousness of the people of Mecca and other Arabs was secured, and their interests were upheld, the Ka'ba was described as the thing that stands for them, because it is the cause of their standing.

The word al-nas (the people) here refers to a specific known group of people, so the definite article is for prior reference (al-'ahd). What is meant by them is the Arabs, because they are the ones who benefited from the Ka'ba and its rites, to the exclusion of other nations such as the Persians and the Romans. As for the benefits of trade and the like that these peoples obtained through commerce, these were a consequence of the presence of the inhabitants, not because the house is sacred, unless one intends a remote causation, namely that without the sanctity of the Ka'ba and the sanctity of the months for the pilgrimage, fear would have prevailed in those regions, and the nations would not have been able to trade there.

The Ka'ba was a means of establishment for the people because when Allah commanded Abraham to settle his wife and his son Isma'il in Mecca, and intended that the Arab origins (the Musta'riba, those Arabs who became Arabized through assimilation, who were the descendants of Isma'il) would be raised in that place, so that they would grow into a nation of noble opinions, proud spirits, and steadfast hearts, because He had decreed that this nation would be the first to receive the religion He willed to be the most excellent and firmest of religions, and that from it the true faith and virtuous morals would spread, He established for them a land remote from attachment to the adornments of life. They grew up with an aversion to oppression, and they received a righteous way of life, by which they were raised upon the oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and the call to Him. He established for them in it the Ka'ba as a landmark of the oneness of Allah, the Exalted, and placed in their souls and the souls of their neighbors the reverence for it and its sanctity. He called their neighbors to its pilgrimage as much as they were able, and He caused people to respond to that call. So the existence of the Ka'ba became beneficial to the inhabitants of its land, through the benefits of companionship with those who came to it, and the benefit of what they brought of provisions, and what the merchants brought during the times when people visited it. Thus its inhabitants were never afflicted by hunger or destitution, and Allah placed contentment in their souls, so their provision was sufficient. This is what Abraham prayed for in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in a valley without cultivation near Your Sacred House, our Lord, that they may establish prayer. So make hearts among the people incline toward them and provide for them from the fruits that they may be grateful﴾ (14:37). So the Ka'ba was a means of establishment for them, by which the sustenance of their livelihood was made straight. This is an establishment specific to its people.

Then the descendants of Isma'il spread out, and many tribes of the Qahtanite Arabs joined them, and the lands of the Arabs became populated. All of its people followed the religion of Abraham. So from their dispersal came what naturally produces, among a large nation, disagreement, mutual domination, and fighting that leads to annihilation. Then they found the sanctity of the three months of the pilgrimage and the sanctity of the month of 'umra (lesser pilgrimage), which is Rajab, which Mudar (most of the descendants of Isma'il) established, and most Arabs followed them. They found those four months compelling them to make peace during them, so peace prevailed among them for a third of the year. During those months they put their affairs in order, preserved their lives, and their leaders, elders, and men of judgment worked to make peace among them concerning the vengeances and grudges that had arisen. So this is part of the Ka'ba's establishment for them, because the sacred months are among the effects of the Ka'ba, since they are the time of the hajj and 'umra to the Ka'ba.

Abraham had made for the Ka'ba a spacious, vast area that surrounds it on all sides for many miles, which is the sanctuary (al-haram), so whoever entered it was safe. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched from around them?﴾ (29:67). So this was a continuous security for the people of Mecca and its sanctuary, and a security to which whoever was afflicted with fear from outside its people might flee by entering it as a refuge. To confirm its security, Allah made its wild animals and beasts safe, to strengthen its sanctity in hearts. Thus the Ka'ba was a means of establishment for every Arab whenever injustice struck him.

The people of Mecca and its sanctuary used to travel through the lands of the Arabs in safety, and no one would harm them. They engaged in trade and entered the lands of the Arab tribes, bringing them what they needed and taking from them what they did not need, in order to deliver it to those who needed it. Had it not been for them, no merchant from any tribe could have traveled through the lands, and trade and benefits would have ceased. For this reason the Quraysh were described among the Arabs as merchants, and for this reason they established the two journeys of winter and summer, about which Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿For the accustoming of Quraysh, their accustoming [to] the caravan of winter and summer﴾ (106:1-2). Through all of this the nation of the Arabs remained preserved in the natural disposition (al-jibilla) that Allah willed for them to be shaped upon. Thereafter they were prepared to receive the call of Muhammad (ﷺ) and carry it to the nations, as Allah, the Exalted, willed, and through this His purpose was fulfilled.

If you wish to extend this, say: The Ka'ba was a means of establishment for the people, namely the Arabs, since it was the cause of their guidance to monotheism and their following of the hanifiyya (the pure monotheistic faith of Abraham). It preserved for them a remnant of that hanifiyya throughout the entirety of their pre-Islamic period, so they never lost the benefits of its good. When Islam came, the hajj to it became among the most excellent acts, and through it sins are expiated. So from this perspective the Ka'ba was a means of establishment for the people in matters of their afterlife, to the degree that they hold fast to what the Ka'ba was made to uphold.

Joining the sacred month to the Ka'ba is similar to the conjunction of a specific item with a general category, given that the Ka'ba is intended to include what is associated with it and what follows from it, since the sacred months only acquired their sanctity from being the months of the hajj and 'umra to the Ka'ba, as you know. The definite article in al-shahr (the month) is generic, as was discussed earlier in His saying ﴿nor the sacred month﴾ (5:2). There is no reason to restrict it here to some of those months. The same applies to the joining of the offerings and the garlands.

That the offering is a means of establishment for the people is evident, because the Arab owners of livestock benefit from selling it to the pilgrims, and the poor Arabs benefit from its meat, which is given by the pilgrims. So it is a means of establishment for them.

The same applies to the garlands, since they benefit from them: they make from their braids a great material for spinning and weaving, so these are a means of establishment for their poor. The reason for singling them out for mention here, although they are among the least of the effects of the hajj, is to point out that all the associated elements of the Ka'ba are a means of establishment for the people, even the least of these associated elements, which is the garlands. How much more so for the rest of them, such as the coverings of the sacrificial camels, their sandals, and the covering of the Ka'ba? Also, the garlands are never absent from any offering among the offerings, unlike the coverings and the sandals. The same is found in the saying of Abu Bakr: "By Allah, if they withheld from me a rope (iqal) ..." etc. . . .

Ibn ʿAshur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 97 (part 2 of 2):

His saying ﴿That is so that you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ and so on, is connected to the preceding statement by means of the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil, the particle of causal purpose) in His saying "li-taʿlamū" (so that you may know). The placement of the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) between the two statements serves to strengthen the connection while also drawing attention to the exalted status of what is pointed to, namely the "making" (al-jaʿl) derived from His saying: ﴿Allah made the Kaʿba﴾. Thus the placement of the demonstrative here resembles the placement of the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and for this reason the sentence resembles a resumptive new sentence (al-mustaʾnaf) while not being one, because what the demonstrative refers to is the preceding statement, and the function of the lam of causation is to link to the preceding statement. So there is nothing new in this sentence beyond the causal explanation, and causation is a connection, not a resumption, since resumption is a separation. There is nothing in the preceding statement suitable for the lam of causation to attach to except His saying "made" (jaʿala). The demonstrative refers only to the "making" derived from His saying "made." The meaning is: Allah made the Kaʿba a means of establishment for the people so that you may know that Allah knows, etc., i.e., that among the wisdoms for which He made the Kaʿba a means of establishment for the people is that you may know that He knows. The making of the Kaʿba as a means of establishment is intended, first and foremost, for the welfare of the people, since it is that upon which it was made; then it is intended for the people's knowledge that He, exalted is He, is All-Knowing. There may also be other wisdoms in it, because the lam of causation does not indicate that the causal explanation of a declarative ruling is restricted to what follows it, since a single act may have multiple causes. These are causes of appointment (ʿilal jaʿliyya), not causes of bringing into existence (ʿilal ijadiyya). The mention of this particular cause, rather than others, is due to the great importance of it, because it is a path to knowing one of the attributes of Allah, and from knowing it come many benefits for those who know it, in obedience, in awe, in acknowledging the incapacity of anyone other than Him, and other things. Thus the attainment of this knowledge is one of the ends for which Allah made the Kaʿba a means of establishment.

The intended meaning is that He knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth before it occurs, because He made the causal explanation attached to the making of the Kaʿba and what follows it as a means of establishment for the people. Its function as a means of establishment for the people was realized after the time of its making by a period, and parts of it have occurred one after another across distant times, as is evident. As for His knowing that after it occurs, it needs no proof, because that is more evident, and because many created beings have known those conditions after they occurred.

Page 60

The manner in which the making of the Kaʿba as a means of establishment for the people, and what is joined to it, indicates that He, exalted is He, knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, is that He, exalted is He, commanded the building of the Kaʿba in the time of Ibrahim. On that day no one knew anything except that Ibrahim had taken it as a place of worship, and Makka at that time had few inhabitants. Then Allah commanded the pilgrimage to the Kaʿba, the sanctity of its sacred precinct, and the sanctity of those who go to it, and He appointed for the people months for travel to it and offerings they drive to it. In all of this there is great welfare and barriers against many harms that would have afflicted the Arabs had the Kaʿba not been brought into being, as we explained earlier. Thus the Kaʿba was the cause of their survival until Allah brought Islam. There is no doubt that the One who commanded its building knew that there would be a great nation there, and that this nation would praise the outcome of the building of the Kaʿba and what came with it of its effects. That was a preparation for what He knew of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) among them, and their being made the bearers of his law to the nations, and what followed from that of the great power of the Muslims and the building of the civilization of Islam. Then He knows what is on the earth, and He is not on the earth, by evidence of observation, or by His exaltedness above deficiency. So it is necessary that He is knowing of what is in the heavens, because the heavens are either equal to the earth in that He, exalted is He, does not dwell in them and they are not nearer to Him than the earth, as is the specific belief, so His knowledge of what is in the heavens is established by analogical equality; or He, exalted is He, is in the highest place and most noble realm, so His knowledge of what is in the heavens would be more fitting than His knowledge of what is in the earth, because the earth is nearer to Him and He is more concerned with it. Thus the argument is complete for both parties.

As for the indication of this regarding His being knowing of every thing, it is that from what has been established of this knowledge, which has been confirmed of His knowledge of what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, there are kinds of known things, both grand and subtle; knowledge of them before they occur is inevitable. If He did not know all things, He would not be free of ignorance of some of them, and that ignorance would prevent His knowledge of much that His management depends upon knowing that unknown. Yet He did not ordain the making of the Kaʿba as a means of establishment, and what arose from that, except through the generality of His knowledge of things; and had His comprehensiveness not been, the ordainment of that decree would not have been completed.

[Page 61]

This is an initial resumptive statement (*istinaf ibtida'i*) and a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) of what precedes it: the prohibition of hunting for one in the state of ihram, the permission to hunt sea game, and the reminder of the favours Allah bestowed on them through what He made for the Ka'bah. The purpose is to reassure them about the restrictions these rulings place on their conduct, so that they know these restrictions serve their own good. The verse then concludes with a reminder that Allah is watching over them, and that He will recompense every doer for what he has done, whether good or evil. The opening of the sentence with ﴿اعْلَمُوا﴾ (know) serves to emphasise its content, as already explained at the verse ﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّكُم مُّلَاقُوهُ﴾ ("Fear Allah and know that you will meet Him") [al-Baqarah: 223] in Surat al-Baqarah. The phrase ﴿أنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ وأنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ("that Allah is severe in punishment and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful") has covered all the categories of how Allah deals with people: He is severe in punishment towards those who oppose His rulings, and Forgiving towards those who repent and do righteous deeds. Opening the sentence with the word ﴿اعْلَمُوا﴾ serves to emphasise the report, as already explained at the verse ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّكُم مُّلَاقُوهُ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The sentence ﴿ما عَلى الرَّسُولِ إلّا البَلاغُ﴾ ("The Messenger's duty is only to convey") is a parenthetical clause (*mu'taridah*), with which an allusion to threat and promise is concluded. Its meaning is to absolve people of blame, since the Messenger has already conveyed to them what Allah wished from them, so they have no excuse for negligence. The favour belongs to Allah and His Messenger in what they have guided them to of good.

The restriction (*qasr*) here is not absolute, because the Messenger has duties other than conveying the message, such as worshipping Allah, going out to jihad, and the obligations Allah imposed on him, such as the night prayer. Therefore it is determined that the meaning of the restriction is: his duty is only to convey, that is, not to compel you to faith. The restriction is thus relative (*idafi*), and so it does not contradict the fact that the Messenger has many other duties.

The use of the preposition ﴿عَلى﴾ (upon) rather than ﴿اللَّام﴾ (to/for) or similar particles indicates that what is being rejected is something that might be presumed to be binding on the Messenger insofar as he claims to convey a message from Allah.

The words ﴿واللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ ما تُبْدُونَ وما تَكْتُمُونَ﴾ ("And Allah knows what you reveal and what you conceal") are conjoined to the clause ﴿اعْلَمُوا أنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ ("Know that Allah is severe in punishment"). This clause completes the allusion to threat and promise, reminding them that nothing of their deeds, outward or inward, is hidden from Him. The placement of the subject before the verbal predicate here serves to affirm the strength of the judgement, and not to restrict it, since the context does not call for restriction.

[Page 62]

The mention of ﴿ما تُبْدُونَ﴾ (what you reveal) is intended, together with ﴿ما تَكْتُمُونَ﴾ (what you conceal), to be general and comprehensive. Otherwise the purpose is to teach them that Allah knows what they keep secret. As for what they reveal, it might not be thought that Allah does not know it, so it is mentioned explicitly.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, commentary on Surah al-Ma'idah 5:100:

﴿Say: The corrupt and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of the corrupt impresses you. So fear God, O people of understanding, that you may prosper.﴾

When His words ﴿Know that God is severe in punishment, and that God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 98] and His words ﴿God knows what you disclose and what you conceal﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 99] made known that people are of two groups, obedient and disobedient, one group opposed the Messenger and did not comply. These were the remaining people of polytheism and the hypocrites who supported them. Perhaps they used to show the tribes that they were a large multitude, and that such a multitude could not be in error. So God removed the illusions that had settled in their souls, which became a trial or a misguided argument by which some of them deceived the guided Muslims.

The verse therefore indicates that there had appeared an abundance of corrupt things, and it was feared that they would seduce those who possessed only a small number of righteous things. It is possible that this abundance is an abundance of numbers among people, since it is well known in the customs of the Arabs, both in the pre-Islamic period and at the beginning of Islam, to take pride in abundance and to be impressed by it. Al-A'sha said:

*You are not among them the most in pebbles,*
*but honour belongs only to the one who outnumbers.*

Al-Samaw'al, or 'Abd al-Malik al-Harithi, said:

*They reproach us that our number is few,*
*and indeed the one who is few in number...*

Al-'Anbari marvelled when he blamed his people, and he said:

*But my people, though they are many in number,*
*are not, in any way, among the evil, even if they are humiliated.*

Al-Suddi said: The abundance of the corrupt are the polytheists, and the good are the believers. This meaning fits if the revelation of this verse was before the Farewell Pilgrimage, when the polytheists were more numerous than the Muslims. However, this entire surah was revealed in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, so it is possible that it is an indication of the abundance of the Arab Christians in Syria and Iraq and the borders of Syria, because the Muslims had by then set their sights on those regions. It was also said: what is meant is the unlawful and the lawful of wealth, and this was transmitted from al-Hasan.

The meaning of ﴿لا يَسْتَوِي﴾ (la yastawi, "are not equal") is the negation of equality, which is similarity, closeness and resemblance. What is intended by it is the affirmation of superiority between the two by way of *kinaya* (indirect expression, implication). The context is what determines which is superior and which is inferior: making one of them corrupt and the other good shows that the intended meaning is to prefer the good. This was already discussed at His words ﴿لَيْسُوا سَواءً﴾ (laysu sawa'an, "they are not equal") [Al 'Imran: 113] in Surah Al 'Imran.

Since it is known that the corrupt is not equal to the good, and that the gap between them is wide, the listener understands from this that the purpose is to draw his understanding towards distinguishing the corrupt from the good in every matter in which one of them is confused with the other. This opens the insight of the heedless, so that they do not fall into the pit of confusion, and so that they know that there is a corrupt thing that has wrapped itself in the garment of the good and so has been disguised before the observers. For this reason He said ﴿ولَوْ أعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَةُ الخَبِيثِ﴾ (even if the abundance of the corrupt impresses you). The corrupt thing meant in the verse is something that was clothed in abundance and so pleased the eyes of the observers because of its multitude. Thus He opened their eyes to reflect upon it, so that they would know its corruption and its abundance would not impress them.

So His words ﴿ولَوْ أعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَةُ الخَبِيثِ﴾ are part of what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say, i.e., "Say all of this to them." The kaf (ك) in ﴿أعْجَبَكَ﴾ is for address, and the one addressed by it is not specific, but rather everyone who is fit for address, like ﴿ولَوْ تَرى إذْ وُقِفُوا عَلى النّارِ﴾ (If you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire) [al-An'am: 27], meaning: even if the abundance of the corrupt impresses whoever is impressed. You have already known the aspect of being impressed by abundance from the beginning of this verse.

His words ﴿ولَوْ أعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَةُ الخَبِيثِ﴾ do not necessarily imply that every corrupt thing is abundant, nor that it must be more numerous than the good of its own kind, for the good dates, wheat and fruits are more numerous than their corrupt counterparts. Rather, what is meant is that the abundance of the corrupt should not impress you when it is abundant, so that it distracts you from reflecting on its corruption and drives you to follow it because of its abundance. That is, "But look at things by their qualities and meanings, not by their forms and structures." Alternatively, the abundance of the corrupt at that time was due to the large numbers of the misguided religious communities.

[Page 64]

The matter of being impressed (al-i'jab) will be discussed at His words ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ أمْوالُهم ولا أوْلادُهُمْ﴾ (So let not their wealth or their children impress you) [al-Tawbah: 55] in Surah Bara'ah.

In the *Tafsir* of Ibn 'Arafa, he said: I had debated with Ibn 'Abd al-Salam and I said to him: this indicates the preference of the majority in testimony, because they differ when two just witnesses testify to a matter and ten just witnesses testify to its opposite. The well-known view is that there is no difference between ten and two just witnesses, since both are complete. In the school of law there is another view that preference is given to the majority. So His words ﴿ولَوْ أعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَةُ الخَبِيثِ﴾ indicate that abundance has a consideration, in that it was dropped here only because of the corruption. Ibn 'Abd al-Salam did not agree with me on this in any way. Then I found that Ibn al-Munir mentioned it in exactly the same words. End of quotation.

The *waw* in His words ﴿ولَوْ أعْجَبَكَ﴾ is the *waw* of circumstance (waw al-hal), and *law* (لَوْ) is for concession (ittisaliyya, "even if"). The explanation of their meanings has already been given at His words ﴿فَلَنْ يُقْبَلَ مِن أحَدِهِمْ مِلْءُ الأرْضِ ذَهَبًا ولَوِ افْتَدى بِهِ﴾ (Not one of them would be accepted with earth full of gold, even if he offered it as ransom) [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surah Al 'Imran.

The consequence drawn by His words ﴿فاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ يا أُولِي الألْبابِ﴾ (So fear God, O people of understanding) from this indicates that God wants us to exercise thought in distinguishing the corrupt from the good, to investigate realities, and not to be deceived by dazzling and false appearances. The command to be God-fearing (taqwa) necessarily entails the command to examine the distinction of actions, until what is taqwa is known apart from what is not.

A parallel to this argument is the reasoning of the scholars for the obligation of *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning) from His words ﴿فاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ ما اسْتَطَعْتُمْ﴾ (So fear God as much as you are able) [al-Taghabun: 16], because among what falls under ability is *ijtihad* for one who is qualified for it and who has acquired its tools. For this reason He said here "O people of understanding," addressing people by a quality, to indicate that the creation of intellects in them enables them to distinguish the corrupt from the good, in order to follow the good and reject the corrupt. Among the most important matters in which obedience to this command appears is reflection upon the evidences of the truthfulness of the Messenger's claim, and that one should not need to seek signs and miracles, like those of whom God reported: ﴿وقالُوا لَنْ نُؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتّى تَفْجُرَ لَنا مِنَ الأرْضِ يَنْبُوعًا﴾ (They said: We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush for us from the earth) [al-Isra': 90], and that one should distinguish between the state of the Messenger and the state of sorcerers and soothsayers, even if their number is large.

His words ﴿لَعَلَّكم تُفْلِحُونَ﴾ (that you may prosper) bring near the attainment of success by them if they fear God in this way, which includes distinguishing the corrupt from the good, and not being deceived by the abundance of the corrupt and the scarcity of the good in this matter.

Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on Surah 5, verses 101–102 (part 1 of 2):

﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you. But if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be disclosed to you. Allah has pardoned them, and Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿A people before you asked about them and then became disbelievers because of them.﴾

This is a fresh resumption (istinaf ibtida'i) introducing the prohibition against returning to matters that some of the believers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about. These were not matters of religious law but personal affairs particular to them. They were forbidden to burden the Messenger with such questions, after he had first stated the nature of his mission in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey (the message)﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 99]. This is suitable as an introduction to the content of this verse and to the content of the preceding verse, which is His saying: ﴿Say: the evil and the good are not equal﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100]. Both verses are linked to the verse ﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 99], and neither of these two verses is linked to the other.

The reports differ in specifying the kind of these things about which they asked. The soundest of these is the hadith of Musa ibn Anas ibn Malik from his father, in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim), who said: "The people questioned the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until they pressed him with questions. He ascended the pulpit one day and said: 'Do not ask me about anything except that I will make it clear to you.' A man who used to be disputed about was called by other than his father's name, so he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Hudhafah.'" That is, he called him by the father whom he was known by.

The questioner was 'Abd Allah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi, as occurs in some narrations of the hadith. In a narration of Muslim from Abu Musa: "Then another man stood and said: 'Who is my father?' He said: 'Your father is Salim, the freedman of Shaybah.'" In some narrations of this report outside the Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah: "Another man stood and said: 'Where is my father?' In another narration: 'Where am I?' He said: 'In the Fire.'"

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: "There were some people, that is, of the hypocrites, who used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mockingly. A man whose camel had strayed would say: 'Where is my camel?' Another man would say: 'Who is my father?' And a traveller would say: 'What has befallen me on my journey?' So Allah revealed concerning them this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you.﴾"

The scholars said: Al-Bukhari alone related it. Its meaning is that it is an opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, and it does not fit the opening of the verse with the address "O you who have believed," unless what is meant is a warning to the believers against such matters out of heedlessness of the intentions of those who mock, as in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say "ra'ina"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104]. Or the intended "those who have believed" are those who displayed faith, since the tone of the address in this verse is free of any hint toward the intent of the mockers, unlike His saying: "Do not say ra'ina," for He followed it with: ﴿And for the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 104].

Al-Tirmidhi and al-Daraqutni related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "When the verse ﴿And due to Allah from the people is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97] was revealed, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, every year?' He remained silent, so they repeated. He said: 'No. Had I said yes, it would have become obligatory.' So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not ask about things which, if they were disclosed to you, would distress you.﴾" He said: "This is a hasan gharib hadith." Al-Tabari related something similar from Abu Umamah and from Ibn 'Abbas. The interpretation of these chains is that the verse was recited at the time this question occurred, while its revelation was before the event; so the narrators thought it was revealed at that time. The meaning according to this is that the community is in latitude when no ruling has been legislated for it, so people have latitude in ijtihad when an incident befalls them after the Messenger (ﷺ). When they ask and are answered by the Messenger (ﷺ), acting upon what they were answered with becomes binding upon them. Conditions and eras may differ, and they would then be in hardship if they sought to change it. So the meaning of ﴿if they were disclosed to you, would distress you﴾ on this view is that they would distress some of them, or distress them in some circumstances, when it is burdensome for them.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 103:**

﴿God did not ordain any bahira, sa'iba, wasila or ham. But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God, and most of them do not reason.﴾

[Page 71]

This is a fresh, independent resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*). It comes to distinguish between what the people of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) had innovated, as deviations from the *hanifiyya* (the pure monotheistic religion of Abraham), and what God had highlighted among their practices concerning the rites of the Hajj. When God stated that He made the Ka'ba a means of support (*qiyam*) for people, and made the offerings (*hady*) and the garlands (*qala'id*) a means of support for them, He then explained here that there are matters which God did not ordain, but which the people of misguidance instituted, so that He might distinguish the wicked from the good. This serves as an elaboration of the verse ﴿Say: The wicked and the good are not equal﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 100]. The *bahira* and what is conjoined with it here resemble the *hady* in that their benefits and their very beings are dedicated, while alive, to their idols, just as offerings are brought to the Ka'ba slaughtered (*muzakkat*). In the Jahiliyya they claimed that God had legislated this for them, and they mixed it with the offerings. For this reason God said: ﴿Say: Bring forward your witnesses who will testify that God has forbidden this﴾ [al-An'am: 150], and He said in this verse: ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God.﴾ Thus, addressing the distinction between the *hady* and the *bahira*, the *sa'iba* and similar things, is like addressing the demonstration that there is no distinction between the *tawaf* and the *sa'y* between al-Safa and al-Marwa, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the rites of God﴾ [al-Baqara: 158], as has preceded there. We have already cited what Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: that some people asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the *bahira*, the *sa'iba* and similar things, and then this verse was revealed.

What further strengthens what I have mentioned is that God opened this verse with His saying ﴿God did not ordain﴾, so that it would be a counterpart to His saying in the other verse ﴿God made the Ka'ba…﴾. Had it not been for the many verses that intervene between the two verses, this verse would have been conjoined to the first by a conjunctive particle. However, the disjunction here is more fitting, so that the sentence stands independently, which conveys greater emphasis on what it contains.

The *ja'l* (making, ordaining) here means command and legislation, because the original sense of *ja'ala*, when it takes a single object, is creation and bringing into being; then it is extended to decreeing and prescribing, as in their saying: "He imposed a *ju'ala* upon him." Here it is likewise, and it returns to the meaning of decreeing and commanding. This is unlike what occurs in His saying ﴿God made the Ka'ba, the Sacred House, a means of support for people﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 97]. The intent here is the negation of legislating these categories of realities, though they exist in actuality. Therefore, the negation of their being made is necessarily to be understood as the negation of command and legislation, and this is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for not being pleased with it and for anger against the one who instituted it, just as a man says to someone who has done something: "I did not command you to do this." The intent is not to permit it or to give the choice of doing or abandoning it, as may be inferred from the context. Similar to this is His saying ﴿Say: Bring forward your witnesses who will testify that God has forbidden this﴾ [al-An'am: 150], for it is a metonymy for anger against those who forbade it, and the intent is not that they may refrain from it.

[Page 72]

The superfluous *min* (من) is introduced after the negation to make explicit that the negation is a negation of the genus, not a negation of specific individual instances. It is equivalent to saying "There is no bahira and no sa'iba," while fulfilling the requirement of the context, which is to explain that this is not from God's making, and that He does not approve of it; therefore it is forbidden.

The *bahira*, with a fatha on the *ba'* and a kasra on the unpointed *ha'*, is of the pattern *fa'ila* in the sense of *maf'ula*, i.e., *mabhura* (cut open). *Al-bahr* means "the cutting"; it is said: *bahara* means "he cut." In the hadith about digging Zamzam: that 'Abd al-Muttalib *bahara*ed it *bahr*, i.e., cut it open and widened it. So the *bahira* is the she-camel. They would slit her ear lengthwise into two halves as a sign that she was set free; that is, she is not ridden, not slaughtered, not prevented from water or pasture, and not shorn; her milk belongs to their *taghut* (idols), and none drinks her milk except a guest. It is apparent that one would drink it if there was a feast for visiting the idol or for the entertainment of its servant (*sadin*). Every tribe of the Arabs would have their *bahair* for their idol, and the tribes had idols, each tribe worshipping one idol or more.

They would make her a *bahira* when she had borne ten offspring, according to the view of the majority of the lexicographers. It was said: when she had borne five offspring and the fifth was a male. If she died a natural death, the eating of her flesh was permitted for men and forbidden for women.

The *sa'iba* is a camel or she-camel dedicated as a vow for recovery from an illness or for return from a journey, when one says: "I dedicate it to God as a *sa'iba*." The *ta'* in it is for intensification of the attribute, like the *ta'* in *nassaba* (a great genealogist); therefore one says "a slave *sa'iba*." It is an active participle in the sense of being released and left unattended. It was also said that it is an active form in the sense of a passive, i.e., *musayyab* (let loose).

The ruling for the *sa'iba* is like that of the *bahira* regarding the prohibition of benefiting from it, so it is like manumission. They would hand it over to the *sadana* (servants of the idols) so that they might feed the wayfarers from its milk. Its mark was that a piece of the skin of the back vertebrae would be cut, and it was called *sarim*, its plural being *surum*. If the she-camel bore ten offspring, all of them females in succession, they would also set her free, and she was a *sa'iba*. What a *sa'iba* bears is a *bahira* according to some of them. It is apparent that its like is a *sa'iba* as well.

[Page 73]

The *wasila* among sheep is the ewe that bears female after female, so the mother is called *wasila* because she has connected one female to another female. Thus Malik explained it in the transmission of Ibn Wahb from him. According to this transmission, the *wasila* is that which is offered in devotion, and the application of the negation of making to it is evident. The majority said: the *wasila* is that the ewe bears five or seven offspring (according to the differing terminology of the tribes). If the last is a male, they would slaughter it for the houses of the *taghut*; if it was female, they would spare it, that is, for the *taghut*; and if the offspring were twins (male and female), they would spare both and say: "The female has connected with her brother, so she prevented him from being slaughtered." According to this interpretation, the *wasila* is a state among the reproductive states of sheep, and it is this which God annulled; they did not address the remaining conditions of the ewe. The more apparent view is that *wasila* is the name for the ewe that has connected seven female offspring, combining the explanation of Malik with the explanation of others. The ewe is set free for the *taghut*, and what they mentioned of slaughtering its male or female offspring is among the consequences of the entitlement to its being set free, so that the verse would encompass all its conditions. From Ibn Ishaq: the *wasila* is the ewe which, in five births, gives birth to ten females; whatever she bears after that is for the males among them only, not for the women, unless one of them dies, in which case men and women share in eating it.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: the *wasila* among camels is when the she-camel, at the beginning of the camels' birthing, bears a female, and then in the end of the year bears another female in succession; they would then dedicate her to their *taghut*. Sa'id said this from himself and did not narrate it from the Prophet (ﷺ). There occurs in the context of al-Bukhari an ambiguity by which some commentators were misled, and this was pointed out in *Fath al-Bari*. In all these aspects, the *wasila* is a *fa'ila* in the sense of *fa'ila* (active).

The *ham* is the stallion camel when ten offspring have been produced from his loins; he is then prevented from being ridden or carried upon, but is not prevented from pasture or water. They say: he has protected his back, that is, he became a cause of his own protection, so he is a *ham*. Ibn Wahb said from Malik: they would place upon him the feathers of peacocks and let him loose. The apparent meaning is that he is in the position of the *sa'iba*: he is not eaten until he dies, and his wool is used for the idols.

His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God﴾ is a *istidrak* (corrective exception) to remove what the polytheists imagined, namely the belief that these were from God's legislation, owing to the long continuity of practising them for centuries. By "those who disbelieve" here is meant all the polytheists, for they lie in attributing these things to the rites of God, since they all report what contradicts reality. Falsehood (*kadhib*) is a report that contradicts reality.

The disbelievers are of two groups: the elite and the common. As for the elite, they are those who originated these misguidances for various purposes and attributed them to God. The most renowned and the most mendacious of these is 'Amr ibn 'Amir ibn Luhayy, with a *damma* on the *lam* and a fatha on the unpointed *ha'* and a shaddah on the *ya'*, al-Khuza'i. In the Sahih, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw 'Amr ibn 'Amir ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i dragging his *qusb* (intestines) in the Fire." *Qusb*, with a *damma* on the *qaf* and quiescence of the unpointed *sad*, means his intestines. "And he was the first to let loose the *sawa'ib*." Among them also is Junada ibn 'Awf. From Malik, that among them was a man from the Banu Mudlij who was the first to cut open the *bahira*, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw him with 'Amr in the Fire." Ibn al-'Arabi narrated it. In another narration: "'Amr ibn Luhayy was the first to cut open the *bahira* and let loose the *sa'iba*." The most authentic and most renowned narrations from the Messenger of God are: "'Amr ibn Luhayy was the first to let loose the *sawa'ib*," and he did not mention the *bahira*.

As for the common people, they are those who followed these misguiding leaders without insight, and they are the ones intended by His saying: "and most of them do not reason." Since the majority is described as lacking understanding, it becomes certain that the minority are those who devised these misguidances and adorned them for the people.

*Al-iftira'* means falsehood (*kadhib*). It was already discussed at His saying ﴿Whoever fabricates lies against God after that﴾ [Al 'Imran: 94] in the surah of Al 'Imran.

[Page 75]

In calling what the disbelievers did of these things a fabrication and a lie, and in negating that God commanded it, there is an indication that those innovations do not bring one closer to God's good pleasure, for two reasons. The first is that they are attributed to the gods and idols, and that is association (*shirk*) and great disbelief. The second is that what is dedicated from them to God, such as the *sa'iba*, is a practice whose harm outweighs its benefit, because in letting an animal go free there is harm to it, since perhaps it finds no pasture or shelter, perhaps beasts of prey attack it, and in it there is the nullification of its usefulness until it dies a natural death. What is obtained from the milk of some of them for the guest and the wayfarer is only a meagre benefit set against the surrounding harms.

The conjunction *waw* here indicates a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The clause is a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) relating to the words ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("those who disbelieved"). That is, they attribute to God, falsely, what He did not command, and when they are called to follow what God has commanded in truth, or to reflect upon it, they turn away and cling to what their fathers followed. Their condition is strange: they accept their fathers' claim that God commanded them the misguided practices they invented, such as the *bahirah* and the *sa'ibah* and what resembles them, while they turn away from the call of the truthful Messenger, having no proof for the first, and turning away from considering the proof of the second, or obstinately denying it after knowing it.

The imperative in His words ﴿تَعالَوْا﴾ ("come") is used to request approach, the lending of attention, the turning of thought, and the attendance of the Messenger's assembly (ﷺ) and not turning away from him. Thus it is used in both its literal and its figurative sense. The discussion of the verb *ta'ala* has already been presented in the discussion of the parallel of this verse in Surat al-Nisa'.

﴿ما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ ("what God has sent down") refers to the Qur'an. The phrase ﴿وإلى الرَّسُولِ﴾ ("and to the Messenger") is conjoined to it because he guides them to understanding the Qur'an. The preposition *ila* ("to") is repeated because the two senses of approach differ with respect to the two complements of *ta'alaw*; the repetition of the particle is an indication that both the literal and figurative senses of *ta'alaw* are intended.

His words ﴿قالُوا حَسْبُنا﴾ mean "our sufficiency," i.e., "what is enough for us," if *hasbuna* is taken as a plain noun with ﴿ما وجَدْنا﴾ as its predicate; or "it suffices us" if *hasb* is taken as a verb-like noun (*ism fi'l*) with ﴿ما وجَدْنا﴾ as its subject. This has already been discussed at His words ﴿وقالُوا حَسْبُنا اللَّهُ ونِعْمَ الوَكِيلُ﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173] in Surat Al 'Imran.

The preposition *'ala* in His words ﴿ما وجَدْنا عَلَيْهِ آباءَنا﴾ is figurative, denoting firm attachment to a state, and it has been discussed under His words ﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلى هُدًى مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾.

His words ﴿أوَ لَوْ كانَ آباؤُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ etc. have been treated earlier in relation to their parallel in Surat al-Baqarah, at His words ﴿وإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ اتَّبِعُوا ما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ قالُوا بَلْ نَتَّبِعُ ما ألْفَيْنا عَلَيْهِ آباءَنا أوَلَوْ كانَ آباؤُهُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 170], the verse.

This verse has no connection with the question of *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning) and *taqlid* (imitation of the jurists) as some commentators have imagined, because this verse concerns a dispute between the people of what God has sent down and the people of fabrication against God. As for *ijtihad* and *taqlid* in the subsidiary matters of Islam, all of that falls under following what God has sent down. Therefore, making this verse address that question is forcing the verse into this meaning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 105:

﴿O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul. Those who have gone astray cannot harm you if you are guided. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding statement that closes a passage and draws out a general principle). It follows naturally from what precedes it. When Allah mentioned the obstinacy of the polytheists and their turning away from the call to goodness, He followed it with teaching the Muslims the limits of debate and argument once obstinacy has become evident. He also excused the Muslims for having fulfilled what Allah obligated on them of calling to goodness. So here He informed them that the attainment of the effect of the call to goodness is not their responsibility. Rather, the caller is obligated to exert his effort, and he bears no further responsibility if the one called does not listen to the call, as Allah says: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56].

*'Alaykum* (عَلَيْكُمُ) is an *ism fi'l* (a noun functioning as a verb) meaning "hold fast to" or "keep to." Its original form is that one says: *'alayka an taf'ala kadhā* ("upon you is that you do such-and-such"), which would be a sentence consisting of a predicate (*khabar*) placed first and a subject (*mubtada'*) placed after it, with *'alā* indicating figurative elevation. It was as if they made the doing of such-and-such an act elevated over the addressee and within his power, as an emphasis on the meaning of obligation. Then, when this became common in their speech, they said *'alayka kadhā*, composing the sentence from a prepositional phrase functioning as predicate and a noun denoting a thing as subject, with the implied meaning *'alayka fi'la kadhā* ("upon you is the doing of such-and-such"). This is because that entity is not described as elevated over the addressee, meaning as being within his capacity. So the sentence is by way of implication. This is like the relation of prohibition and permission to things in His saying: ﴿Prohibited to you is carrion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and His saying: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Among this is what is reported: *'alaykumu al-du'ā'*, "upon you is the supplication, and upon Me is the answering," and among it their saying: *'alayya alīyah* ("an oath is incumbent upon me") and *'alayya nadhr* ("a vow is incumbent upon me"). Then usage increased, and they treated *'alā* in the manner of an imperative verb, making it mean the command to the addressee to keep to something, and they put the noun after it in the accusative as the object. This became widespread in their speech, so the grammarians named it *ism fi'l*, because it was made like a noun for a particular command. It is as if you took the verb *(ilzam)* ("keep to!"), named it *(ʿalā)*, and brought out the pronoun accompanying it and attached it to *(ʿalā)* in the form of the pronoun that is customarily connected to it, which is the pronoun of the genitive. So one says *'alayka*, *'alaykumā*, and *'alaykum*. For this reason it is not attributed to pronouns of the third person, because the absent one is not addressed with the imperative form, but is commanded through the particle of command (*lām al-amr*).

So His saying ﴿upon you is your own soul﴾ is with *anfusakum* in the accusative, meaning "keep to your own souls," that is, "be keen upon your own souls." The context clarifies what is to be kept to, namely, persistence in guidance, by the indication of His saying ﴿if you are guided﴾, and this implies turning away from others, which He has made explicit by His saying ﴿those who have gone astray cannot harm you﴾.

So the clause ﴿those who have gone astray cannot harm you﴾ stands in the place of an explanation with respect to the preceding clause, and therefore it is disconnected from it (*fuṣila*). This is because the command to them to keep to their own souls is intended to remove the grief and regret that had befallen them over the refusal of those who went astray to accept guidance, and the fear that this might be due to a shortcoming in their call. So it was said to them: ﴿upon you is your own soul﴾, meaning, "occupy yourselves with perfecting your own guidance." Therefore the verb *(yaḍurrukum)* ("harms you") is in the nominative.

His saying ﴿if you are guided﴾ is an adverbial phrase of time containing the meaning of a condition, and it is linked to *(yaḍurrukum)*. Guidance encompasses everything Allah has commanded them. Among that is calling people to goodness, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong. So if they fall short in calling to goodness and in arguing for it, and remain silent about wrongdoing, then the one who has gone astray will harm them, because the sin of his error is borne upon them.

[p. 78]

Therefore one should not suppose that this verse is a dispensation for the Muslims to abandon calling to goodness, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong, because all of that is obligatory by evidences with which the Sharia is replete. So all of that falls within the condition of ﴿if you are guided﴾.

Because of what His saying ﴿upon you is your own soul﴾ implies of turning away from another group, namely the one specified by ﴿those who have gone astray﴾, and because of what His saying ﴿if you are guided﴾ contains of the obscurity of the ramifications of the types of guidance, some people in antiquity were confused about this verse. They doubted whether its meaning was a license to abandon enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. This doubt arose in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Tirmidhi reported from Abu Umayya al-Sha'bani that he said: "I asked Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani about it, and he said to me: 'You have asked about it one who knows. I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "Rather, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, until you see avarice obeyed, desire followed, the world preferred, and every person of opinion admiring his own opinion. Then, upon you is the care of your own self, and leave the common people."'" It also occurred in the time of Abu Bakr. The compilers of the Sunan reported that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq was informed that some people interpreted the verse as meaning the removal of the obligation to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. So he ascended the pulpit, praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, you recite this verse: ﴿O you who have believed, upon you is your own soul. Those who have gone astray cannot harm you if you are guided﴾, and you place it in other than its proper place. I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, when people see wrongdoing and do not change it, Allah is about to encompass them with His punishment. And indeed, when people see the wrongdoer and do not restrain his hands, Allah is about to encompass them with a punishment from Him.'" It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud that this verse was recited in his presence, and he said: "This is not its time. It is now accepted, that is, the advice. But a time is about to come when you command and it will not be accepted from you. Then, upon you is your own soul," meaning that fighting is not obligatory upon them so that their advice may be accepted.

Also from him: "When hearts differ, and you are clothed in factions, and some of you taste the violence of others, then it is each man and himself."

And from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar that he said: "Indeed it, that is this verse, is not for me nor for my companions, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Let the present one convey to the absent one.' So we were the present ones and you are the absent ones. But this verse is for people who will come after us. If they say it, it will not be accepted from them."

[p. 79]

The referent of this verse is the referent of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning changing what is wrong: "Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand. If he is not able, then with his tongue. If he is not able, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith." For the meaning of ability (*istiṭā'ah*) is being empowered to effect the change without harm befalling him or befalling the people in general, such as strife. So the verse indicates turning away from that when it is established that there is no benefit after beginning it. It also applies when obstinacy has become evident and there is no acceptance of advice, as the hadith of Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani indicates. Likewise, if harm is feared to befall the caller without any benefit, as indicated by the statement of Ibn Mas'ud mentioned just above.

His saying ﴿to Allah is your return, all of you﴾ is an excuse for the one who is guided and a warning to the one who has gone astray. He placed the prepositional phrase first for the sake of emphasis on the object of this return, and to instill awe in the hearts of the listeners. He emphasized the pronoun of the addressees with *jamī'an* ("all of you") to make explicit the generality, and that the speech is not by way of predominance (*taghlīb*, the grammatical convention of using a masculine plural form to include both sexes). And what is meant by "He will inform you of what you used to do" is a metonymy for showing the effect of that, namely the reward for the one who is guided and calls to goodness, and the punishment for the one who has gone astray and turns away from the call.

The word *al-marji'* (المَرْجِعُ, "return") is undoubtedly a *maṣdar mīmī* (a noun of place or action formed with the prefixed *mīm*). This is evidenced by its being governed by *ilā* ("to"). It is one of the mimi verbal nouns with a kasra on the 'ayn, which is rare, because the well-known mimi form from (*yafʿilu*) with a kasra on the 'ayn is that it has a fatha on the 'ayn.

[Page 80]

These verses begin a new section, an independent beginning, to legislate the rules for securing bequests, because this is one of the legislative provisions that this surah includes, to confirm the completion of the religion and to cover what Muslims may need to act upon. Its place here is something we will mention.

Bequest (al-wasiyyah) had already been prescribed by the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. The discussion of the beginning of its legislation, and of what of that verse's ruling was abrogated (naskh) and what was confirmed, has preceded in its proper place there. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was keen on bequest and commanded it, so it became well known and practised from an early time in Islam. It was also known in the pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyyah), as has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. A man would make his bequest to the person he wished to name in the presence of his heirs and relatives, so no dispute would arise among them after his death, together with the sanctity of the bequest in people's souls and their eagerness to carry it out, in preservation of the right of the deceased, since he has no means of securing his right himself. For this reason the Qur'an dispensed with legislating for securing bequests by witnessing, unlike what had preceded regarding securing transactions by the verse ﴿And call two witnesses when you trade⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and securing debt by the verse ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and so on. Thus this verse completed the explanation of securing bequests, out of concern for them and because bequests deserve to be secured, since the defence of them is weak. This is because in trades and debts there are two parties who know the form of what was contracted, and each defends its interests, so the truth becomes clear through their striving to establish right in them. Bequest, by contrast, has only one party, the party of the beneficiary, because the testator has died, and the beneficiary is weak, having no knowledge of what the testator contracted or what he left. So bequests were exposed to loss, wholly or in part.

The Arabs in the pre-Islamic period used to entrust their bequests at death to someone they trusted from among their companions, or the elders of their tribe, or someone who was present at the testator's dying, or someone who had been told by the testator of his intention. Nizar ibn Ma'd made a concise bequest and referred his sons to al-Ufa al-Jurhumi to explain to them the detailed meaning of what he intended by it.

At the end of the life of the Messenger, upon him be peace and blessings, an event occurred that was the cause of the revelation of this verse. Perhaps its occurrence coincided with the revelation of the verses that precede it, so this verse came after them in this place of the surah.

That is: in the ninth year after the Hijrah a case arose, namely that two men, one of them Tamim al-Dari al-Lakhmi and the other 'Adi ibn Badda', were Christian Arabs and merchants, and they were from the people of Dara'in, and they used to trade between Syria, Makkah and Madinah. A man named Budayl ibn Abi Maryam, a client (mawla) of Banu Sahm, who was a Muslim, went out with them from Madinah on a trade journey to Syria. Budayl fell ill, it was said in Syria and it was said on the road, by land or by sea. With him among his goods was a cup of silver inlaid with gold, which he intended for the king of Syria. When his illness grew severe, he took a document and wrote in it what he had of goods and wealth, and placed it among the folds of his baggage, and handed what he had to Tamim and 'Adi, and charged them to deliver it to his clients from Banu Sahm. Budayl was a client of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, so his walā' after his death belonged to his son 'Amr ibn al-'As. Some of the commentators say that Budayl's walā' belonged to 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Wada'ah. What supports their view is that al-Muttalib swore together with 'Amr ibn al-'As that the cup belonged to Budayl ibn Abi Maryam. When the two returned, they sold the cup in Makkah for a thousand dirhams, and returned to Madinah, and they delivered what belonged to Budayl to his clients. When they unfolded it, they found the document, and they said to Tamim and 'Adi: "Where is the cup?" They denied that he had given them a cup. Then the cup was found after some time being sold in Makkah, and 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah stood against the one who had it, and he said: "He bought it from Tamim and 'Adi." In another report, when Tamim became Muslim in the ninth year, he felt guilty for what he had done, so he informed 'Amr ibn al-'As of the matter of the cup, and gave him the five hundred dirhams that had come to him from its price. 'Amr then demanded the remainder of the price from 'Adi, who denied that he had sold it. This is the best of what has been related about the cause of the revelation of this verse. al-Bukhari related it as a suspended report (ta'liq) in the Book of Bequests. al-Tirmidhi related it in the Book of Tafsir, and said: "Its chain is not sound." Although it does not fully meet the conditions of soundness, it became widely known and was received with acceptance, and al-Bukhari transmitted it with a chain in his History.

[Page 82]

The reports agree that the two parties brought their dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed concerning it. So 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah swore that Tamim and 'Adi had concealed the cup, and that Budayl, its owner, had neither sold it nor let it leave his hand. 'Adi handed them five hundred dirhams, and he was at that time a Christian. It is said that this 'Adi later became Muslim, and Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mandah counted him among the Companions. It is also said that he died a Christian, and Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred this view; it is the opinion of Abu Nu'aym, and it is related from Muqatil. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr did not mention him among the Companions. It is possible that the revelation came before the litigants' appeal in the case of the cup, and it is possible that it came after the Prophet's (ﷺ) judgment in that case, so that it would be legislation for similar cases that might occur.

And (baynakum): the original of (bayn) is a noun of indefinite place situated between two things, specified by what follows it in construction. Here it is used figuratively for a matter connected with several things. It is in the genitive, as it is the object of the construct phrase (idafah) of (shahadah) to it, by extension (ittisa'). Its original form was (shahadatun), with tanwin and nominative case, and (baynakum) in the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf). Then (bayn) moved out of the adverbial function into full nominal function, just as it moved out of it in the words of Allah, ﴿Certainly the connection between you has been severed⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-An'am: 94], in the reading of a group of the ten readers, who read (baynakum) in the nominative.

(Shahadatu) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (ithnan), "two." ﴿When death approaches one of you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ is a temporal adverbial clause referring to the future. (Idha) here does not carry the meaning of a conditional, and the adverbial is connected to (shahadatu) because it contains the sense of a verb, meaning: "let two witness when death approaches one of you," that is, it is obligatory upon him to have it witnessed, and it is obligatory upon them to bear witness, in accordance with the words of Allah, ﴿and let the witnesses not refuse when they are called⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. ﴿At the time of the bequest⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when death approaches one of you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, an exact substitute (badal mutabiq), since the time when death approaches is generally the time when people make their bequests. This second temporal expression is brought so that through this substitution one may reach the intended matter, which is the bequest. The Arabs, when they saw the sign of death on a sick person, would say: "Make your bequest (awsi)." They said this to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when the physician informed him that his wound was in his bowels.

The meaning of the approach of death is the appearance of its signs, because in that state a person imagines that death has come to him to make him a dead person. The intended meaning is not the occurrence of the death-rattle (ghargharah), because what is required of the testator to do takes a long time. This has been discussed earlier at the words of Allah, ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words (ithnan) are the predicate of (shahadatu), that is: the witnessing concerning the bequest is the witnessing of two. So the genitive-governing noun was omitted (hadhf al-mudaf), and the genitive that was dependent on it took its place and received its case ending. The indication is clear, and the purpose is brevity. So the referent of (ithnan) is two witnesses, by the indication of His words, ﴿witnessing among you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ and His words, (﴿just men⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾). These two witnesses are the executors (wasiyyan) of the deceased in the description of his bequest and in conveying it, unless the testator appoints someone other than them as executor, in which case they will be witnesses to that.

Al-'adl and al-'adalah are synonymous, that is, persons characterised by justice.

The meaning of (minkum) is "from among the believers," as is required by the address ﴿O you who have believed⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, because when a speaker addresses his listener with a description and then follows it with something indicating part of that description, its meaning is that he is part of those who bear that description, as the Ansar said on the day of Saqifah: "There is an amir from us and an amir from you." So the discussion concerns the bequest of believers. On this view the majority of the commentators proceeded; it is the opinion of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, and the four Imams. It is the view upon which one must rely, and it is the apparent meaning of the description with the word (minkum) in its occurrences in the Qur'an.

Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah said: the meaning of His words (minkum) is "from among your kin and relatives." The consequence of the first interpretation is that the meaning of its opposite, (min ghayrikum), "from other than you," is that they are from outside your religious community. Some of those who held the first interpretation acted upon this and permitted the testimony of a non-Muslim during travel concerning bequests specifically, and they restricted that to a dhimmi. This is the view of Ahmad, al-Thawri, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and it is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Musa. Another group held that this was abrogated (mansukh) by the words of Allah, ﴿and call to witness two just men from among you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i, and it is attributed to Zayd ibn Aslam. The complete statement concerning the full form of the testimony of bequest has been concluded with His words, ﴿two just men from among you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

[Page 84]

His words, ﴿or two others from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ and so on, are a detailing of the situation that arises during travel.

(Aw) here is for division, not for choice, and the division is by consideration of the difference between the two states: the state of one who is present and the state of one who is travelling. For this reason it is joined with the phrase ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, so this is a restriction on His words, ﴿or two others from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

The condition in ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ has an omitted answer (jawab al-shart), indicated by His words, ﴿or two others from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾. The estimated sense is: "if you are travelling in the land, then the testimony is of two others from other than you." So the resort to the testimony of two non-Muslim witnesses, according to the one who holds this view, is restricted by the condition ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

Striking in the land (al-darb fi al-ard) means journeying in it, and what is meant by it is travel (safar). It has preceded at the words of Allah, ﴿And they said to their brothers when they struck out in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The meaning of ﴿then the disaster of death strikes you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ is that it befalls you. The verb is used with the meaning of nearing and approaching, as in the words of Allah, ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them offspring⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Nisa': 9], that is, if they were about to leave offspring behind. This is a usage of verbs, and from it is the saying in the iqamah: "The prayer has been established" (qad qamati al-salah).

He joined (﴿then the disaster struck you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾) to ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, so it was part of the content of His words before it, ﴿when death approaches one of you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾. It was repeated here to link the speech after it had been separated from that by adverbials and conditions.

The plural pronoun in (asabatkum) is like the plural pronoun in ﴿you strike in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

Al-musibah is the event that befalls a person of evil and harm, and it has preceded at the words of Allah, ﴿So if a disaster befalls you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Nisa': 72], in Surat al-Nisa'.

The clause (tahbisunahuma) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to (ākharani), according to the one who made His words ﴿from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾

[Page 85]

[p. 86] in the sense of "from outside your religious community." As for the one who takes it to mean "from outside your tribe," then [ākharān] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to [ithnān] and [ākharān], since the two are joined by [aw] (or). They are then one of two categories, and the oath is required when there is suspicion. An oath on this interpretation is remote, since there is no cause for suspicion regarding two upright Muslim witnesses.

The plural pronoun in [tahbisūnahumā] is like the pronouns in [ḍarabtum] and [aṣābatkum]. All of them are used in the distributive (badalī) plural rather than the comprehensive (shumūlī) plural, because every one of the addressees is capable of being subject to this ruling, though it befalls only some of them. Thus the plural pronouns addressing the audience all stand in the place of what the context requires. The plural form was used to convey generality, to prevent the assumption that this legislation applies only to two specific persons, since the occasion of revelation concerned two persons. Alternatively, the address and the plural are directed to the Muslims and their rulers.

[al-ḥabs] means holding back, i.e., preventing someone from departing. It may be by compulsion, as in imprisoning a criminal in a house or shackling him in chains. It may also mean waiting, as in the ḥadīth of ʿItbān ibn Mālik: "The Messenger of God and Abū Bakr came to me in the morning..." until he said, "and we detained him for a khazīr (a dish) that we had prepared," i.e., we kept him. This is the meaning intended in the verse: you hold them back and do not let them leave you until they have borne the bequest. It does not mean imprisonment or anything close to it, because God the Exalted said: ﴿neither the scribe nor the witness be harmed﴾ [al-Baqara: 282].

His words ﴿after the prayer﴾ specify the time for bringing them and holding them for the giving of this testimony. The use of [min] (from), which denotes a starting point, indicates the proximity of the time after, i.e., close to the end of the prayer. The verse may also mean a prayer of the Muslims' prayers, and some scholars interpreted it this way, saying: it is the ʿAṣr prayer. It is related that "the Prophet ﷺ had Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Badde swear an oath after the ʿAṣr prayer in the case of the cup," and this is the view of Qatāda, Saʿīd, Shurayḥ and al-Shaʿbī. Others said it is the Ẓuhr prayer, and this is reported from al-Ḥasan. It may also mean "after the prayer of their religion," on the interpretation of "from other than you" as "from outside the people of your religion." It is reported from al-Suddī and Ibn ʿAbbās, i.e., you bring them immediately after they have performed their prayer, because that is close to their turning to the fear of God and standing before Him in worship.

His words ﴿they both swear by God﴾ are conjoined to [tahbisūnahumā] (you hold them), so it is understood that their detention after the prayer is for the purpose of their swearing by God. The pronoun in [yuqsimān] refers back to [ākharān] (two others). Thus the oath is sworn by the two bequest witnesses, who are not Muslims, in order to increase confidence in their testimony, since the uprightness of a non-Muslim is not relied upon.

His words ﴿if you doubt﴾: the statements of the exegetes concur that this conditional is connected to [tahbisūnahumā] and what is conjoined to it. The answer to the condition is omitted, being indicated by what precedes it, for the sake of concision (ījāz). Had it not been placed first, it would have said: "or two others from outside your group, if you doubt them, you hold them back," and so on. This interpretation implies that if no doubt arises about their truthfulness, it would not be required to bring them after the prayer and to have them swear, so this is left to the discretion of the guardian (walī). The conditional clause is parenthetical between the verb of swearing and its answer.

In my view, the more correct position is that his words ﴿if you doubt﴾ are part of the speech that the two witnesses themselves utter, meaning: the two witnesses say, "If you doubt our testimony, then we swear by God that we will not exchange it for any price, even if it concerns a near kinsman, and we will not conceal the testimony," i.e., they say this to reassure the soul of the testator, because uprightness is a presumption of truthfulness, while there remains the possibility of something contrary to it that is not known. The presumption of truthfulness is thus reinforced by the oath. This speech is therefore prescribed for every witness, so that all circumstances are equal, and so that the imposition of the oath in some circumstances does not become a burden on the two witnesses upon whom the oath is imposed, since the oath implies an insinuation of doubt about their truthfulness. The imposition of the oath by the Lawgiver thus removes the embarrassment between them and the guardian, since the oath being a condition from God provides an excuse for demanding it, as the majority of our jurists said regarding the judicial oath imposed upon one who establishes a right against a dead or absent person, that it is obligatory before the ruling in every case, even if the rightful heir waives it. I have not found any exegete who pursued this meaning except al-Kawāshī's statement in his *Talkhīṣ al-Tafsīr*: "Some stop at [yuqsimān] and begin with [billāh] as an oath, but I do not like this." And apart from that, what al-Ṣaffāqusī related in his *Iʿrāb* from al-Jurjānī: that there is an omitted statement here, its estimate being: "they both swear by God and say." Al-Ṣaffāqusī did not discern what led al-Jurjānī to posit this statement. I do not think he was moved to it except by making his words ﴿if you doubt﴾ part of the speech of the two witnesses.

The answer to the condition is omitted and indicated by the answer to the oath, since the oath has priority for the answer because it precedes the condition.

His words ﴿we will not exchange it for any price﴾ etc. are the content of the oath. The meaning of "we will not exchange it for any price" is: we will not take in exchange for the matter we have sworn to any price, i.e., any compensation. The pronoun in [bihi] refers to the oath understood from [yuqsimān]. The indefinite [thaman] in a negative context conveys the generality of every price. The word "price" means compensation: we will not substitute what we have sworn to with any compensation, whatever that compensation may be. The pronoun [bihi] may also refer to the matter sworn to, which is what they were entrusted with, namely the wording of the testator's bequest in all its contents.

His words ﴿even if it concerns a near kinsman﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of [thaman], which is in the sense of compensation, meaning: even if the compensation were a near kinsman, i.e., a near relative of ours. [Law] (even if) is a conditional particle that conveys emphasis. If a near kinsman would not be accepted by them as compensation for altering their testimony, then what is less than that is even less acceptable. This is because the greatest thing that drives a person to partiality in the custom of the tribes is zeal and support for a relative, so bribes and personal benefits appear small in comparison. The concealed pronoun in [kāna] refers to [thaman].

The meaning of the compensation being "of near kinship" is that it is the pleasing or benefiting of the near kinsman. The statement therefore contains an elided noun, which is part of what is called *dalālat al-iqtiḍāʾ* (implication required by the sense), because it makes no sense to make the compensation itself the near kinsman. It is therefore determined that what is meant is something of his relations that the context specifies. A parallel is ﴿forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 23].
