The manner in which this conditional with [law] conveys meaning, and why it is called *waṣliyya* (connective), was discussed earlier at His words ﴿even if he were to offer it as ransom﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 91] in the chapter of Āl ʿImrān.

His words [wa-lā naktum] (nor do we conceal) are conjoined to [lā nashtarī] (we will not exchange), because the intent of making them swear is that they render the testimony as they received it, so that they change nothing of it and conceal none of it at all.

The attribution of the testimony to the name of God (the Majesty) magnifies its importance in the eyes of the witness and others, because when God commanded its rendering as it is and urged it, He attributed it to His name to protect it from alteration. Thus the explicit mention of His name serves to remind the witness of Him at the moment of the oath.

In His words ﴿nor do we conceal﴾ there is evidence that the word "testimony" here has its customary meaning, which is reporting a specific matter that arises in such disputes. It does not mean the oath, as some exegetes supposed; we will not dwell at length refuting this, since the wording itself refutes it.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinners﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) of explanatory type (bayānī), because it is an answer to an implied question, as shown by the presence of [idhan], which is a particle of response. The two witnesses sensed a question from the one to whom they swore, when they said: "we will not exchange it for any price, nor conceal the testimony of God." He might have said to himself: "Perhaps you will not fulfill what you have sworn," so they replied: "Indeed, then we would be among the sinners," i.e., we know that the consequence of failing to fulfill what we have sworn is that we would be among the sinners, and we do not accept that.

[al-ātham] is the one who commits sin. It is known that sin is violating the oath by the occurrence of the sentence as a resumption together with [idhan], which indicates an answer to a statement stirring in the soul of the deceased's heirs.

His words ﴿But if it is discovered that the two had incurred sin, then two others...﴾, i.e., if it becomes clear that they concealed or altered and broke their oath, their testimony is invalidated, because His words ﴿two others shall take their place﴾ are a consequence of the invalidation of their testimony. Thus what expresses the invalidation of their testimony is omitted for concision, as in His words ﴿Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ [al-Baqara: 60], i.e., he struck, and it gushed forth.

[ʿuthira] means it became evident and clear. The original sense of [ʿathara] is that a walker's foot strikes a protruding object on the ground that he did not anticipate or guard against, so that the movement of his walking is disturbed, so that he may fall or be shaken. Its verbal noun is [ʿithār] and [ʿuthūr]. It was then used figuratively for finding something one had not expected to find. This became so widespread that it became almost literal, so in usage they restricted the literal meaning to one of the two verbal nouns, [ʿithār], and restricted the figurative meaning to the other verbal noun, [ʿuthūr].

The meaning of [istaḥaqqā ithman] (they had incurred sin) is that it was established that they committed what makes them sinners, so sin became incumbent upon them, i.e., fell upon them; the [sīn] and [tā'] here are for emphasis. The sin meant is that from which they disowned themselves in His words ﴿we will not exchange it for any price, even if it concerns a near kinsman, nor conceal the testimony of God.﴾ So the sin is one of these two: that it becomes evident they took compensation for themselves or others in exchange for what they were entrusted with, or that it becomes evident they concealed the testimony, i.e., part of it. The essence of the sin is that what discredits their truthfulness becomes clear by proof of establishment.

His words [fa-ākharān] means two other men, because the description [ākhar] applies to what differs either in essence or in attribute while being similar in the genus under discussion, and what is discussed here is two persons. The meaning is therefore: two others who take their place in establishing the bequest. [Yaqūmān maqāmahumā] means they make up for that testimony. The word [maqām] originally denotes the place of standing; then it is used for a place of any activity even if no standing occurs there; then it is used for the activity which by its nature occurs in a place where the agent stands, and this applies to important activity. God the Exalted said: ﴿If my standing [among you] and my reminding you is burdensome to you﴾ [Yūnus: 71]. Thus the standing (maqām) of the two witnesses is establishing the bequest. The [min] in His words ﴿from among those against whom [the claim] was established﴾ is partitive, meaning: two others who are from the group of those against whom it was established.

[al-istiḥqāq] means that a thing is deserving of another thing. It takes its object directly, as in His words ﴿they had incurred sin﴾, and the object is the thing deserved. When the deservingness arises from a dispute, the verb takes as its object the one who has the right by [ʿalā], which indicates elevation, in the sense of obligation upon him even if he dislikes it; it is as if they implied in it the sense of [wajaba] (was obligatory), as in God the Exalted's words ﴿It is incumbent upon me not to say about God except the truth﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 105]. One says: Zayd deserved from ʿAmr such-and-such, i.e., a right became due to Zayd from ʿAmr, so he took it from him.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿was established against them﴾ in the passive voice. The omitted subject in His words ﴿was established against them﴾ is an unspecified claimant, who is the one who benefited from the false testimony and oath, so that he obtained from the testator's estate what the testator had not left him, and overpowered the testator's heir in this. Thus those against whom it was established are the testator's heirs, who were entitled to his property by some mode of inheritance, but were deprived of part of it.

His words [ʿalayhim] (against them) stand in the place of the deputy of the subject of [istuḥiqqa].

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 3 of 4):

His saying: (﴿al-awlayan﴾) is the dual of awlā, meaning the most deserving and most entitled, i.e., "the two most deserving" of having their word accepted. Its referent (mā ṣadaquhu) is the same as that of (ākharān), and it refers back to it. Thus it is permissible for it to be made a predicate of ākharān: since ākharān was qualified by the clause ﴿who will stand in their place﴾, it became valid to begin with it, meaning: "two other persons, they are the most deserving of having their word accepted, rather than the two accused witnesses."

It was defined with the article (al-) because it is known to the addressee in mind: when the listener hears His saying ﴿if it is discovered that the two of them have incurred sin﴾, he anticipates learning who is most deserving of having their word accepted in this matter, so he is told: "two others who are the most deserving of it." It is also permissible for (al-awlayan) to be the subject (mubtada') and ﴿two others who will stand﴾ its predicate (khabar). The predicate is placed first to hasten the benefit, because the listener awaits the ruling after His saying ﴿if it is discovered that the two of them have incurred sin﴾; that discovery of the lie of the two witnesses voids their testimony and their oath, so how is the judgment in that case? So the answer is hastened. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for (ākharān), or for the pronoun in (yaqumān), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "they are the most deserving." The rhetorical point of the definiteness holds in all these cases.

Ḥamzah, and Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf read (al-awwalīn) with the wāw doubled and fatḥah, the lām kasrah and the yā' sākinah, the plural of awwal, which is used figuratively in the sense of "the foremost" and "the ones who are first to be addressed." Thus "those against whom it is deserved" are the guardians of the testator, since the legatee deserved the bequest from the estate's property that belonged to the guardians, i.e., the heirs were it not for the bequest. It is in the genitive as an adjective of ﴿those against whom it is deserved﴾.

Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim read (istaḥaqqa) in the active form, so (al-awlayan) is the subject (fā'il) of (istaḥaqqa), and His saying ﴿so they swear by God﴾ is a consequence of His saying ﴿who will stand in their place﴾.

The meaning of ﴿our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾ is that they are more deserving that their testimony be accepted than the two about whom it was discovered that they had incurred sin.

The meaning of (aḥaqq) is that it is the truth, so the comparative form is stripped of comparison.

His saying ﴿nor have we transgressed﴾ is an emphasis on the claim of being more worthy, because being more worthy refers to their benefit by establishing what the two foreign witnesses concealed. Had it not been so in reality, it would have been falsehood and aggression on their part against the property of those who conveyed the bequest. The meaning: "we have not transgressed against the two witnesses by accusing them of concealing part of the estate."

His saying ﴿for then we would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾ means: were we to transgress, we would be wrongdoers. Its purpose is to signal that they are mindful of what follows from transgression and wrongdoing, and in this there is added restraint.

The oath included an affirmation of the truth of their report, a sworn assertion establishing their right; so it is of the kind of oath by which a right is established together with a customary witness, namely the witness of suspicion (tuhmah), which was found against the two witnesses who convey the bequest.

The discussion of (idhan) here is like the discussion of His saying ﴿for then we would indeed be among the sinners﴾.

The meaning is that if the testimony of the two witnesses of the bequest is invalidated, the oath passes to the legatee, whether the legatee is one person or several. The verse was phrased in the dual in consideration of the case in which it was revealed, namely the case of Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Baddāʾ, for the heirs of the owner of the estate were two: ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿah, both of Banū Sahm, and they were the clients (mawlā) of Budayl ibn Abī Maryam al-Sahmī, the owner of the cup. Some exegetes mention that they were the clients of Budayl; others say that his client was ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ. The apparent sense of al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿah being made to swear is that he had a clientage relation with Budayl, since in Islam no one is known to swear who does not benefit from the oath. If the claimant is one person, he swears alone; if the claimants are a group, they all swear and are entitled. No one has said that if the claimant is one, someone who is not entitled swears with him, nor that if the claimants are three or more, two of them swear and all of them are entitled. So the restriction to two in the oaths of the two most deserving looks to the story of the occasion of revelation, and the verse would on this view be specific to that case. What differs from that case is governed by what is known in the Sharia regarding entitlement and suspicion.

This view implies that the verse was revealed before the Messenger's ﷺ judgment regarding the bequest of Budayl ibn Abī Maryam. This is apparent in some reports of the account, while some reports imply that the verse was revealed after the Messenger ﷺ had ruled. In that case it is necessarily a legislation for the like of that case that arises in the future, and so it is necessary to adopt the first view regarding the requirement that the two most deserving be two, if that is possible.

A case remains that the verse does not cover, such as when the dying person finds only one Muslim, or one non-Muslim, or finds two, one of whom is Muslim and the other not. All of these follow their known rulings in all judgments: the oath of the one who has a witness, or the oath of the denier.

The referent of His saying (﴿that is closer﴾) is the ruling previously mentioned, from His saying ﴿you shall detain them after the prayer﴾ up to His saying ﴿for then we would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾.

(Adnā) means "closer," and nearness here is figurative for nearness of knowledge, which is conjecture, i.e., more conducive to a conjecture of truthfulness.

The pronoun in (﴿ya'tū﴾) refers to the witnesses, who are: the two others from among you, and the two others who stand in their place, meaning that each one of them should come. The pronoun was made plural in view of distribution.

The meaning is that what God has prescribed of documentation and precision, and of rejecting testimony upon the emergence of doubt, is more conducive to a conjecture of the occurrence of truthfulness, because of the abundance of care exercised toward both parties, which negates heedlessness and laxity, let alone falsehood and injustice, while guarding against bad reputation.

The meaning of ﴿that they should bring the testimony﴾ is that they should render the testimony. Rendering it and reporting it is treated as bringing something from a place.

The meaning of His saying ﴿in its proper form (ʿalā wajhihā)﴾ is: according to its sunnah and what constitutes its completeness and perfection. The word "face" (wajh) in such a case is used figuratively for the best and most complete of a thing, by analogy to the human face, being the member by which a person is recognized and distinguished from others. Since this sense was intended as a metaphor, and became common in their speech, they said: "He brought such-and-such a thing ʿalā wajhihi," treating the thing as brought, and describing it as brought fully in its face, i.e., in its complete state. So the particle (ʿalā) is for figurative elevation, meaning firmness, like ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the testimony, and this serves as an indication that the word "face" is not used in its literal sense.

The sunnah of testimony and its perfection is its truthfulness, firmness in it, and attention to what one is heedless of among various conditions that one may lightly regard at the time and whose neglect may have consequences that squander rights. That is, this teaches them the way of firmness in bearing and rendering, and of seeking truthfulness, and it falls under the principle that a witness must maintain alertness.

The verse contains an allusion to the wisdom behind legislating the counter-testimony (i'dhār) in testimony by challenge or counter-claim, since this drives the witnesses to firmness in conforming their testimony to reality, because challenge and counter-claim uncover the truth.

His saying ﴿or they fear that oaths will be turned back after their oaths﴾ is coordinated with His saying (that they should bring) in view of what is connected to it of prepositional phrases, because the clause ﴿they bring the testimony in its proper form﴾ conveys bringing it truthfully without deficiency, from a motive within the witnesses themselves. That is why we estimated it as meaning that they should know what true testimony is. The coordinated clause thus conveys a restraint for the witnesses from within themselves, and the second clause conveys a restraint that is the expectation of their lie being exposed.

The meaning of ﴿that oaths be turned back﴾ is that oaths return to the heirs of the testator after the oaths of the two witnesses. Thus "turning back" is figurative for transfer, like the saying: "he turned the oath against him," so that they are reproached for it among people. The particle (or) is for division, and this division conveys the preference of what the demonstrative in His saying ﴿that is closer﴾ etc. had summarized. . . The plural (al-aymān) is used in view of the general application of the verse to all similar cases of bequests, since the Arabs often depart from the dual; an example is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If you two repent to God, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

This weighty ruling is concluded with an exhortation to the whole community, so He said (﴿and fear God﴾), the verse.

His saying (﴿and listen﴾) is a command to listening, used figuratively for obedience, as was mentioned previously in His saying ﴿when you said, we hear and we obey﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 7] in this surah.

His saying ﴿and God does not guide the defiant people﴾ is an encouragement to piety and obedience to God in what He commanded and forbade, and a warning against opposing that, because following God's command is guidance, and turning away from it is defiance. ﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾, that is, those who turn away from God's command, for that is not to be taken lightly, since it leads to a rust upon the heart so that guidance no longer penetrates it thereafter. So do not be like them, and be among the guided.

This is the exegesis of the verses. I have sought the clearest meanings and those most in accord with the Sharia, and I have elaborated in explaining them to remove what is obscure under their eloquent brevity. Al-Ṭībī transmitted from al-Zajjāj that this verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in terms of grammar. Al-Fakhr said: al-Wāḥidī reported from ʿUmar: "This verse is the most intractable of this surah's rulings." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, on the authority of Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib: "These verses are, according to the people of meanings, among the most difficult in the Qur'an in grammar, meaning, and ruling." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "This is the speech of one on whom the snow has not fallen in its exegesis," and that is clear from his book.

For the purpose of completing the meanings of the verses in sequence, I avoided discussing the rulings they yield and the disagreement of the scholars of Islam about them in the course of their exegesis, and I postponed that to this place, now that I have finished explaining their meanings.

They comprise two principles: the first is the command to call witnesses to a bequest; the second is the judgment in the case of Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Baddāʾ with the heirs of Budayl ibn Abī Maryam.

The first principle is from His saying ﴿testimony among you﴾ to His saying ﴿nor do we conceal the testimony of God﴾. The second principle is from His saying ﴿if it is discovered that the two of them have incurred sin﴾ to His saying ﴿after their oaths﴾. From this one arrives at knowledge of the manner of judgment in cases like that one, in which witnesses are suspected.

His saying ﴿testimony among you﴾, the verse, is an explanation of the manner of testimony, and it contains the command to it, but he turned away from mentioning the command because people are accustomed to entrusting their bequests to the place of their trust.

The most important rulings derived from the verse are three: the first is the calling of non-Muslim witnesses in matters of Muslims' rights, according to the opinion of those who took it to be the meaning of His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own﴾.

The second is making the witness swear that he is truthful in his testimony.

The third is aggravating the oath by time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 106–108 (part 4 of 4):

As for the first ruling, it is indicated by His, the Exalted, saying ﴿or two others from among other than you﴾. We have already explained that the more apparent view is that the "otherness" (al-ghayriyyah) is otherness in religion. Scholars have differed concerning the acceptance of the testimony of non-Muslims in matters arising among Muslims. The majority (al-jumhur) held that the ruling of this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] and His saying ﴿of those whom you approve as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i. A group, however, held that the verse is muhkam (non-abrogated), and among them some made it specific to the witnesses to a bequest (wasiyyah) during travel when there are no Muslims with the testator. This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari ruled accordingly in a bequest of this kind during his judgeship in Kufa, and said: "This is a matter that did not occur after what occurred in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Sufyan al-Thawri, and a group. They say: there is no abrogation in Surat al-Ma'idah, following Ibn 'Abbas. Among them are those who interpreted His saying "from other than you" as meaning "from other than your tribe," and this is the view of al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal analogized the remaining contracts in which witnessing during travel is recorded to the testimony of bequest, and said that the testimony of the People of the Dhimmah against Muslims during travel is valid, and he went further, making it without an oath.

The more apparent view in my opinion is that the ruling of the verse is not abrogated, and that the acceptance of the testimony of non-Muslims is specific to the bequest during travel where no Muslims are found, out of necessity. The reason the bequest is specific to this ruling is that it arises in a situation for which a person cannot prepare beforehand, so he is excused for calling non-Muslims to witness in that situation, out of fear that it may be lost; unlike other contracts, for which one can prepare in advance and secure them by other means. Thus this ruling is a concession (rukhsah).

The wisdom for which the testimony of non-Muslims is not accepted in the Islamic law except in necessity, according to those who hold that it is applied in necessity, is that accepting testimony is a form of certification and attestation of the witness and an elevation of his standing, since his report becomes decisive for rights. Some of the early judges used to say to the witnesses: "Fear Allah concerning us, for you are the judges and we are the executors." Since our Messenger ﷺ called people to follow his religion and the People of the Book turned away from it, they are not worthy that his community certify them and mark them as truthful, while they denied our Messenger. Also, one whose religion is not our religion, we do not know the limits of what restrains him from lying in his report, nor the scope of restriction and latitude in his actions arising from his beliefs, for perhaps his religion permits him to lie, especially if his testimony concerns a right of someone who differs from him in religion. We have observed of them that they do not exercise caution regarding the rights of those who are not of their religion. Allah, the Exalted, said quoting them: ﴿That is because they say: "There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], where "the unlettered" means the Muslims. Therefore, he is not a place of expectation for justice, nor is his degree of justice fixed in him. This is the state of most of them, though among them is one about whom Allah said: ﴿Of them is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]; but the ruling follows the majority.

As for the ruling on making the witness swear to the truth of his testimony, nothing has come in the transmitted reports except in this place. As for those who said that the acceptance of the testimony of the disbeliever is abrogated, the oath of the two disbelieving witnesses to a bequest is abrogated by implication, and this is the view of the majority. As for those who held it muhkam, they differed: some restricted the oath to the two witnesses to a bequest from among non-Muslims, and some reasoned from the cause for prescribing the oath of two witnesses from among non-Muslims, and analogized to it the oath of two witnesses when doubt attaches to them even if they are Muslims. This has no basis, since Allah made justice a condition for both of them, and justice is incompatible with doubt. Yes, it may be said: this applies when justice is unavailable or weakened at certain times and there arises necessity to call upon non-just witnesses, as is the state of most Islamic lands today; so it is not far-fetched that there is a basis in judgment for making a witness of unknown condition swear. The matter is set out at length in the books of jurisprudence.

As for the ruling on intensifying the oath, it has been derived from the verse that the oath falls after the prayer (al-salah), and this became a basis for intensifying the oath in the view of some scholars. Intensification of the oath may involve time, place, and wording. In all of these there is disagreement among the scholars. The verse contains nothing to be relied upon for any of these three except His saying: ﴿after the prayer﴾; and I have explained that the more apparent view is that it is specific to the bequest. As for intensification by place and by wording, its detail is found in the books of differences of opinion.

[Page 80]

These verses begin a new section, an independent beginning, to legislate the rules for securing bequests, because this is one of the legislative provisions that this surah includes, to confirm the completion of the religion and to cover what Muslims may need to act upon. Its place here is something we will mention.

Bequest (al-wasiyyah) had already been prescribed by the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. The discussion of the beginning of its legislation, and of what of that verse's ruling was abrogated (naskh) and what was confirmed, has preceded in its proper place there. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was keen on bequest and commanded it, so it became well known and practised from an early time in Islam. It was also known in the pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyyah), as has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. A man would make his bequest to the person he wished to name in the presence of his heirs and relatives, so no dispute would arise among them after his death, together with the sanctity of the bequest in people's souls and their eagerness to carry it out, in preservation of the right of the deceased, since he has no means of securing his right himself. For this reason the Qur'an dispensed with legislating for securing bequests by witnessing, unlike what had preceded regarding securing transactions by the verse ﴿And call two witnesses when you trade⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and securing debt by the verse ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and so on. Thus this verse completed the explanation of securing bequests, out of concern for them and because bequests deserve to be secured, since the defence of them is weak. This is because in trades and debts there are two parties who know the form of what was contracted, and each defends its interests, so the truth becomes clear through their striving to establish right in them. Bequest, by contrast, has only one party, the party of the beneficiary, because the testator has died, and the beneficiary is weak, having no knowledge of what the testator contracted or what he left. So bequests were exposed to loss, wholly or in part.

The Arabs in the pre-Islamic period used to entrust their bequests at death to someone they trusted from among their companions, or the elders of their tribe, or someone who was present at the testator's dying, or someone who had been told by the testator of his intention. Nizar ibn Ma'd made a concise bequest and referred his sons to al-Ufa al-Jurhumi to explain to them the detailed meaning of what he intended by it.

At the end of the life of the Messenger, upon him be peace and blessings, an event occurred that was the cause of the revelation of this verse. Perhaps its occurrence coincided with the revelation of the verses that precede it, so this verse came after them in this place of the surah.

That is: in the ninth year after the Hijrah a case arose, namely that two men, one of them Tamim al-Dari al-Lakhmi and the other 'Adi ibn Badda', were Christian Arabs and merchants, and they were from the people of Dara'in, and they used to trade between Syria, Makkah and Madinah. A man named Budayl ibn Abi Maryam, a client (mawla) of Banu Sahm, who was a Muslim, went out with them from Madinah on a trade journey to Syria. Budayl fell ill, it was said in Syria and it was said on the road, by land or by sea. With him among his goods was a cup of silver inlaid with gold, which he intended for the king of Syria. When his illness grew severe, he took a document and wrote in it what he had of goods and wealth, and placed it among the folds of his baggage, and handed what he had to Tamim and 'Adi, and charged them to deliver it to his clients from Banu Sahm. Budayl was a client of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, so his walā' after his death belonged to his son 'Amr ibn al-'As. Some of the commentators say that Budayl's walā' belonged to 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Wada'ah. What supports their view is that al-Muttalib swore together with 'Amr ibn al-'As that the cup belonged to Budayl ibn Abi Maryam. When the two returned, they sold the cup in Makkah for a thousand dirhams, and returned to Madinah, and they delivered what belonged to Budayl to his clients. When they unfolded it, they found the document, and they said to Tamim and 'Adi: "Where is the cup?" They denied that he had given them a cup. Then the cup was found after some time being sold in Makkah, and 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah stood against the one who had it, and he said: "He bought it from Tamim and 'Adi." In another report, when Tamim became Muslim in the ninth year, he felt guilty for what he had done, so he informed 'Amr ibn al-'As of the matter of the cup, and gave him the five hundred dirhams that had come to him from its price. 'Amr then demanded the remainder of the price from 'Adi, who denied that he had sold it. This is the best of what has been related about the cause of the revelation of this verse. al-Bukhari related it as a suspended report (ta'liq) in the Book of Bequests. al-Tirmidhi related it in the Book of Tafsir, and said: "Its chain is not sound." Although it does not fully meet the conditions of soundness, it became widely known and was received with acceptance, and al-Bukhari transmitted it with a chain in his History.

[Page 82]

The reports agree that the two parties brought their dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed concerning it. So 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah swore that Tamim and 'Adi had concealed the cup, and that Budayl, its owner, had neither sold it nor let it leave his hand. 'Adi handed them five hundred dirhams, and he was at that time a Christian. It is said that this 'Adi later became Muslim, and Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mandah counted him among the Companions. It is also said that he died a Christian, and Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred this view; it is the opinion of Abu Nu'aym, and it is related from Muqatil. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr did not mention him among the Companions. It is possible that the revelation came before the litigants' appeal in the case of the cup, and it is possible that it came after the Prophet's (ﷺ) judgment in that case, so that it would be legislation for similar cases that might occur.

And (baynakum): the original of (bayn) is a noun of indefinite place situated between two things, specified by what follows it in construction. Here it is used figuratively for a matter connected with several things. It is in the genitive, as it is the object of the construct phrase (idafah) of (shahadah) to it, by extension (ittisa'). Its original form was (shahadatun), with tanwin and nominative case, and (baynakum) in the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf). Then (bayn) moved out of the adverbial function into full nominal function, just as it moved out of it in the words of Allah, ﴿Certainly the connection between you has been severed⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-An'am: 94], in the reading of a group of the ten readers, who read (baynakum) in the nominative.

(Shahadatu) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is (ithnan), "two." ﴿When death approaches one of you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ is a temporal adverbial clause referring to the future. (Idha) here does not carry the meaning of a conditional, and the adverbial is connected to (shahadatu) because it contains the sense of a verb, meaning: "let two witness when death approaches one of you," that is, it is obligatory upon him to have it witnessed, and it is obligatory upon them to bear witness, in accordance with the words of Allah, ﴿and let the witnesses not refuse when they are called⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. ﴿At the time of the bequest⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when death approaches one of you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, an exact substitute (badal mutabiq), since the time when death approaches is generally the time when people make their bequests. This second temporal expression is brought so that through this substitution one may reach the intended matter, which is the bequest. The Arabs, when they saw the sign of death on a sick person, would say: "Make your bequest (awsi)." They said this to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab when the physician informed him that his wound was in his bowels.

The meaning of the approach of death is the appearance of its signs, because in that state a person imagines that death has come to him to make him a dead person. The intended meaning is not the occurrence of the death-rattle (ghargharah), because what is required of the testator to do takes a long time. This has been discussed earlier at the words of Allah, ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], in Surat al-Baqarah.

His words (ithnan) are the predicate of (shahadatu), that is: the witnessing concerning the bequest is the witnessing of two. So the genitive-governing noun was omitted (hadhf al-mudaf), and the genitive that was dependent on it took its place and received its case ending. The indication is clear, and the purpose is brevity. So the referent of (ithnan) is two witnesses, by the indication of His words, ﴿witnessing among you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ and His words, (﴿just men⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾). These two witnesses are the executors (wasiyyan) of the deceased in the description of his bequest and in conveying it, unless the testator appoints someone other than them as executor, in which case they will be witnesses to that.

Al-'adl and al-'adalah are synonymous, that is, persons characterised by justice.

The meaning of (minkum) is "from among the believers," as is required by the address ﴿O you who have believed⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, because when a speaker addresses his listener with a description and then follows it with something indicating part of that description, its meaning is that he is part of those who bear that description, as the Ansar said on the day of Saqifah: "There is an amir from us and an amir from you." So the discussion concerns the bequest of believers. On this view the majority of the commentators proceeded; it is the opinion of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Qatadah, and the four Imams. It is the view upon which one must rely, and it is the apparent meaning of the description with the word (minkum) in its occurrences in the Qur'an.

Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah said: the meaning of His words (minkum) is "from among your kin and relatives." The consequence of the first interpretation is that the meaning of its opposite, (min ghayrikum), "from other than you," is that they are from outside your religious community. Some of those who held the first interpretation acted upon this and permitted the testimony of a non-Muslim during travel concerning bequests specifically, and they restricted that to a dhimmi. This is the view of Ahmad, al-Thawri, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and it is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Musa. Another group held that this was abrogated (mansukh) by the words of Allah, ﴿and call to witness two just men from among you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Talaq: 2]. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i, and it is attributed to Zayd ibn Aslam. The complete statement concerning the full form of the testimony of bequest has been concluded with His words, ﴿two just men from among you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

[Page 84]

His words, ﴿or two others from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ and so on, are a detailing of the situation that arises during travel.

(Aw) here is for division, not for choice, and the division is by consideration of the difference between the two states: the state of one who is present and the state of one who is travelling. For this reason it is joined with the phrase ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, so this is a restriction on His words, ﴿or two others from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

The condition in ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ has an omitted answer (jawab al-shart), indicated by His words, ﴿or two others from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾. The estimated sense is: "if you are travelling in the land, then the testimony is of two others from other than you." So the resort to the testimony of two non-Muslim witnesses, according to the one who holds this view, is restricted by the condition ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

Striking in the land (al-darb fi al-ard) means journeying in it, and what is meant by it is travel (safar). It has preceded at the words of Allah, ﴿And they said to their brothers when they struck out in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The meaning of ﴿then the disaster of death strikes you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ is that it befalls you. The verb is used with the meaning of nearing and approaching, as in the words of Allah, ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them offspring⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Nisa': 9], that is, if they were about to leave offspring behind. This is a usage of verbs, and from it is the saying in the iqamah: "The prayer has been established" (qad qamati al-salah).

He joined (﴿then the disaster struck you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾) to ﴿if you are travelling in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾, so it was part of the content of His words before it, ﴿when death approaches one of you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾. It was repeated here to link the speech after it had been separated from that by adverbials and conditions.

The plural pronoun in (asabatkum) is like the plural pronoun in ﴿you strike in the land⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾.

Al-musibah is the event that befalls a person of evil and harm, and it has preceded at the words of Allah, ﴿So if a disaster befalls you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Nisa': 72], in Surat al-Nisa'.

The clause (tahbisunahuma) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to (ākharani), according to the one who made His words ﴿from other than you⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾

[Page 85]

[p. 86] in the sense of "from outside your religious community." As for the one who takes it to mean "from outside your tribe," then [ākharān] is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to [ithnān] and [ākharān], since the two are joined by [aw] (or). They are then one of two categories, and the oath is required when there is suspicion. An oath on this interpretation is remote, since there is no cause for suspicion regarding two upright Muslim witnesses.

The plural pronoun in [tahbisūnahumā] is like the pronouns in [ḍarabtum] and [aṣābatkum]. All of them are used in the distributive (badalī) plural rather than the comprehensive (shumūlī) plural, because every one of the addressees is capable of being subject to this ruling, though it befalls only some of them. Thus the plural pronouns addressing the audience all stand in the place of what the context requires. The plural form was used to convey generality, to prevent the assumption that this legislation applies only to two specific persons, since the occasion of revelation concerned two persons. Alternatively, the address and the plural are directed to the Muslims and their rulers.

[al-ḥabs] means holding back, i.e., preventing someone from departing. It may be by compulsion, as in imprisoning a criminal in a house or shackling him in chains. It may also mean waiting, as in the ḥadīth of ʿItbān ibn Mālik: "The Messenger of God and Abū Bakr came to me in the morning..." until he said, "and we detained him for a khazīr (a dish) that we had prepared," i.e., we kept him. This is the meaning intended in the verse: you hold them back and do not let them leave you until they have borne the bequest. It does not mean imprisonment or anything close to it, because God the Exalted said: ﴿neither the scribe nor the witness be harmed﴾ [al-Baqara: 282].

His words ﴿after the prayer﴾ specify the time for bringing them and holding them for the giving of this testimony. The use of [min] (from), which denotes a starting point, indicates the proximity of the time after, i.e., close to the end of the prayer. The verse may also mean a prayer of the Muslims' prayers, and some scholars interpreted it this way, saying: it is the ʿAṣr prayer. It is related that "the Prophet ﷺ had Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Badde swear an oath after the ʿAṣr prayer in the case of the cup," and this is the view of Qatāda, Saʿīd, Shurayḥ and al-Shaʿbī. Others said it is the Ẓuhr prayer, and this is reported from al-Ḥasan. It may also mean "after the prayer of their religion," on the interpretation of "from other than you" as "from outside the people of your religion." It is reported from al-Suddī and Ibn ʿAbbās, i.e., you bring them immediately after they have performed their prayer, because that is close to their turning to the fear of God and standing before Him in worship.

His words ﴿they both swear by God﴾ are conjoined to [tahbisūnahumā] (you hold them), so it is understood that their detention after the prayer is for the purpose of their swearing by God. The pronoun in [yuqsimān] refers back to [ākharān] (two others). Thus the oath is sworn by the two bequest witnesses, who are not Muslims, in order to increase confidence in their testimony, since the uprightness of a non-Muslim is not relied upon.

His words ﴿if you doubt﴾: the statements of the exegetes concur that this conditional is connected to [tahbisūnahumā] and what is conjoined to it. The answer to the condition is omitted, being indicated by what precedes it, for the sake of concision (ījāz). Had it not been placed first, it would have said: "or two others from outside your group, if you doubt them, you hold them back," and so on. This interpretation implies that if no doubt arises about their truthfulness, it would not be required to bring them after the prayer and to have them swear, so this is left to the discretion of the guardian (walī). The conditional clause is parenthetical between the verb of swearing and its answer.

In my view, the more correct position is that his words ﴿if you doubt﴾ are part of the speech that the two witnesses themselves utter, meaning: the two witnesses say, "If you doubt our testimony, then we swear by God that we will not exchange it for any price, even if it concerns a near kinsman, and we will not conceal the testimony," i.e., they say this to reassure the soul of the testator, because uprightness is a presumption of truthfulness, while there remains the possibility of something contrary to it that is not known. The presumption of truthfulness is thus reinforced by the oath. This speech is therefore prescribed for every witness, so that all circumstances are equal, and so that the imposition of the oath in some circumstances does not become a burden on the two witnesses upon whom the oath is imposed, since the oath implies an insinuation of doubt about their truthfulness. The imposition of the oath by the Lawgiver thus removes the embarrassment between them and the guardian, since the oath being a condition from God provides an excuse for demanding it, as the majority of our jurists said regarding the judicial oath imposed upon one who establishes a right against a dead or absent person, that it is obligatory before the ruling in every case, even if the rightful heir waives it. I have not found any exegete who pursued this meaning except al-Kawāshī's statement in his *Talkhīṣ al-Tafsīr*: "Some stop at [yuqsimān] and begin with [billāh] as an oath, but I do not like this." And apart from that, what al-Ṣaffāqusī related in his *Iʿrāb* from al-Jurjānī: that there is an omitted statement here, its estimate being: "they both swear by God and say." Al-Ṣaffāqusī did not discern what led al-Jurjānī to posit this statement. I do not think he was moved to it except by making his words ﴿if you doubt﴾ part of the speech of the two witnesses.

The answer to the condition is omitted and indicated by the answer to the oath, since the oath has priority for the answer because it precedes the condition.

His words ﴿we will not exchange it for any price﴾ etc. are the content of the oath. The meaning of "we will not exchange it for any price" is: we will not take in exchange for the matter we have sworn to any price, i.e., any compensation. The pronoun in [bihi] refers to the oath understood from [yuqsimān]. The indefinite [thaman] in a negative context conveys the generality of every price. The word "price" means compensation: we will not substitute what we have sworn to with any compensation, whatever that compensation may be. The pronoun [bihi] may also refer to the matter sworn to, which is what they were entrusted with, namely the wording of the testator's bequest in all its contents.

His words ﴿even if it concerns a near kinsman﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of [thaman], which is in the sense of compensation, meaning: even if the compensation were a near kinsman, i.e., a near relative of ours. [Law] (even if) is a conditional particle that conveys emphasis. If a near kinsman would not be accepted by them as compensation for altering their testimony, then what is less than that is even less acceptable. This is because the greatest thing that drives a person to partiality in the custom of the tribes is zeal and support for a relative, so bribes and personal benefits appear small in comparison. The concealed pronoun in [kāna] refers to [thaman].

The meaning of the compensation being "of near kinship" is that it is the pleasing or benefiting of the near kinsman. The statement therefore contains an elided noun, which is part of what is called *dalālat al-iqtiḍāʾ* (implication required by the sense), because it makes no sense to make the compensation itself the near kinsman. It is therefore determined that what is meant is something of his relations that the context specifies. A parallel is ﴿forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 23]. The manner in which this conditional with [law] conveys meaning, and why it is called *waṣliyya* (connective), was discussed earlier at His words ﴿even if he were to offer it as ransom﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 91] in the chapter of Āl ʿImrān.

His words [wa-lā naktum] (nor do we conceal) are conjoined to [lā nashtarī] (we will not exchange), because the intent of making them swear is that they render the testimony as they received it, so that they change nothing of it and conceal none of it at all.

The attribution of the testimony to the name of God (the Majesty) magnifies its importance in the eyes of the witness and others, because when God commanded its rendering as it is and urged it, He attributed it to His name to protect it from alteration. Thus the explicit mention of His name serves to remind the witness of Him at the moment of the oath.

In His words ﴿nor do we conceal﴾ there is evidence that the word "testimony" here has its customary meaning, which is reporting a specific matter that arises in such disputes. It does not mean the oath, as some exegetes supposed; we will not dwell at length refuting this, since the wording itself refutes it.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, then we would be among the sinners﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) of explanatory type (bayānī), because it is an answer to an implied question, as shown by the presence of [idhan], which is a particle of response. The two witnesses sensed a question from the one to whom they swore, when they said: "we will not exchange it for any price, nor conceal the testimony of God." He might have said to himself: "Perhaps you will not fulfill what you have sworn," so they replied: "Indeed, then we would be among the sinners," i.e., we know that the consequence of failing to fulfill what we have sworn is that we would be among the sinners, and we do not accept that.

[al-ātham] is the one who commits sin. It is known that sin is violating the oath by the occurrence of the sentence as a resumption together with [idhan], which indicates an answer to a statement stirring in the soul of the deceased's heirs.

His words ﴿But if it is discovered that the two had incurred sin, then two others...﴾, i.e., if it becomes clear that they concealed or altered and broke their oath, their testimony is invalidated, because His words ﴿two others shall take their place﴾ are a consequence of the invalidation of their testimony. Thus what expresses the invalidation of their testimony is omitted for concision, as in His words ﴿Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ [al-Baqara: 60], i.e., he struck, and it gushed forth.

[ʿuthira] means it became evident and clear. The original sense of [ʿathara] is that a walker's foot strikes a protruding object on the ground that he did not anticipate or guard against, so that the movement of his walking is disturbed, so that he may fall or be shaken. Its verbal noun is [ʿithār] and [ʿuthūr]. It was then used figuratively for finding something one had not expected to find. This became so widespread that it became almost literal, so in usage they restricted the literal meaning to one of the two verbal nouns, [ʿithār], and restricted the figurative meaning to the other verbal noun, [ʿuthūr].

The meaning of [istaḥaqqā ithman] (they had incurred sin) is that it was established that they committed what makes them sinners, so sin became incumbent upon them, i.e., fell upon them; the [sīn] and [tā'] here are for emphasis. The sin meant is that from which they disowned themselves in His words ﴿we will not exchange it for any price, even if it concerns a near kinsman, nor conceal the testimony of God.﴾ So the sin is one of these two: that it becomes evident they took compensation for themselves or others in exchange for what they were entrusted with, or that it becomes evident they concealed the testimony, i.e., part of it. The essence of the sin is that what discredits their truthfulness becomes clear by proof of establishment.

His words [fa-ākharān] means two other men, because the description [ākhar] applies to what differs either in essence or in attribute while being similar in the genus under discussion, and what is discussed here is two persons. The meaning is therefore: two others who take their place in establishing the bequest. [Yaqūmān maqāmahumā] means they make up for that testimony. The word [maqām] originally denotes the place of standing; then it is used for a place of any activity even if no standing occurs there; then it is used for the activity which by its nature occurs in a place where the agent stands, and this applies to important activity. God the Exalted said: ﴿If my standing [among you] and my reminding you is burdensome to you﴾ [Yūnus: 71]. Thus the standing (maqām) of the two witnesses is establishing the bequest. The [min] in His words ﴿from among those against whom [the claim] was established﴾ is partitive, meaning: two others who are from the group of those against whom it was established.

[al-istiḥqāq] means that a thing is deserving of another thing. It takes its object directly, as in His words ﴿they had incurred sin﴾, and the object is the thing deserved. When the deservingness arises from a dispute, the verb takes as its object the one who has the right by [ʿalā], which indicates elevation, in the sense of obligation upon him even if he dislikes it; it is as if they implied in it the sense of [wajaba] (was obligatory), as in God the Exalted's words ﴿It is incumbent upon me not to say about God except the truth﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 105]. One says: Zayd deserved from ʿAmr such-and-such, i.e., a right became due to Zayd from ʿAmr, so he took it from him.

The majority (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿was established against them﴾ in the passive voice. The omitted subject in His words ﴿was established against them﴾ is an unspecified claimant, who is the one who benefited from the false testimony and oath, so that he obtained from the testator's estate what the testator had not left him, and overpowered the testator's heir in this. Thus those against whom it was established are the testator's heirs, who were entitled to his property by some mode of inheritance, but were deprived of part of it.

His words [ʿalayhim] (against them) stand in the place of the deputy of the subject of [istuḥiqqa].

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 5, verses 106–108 (part 3 of 4):

His saying: (﴿al-awlayan﴾) is the dual of awlā, meaning the most deserving and most entitled, i.e., "the two most deserving" of having their word accepted. Its referent (mā ṣadaquhu) is the same as that of (ākharān), and it refers back to it. Thus it is permissible for it to be made a predicate of ākharān: since ākharān was qualified by the clause ﴿who will stand in their place﴾, it became valid to begin with it, meaning: "two other persons, they are the most deserving of having their word accepted, rather than the two accused witnesses."

It was defined with the article (al-) because it is known to the addressee in mind: when the listener hears His saying ﴿if it is discovered that the two of them have incurred sin﴾, he anticipates learning who is most deserving of having their word accepted in this matter, so he is told: "two others who are the most deserving of it." It is also permissible for (al-awlayan) to be the subject (mubtada') and ﴿two others who will stand﴾ its predicate (khabar). The predicate is placed first to hasten the benefit, because the listener awaits the ruling after His saying ﴿if it is discovered that the two of them have incurred sin﴾; that discovery of the lie of the two witnesses voids their testimony and their oath, so how is the judgment in that case? So the answer is hastened. It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for (ākharān), or for the pronoun in (yaqumān), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "they are the most deserving." The rhetorical point of the definiteness holds in all these cases.

Ḥamzah, and Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, and Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf read (al-awwalīn) with the wāw doubled and fatḥah, the lām kasrah and the yā' sākinah, the plural of awwal, which is used figuratively in the sense of "the foremost" and "the ones who are first to be addressed." Thus "those against whom it is deserved" are the guardians of the testator, since the legatee deserved the bequest from the estate's property that belonged to the guardians, i.e., the heirs were it not for the bequest. It is in the genitive as an adjective of ﴿those against whom it is deserved﴾.

Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim read (istaḥaqqa) in the active form, so (al-awlayan) is the subject (fā'il) of (istaḥaqqa), and His saying ﴿so they swear by God﴾ is a consequence of His saying ﴿who will stand in their place﴾.

The meaning of ﴿our testimony is more worthy than their testimony﴾ is that they are more deserving that their testimony be accepted than the two about whom it was discovered that they had incurred sin.

The meaning of (aḥaqq) is that it is the truth, so the comparative form is stripped of comparison.

His saying ﴿nor have we transgressed﴾ is an emphasis on the claim of being more worthy, because being more worthy refers to their benefit by establishing what the two foreign witnesses concealed. Had it not been so in reality, it would have been falsehood and aggression on their part against the property of those who conveyed the bequest. The meaning: "we have not transgressed against the two witnesses by accusing them of concealing part of the estate."

His saying ﴿for then we would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾ means: were we to transgress, we would be wrongdoers. Its purpose is to signal that they are mindful of what follows from transgression and wrongdoing, and in this there is added restraint.

The oath included an affirmation of the truth of their report, a sworn assertion establishing their right; so it is of the kind of oath by which a right is established together with a customary witness, namely the witness of suspicion (tuhmah), which was found against the two witnesses who convey the bequest.

The discussion of (idhan) here is like the discussion of His saying ﴿for then we would indeed be among the sinners﴾.

The meaning is that if the testimony of the two witnesses of the bequest is invalidated, the oath passes to the legatee, whether the legatee is one person or several. The verse was phrased in the dual in consideration of the case in which it was revealed, namely the case of Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Baddāʾ, for the heirs of the owner of the estate were two: ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿah, both of Banū Sahm, and they were the clients (mawlā) of Budayl ibn Abī Maryam al-Sahmī, the owner of the cup. Some exegetes mention that they were the clients of Budayl; others say that his client was ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ. The apparent sense of al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿah being made to swear is that he had a clientage relation with Budayl, since in Islam no one is known to swear who does not benefit from the oath. If the claimant is one person, he swears alone; if the claimants are a group, they all swear and are entitled. No one has said that if the claimant is one, someone who is not entitled swears with him, nor that if the claimants are three or more, two of them swear and all of them are entitled. So the restriction to two in the oaths of the two most deserving looks to the story of the occasion of revelation, and the verse would on this view be specific to that case. What differs from that case is governed by what is known in the Sharia regarding entitlement and suspicion.

This view implies that the verse was revealed before the Messenger's ﷺ judgment regarding the bequest of Budayl ibn Abī Maryam. This is apparent in some reports of the account, while some reports imply that the verse was revealed after the Messenger ﷺ had ruled. In that case it is necessarily a legislation for the like of that case that arises in the future, and so it is necessary to adopt the first view regarding the requirement that the two most deserving be two, if that is possible.

A case remains that the verse does not cover, such as when the dying person finds only one Muslim, or one non-Muslim, or finds two, one of whom is Muslim and the other not. All of these follow their known rulings in all judgments: the oath of the one who has a witness, or the oath of the denier.

The referent of His saying (﴿that is closer﴾) is the ruling previously mentioned, from His saying ﴿you shall detain them after the prayer﴾ up to His saying ﴿for then we would indeed be among the wrongdoers﴾.

(Adnā) means "closer," and nearness here is figurative for nearness of knowledge, which is conjecture, i.e., more conducive to a conjecture of truthfulness.

The pronoun in (﴿ya'tū﴾) refers to the witnesses, who are: the two others from among you, and the two others who stand in their place, meaning that each one of them should come. The pronoun was made plural in view of distribution.

The meaning is that what God has prescribed of documentation and precision, and of rejecting testimony upon the emergence of doubt, is more conducive to a conjecture of the occurrence of truthfulness, because of the abundance of care exercised toward both parties, which negates heedlessness and laxity, let alone falsehood and injustice, while guarding against bad reputation.

The meaning of ﴿that they should bring the testimony﴾ is that they should render the testimony. Rendering it and reporting it is treated as bringing something from a place.

The meaning of His saying ﴿in its proper form (ʿalā wajhihā)﴾ is: according to its sunnah and what constitutes its completeness and perfection. The word "face" (wajh) in such a case is used figuratively for the best and most complete of a thing, by analogy to the human face, being the member by which a person is recognized and distinguished from others. Since this sense was intended as a metaphor, and became common in their speech, they said: "He brought such-and-such a thing ʿalā wajhihi," treating the thing as brought, and describing it as brought fully in its face, i.e., in its complete state. So the particle (ʿalā) is for figurative elevation, meaning firmness, like ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the testimony, and this serves as an indication that the word "face" is not used in its literal sense.

The sunnah of testimony and its perfection is its truthfulness, firmness in it, and attention to what one is heedless of among various conditions that one may lightly regard at the time and whose neglect may have consequences that squander rights. That is, this teaches them the way of firmness in bearing and rendering, and of seeking truthfulness, and it falls under the principle that a witness must maintain alertness.

The verse contains an allusion to the wisdom behind legislating the counter-testimony (i'dhār) in testimony by challenge or counter-claim, since this drives the witnesses to firmness in conforming their testimony to reality, because challenge and counter-claim uncover the truth.

His saying ﴿or they fear that oaths will be turned back after their oaths﴾ is coordinated with His saying (that they should bring) in view of what is connected to it of prepositional phrases, because the clause ﴿they bring the testimony in its proper form﴾ conveys bringing it truthfully without deficiency, from a motive within the witnesses themselves. That is why we estimated it as meaning that they should know what true testimony is. The coordinated clause thus conveys a restraint for the witnesses from within themselves, and the second clause conveys a restraint that is the expectation of their lie being exposed.

The meaning of ﴿that oaths be turned back﴾ is that oaths return to the heirs of the testator after the oaths of the two witnesses. Thus "turning back" is figurative for transfer, like the saying: "he turned the oath against him," so that they are reproached for it among people. The particle (or) is for division, and this division conveys the preference of what the demonstrative in His saying ﴿that is closer﴾ etc. had summarized. . . The plural (al-aymān) is used in view of the general application of the verse to all similar cases of bequests, since the Arabs often depart from the dual; an example is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿If you two repent to God, your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4].

This weighty ruling is concluded with an exhortation to the whole community, so He said (﴿and fear God﴾), the verse.

His saying (﴿and listen﴾) is a command to listening, used figuratively for obedience, as was mentioned previously in His saying ﴿when you said, we hear and we obey﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 7] in this surah.

His saying ﴿and God does not guide the defiant people﴾ is an encouragement to piety and obedience to God in what He commanded and forbade, and a warning against opposing that, because following God's command is guidance, and turning away from it is defiance. ﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾, that is, those who turn away from God's command, for that is not to be taken lightly, since it leads to a rust upon the heart so that guidance no longer penetrates it thereafter. So do not be like them, and be among the guided.

This is the exegesis of the verses. I have sought the clearest meanings and those most in accord with the Sharia, and I have elaborated in explaining them to remove what is obscure under their eloquent brevity. Al-Ṭībī transmitted from al-Zajjāj that this verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in terms of grammar. Al-Fakhr said: al-Wāḥidī reported from ʿUmar: "This verse is the most intractable of this surah's rulings." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, on the authority of Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib: "These verses are, according to the people of meanings, among the most difficult in the Qur'an in grammar, meaning, and ruling." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "This is the speech of one on whom the snow has not fallen in its exegesis," and that is clear from his book.

For the purpose of completing the meanings of the verses in sequence, I avoided discussing the rulings they yield and the disagreement of the scholars of Islam about them in the course of their exegesis, and I postponed that to this place, now that I have finished explaining their meanings.

They comprise two principles: the first is the command to call witnesses to a bequest; the second is the judgment in the case of Tamīm al-Dārī and ʿAdī ibn Baddāʾ with the heirs of Budayl ibn Abī Maryam.

The first principle is from His saying ﴿testimony among you﴾ to His saying ﴿nor do we conceal the testimony of God﴾. The second principle is from His saying ﴿if it is discovered that the two of them have incurred sin﴾ to His saying ﴿after their oaths﴾. From this one arrives at knowledge of the manner of judgment in cases like that one, in which witnesses are suspected.

His saying ﴿testimony among you﴾, the verse, is an explanation of the manner of testimony, and it contains the command to it, but he turned away from mentioning the command because people are accustomed to entrusting their bequests to the place of their trust.

The most important rulings derived from the verse are three: the first is the calling of non-Muslim witnesses in matters of Muslims' rights, according to the opinion of those who took it to be the meaning of His saying ﴿or two others from outside your own﴾.

The second is making the witness swear that he is truthful in his testimony.

The third is aggravating the oath by time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 106–108 (part 4 of 4):

As for the first ruling, it is indicated by His, the Exalted, saying ﴿or two others from among other than you﴾. We have already explained that the more apparent view is that the "otherness" (al-ghayriyyah) is otherness in religion. Scholars have differed concerning the acceptance of the testimony of non-Muslims in matters arising among Muslims. The majority (al-jumhur) held that the ruling of this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and call to witness two just men from among you﴾ [al-Talaq: 2] and His saying ﴿of those whom you approve as witnesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. This is the view of Malik, Abu Hanifah, and al-Shafi'i. A group, however, held that the verse is muhkam (non-abrogated), and among them some made it specific to the witnesses to a bequest (wasiyyah) during travel when there are no Muslims with the testator. This is the view of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari ruled accordingly in a bequest of this kind during his judgeship in Kufa, and said: "This is a matter that did not occur after what occurred in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." This is also the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Sufyan al-Thawri, and a group. They say: there is no abrogation in Surat al-Ma'idah, following Ibn 'Abbas. Among them are those who interpreted His saying "from other than you" as meaning "from other than your tribe," and this is the view of al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah.

Ahmad ibn Hanbal analogized the remaining contracts in which witnessing during travel is recorded to the testimony of bequest, and said that the testimony of the People of the Dhimmah against Muslims during travel is valid, and he went further, making it without an oath.

The more apparent view in my opinion is that the ruling of the verse is not abrogated, and that the acceptance of the testimony of non-Muslims is specific to the bequest during travel where no Muslims are found, out of necessity. The reason the bequest is specific to this ruling is that it arises in a situation for which a person cannot prepare beforehand, so he is excused for calling non-Muslims to witness in that situation, out of fear that it may be lost; unlike other contracts, for which one can prepare in advance and secure them by other means. Thus this ruling is a concession (rukhsah).

The wisdom for which the testimony of non-Muslims is not accepted in the Islamic law except in necessity, according to those who hold that it is applied in necessity, is that accepting testimony is a form of certification and attestation of the witness and an elevation of his standing, since his report becomes decisive for rights. Some of the early judges used to say to the witnesses: "Fear Allah concerning us, for you are the judges and we are the executors." Since our Messenger ﷺ called people to follow his religion and the People of the Book turned away from it, they are not worthy that his community certify them and mark them as truthful, while they denied our Messenger. Also, one whose religion is not our religion, we do not know the limits of what restrains him from lying in his report, nor the scope of restriction and latitude in his actions arising from his beliefs, for perhaps his religion permits him to lie, especially if his testimony concerns a right of someone who differs from him in religion. We have observed of them that they do not exercise caution regarding the rights of those who are not of their religion. Allah, the Exalted, said quoting them: ﴿That is because they say: "There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], where "the unlettered" means the Muslims. Therefore, he is not a place of expectation for justice, nor is his degree of justice fixed in him. This is the state of most of them, though among them is one about whom Allah said: ﴿Of them is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]; but the ruling follows the majority.

As for the ruling on making the witness swear to the truth of his testimony, nothing has come in the transmitted reports except in this place. As for those who said that the acceptance of the testimony of the disbeliever is abrogated, the oath of the two disbelieving witnesses to a bequest is abrogated by implication, and this is the view of the majority. As for those who held it muhkam, they differed: some restricted the oath to the two witnesses to a bequest from among non-Muslims, and some reasoned from the cause for prescribing the oath of two witnesses from among non-Muslims, and analogized to it the oath of two witnesses when doubt attaches to them even if they are Muslims. This has no basis, since Allah made justice a condition for both of them, and justice is incompatible with doubt. Yes, it may be said: this applies when justice is unavailable or weakened at certain times and there arises necessity to call upon non-just witnesses, as is the state of most Islamic lands today; so it is not far-fetched that there is a basis in judgment for making a witness of unknown condition swear. The matter is set out at length in the books of jurisprudence.

As for the ruling on intensifying the oath, it has been derived from the verse that the oath falls after the prayer (al-salah), and this became a basis for intensifying the oath in the view of some scholars. Intensification of the oath may involve time, place, and wording. In all of these there is disagreement among the scholars. The verse contains nothing to be relied upon for any of these three except His saying: ﴿after the prayer﴾; and I have explained that the more apparent view is that it is specific to the bequest. As for intensification by place and by wording, its detail is found in the books of differences of opinion.

[Page 80]

These verses begin a new section, an independent beginning, to legislate the rules for securing bequests, because this is one of the legislative provisions that this surah includes, to confirm the completion of the religion and to cover what Muslims may need to act upon. Its place here is something we will mention.

Bequest (al-wasiyyah) had already been prescribed by the verse of al-Baqarah: ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180]. The discussion of the beginning of its legislation, and of what of that verse's ruling was abrogated (naskh) and what was confirmed, has preceded in its proper place there. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was keen on bequest and commanded it, so it became well known and practised from an early time in Islam. It was also known in the pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyyah), as has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. A man would make his bequest to the person he wished to name in the presence of his heirs and relatives, so no dispute would arise among them after his death, together with the sanctity of the bequest in people's souls and their eagerness to carry it out, in preservation of the right of the deceased, since he has no means of securing his right himself. For this reason the Qur'an dispensed with legislating for securing bequests by witnessing, unlike what had preceded regarding securing transactions by the verse ﴿And call two witnesses when you trade⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and securing debt by the verse ﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term⁠﻿﻿﻿﻿...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and so on. Thus this verse completed the explanation of securing bequests, out of concern for them and because bequests deserve to be secured, since the defence of them is weak. This is because in trades and debts there are two parties who know the form of what was contracted, and each defends its interests, so the truth becomes clear through their striving to establish right in them. Bequest, by contrast, has only one party, the party of the beneficiary, because the testator has died, and the beneficiary is weak, having no knowledge of what the testator contracted or what he left. So bequests were exposed to loss, wholly or in part.

The Arabs in the pre-Islamic period used to entrust their bequests at death to someone they trusted from among their companions, or the elders of their tribe, or someone who was present at the testator's dying, or someone who had been told by the testator of his intention. Nizar ibn Ma'd made a concise bequest and referred his sons to al-Ufa al-Jurhumi to explain to them the detailed meaning of what he intended by it.

At the end of the life of the Messenger, upon him be peace and blessings, an event occurred that was the cause of the revelation of this verse. Perhaps its occurrence coincided with the revelation of the verses that precede it, so this verse came after them in this place of the surah.

That is: in the ninth year after the Hijrah a case arose, namely that two men, one of them Tamim al-Dari al-Lakhmi and the other 'Adi ibn Badda', were Christian Arabs and merchants, and they were from the people of Dara'in, and they used to trade between Syria, Makkah and Madinah. A man named Budayl ibn Abi Maryam, a client (mawla) of Banu Sahm, who was a Muslim, went out with them from Madinah on a trade journey to Syria. Budayl fell ill, it was said in Syria and it was said on the road, by land or by sea. With him among his goods was a cup of silver inlaid with gold, which he intended for the king of Syria. When his illness grew severe, he took a document and wrote in it what he had of goods and wealth, and placed it among the folds of his baggage, and handed what he had to Tamim and 'Adi, and charged them to deliver it to his clients from Banu Sahm. Budayl was a client of al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, so his walā' after his death belonged to his son 'Amr ibn al-'As. Some of the commentators say that Budayl's walā' belonged to 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Wada'ah. What supports their view is that al-Muttalib swore together with 'Amr ibn al-'As that the cup belonged to Budayl ibn Abi Maryam. When the two returned, they sold the cup in Makkah for a thousand dirhams, and returned to Madinah, and they delivered what belonged to Budayl to his clients. When they unfolded it, they found the document, and they said to Tamim and 'Adi: "Where is the cup?" They denied that he had given them a cup. Then the cup was found after some time being sold in Makkah, and 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah stood against the one who had it, and he said: "He bought it from Tamim and 'Adi." In another report, when Tamim became Muslim in the ninth year, he felt guilty for what he had done, so he informed 'Amr ibn al-'As of the matter of the cup, and gave him the five hundred dirhams that had come to him from its price. 'Amr then demanded the remainder of the price from 'Adi, who denied that he had sold it. This is the best of what has been related about the cause of the revelation of this verse. al-Bukhari related it as a suspended report (ta'liq) in the Book of Bequests. al-Tirmidhi related it in the Book of Tafsir, and said: "Its chain is not sound." Although it does not fully meet the conditions of soundness, it became widely known and was received with acceptance, and al-Bukhari transmitted it with a chain in his History.

[Page 82]

The reports agree that the two parties brought their dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed concerning it. So 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'ah swore that Tamim and 'Adi had concealed the cup, and that Budayl, its owner, had neither sold it nor let it leave his hand. 'Adi handed them five hundred dirhams, and he was at that time a Christian. It is said that this 'Adi later became Muslim, and Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mandah counted him among the Companions. It is also said that he died a Christian, and Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred this view; it is the opinion of Abu Nu'aym, and it is related from Muqatil. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr did not mention him among the Companions. It is possible that the revelation came before the litigants' appeal in the case of the cup, and it is possible that it came after the Prophet's (ﷺ) judgment in that case, so that it would be legislation for similar cases that might occur.

And (baynakum): the original of (bayn) is a noun of indefinite place situated between two things, specified by what follows it in construction. Here it is used figuratively for a matter connected with several things. It is in the genitive, as it is the object of the construct phrase (idafah) of (shahadah) to it, by extension (ittisa'). Its original form was (shahadatun), with tanwin and nominative case, and (baynakum) in the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf).
