Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 111:

﴿And when I inspired the disciples, saying: "Believe in Me and My Messenger." They said: "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾

It is permissible that this be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿When I strengthened you with the Holy Spirit﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110], so that it is part of what God says to Jesus on the Day when God gathers the Messengers. The belief of the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) is a blessing upon Jesus, for had they not believed in him, he would not have found anyone to follow his religion, and so he would not obtain the reward that renews itself with the renewed guidance of generations by his religion until its abrogation (naskh) came with Islam.

The meaning of the "inspiration" (wahy) to the disciples is their being inspired (ilham) upon hearing the call of Jesus to hasten to affirm him. Thus the "inspiration" here is not the revelation by which Jesus called them. It is permissible that the revelation which was sent down to Jesus, to call the Children of Israel to his religion, is meant. The disciples were singled out here for honour (tanwih) by them, to the extent that it is as though the call by revelation was only for their sake, because that [call] was addressed to all the Children of Israel, and most of them disbelieved, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples: "Who are my helpers toward God?" The disciples said: "We are the helpers of God." Then a group of the Children of Israel believed, and a group disbelieved﴾ [al-Saff: 14].

Page 104

Thus the disciples were foremost in faith; they did not waver concerning the truthfulness of Jesus.

And "an" (أنْ) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) of the inspiration that God cast into the hearts of the disciples.

The separation of the clause "They said: 'We believe'" is because it is the answer to what contains the meaning of speech, namely "We inspired" (awhayna), following the method of separation in dialogue, as was mentioned earlier in Surah al-Baqarah. It is an inner speech (qawl nafsi) that occurred when God cast into their hearts the affirmation of Jesus, so it is as if He addressed them and they answered him. The address in their saying "and bear witness" is to God, exalted is He. They spoke that only in inner speech in their own language, so God related its meaning with what His saying conveys: ﴿and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾. He named their faith "Islam" because it was a firmly rooted affirmation by which they had risen above the rank of the faith of the general body of those who believed in the Messiah other than them. Thus they were similar to the faith of Jesus, which is the faith of the Prophets and the truthful (al-Siddiqiyyin). I have already set out its explanation in my commentary on His saying: ﴿but he was a upright Muslim (hanifan musliman)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67] in Surah Al 'Imran, and in my commentary on His saying: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah: 132] in Surah al-Baqarah, so refer back to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 112–113:

﴿When the disciples said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?" He said: "Be mindful of Allah, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿They said: "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truly to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾

The clause ﴿When the disciples said﴾ may be part of the speech that Allah addresses to Jesus on the Day when He gathers the Messengers. In that case "idh" (when) is an adverbial phrase (zarf) linked to the verb of their saying "We believe" (qalu amanna), and it is among the things Allah reminds Jesus of on the Day He gathers the Messengers. It is related according to how it occurred in the world, and this does not necessitate that their request for the table took place at the very beginning of their faith, but rather at another time. Their saying "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims" (5:111) may be repeated from them on various occasions, such as when they hear the Jews denying Jesus, or when they witness signs at the hand of Jesus, or when they say it to renew the remembrance of faith, like the sincere (siddiqun) who take account of themselves and polish their faith, so they say at every renewal: "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims." As for what al-Kashshaf and its followers have established, it is not fitting to interpret the speech by it.

The clause ﴿When the disciples said﴾ may also be an independent sentence (ibtida'iyya) with the implied meaning "Remember," in the style of His saying, ﴿When Moses said to his family: "I have perceived a fire"﴾ (27:7) in Surah al-Naml. The speech then serves as a transition (takhallus) to mentioning the story of the table, for the relevance of relating what passed between Jesus and the disciples in His saying, ﴿And when I inspired the disciples: "Believe in Me and in My Messenger"﴾ (5:111).

They began their address to Jesus by calling him by his name, to indicate that what they were about to say was a matter involving a proposal and a burden upon him. Likewise, it is the habit of one who addresses someone from whom he seeks a burden to prolong his address, seeking to attract his attention so that he may be more receptive to the intended meaning.

His saying, ﴿Can your Lord﴾, follows an Arabic manner of making a request or supplication. They say to one capable of a matter: "Are you able to do such-and-such?", meaning a request for an excuse for him should he not grant your desire, and that the questioner does not like to burden the one asked with what is difficult for him. This is a kinaya (allusion), so the literal meaning implying doubt about the ability of the one asked is not what is intended. Rather, the inferior says this to the superior, and about something which the questioner knows is within the ability of the one asked. Thus the indicator of the allusion is that the one asked is certain that the questioner knows his ability. From this is what came in the hadith of Yahya al-Mazini that a man said to 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd: "Can you show me how the Messenger of Allah used to perform ablution?" The questioner knows that this is not difficult for 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd. Therefore, the words of the disciples as related in the Qur'an in this form are only a wording from their own language indicating gentleness and courtesy in asking, as is fitting for people of pure faith. It is not doubt about the power of Allah, the Exalted, but they asked for a sign to increase the reassurance of their hearts in faith, by moving from rational proof to sensory proof, for souls are more at ease with what is perceived by the senses. Likewise, Abraham's request in his saying, ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ (2:260) was not doubt about the state. This is the interpretation followed by the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) such as Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, in contrast to what is in al-Kashshaf.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿yastati'u﴾ with the yā' of the third person and ﴿rabbuka﴾ in the nominative. Al-Kisa'i read ﴿hal tastati'u rabbaka﴾ with the tā' of the second person and the nasb of the rā' of "rabbaka" as the object, so the meaning is: "Can you ask your Lord on our behalf?" Here istita'a (being able) is used to express seeking obedience, i.e., granting the request. It was also said that there is an elided modifier, the sense being: "Can you ask the question of your Lord?", so the modifier's position is given to the modified in its grammatical case. In the narration of al-Tabari from 'A'isha she said: "The disciples were too knowledgeable of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to say: 'Can your Lord...'; rather they said: 'Can you ask your Lord...'" And from Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "The Prophet recited to us: ﴿hal tastati'u rabbaka﴾."

The name ﴿ma'idah﴾ is the tray (khiwan) upon which food is placed; it is a name for a composite meaning, indicating the food and what it is placed upon. The khiwan, with kasra or damma on the kha', is a wooden table with legs made to place food on for eating; they agreed that it is a loanword (mu'arrab). Al-Jawaliqi said: it is 'ajami (non-Arabic). In the hadith of Qatada from Anas, he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never ate on a khiwan, nor in a small dish." Qatada said: "I said to Anas: 'Then on what did you eat?' He said: 'On the sufra (leather spread).'" It was also said that ma'idah is the name of food even if it is not in a container nor on a khiwan. Some verifiers among the lexicographers affirmed this, and perhaps it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) by the relation of locality ( 'alaqat al-mahall). Al-Qurtubi mentioned that the Arabs did not have ma'idat; rather they had the sufra. As for what occurred in the hadith, the saying of Ibn 'Abbas regarding the lizard (dabb): "If it were forbidden, it would not have been eaten at the ma'idah of the Messenger of Allah," what is meant is the food placed on a sufra. The name sufra has become predominantly applied to a round leather container with handles by which it is lifted when carried on a journey; it was named sufra because the traveller takes it. The disciples requested that the table be sent down from heaven because they desired it to be a departure from custom, not something made in the earthly world, so it was necessary that it come from a higher world.

When Jesus answered them, ﴿Be mindful of Allah, if you are believers﴾, it was a command to constancy in piety and to the non-wavering of faith. For this reason he used ﴿in﴾ (if), which implies doubt about faith, so that the one who calls for that request would know, lest what they had asked arise from doubt about the truthfulness of their Messenger. They asked for a miracle by which they would know his truthfulness after they had believed in him. This is close to Allah's saying to Abraham, as related in ﴿He said: "Do you not believe?"﴾ (2:260), that is, were you not free of seeking sensory proof? So the meaning of piety in the words of Jesus includes faith and its branches. It was also said that he forbade them from seeking miracles, meaning: if you are believers, then your faith has been established, so what is the need for a miracle? They answered him on that by saying they did not want it out of weakness in their faith; they only wanted the blessing of eating food sent down from the presence of Allah as an honour for them. For this reason they added to it and did not limit themselves to "that we may eat," since their purpose in eating was not to ward off hunger but rather the honour of eating from something sent down from heaven. This is like the eating of Abu Bakr from the food that his guest ate in his house when they waited for him with supper until part of the night had passed; Abu Bakr arrived and became angry at their leaving the food. When they began to eat, the food increased, so Abu Bakr said to his wife: "What is this, O sister of Banu Firas?" And the next day he carried some of that food to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he ate from it.

For this reason the disciples said ﴿and that our hearts may be reassured﴾, that is, by witnessing this miracle, for sensory proof is clearer to the soul. ﴿And that we may know that you have indeed spoken truly to us﴾, that is, we may know with knowledge of necessity, not knowledge by inference, so that they attain both kinds of knowledge. ﴿And that we may be among its witnesses﴾, that is, among those who witness this miracle, so that we may convey it to those who did not witness it. These are four benefits of asking for the sending down of the table, all of them degrees of the virtue that people like them desire.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿among its witnesses﴾ is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fasila).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verses 112–113:

﴿When the disciples said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food from heaven?" He said: "Be mindful of Allah, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿They said: "We wish to eat from it, and that our hearts may be reassured, and that we may know that you have indeed spoken truly to us, and that we may be among its witnesses."﴾

The clause ﴿When the disciples said﴾ may be part of the speech that Allah addresses to Jesus on the Day when He gathers the Messengers. In that case "idh" (when) is an adverbial phrase (zarf) linked to the verb of their saying "We believe" (qalu amanna), and it is among the things Allah reminds Jesus of on the Day He gathers the Messengers. It is related according to how it occurred in the world, and this does not necessitate that their request for the table took place at the very beginning of their faith, but rather at another time. Their saying "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims" (5:111) may be repeated from them on various occasions, such as when they hear the Jews denying Jesus, or when they witness signs at the hand of Jesus, or when they say it to renew the remembrance of faith, like the sincere (siddiqun) who take account of themselves and polish their faith, so they say at every renewal: "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims." As for what al-Kashshaf and its followers have established, it is not fitting to interpret the speech by it.

The clause ﴿When the disciples said﴾ may also be an independent sentence (ibtida'iyya) with the implied meaning "Remember," in the style of His saying, ﴿When Moses said to his family: "I have perceived a fire"﴾ (27:7) in Surah al-Naml. The speech then serves as a transition (takhallus) to mentioning the story of the table, for the relevance of relating what passed between Jesus and the disciples in His saying, ﴿And when I inspired the disciples: "Believe in Me and in My Messenger"﴾ (5:111).

They began their address to Jesus by calling him by his name, to indicate that what they were about to say was a matter involving a proposal and a burden upon him. Likewise, it is the habit of one who addresses someone from whom he seeks a burden to prolong his address, seeking to attract his attention so that he may be more receptive to the intended meaning.

His saying, ﴿Can your Lord﴾, follows an Arabic manner of making a request or supplication. They say to one capable of a matter: "Are you able to do such-and-such?", meaning a request for an excuse for him should he not grant your desire, and that the questioner does not like to burden the one asked with what is difficult for him. This is a kinaya (allusion), so the literal meaning implying doubt about the ability of the one asked is not what is intended. Rather, the inferior says this to the superior, and about something which the questioner knows is within the ability of the one asked. Thus the indicator of the allusion is that the one asked is certain that the questioner knows his ability. From this is what came in the hadith of Yahya al-Mazini that a man said to 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd: "Can you show me how the Messenger of Allah used to perform ablution?" The questioner knows that this is not difficult for 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd. Therefore, the words of the disciples as related in the Qur'an in this form are only a wording from their own language indicating gentleness and courtesy in asking, as is fitting for people of pure faith. It is not doubt about the power of Allah, the Exalted, but they asked for a sign to increase the reassurance of their hearts in faith, by moving from rational proof to sensory proof, for souls are more at ease with what is perceived by the senses. Likewise, Abraham's request in his saying, ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ (2:260) was not doubt about the state. This is the interpretation followed by the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) such as Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, in contrast to what is in al-Kashshaf.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿yastati'u﴾ with the yā' of the third person and ﴿rabbuka﴾ in the nominative. Al-Kisa'i read ﴿hal tastati'u rabbaka﴾ with the tā' of the second person and the nasb of the rā' of "rabbaka" as the object, so the meaning is: "Can you ask your Lord on our behalf?" Here istita'a (being able) is used to express seeking obedience, i.e., granting the request. It was also said that there is an elided modifier, the sense being: "Can you ask the question of your Lord?", so the modifier's position is given to the modified in its grammatical case. In the narration of al-Tabari from 'A'isha she said: "The disciples were too knowledgeable of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to say: 'Can your Lord...'; rather they said: 'Can you ask your Lord...'" And from Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "The Prophet recited to us: ﴿hal tastati'u rabbaka﴾."

[Page 108]

It is part of the speech that God addresses to Jesus on the day when God gathers the Messengers. This sentence, ﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O God, our Lord, send down upon us a table from heaven, to be for us a festival for the first and the last of us, and a sign from You. And provide for us, for You are the best of providers"﴾, and so on, is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between the sentence ﴿And when I inspired the Disciples﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 111] and the sentence ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people..."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and so on.

If, however, his saying ﴿When the Disciples said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 112], and so on, is the beginning of a speech, with the verb "mention" (udhkur) understood, then the sentence ﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O God, our Lord"﴾, and so on, is a reply to the Disciples' words ﴿O Jesus, son of Mary, can your Lord...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 112], and so on, in the manner of relating dialogues.

His saying ﴿O God, our Lord, send down upon us a table﴾ contains two invocations, since his saying "our Lord" (rabbana) is with the vocative particle understood. He repeated the invocation for the sake of emphasis in supplication. The phrase "our Lord" is neither an apposition (badal) nor a clarifying attribute (bayan) of the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah), because, according to the majority of grammarians, the invocation "O God" (Allahumma) is not followed, since it operates like the names of sounds (asma' al-aswat) on account of the change that has affected it, until it became like the names of verbs (asma' al-af'al). Some grammarians permitted its being followed. In any case, considering it a second invocation is more eloquent here, especially since the invocation of God, "our Lord", with the vocative particle omitted, is common, as in the final verses of Surah Al 'Imran.

Jesus combined the invocation by the Essential Name, which comprises the attributes of Majesty, with the invocation by the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), for himself and for the Disciples, seeking God's compassion so that He would answer their supplication.

The meaning of ﴿to be for us a festival﴾ is: the remembrance of its descent will be by making the day that coincides with the day of its descent a festival every year. Thus the attribution of "being a festival" to the table is a figurative attribution (isnad majazi); in reality the festival is the day that coincides with the day of its descent. For this reason He said ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾, meaning for the first generation of the Christian community and its last, namely those with whom Christianity was concluded at the Muhammadan mission.

The festival ('id) is a name for a day that returns every year as a remembrance of a blessing or an event that took place on it, for giving thanks or for taking lessons. Its mention has occurred in the speech of the Arabs.

[Page 109]

The most famous of the festivals of the Arabs among the Christians is what al-'Ajjaj said:

"As a Christian returns to the festival."

And like the day of al-Sabasib, in the words of al-Nabighah:

"They are greeted with basil on the day of al-Sabasib."

This is the festival of Palm Sunday (al-Sha'anin) among the Christians.

The Prophet (ﷺ) called the day of Eid al-Fitr a festival, in his saying to Abu Bakr when he forbade the slave-girls who were singing at 'A'ishah's: "Every people has a festival, and this is our festival." He also called the day of sacrifice a festival, in his saying: "Two months of festival that do not diminish: Ramadan and Dhu al-Hijjah."

The word 'id is derived from 'awd (returning). It is a noun on the pattern fi'l, so its waw was changed to ya' because it occurs after a consonantal kasrah. They pluralized it as a'yad with a ya', contrary to analogy, because the analogy of the plural is to return things to their roots; the analogy of its plural would be a'wad, but they pluralized it as a'yad. And they diminutived it as 'uyayd, to distinguish it from the plural and diminutive of 'ud (a stick or wood).

Your saying "for the first of us" (li-awwalina) is an apposition (badal) of part from whole (badl ba'd min kull) of the pronoun in your saying "for us" (lana). The conjunction of "and the last of us" (wa-akhirina) to it makes the whole, in effect, an apposition of the matching kind (badal mutabiq). He has manifested the preposition lam in the apposition, and the rule of an apposition is that the governing element that governed the head noun should not appear in it, because the apposition being a follower of the head noun in case is incompatible with mentioning the governing element that governed the followed noun. For this reason the grammarians said that the apposition is in the intention of repeating the governing element; that is, the governing element is intended but not expressed. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in al-Mufassal that the governing element of an apposition may be expressed, and he took this as evidence that it is mostly intended, and he did not restrict this to a specific type of governing element. He gave as an example God's saying: ﴿For those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful, We would make for their houses roofs of silver﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 33], and His saying in Surah al-A'raf: ﴿The notables of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75]. In al-Kashshaf he said regarding this verse ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾ that it is an apposition of "for us" with the repetition of the governing element. He also permitted apposition in the verse of al-Zukhruf. Then he said: "It is also permissible that the two lams be like the two lams in your saying: 'I gave him a garment for his shirt,' meaning that the first lam is connected with 'shall be' and the second is connected with 'festival'."

[Page 110]

I have surveyed what I have reached of the sources of its usage, and what has resulted for me is that the original governing element, of a verb or its equivalent, is not repeated with the apposition. As for the complementary governing element, that is, the preposition only, it is the one whose repetition has occurred in verses of the Qur'an, such as God's saying ﴿The notables of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75] in Surah al-A'raf, and the verse of Surah al-Zukhruf, and His saying ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters of dates hanging low﴾ [al-An'am: 99]. This is because the preposition completes the action of the verb to which it is attached, since it transfers the intransitive verb to its object in a meaning that the verb does not reach by its own verbal noun. So the preposition is not a strong governing element, but it completes the governing element to which it is attached.

Then it is incumbent upon us to seek the motive for manifesting the preposition in the apposition in the places where it appears. Ibn Ya'ish, in his commentary on al-Mufassal, attributed this to emphasis (ta'kid). He said: "Because the particle may be repeated for the purpose of emphasis." This is not convincing to us, because emphasis also needs a motive that calls for it.

So whatever manifested the preposition in these verses, its requirement for manifesting it was either the intention of depicting the situation, as in most of the verses, or the removal of ambiguity. The latter is specific to the verse of al-A'raf, lest the listener suppose that "those who believed" is part of the speech, and that "who" (man) is an interrogative, so he thinks they are asking about specifying those among the people who believed. The meaning of emphasis is nonetheless present in every case, because it is inherent in the repetition of the word. As for what is not a governing element, it is the interrogative. The manifestation of the interrogative hamzah in an apposition to an interrogative noun is obligatory, as in: "Where will you alight? In the house or in the courtyard?" and "Who is it? Sa'id or 'Ali?"

This festival mentioned in this verse is not known among the Christians. However, they mention that Jesus, peace be upon him, ate with the Disciples at a table on the night of the Feast of the Passover (Fisah), which is the night from whose morning they believe he was crucified. So perhaps the meaning of its being a festival is that it was made the day of Passover a festival in Christianity, as it was a festival in Judaism. Thus it became a festival through a difference of consideration, even though the day is one, because the Christians adapted the festivals of the Jews to other occasions fitting for Christianity, in order to erase the traces of Judaism.

[Page 111]

The sentence ﴿He said: "I am sending it down to you"﴾ is God's answer to Jesus's supplication, which is why it is separated in the manner of dialogue.

The statement is emphasized with "indeed" (inna), to affirm the promise. The meaning is: "I am sending it down to you now." So it is a response, not a promise.

His saying ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves afterwards﴾ is a consequence of granting their desire, and a warning to them against falling into disbelief after faith, informing them of the importance of faith in God's sight. So the reward for His answering them is that they should not return to disbelief. If they do return, they will be punished with a punishment more severe than the punishment of the rest of the disbelievers, because the evidence of reason and the senses has converged for them, so they have no excuse left.

The pronoun in the object position in His saying ﴿I shall punish him﴾ is the pronoun of the verbal noun (damir al-masdar). It is in the position of the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), not a direct object (maf'ul bihi). That is: "I shall not punish any one of the worlds with that punishment," that is, with the like of that punishment.

The story of the request for the table has ended at this point, and the account of what happened after its descent has been omitted, because it has no effect on the purpose of the story. That purpose is the lesson of the state of the Disciples' faith and their attachment to what increases them in certainty, and their nearness to their Lord, and their attaining the rank of witnesses over those who come after them, and the supplication of the Messiah that indicates his servanthood, and his dignity before his Lord, since He answered his call, and the vastness of power. As for the detailed description of what the table contained and what passed between them when it descended, there is no lesson in it. The commentators have overloaded it with reports of weak chains of transmission, apart from what al-Tirmidhi transmitted in the chapters of tafsir from al-Hasan ibn Qaza'ah, with his chain back to 'Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The table was sent down from heaven as bread and meat," the hadith. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This hadith has been transmitted by more than one person from 'Ammar ibn Yasir as a mawquf (a report ending with a Companion); we do not know it as marfu' (traced to the Prophet) except through the hadith of al-Hasan ibn Qaza'ah, and we do not know any basis for the marfu' hadith."

The commentators differed as to whether the table descended from heaven or did not descend. From Mujahid and al-Hasan it is reported that when they heard His saying: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves afterwards﴾, and so on, they feared, and they refrained from asking for its descent, so it did not descend. The majority said: it descended. This is the apparent meaning, because His saying ﴿I am sending it down to you﴾ is a promise that is not broken, and is not conditional on any condition. But it is followed by a warning against

[Page 112]

disbelief, and its effect is present among the Disciples, and they are not among those who fear a return to disbelief, whether the table descended or did not descend.

As for the Christians, they do not know the report of the table's descent from heaven, and how many reports they have neglected in the Gospels.

He also permitted apposition in the verse of al-Zukhruf. Then he said: "It is also permissible that the two lams be like the two lams in your saying: 'I gave him a garment for his shirt,' meaning that the first lam is connected with 'shall be' and the second is connected with 'festival'."

[Page 110]

I have surveyed what I have reached of the sources of its usage, and what has resulted for me is that the original governing element, of a verb or its equivalent, is not repeated with the apposition. As for the complementary governing element, that is, the preposition only, it is the one whose repetition has occurred in verses of the Qur'an, such as God's saying ﴿The notables of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 75] in Surah al-A'raf, and the verse of Surah al-Zukhruf, and His saying ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, are clusters of dates hanging low﴾ [al-An'am: 99]. This is because the preposition completes the action of the verb to which it is attached, since it transfers the intransitive verb to its object in a meaning that the verb does not reach by its own verbal noun. So the preposition is not a strong governing element, but it completes the governing element to which it is attached.

Then it is incumbent upon us to seek the motive for manifesting the preposition in the apposition in the places where it appears. Ibn Ya'ish, in his commentary on al-Mufassal, attributed this to emphasis (ta'kid). He said: "Because the particle may be repeated for the purpose of emphasis." This is not convincing to us, because emphasis also needs a motive that calls for it.

So whatever manifested the preposition in these verses, its requirement for manifesting it was either the intention of depicting the situation, as in most of the verses, or the removal of ambiguity. The latter is specific to the verse of al-A'raf, lest the listener suppose that "those who believed" is part of the speech, and that "who" (man) is an interrogative, so he thinks they are asking about specifying those among the people who believed. The meaning of emphasis is nonetheless present in every case, because it is inherent in the repetition of the word. As for what is not a governing element, it is the interrogative. The manifestation of the interrogative hamzah in an apposition to an interrogative noun is obligatory, as in: "Where will you alight? In the house or in the courtyard?" and "Who is it? Sa'id or 'Ali?"

This festival mentioned in this verse is not known among the Christians. However, they mention that Jesus, peace be upon him, ate with the Disciples at a table on the night of the Feast of the Passover (Fisah), which is the night from whose morning they believe he was crucified. So perhaps the meaning of its being a festival is that it was made the day of Passover a festival in Christianity, as it was a festival in Judaism. Thus it became a festival through a difference of consideration, even though the day is one, because the Christians adapted the festivals of the Jews to other occasions fitting for Christianity, in order to erase the traces of Judaism.

[Page 111]

The sentence ﴿He said: "I am sending it down to you"﴾ is God's answer to Jesus's supplication, which is why it is separated in the manner of dialogue.

The statement is emphasized with "indeed" (inna), to affirm the promise. The meaning is: "I am sending it down to you now." So it is a response, not a promise.

His saying ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves afterwards﴾ is a consequence of granting their desire, and a warning to them against falling into disbelief after faith, informing them of the importance of faith in God's sight. So the reward for His answering them is that they should not return to disbelief. If they do return, they will be punished with a punishment more severe than the punishment of the rest of the disbelievers, because the evidence of reason and the senses has converged for them, so they have no excuse left.

The pronoun in the object position in His saying ﴿I shall punish him﴾ is the pronoun of the verbal noun (damir al-masdar). It is in the position of the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), not a direct object (maf'ul bihi). That is: "I shall not punish any one of the worlds with that punishment," that is, with the like of that punishment.

The story of the request for the table has ended at this point, and the account of what happened after its descent has been omitted, because it has no effect on the purpose of the story. That purpose is the lesson of the state of the Disciples' faith and their attachment to what increases them in certainty, and their nearness to their Lord, and their attaining the rank of witnesses over those who come after them, and the supplication of the Messiah that indicates his servanthood, and his dignity before his Lord, since He answered his call, and the vastness of power. As for the detailed description of what the table contained and what passed between them when it descended, there is no lesson in it. The commentators have overloaded it with reports of weak chains of transmission, apart from what al-Tirmidhi transmitted in the chapters of tafsir from al-Hasan ibn Qaza'ah, with his chain back to 'Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The table was sent down from heaven as bread and meat," the hadith. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This hadith has been transmitted by more than one person from 'Ammar ibn Yasir as a mawquf (a report ending with a Companion); we do not know it as marfu' (traced to the Prophet) except through the hadith of al-Hasan ibn Qaza'ah, and we do not know any basis for the marfu' hadith."

The commentators differed as to whether the table descended from heaven or did not descend. From Mujahid and al-Hasan it is reported that when they heard His saying: ﴿Whoever among you disbelieves afterwards﴾, and so on, they feared, and they refrained from asking for its descent, so it did not descend. The majority said: it descended. This is the apparent meaning, because His saying ﴿I am sending it down to you﴾ is a promise that is not broken, and is not conditional on any condition. But it is followed by a warning against

[Page 112]

disbelief, and its effect is present among the Disciples, and they are not among those who fear a return to disbelief, whether the table descended or did not descend.

As for the Christians, they do not know the report of the table's descent from heaven, and how many reports they have neglected in the Gospels.

[p. 112]

﴿And when God says: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God'?" He will say: "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. Had I said it, You would have known it. You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ ﴿"I told them only what You commanded me: 'Worship God, my Lord and your Lord.' I was a witness over them as long as I was among them. But when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things."﴾ ﴿"If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise."﴾

﴿And when God says﴾ is coordinated with His words (al-Ma'idah: 110): ﴿when God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you"﴾. So this is what God will say on the Day when He gathers the Messengers, and it is not something He said in this world, because the worship of Jesus came into being after his being raised up, and also because of His words (al-Ma'idah: 119): ﴿This is a day on which the truthful will profit from their truthfulness﴾. The exegetes have unanimously agreed that the intended day here is the Day of Resurrection. And His words ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people..."﴾ are a statement He will make on the Day of Resurrection. This is the beginning of the rebuke of the Christians, after He had finished rebuking the Jews from His words ﴿when God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you"﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 110) up to here. The rebuke of the Christians is the aim of these verses, as was previously mentioned at His words, exalted is He, ﴿On the day God gathers the Messengers﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 109) and what follows. So the interrogation here is like the interrogation in His words, exalted is He, to the Messengers: ﴿What was your response?﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 109). God knows that Jesus did not say that, but the purpose is to announce the lie of those among the Christians who disbelieved.

[p. 113]

The placing of the subject ﴿You﴾ before the verbal predicate in ﴿Did you say to the people﴾ indicates that the question is directed at restricting the statement to him, rather than to anyone else, although the statement itself has certainly taken place. The statement of those who said, "Take Jesus and his mother as two gods," has occurred. The question was addressed to Jesus, "Did you tell them this?", as a veiled intimidation and threat, implying that punishment will fall upon whoever said this statement, if Jesus disowns it. Thus their rabbis who invented this saying will know that they are the intended target.

The meaning is that if he himself did not say this, then there is no excuse for those who said it, because they claimed that they follow the sayings and teachings of Jesus. Had he been the one who said it, he would have said, "Take me and my mother." For this reason the expression in the verse came with these two words.

By "the people" is meant the people of his religion.

His words ﴿besides God﴾ are connected to ﴿Take me﴾, and the particle (min) here is a connective and emphatic particle.

The word dūna (besides) is a noun denoting a place that is beyond something, and it often refers to a figurative place, meaning difference, so it carries the sense of "other than." Refer to what has been mentioned just before at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Do you worship besides God what has no power to harm or benefit you?﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 76). The meaning is: "Take me and my mother as two gods other than God."

This usage is widespread in the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides God, rivals whom they love as they love God﴾ (al-Baqarah: 165), and He says: ﴿They worship besides God what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with God"﴾ (Yunus: 18), and other verses in which the polytheists are addressed, although they associated others with God and did not deny God's divinity.

He mentioned this complement as a reproach to them, to make clear the abomination of attributing divinity to other than God. For when the Christians claimed that God indwells the essence of Jesus, divinity was divided and oneness was nullified. The explanation of this doctrine has been given previously in the commentary on His words, exalted is He, ﴿Those who say that God is the Messiah, son of Mary, have certainly disbelieved﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 17) in this surah.

Jesus's response, peace be upon him, with the words "Glory be to You" is a declaration of God's transcendence above the content

[p. 114]

of that statement. The priority of glorifying God, exalted is He, was more important than clearing himself, though it also serves as a preface to disassociation, because if he glorifies God above such a thing, then he surely would not command anyone to it. The discussion of (Subḥānaka, "Glory be to You") was given before at His words, exalted is He, ﴿They said: "Glory be to You, we have no knowledge"﴾ (al-Baqarah: 32) in Surat al-Baqarah.

He cleared himself, saying: ﴿It is not for me to say what I have no right to say.﴾ The sentence ﴿It is not for me to say﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, because it is the answer to the question. The sentence ﴿Glory be to You﴾ is a preface.

His words ﴿It is not for me (mā yakūnu lī)﴾ are an intensification in clearing himself from that, meaning: there does not exist with me the saying of what is not right for me. So the lām in ﴿lī﴾ denotes entitlement, meaning: there is no right for me to say it. This is more emphatic than "I did not say it," because it negates that he has any entitlement to that saying.

The bāʾ in His words (bi-ḥaqq, "with right") is an extra particle in the predicate of (laysa, "is not"), for emphasis of the negation which (laysa) denotes. The lām in His words ﴿lī bi-ḥaqq (not with right to me)﴾ is connected to the word (ḥaqq) according to the view of the verifying grammarians, that it is permissible to front a complement before its governed item when it is governed by a preposition. The prepositional phrase was fronted to make explicit that it is an adverbial complement (ẓarf laghw) connected to (ḥaqq), lest it be thought to be a settled adverbial (ẓarf mustaqarr) qualifying (ḥaqq), so that it might be understood that he denied that this was a right for him, while it is a right for others, namely those who said it and disbelieved in Him. It was also to give priority to what indicates his disassociation from it, by stating that it is not his. The statement has established, in the manner of the theological method, the emphasis that this is not a right for him, because he denied that it would be permitted for him to say what is not befitting for him. Thus it is known that this is not a right for him, and that he did not say it because it is not of that kind. This is an emphasis of the utmost eloquence and artistry.

Then he ascended further in clearing himself, saying: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it.﴾ The sentence is a new (independent) sentence, because it is evidence and proof for the content of the sentence before it, so it functioned as an explanation, and therefore it was separated. The pronoun in the accusative in (qulluhu, "I said it") refers back to the preceding speech. Placing the saying in the accusative as a singular noun when it has the sense of a whole sentence is common, like His words, exalted is He, (﴿No! It is a word he is saying﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 100)). He thus argued for the negation of his saying it by saying that God knows that he did not say it, because he is certain that he did not say it, so he referred the matter to God's knowledge, exalted is He. This is like the saying of the Arabs: "God knows that I did not do it," as al-Harith ibn 'Abbad said:

"I was not among its (the war's) warriors, God knows, and I am today burning in its heat."

[p. 115]

Therefore He said: ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾, so the sentence ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾ is an explanation of the conditional clause ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾, and therefore it was separated.

The word (nafs, "soul") is applied to the intellect and to that by which a human is human, namely the human spirit, and it is applied to the essence. The meaning here is: You know what I believe, that is, You know what I know, because in common usage the soul is the seat of knowledge.

His words ﴿and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾ are an interjected clause arising from ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾, aiming to combine the two matters at one time and in every state. This is an exaggeration in glorifying God, and it has no effect on clearing himself and disassociating, so the conjunction (wa) is interjectory.

The annexation of "soul" to the Name of Majesty (Allah) here means the knowledge that He has not disclosed to anyone else, that is, "I do not know what You know," meaning of what You alone have knowledge. This was made fitting here by (mushākalah, harmony of expression), as indicated in al-Kashshaf.

Regarding the permissibility of applying "soul" to the essence of God, exalted is He, without mushākalah, there is a difference of opinion. Some scholars prohibited this, and al-Sa'd, al-Sayyid and 'Abd al-Hakim, in the commentaries on al-Miftah and al-Talkhis, held this view. These scholars consider what occurs of this in the Book, such as ﴿and God warns you of Himself﴾ (Al 'Imran: 28), to be among the ambiguous verses (mutashābih). Among the scholars are those who permitted it, such as Imam al-Haramayn, as Ibn 'Arafa transmitted in his commentary at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ (al-An'am: 54) in Surat al-An'am. The repeated usage of it in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ) supports this, as in the Hadith Qudsi: "If he mentions Me in himself, I mention him in Myself."

His words ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ are the reason for His words ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾, and therefore the particle (inna), which denotes causation, was used. Four emphatic elements and a means of restriction are gathered in it: the pronoun of separation (anta) indicates restriction; (inna) is emphatic; the form of restriction; the plural of "unseen" (ghuyūb); and the particle of wonder.

After he had disclaimed that he ordered his community to what they had fabricated, he moved on to explain that he had commanded them the opposite, according to what God, exalted is He, had commanded him, and so he said: ﴿I told them only what You commanded me.﴾ His words ﴿I did not tell them﴾ are an escalation in the answer. It is a resumption equivalent to the first answer, which is "It is not for me to say..." etc. He explicitly stated what he said because the question was about what he said. The meaning: I did not exceed, in what I said,

[p. 116]

the limit of conveying what You commanded me. So the relative pronoun and its clause constitute the object of "I said to them," and it is a singular term signifying sentences, so it was valid for it to be in the accusative after the verb of saying.

The (an) here is explanatory of (amartanī, "You commanded me"), because the command contains the meaning of saying, though not its letters. The sentence ﴿Worship God, my Lord and your Lord﴾ is explanatory of (amartanī). (Amartanī) was chosen over (qulta lī, "You said to me") as an extra mark of courtesy. Since (amartanī) implicitly contains the meaning of saying, the sentence ﴿Worship God, my Lord and your Lord﴾ is what he was commanded to convey to them. So God said to him: "Say to them, ﴿Worship God, my Lord and your Lord﴾." On this basis, ﴿my Lord and your Lord﴾ is part of what God, exalted is He, said, because He commanded him to say this phrase. But since he expressed that by the verb ﴿You commanded me﴾, it was valid to explain it with the explanatory particle (an). So what Jesus said is exactly the wording that God commanded him to say. There is no need for what al-Kashshaf strained to explain. Moreover, the author of al-Intisaf allowed another view, namely that the explanation proceeded by relating the commanded speech in meaning, so that God, exalted is He, said to him: "Tell them that they should worship your Lord and their Lord." When Jesus related it, he said: "Worship God, my Lord and your Lord." This interpretation is the most common among scholars, to the point that they made the verse an example of reporting speech by meaning. I say: this is an eloquent usage. Ibn 'Atiyya said in his commentary on His words, exalted is He, ﴿We established them in the land as We did not establish you﴾ (al-An'am: 6) in Surat al-An'am: "When you report that you said to an absent person, or that it was said to him, or that you commanded that it be said to him, then in eloquent Arabic you may relate the words spoken exactly, using the second-person address, or you may convey the meaning in words, mentioning an absent person without direct address." End of quote. In my view, this is weak in this verse.

Then he disassociated himself from their consequences, saying: ﴿I was a witness over them as long as I was among them﴾, that is, I was observing them and was a watcher preventing them from uttering such a shameful statement.

In ﴿mā dumtu fīhim﴾ (as long as I was among them), (mā) is a temporal verbal particle, and (dāma) is complete, not requiring an accusative complement, and (fīhim, among them) is connected to (dumtu), that is, "among them," and it is not the predicate of (dāma) according to the most apparent view. This is because (dāma) which requires a predicate is that in which continuation upon a specific act is intended, the act being the content of its predicate. But here it has the meaning of remaining: "as long as I remained among them," that is, as long as I remained in this world.

[p. 117]

For this reason he made the next statement follow from it: ﴿So when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them﴾, that is, when You decreed my death, because the one who directly carries out death is the Angel of Death. Death (wafāh) is dying; (tawaffāhu Allāh) means God caused him to die, that is, decreed it for him, and (tawaffāhu malak al-mawt) means the Angel of Death took his soul and caused him to die.

This was mentioned before at His words, exalted is He, ﴿I am taking you (mutawaffīka)﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran.

The meaning is: when You caused me to die, the death became a barrier between me and them, so it was not for me to rebuke them for their misguidance. Therefore he said ﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾. He used the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), which indicates restriction (al-qasr), meaning: it was You who were the Watcher, not I, since no connection remained between me and the worldly life. The meaning is that You know their state and send to them whoever guides them whenever You will. He sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to them, and he guided them by every means of guidance. The furthest means of guidance is informing them of what will happen concerning them on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying ﴿And You are over all things a Witness﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil), and the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), since it is not conjoined to what preceded, so that it would not be in the position of the answer to (lamma) (the "when" clause).

His saying ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ entrusts their affair to Allah, for He is most knowing of what He will recompense them with, because the situation is one of refraining from expressing a desire (for forgiveness), due to the severity of the terror of that Day. The most that Jesus alluded to was that he permitted their forgiveness out of mercy toward them.

His saying ﴿Indeed You, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾: mentioning "al-'Aziz" (the Exalted in Might) is a metonymy (kinayah) for His forgiving from a position of power, and mentioning "al-Hakim" (the Wise) is for its suitability to the act of entrusting, i.e., the One who firmly ordains affairs, knowing what befits them.

[p. 112]

Thus it is known that this is not a right for him, and that he did not say it because it is not of that kind. This is an emphasis of the utmost eloquence and artistry.

Then he ascended further in clearing himself, saying: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it.﴾ The sentence is a new (independent) sentence, because it is evidence and proof for the content of the sentence before it, so it functioned as an explanation, and therefore it was separated. This is like the saying of the Arabs: "God knows that I did not do it," as al-Harith ibn 'Abbad said:

"I was not among its (the war's) warriors, God knows, and I am today burning in its heat."

[p. 115]

Therefore He said: ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾, so the sentence ﴿You know what is in my soul﴾ is an explanation of the conditional clause ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾, and therefore it was separated.

[p. 116]

the limit of conveying what You commanded me. So the relative pronoun and its clause constitute the object of "I said to them," and it is a singular term signifying sentences, so it was valid for it to be in the accusative after the verb of saying.

[p. 117]

This was mentioned before at His words, exalted is He, ﴿I am taking you (mutawaffīka)﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran.

Therefore he said ﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾. He used the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), which indicates restriction (al-qasr), meaning: it was You who were the Watcher, not I, since no connection remained between me and the worldly life. The meaning is that You know their state and send to them whoever guides them whenever You will. He sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to them, and he guided them by every means of guidance. The furthest means of guidance is informing them of what will happen concerning them on the Day of Resurrection.

The most that Jesus alluded to was that he permitted their forgiveness out of mercy toward them.

[p. 112]

﴿And when God says: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God'?" He will say: "Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. Had I said it, You would have known it. You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul. Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen."﴾ ﴿"I told them only what You commanded me: 'Worship God, my Lord and your Lord.' I was a witness over them as long as I was among them. But when You caused me to die, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things."﴾ ﴿"If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise."﴾

﴿And when God says﴾ is coordinated with His words (al-Ma'idah: 110): ﴿when God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you"﴾. So this is what God will say on the Day when He gathers the Messengers, and it is not something He said in this world, because the worship of Jesus came into being after his being raised up, and also because of His words (al-Ma'idah: 119): ﴿This is a day on which the truthful will profit from their truthfulness﴾. The exegetes have unanimously agreed that the intended day here is the Day of Resurrection. And His words ﴿And when God says: "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people..."﴾ are a statement He will make on the Day of Resurrection. This is the beginning of the rebuke of the Christians, after He had finished rebuking the Jews from His words ﴿when God said: "O Jesus, son of Mary, remember My blessing upon you"﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 110) up to here. The rebuke of the Christians is the aim of these verses, as was previously mentioned at His words, exalted is He, ﴿On the day God gathers the Messengers﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 109) and what follows. So the interrogation here is like the interrogation in His words, exalted is He, to the Messengers: ﴿What was your response?﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 109). God knows that Jesus did not say that, but the purpose is to announce the lie of those among the Christians who disbelieved.

[p. 113]

The placing of the subject ﴿You﴾ before the verbal predicate in ﴿Did you say to the people﴾ indicates that the question is directed at restricting the statement to him, rather than to anyone else, although the statement itself has certainly taken place. The statement of those who said, "Take Jesus and his mother as two gods," has occurred. The question was addressed to Jesus, "Did you tell them this?", as a veiled intimidation and threat, implying that punishment will fall upon whoever said this statement, if Jesus disowns it. Thus their rabbis who invented this saying will know that they are the intended target.

The meaning is that if he himself did not say this, then there is no excuse for those who said it, because they claimed that they follow the sayings and teachings of Jesus. Had he been the one who said it, he would have said, "Take me and my mother." For this reason the expression in the verse came with these two words.

By "the people" is meant the people of his religion.

His words ﴿besides God﴾ are connected to ﴿Take me﴾, and the particle (min) here is a connective and emphatic particle.

The word dūna (besides) is a noun denoting a place that is beyond something, and it often refers to a figurative place, meaning difference, so it carries the sense of "other than." Refer to what has been mentioned just before at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Do you worship besides God what has no power to harm or benefit you?﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 76). The meaning is: "Take me and my mother as two gods other than God."

This usage is widespread in the Qur'an. He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And among people are those who take, besides God, rivals whom they love as they love God﴾ (al-Baqarah: 165), and He says: ﴿They worship besides God what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with God"﴾ (Yunus: 18), and other verses in which the polytheists are addressed, although they associated others with God and did not deny God's divinity.

He mentioned this complement as a reproach to them, to make clear the abomination of attributing divinity to other than God. For when the Christians claimed that God indwells the essence of Jesus, divinity was divided and oneness was nullified. The explanation of this doctrine has been given previously in the commentary on His words, exalted is He, ﴿Those who say that God is the Messiah, son of Mary, have certainly disbelieved﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 17) in this surah.

Jesus's response, peace be upon him, with the words "Glory be to You" is a declaration of God's transcendence above the content

[p. 114]

of that statement. The priority of glorifying God, exalted is He, was more important than clearing himself, though it also serves as a preface to disassociation, because if he glorifies God above such a thing, then he surely would not command anyone to it. Almighty God said: "This is a Day on which their truthfulness benefits the truthful. For them are Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the supreme triumph."

This is a response to the statement of Jesus, and therefore the sentence is detached (fasl) in the manner of dialogue.

The demonstrative "this" refers to the Day of Resurrection, which is present at the time this exchange takes place.

The clause "their truthfulness benefits them" (yanfa'u al-sadiqina sidquhum) is a sentence in apposition to which the word "Day" (yawm) is added; that is, "this is the Day of the benefit of truthfulness." Except for Nafi', the other of the Ten Readers read "yawmu" with a damma, the sign of the nominative, because it is the predicate (khabar) of "hadha." Nafi' read it with a fatha, on the basis that it is built (mabni) on fatha because it is added to a verbal clause. The addition of a noun of time to a verbal clause justifies its being built on fatha; if the clause is in the past tense, building is more common, as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"At the time when I reproached grey hair for youth..."

If the clause is in the present tense, both building and inflection (i'rab) are permissible, as in this verse, and this is the verified view (al-tahqiq). The addition of a time adverb to a clause implies that its content occurs within it, so the benefit of truthfulness to its possessors is realized on that Day. The generality of "the truthful" includes the truthfulness uttered on that Day and the truthfulness uttered in this world; the benefit of both becomes manifest on that Day. As for the benefit of truthfulness uttered in this world, it is the attainment of its reward; and as for the benefit of truthfulness uttered in the Hereafter, such as the truthfulness of the Messiah in what he said, it is God's being pleased with the truthful one, or the averting of His wrath from the one who denies him. Thus there is no perplexity in the meaning of the verse.

By "the truthful" (al-sadiqin) is meant those for whom truthfulness was their emblem and who did not deviate from it. Among the first levels of truthfulness is truthfulness of belief, namely that they do not believe anything contrary to what is in reality, of what rational or legal evidence has established. God the Exalted said: "O you who believe, fear God and be with the truthful" [al-Tawbah: 119].

The meaning of truthfulness benefiting its possessor on that Day is that that Day is the Day of Truth, so the truthful person benefits by his truthfulness in it, because truthfulness is good, and so in the realm of truth it has no effect but a good one. This is unlike the situation in the world, the realm where truth and falsehood coexist, for truth may bring harm to its possessor through people's distortion of realities, or through his being held to account for what he reported, such that had he not reported it no one would have known of it. As for what results from it of reward in the Hereafter, that is among the benefit realized on the Day of Resurrection. Ka'b ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, was tested in truthfulness, then he saw the good outcome of it in this world.

The meaning of truthfulness benefiting is that if the report concerns a good matter that the reporter committed, then the truthfulness is good and the matter reported is good, so it is pure benefit, and for it there are two rewards, as in the statement of Jesus: "Glory be to You, it is not for me to say what I have no right to" [al-Ma'idah: 116] to the end of the verse. If the report concerns an ugly matter, then truthfulness does not add ugliness to what is reported, because the ugly thing has already occurred, whether it is reported or not. It deserves an ugly consequence like it. Truthfulness benefits its possessor who committed that ugliness, so he receives the reward of truthfulness, and some of the punishment is lightened for him by the increase of means of kindness shown to him.

The clause "for them are Gardens" (lahum jannat) explains the clause "yanfa'" in terms of being its most complete state of the benefit of truthfulness. The clause "beneath which rivers flow" (tajri min tahtiha al-anhar) is a qualifier of "Gardens," and "abiding" (khalidin) is a circumstantial clause (hal). Likewise the clause "God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him."

The meaning of "they are pleased with Him" is complete gladness at what He has recompensed them with, the Garden and His good pleasure. The original sense of riḍa (pleasure) is that it is the opposite of anger; it is therefore love and its effect of honor and kindness. So God's pleasure is used for His honoring and kindness, like His love in His saying "He loves them." The creatures' pleasure with God is their love of Him and the attainment of what they hoped from Him, such that no longing remains in their souls.

The demonstrative in His saying "that" (dhalika) is for magnifying the thing indicated, which is the Gardens and the good pleasure.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 5, verse 120:**

﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is competent over all things.﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding phrase appended to a passage, signalling its end), since this sentence gathers the servitude of all existing things to Allah, the Exalted. It fits what precedes it, the refutation of the Christians, and it implies that all things are under His disposal, which fits the reward of the truthful mentioned earlier. It also carries the sense of entrusting all that descends to Allah, so it indicates the end of the revelation of the Qur'an according to the view that Surah al-Ma'idah was the last to be revealed. It also points to the approaching death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because the verse conveys submission to Allah and that He is the One who does what He wills.

[Page 120]

The fronting of the prepositional phrase with *li* (lil-lahi, "to Allah") conveys restriction (*qasr*), meaning: to Him and not to other than Him.

The relative pronoun *ma* is used in His words *wa ma fihinna* ("and whatever is in them") rather than *man* ("whoever"), because *ma* is the original form of the indefinite relative, so the predominance of rational beings (*taghlib al-'uqala'*) is not taken into account. The fronting of the prepositional phrase with *'ala* in His words ﴿over all things competent﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 109] is for the sake of observing the rhyme (*fasila*), which is built on two letters with a long vowel between them.

*Wa ma fihinna* is coordinated (*'atf*) on *mulk* (dominion), meaning: to Allah belongs what is in the heavens and the earth, as in Surah al-Baqarah: "To Allah belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth." This conveys the restriction of these things to being Allah's and not to anyone else's. It is not coordinated on "the heavens and the earth," since it would not be proper to say "to Allah belongs the dominion of what is in the heavens and the earth," because dominion (*mulk*) is attributed to regions, horizons and places, as Allah related: ﴿Is not mine the dominion of Egypt?﴾ It is also attributed to the possessor of dominion, as in His words: ﴿over the dominion of Solomon﴾. And it is said: "in the period of the dominion of the Assyrians or the Romans."

[Page 121]

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

**Surah al-An'am**

This surah has no name other than this one from the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). al-Tabarani narrated with his chain to 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surah al-An'am was revealed to me all at once, and seventy thousand angels escorted it, with a loud sound of glorification and praise." It is also reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Anas ibn Malik, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah and Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan that they called it Surah al-An'am. Likewise its name is established in the copies of the Qur'an, the books of tafsir and the Sunnah.

It was named Surah al-An'am (the Cattle) because the word *al-an'am* is repeated in it six times, from His words ﴿And they assign to Allah a portion of what He has created of the tilth and the cattle﴾ [Al-An'am: 136] to His words ﴿for Allah has enjoined this upon you﴾ [Al-An'am: 144].

It is Meccan by consensus. From Ibn 'Abbas: it was revealed in Mecca at night, all at once, as narrated from him by 'Ata', 'Ikrimah and al-'Awfi. This is consistent with the hadith of Ibn 'Umar from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned just above. It is reported that His words ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and evening﴾ [Al-An'am: 52], up to the end of the verse, were revealed during the lifetime of Abu Talib, that is, before the tenth year of the prophetic mission. If this is sound, it serves as a fixed point for the year of revelation of this surah. al-Kalbi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that six verses of it were revealed at Medina: three from His words ﴿And they did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [Al-An'am: 91] to the end of three verses, and three from His words ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden to you﴾ [Al-An'am: 151] to His words ﴿That is what He has enjoined upon you that you may reflect﴾ [Al-An'am: 152]. And from Abu Juhayfah, the verse ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ [Al-An'am: 111] is Medinan.

It was said that the verse ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or says, "It has been revealed to me"﴾ [Al-An'am: 93] was revealed at Medina, based on the cause of its revelation that is mentioned below. It was also said that the verse ﴿Those to whom We have given the Scripture recognize it﴾ [Al-An'am: 20] and the verse ﴿So those to whom We gave the Scripture believe in it﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 47] were both revealed at Medina, based on the causes of their revelation that are mentioned, as will come. Ibn al-'Arabi said in *Ahkam al-Qur'an*, at His words ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden﴾ [Al-An'am: 145], that according to the majority view it was revealed on the day of the revelation of His words ﴿This day I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 3], that is, in the tenth year. Thus these verses are exceptions to the Meccan character of the surah that were appended to it.

[Page 122]

Ibn 'Atiyyah, in his tafsir of His words ﴿And they did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [Al-An'am: 91] from this surah, said: al-Naqqash related that the whole of Surah al-An'am is Medinan. But Ibn al-Hassar said: No report is sound that any part of al-An'am was revealed at Medina. This is the more apparent view, and it is what Abu 'Ubayd, al-Bayhaqi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and what Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed in Mecca all at once, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the scribes, and they wrote it down that same night.

Sufyan al-Thawri and Sharik narrated from Asma' bint Yazid al-Ansariyyah: Surah al-An'am was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) all at once while he was on a journey, and I was holding the reins of his she-camel; its weight was almost breaking the bones of the she-camel. They did not specify this journey or its time. However, this Asma' is not known to have come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before his migration, nor is she counted among those who pledged allegiance at the Second Pledge of al-'Aqabah, so that it could be said she met him before the migration. Rather, the one counted is Asma' bint 'Amr ibn 'Adi. Thus the status of this report is not clear. Perhaps what became confused in it is the recitation of the surah on that journey, with the claim that it was revealed at that time.

They said: No long surah other than this one was revealed all at once. Something similar occurred in the narration of Sharik from Asma' bint Yazid, as you have just learned. So perhaps the wisdom of its revelation all at once was to cut off the pretext of the polytheists when they said: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [Al-Furqan: 32], supposing that its gradual revelation undermined its being a Book. So Allah sent down Surah al-An'am, which is the size of one of the books they knew, such as the Gospel and the Psalms, so that they would know that Allah is capable of that. However, the wisdom of the gradual revelation is more deserving of consideration. Also, so that the inimitability (*i'jaz*) would be realised through the diversity of styles of speech, short, long and medium, for lengthy speech is sometimes required by the occasion, as Qays ibn Kharijah said, boasting of the virtues he possessed: "And a sermon from the time the sun rises until it sets, etc."

Abu Du'ad ibn Jarir al-Iyadi said, praising the orators of Iyad:

*They hurl long sermons, and at times a hinted gesture, for fear of the watchers.*

Know that the revelation of this surah all at once, according to the sound view, does not contradict what is mentioned about the causes of revelation of some of its verses. For if the causes of revelation of those verses were events before the migration, then many causes may have accumulated within a short period before the revelation of this surah, so the revelation of those verses would be consequent upon those events. And if it was after the migration, those verses may be Medinan and appended to Surah al-An'am for related reasons. Moreover, causes of revelation need not coincide with the revelation of the verses of their rulings, for a cause may occur while the legislation of its ruling is delayed.

According to the more correct view, that it is Meccan, this surah is counted as the fifty-fifth in the count of the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surah al-Hijr and before Surah al-Saffat.

Its number of verses is one hundred and sixty-seven in the Medinan and Meccan counts, one hundred and sixty-five in the Kufan count, and one hundred and sixty-four in the Syrian and Basran counts.

**The aims of this surah:**

It opens by informing people that the right to praise belongs to Allah alone, because He is the originator of the worlds, both substances and accidents, so it is known that He alone is the Deity. It also refutes the influence of partners, whether idols or jinn, by establishing that He alone creates the world, its substances and accidents, and creates man and the order of his life and death, by His wisdom and knowledge, while their gods possess no disposal and no knowledge.

It declares Allah free of offspring and consorts. Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini said: In Surah al-An'am are all the foundations of monotheism (*tawhid*).

It admonishes those who turn away from the verses of the Qur'an and who deny the true religion, and it threatens them that there will befall them what befell the earlier generations who denied, and those who disbelieved in the blessings of Allah, and that they harm no one by their denial except themselves.

It warns them of what they will meet at the removal of their souls, and then at the Resurrection.

[Page 124]

It rebukes the polytheists for what they demanded of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely that he display extraordinary signs, mockingly.

It nullifies their belief that Allah inculcated in them the creed of association (*shirk*) with the intention of confounding the Messenger (ﷺ), and it clarifies the reality of the will of Allah.

It establishes the truthfulness of the Qur'an, by the fact that the People of the Book know that it is the truth.

It censures the polytheists for denying the Resurrection, and it affirms that it is certain to occur, and that they will witness punishment after it, and their gods whom they worshipped will disown them, and they will regret that, just as those gods will not avail them anything in the life of this world, for they call upon none but Allah in times of calamity.

It strengthens the Prophet (ﷺ), that he will not be held responsible for the turning away of his people, and it commands him to turn away from them.

It explains the wisdom of Allah's sending of the messengers, which is warning and giving good tidings, and that the function of the messengers is not to inform people of the unseen matters they seek to know.

That people are distinguished by piety and by affiliation to the religion of Allah.

It nullifies what the people of association legislated of the laws of error.

It explains that true piety is not merely depriving oneself of good things, but rather depriving oneself of the desires that stand between the self and perfection and purification.

It presents a parable for the Prophet with his people, using the parable of Abraham with his father and his people; and the prophets and messengers, both those before and those after him, were upon this same parable.

It expresses Allah's favour upon the nation by sending down the Qur'an as guidance for them, just as He sent the Book to Moses, and by making it the seal of the good nations.

It explains the excellence of the Qur'an and of the religion of Islam and what Allah grants its adherents of multiplication of good deeds.

Interspersed throughout this are thunderbolts against the polytheists, praise for the believers, and reminders of blessings contained in the creatures of Allah, and mention of the keys of the unseen.

[Page 125]

Fakhr al-Din said: The Usulis (that is, scholars of the principles of religion) said: The reason it was revealed in one piece is that it contains proofs of monotheism, justice, prophethood, the Hereafter, and the refutation of the doctrines of those who deny attributes and of the atheists. Revelation of what indicates legal rulings may be in the interest that Allah reveals it according to the measure of their needs and in accordance with events, but what indicates the principles of belief He revealed all at once.

It is the most comprehensive of the surahs of the Qur'an regarding the conditions of the Arabs in the time of ignorance (*jahiliyyah*), and the most intense in confronting their disputes and in argument against the foolishness of their conditions, from His words ﴿And they assign to Allah a portion of what He has created of the tilth and the cattle﴾ [Al-An'am: 136], and regarding what they forbade themselves of what Allah had provided for them.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Abbas said: If you wish to know the ignorance of the Arabs, then recite what is beyond the hundred and thirtieth verse of Surah al-An'am: ﴿Those have lost who killed their children in folly without knowledge and forbade what Allah had provided for them, fabricating against Allah. They have certainly gone astray and were not guided.﴾ [Al-An'am: 140]

Many reports have come concerning the excellence of Surah al-An'am and the excellence of some of its verses, from the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, Anas ibn Malik, Ibn 'Abbas and Asma' bint Yazid.
